Electronic transitions of valence electrons
Correct: UV-Vis photons promote electrons, often π → π*, to higher orbitals.
Nuclear spin transitions
Those are probed by NMR with radio waves.
Changes in mass-to-charge ratio
That is mass spectrometry, which does not use absorbed light.
questions.x: UV and visible photons carry a few eV, matching gaps between electronic energy levels, so absorption promotes valence electrons, commonly π → π* or n → π*. Vibrational transitions need lower-energy IR photons, spin flips need radio waves, and mass spectrometry does not involve light absorption.

questions.q: In NMR spectroscopy, what form of electromagnetic radiation flips nuclear spins in the applied magnetic field?
o: Infrared
IR excites bond vibrations.
Radio waves
Correct: spin-state energy gaps in a magnet correspond to radiofrequency photons.
Ultraviolet
UV excites electrons, far above spin-flip energies.
X-rays
X-rays far exceed nuclear spin-flip energies.
questions.x: In a strong magnetic field, nuclei like ¹H have spin states separated by a tiny energy gap. Photons matching that gap are in the radiofrequency range (hundreds of MHz), so NMR uses radio waves to flip spins. IR, UV and X-ray photons carry far more energy than this transition needs.

questions.q: In the ¹H NMR spectrum of an ethyl group (CH₃CH₂–) attached to an atom with no hydrogens, the CH₃ signal is split into a:
o: triplet
Correct: n + 1 rule with the two neighboring CH₂ protons gives 3 lines.
quartet
That is the CH₂ signal, split by three CH₃ protons.
doublet
A doublet needs exactly one neighboring proton.
singlet
The CH₃ has two neighboring protons, so it is split.
questions.x: The n + 1 rule says a signal is split into n + 1 peaks by n equivalent protons on adjacent carbons. The CH₃ has two neighboring CH₂ protons, so it appears as a triplet; the CH₂, with three neighbors, appears as a quartet. Splitting reports neighbors, not the group's own protons.

questions.q: In ¹H NMR, a proton on a carbon bonded to an electronegative oxygen appears:
o: upfield (lower ppm), because it is shielded
Electronegative neighbors deshield protons, not shield them.
at 0 ppm, like TMS
TMS protons are highly shielded; a C–H next to O is not.
only as a singlet
Chemical shift and splitting are separate features.
downfield (higher ppm), because it is deshielded
Correct: oxygen pulls electron density away, exposing the proton to more of the field.
questions.x: Electrons around a proton shield it from the applied field. An electronegative atom like oxygen withdraws electron density, deshielding nearby protons so they resonate at higher frequency, which appears downfield at higher ppm (about 3.3 to 4 ppm for H–C–O). Shielded protons, like those of TMS, appear upfield near 0 ppm.

questions.q: The ¹H NMR spectrum of ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) shows three signals. What are the relative integrations?
o: Integration reflects proton count, not the number of signals.
The OH carries one proton and the CH₂ carries two.
Correct: integration is proportional to the number of equivalent protons.
The three groups have different numbers of protons.
questions.x: In ¹H NMR, the area under each signal is proportional to the number of protons producing it. Ethanol's CH₃, CH₂ and OH groups carry 3, 2 and 1 protons, so the integrations are 3 : 2 : 1. Integration counts protons; splitting, a separate feature, counts neighbors.

questions.q: A mass spectrum shows a molecular ion peak at m/z 122 and a peak of nearly equal height at m/z 124. Which element does the compound most likely contain?
o: Chlorine
Chlorine gives an M+2 peak about one-third the height of M.
Nitrogen
Nitrogen affects odd or even molecular mass, not a strong M+2 peak.
Bromine
Correct: ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br are about equally abundant, giving M and M+2 peaks of similar height.
Oxygen
¹⁸O is rare, so oxygen gives only a tiny M+2 peak.
questions.x: Isotope patterns reveal halogens. Bromine is about 50% ⁷⁹Br and 50% ⁸¹Br, so a molecule with one Br shows M and M+2 peaks of nearly equal height. Chlorine is about 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl, giving an M+2 peak about one third the height of M, which rules it out here.

questions.q: Which of these analytical techniques does NOT rely on a molecule absorbing electromagnetic radiation?
o: Infrared spectroscopy
IR measures absorption of infrared photons.
NMR spectroscopy
NMR measures absorption of radiofrequency photons.
Mass spectrometry
Correct: it ionizes molecules and sorts ions by mass-to-charge ratio.
UV-Vis spectroscopy
UV-Vis measures absorption of ultraviolet and visible photons.
questions.x: IR, UV-Vis and NMR are all absorption spectroscopies: each measures which photon energies a molecule absorbs. Mass spectrometry instead ionizes molecules, often fragments them, and separates the ions by mass-to-charge ratio using electric or magnetic fields. It reveals molecular mass and structure without absorbing light.

questions.q: A fluorescent dye absorbs at 490 nm. Compared with the absorbed light, the emitted light most likely has:
o: a shorter wavelength
Emission cannot exceed the absorbed photon's energy in ordinary fluorescence.
the same wavelength
Some energy is always lost to vibrational relaxation first.
a longer wavelength
Correct: energy is lost to vibrational relaxation before emission, so emitted photons have less energy.
a higher frequency
Lower energy means lower frequency.
questions.x: After absorbing a photon, a fluorescent molecule quickly loses some energy through vibrational relaxation in the excited state before emitting. The emitted photon therefore has less energy, lower frequency and longer wavelength than the absorbed one, a difference called the Stokes shift. Here emission would fall above 490 nm, toward green.

questions.q: Which pairing of radiation type with molecular transition, in order of increasing photon energy, is correct?
o: Radio: rotation; microwave: nuclear spin; IR: electronic; UV: vibration
Swaps several pairings; IR excites vibrations and UV excites electrons.
Radio: nuclear spin; microwave: rotation; IR: vibration; UV: electronic
Correct: each region's photon energy matches progressively larger energy gaps.
Radio: nuclear spin; microwave: electronic; IR: rotation; UV: vibration
Electronic transitions need far more energy than microwaves supply.
Radio: vibration; microwave: rotation; IR: nuclear spin; UV: electronic
Vibrations need IR, and spin flips need radio waves.
questions.x: Photon energy rises from radio to microwave to infrared to ultraviolet, and each region matches a progressively larger molecular energy gap. Nuclear spin flips in a magnet are tiny (radio), molecular rotations are next (microwave), bond vibrations larger (IR), and electronic transitions largest (UV-Vis). Pairing higher-energy radiation with smaller gaps reverses this logic.

questions.q: Lens aberration in which rays striking the outer edge of a spherical lens focus at a different point than central rays is called:
o: chromatic aberration
That results from different wavelengths focusing at different points.
astigmatism
That comes from unequal curvature in different directions.
spherical aberration
Correct: it comes from the lens's spherical shape, not from color.
dispersion
Dispersion is the wavelength dependence of n that causes chromatic aberration.
questions.x: A spherical surface is only an approximation to the ideal focusing shape, so rays hitting the outer edge of a lens bend too much and focus closer than central rays. This blurring is spherical aberration and occurs even with one wavelength. Chromatic aberration, by contrast, comes from different colors focusing at different points.

questions.q: How many neutrons are in one atom of chlorine-37 (Z = 17)?
o: That is the proton count (atomic number), not the neutron count.
Correct: neutrons = A − Z = 37 − 17 = 20.
That is the mass number, which counts protons plus neutrons.
Adds Z to A instead of subtracting it.
questions.note: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
questions.x: The atomic number Z counts protons and fixes the element; the mass number A counts protons plus neutrons. So neutrons N = A − Z = 37 − 17 = 20. The common slip is reporting Z (17) or A (37) itself; neither is the neutron count.

questions.q: Which subatomic particle has nearly the same mass as a proton but carries no charge?
o: Electron
Electrons are charged and about 1/1836 the proton's mass.
Positron
A positron has the electron's tiny mass and a +1 charge.
Neutron
Correct: the neutron's mass is about 1 u, like the proton, and it is neutral.
Alpha particle
An alpha particle is a helium nucleus: about 4 u and a +2 charge.
questions.x: Protons and neutrons are both nucleons with masses of about 1 u, roughly 1836 times the electron's mass. The neutron differs from the proton only in being electrically neutral. A positron is a tempting pick because it is 'unusual', but it is the electron's antiparticle, with the electron's tiny mass and a +1 charge.

questions.q: A species contains 26 protons, 30 neutrons and 23 electrons. Which symbol represents it?
o: ⁵⁶Fe³⁻
Fewer electrons than protons gives a positive charge, not a negative one.
⁵⁶Mn³⁺
Element identity is set by the 26 protons, which makes it iron, not manganese.
⁴⁹Fe³⁺
Mass number counts protons plus neutrons (56), not protons plus electrons.
⁵⁶Fe³⁺
Correct: Z = 26 is Fe, A = 26 + 30 = 56, and charge = 26 − 23 = +3.
questions.x: Read a species in three steps: protons give the element (26 = Fe), protons plus neutrons give the mass number (56), and protons minus electrons give the charge (+3). Having fewer electrons than protons always makes a cation. Changing electrons never changes the element, which rules out manganese.

questions.q: Element X occurs as 70% ⁶³X and 30% ⁶⁵X. What is the approximate average atomic mass of X?
o: Weights the heavier isotope too little.
That is a simple unweighted average of 63 and 65.
Swaps the abundances, weighting the heavier isotope at 70%.
questions.note: Weighted average lands closer to the more abundant isotope.
questions.x: Average atomic mass is the abundance-weighted mean of isotope masses: 0.70 × 63 + 0.30 × 65 = 63.6 u. Because 70% of atoms are the lighter isotope, the average sits closer to 63 than to 65. The simple midpoint (64.0) would only be right for a 50:50 mix.

questions.q: Boron has an average atomic mass of 10.8 u and consists of ¹⁰B and ¹¹B. What is the approximate percent abundance of ¹¹B?
o: That is the abundance of ¹⁰B, not ¹¹B.
A 50:50 mix would average 10.5 u.
Correct: 10x + 11(1 − x) = 10.8 gives x = 0.2 for ¹⁰B, so ¹¹B is 80%.
Too high; that would give an average near 10.92 u.
questions.x: Set up a weighted average with one unknown: if x is the fraction of ¹⁰B, then 10x + 11(1 − x) = 10.8, so x = 0.2 and ¹¹B is 80%. A quick check: 10.8 lies 80% of the way from 10 to 11, so the heavier isotope dominates. The 20% choice is the lighter isotope's abundance, a common mix-up.

questions.q: In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through while a few bounced back. What did this show?
o: Electrons occupy quantized orbits
Quantized orbits came from Bohr's model and line spectra, not this experiment.
Positive charge is spread evenly through the atom
That plum-pudding picture predicted no large-angle deflections.
The nucleus contains neutral neutrons
Neutrons were discovered later by Chadwick.
Mass and positive charge sit in a tiny dense nucleus
Correct: mostly empty space explains pass-through; a dense core explains rare rebounds.
questions.x: Most alpha particles passing straight through means the atom is mostly empty space; the rare large-angle rebounds mean positive charge and nearly all mass are packed into a tiny, dense nucleus. The plum-pudding model, with positive charge spread evenly, predicted only small deflections. Quantized orbits came later from Bohr's work on hydrogen spectra.

questions.q: Which pair of nuclides contains the same number of neutrons?
o: ¹⁴C and ¹⁶O
Correct: ¹⁴C has 14 − 6 = 8 and ¹⁶O has 16 − 8 = 8 neutrons.
¹²C and ¹⁴C
These are isotopes with 6 and 8 neutrons.
¹⁴C and ¹⁴N
Same mass number but 8 versus 7 neutrons.
¹⁶O and ¹⁸O
Isotopes of oxygen with 8 and 10 neutrons.
questions.x: Neutron number is N = A − Z, so compute it for each nuclide: ¹⁴C has 14 − 6 = 8 and ¹⁶O has 16 − 8 = 8. Nuclides with equal N but different Z are called isotones. Isotopes (same Z) like ¹²C and ¹⁴C differ in neutrons, and isobars (same A) like ¹⁴C and ¹⁴N differ in both.

questions.q: Which ion has the same ground-state electron configuration as argon?
o: Na⁺
Na⁺ has 10 electrons, matching neon.
Ca²⁺
Correct: Ca (20 electrons) loses 2 to reach 18, the argon configuration.
Al³⁺
Al³⁺ has 10 electrons, matching neon.
Br⁻
Br⁻ has 36 electrons, matching krypton.
questions.x: Ions are isoelectronic with a noble gas when their electron count matches it. Argon has 18 electrons, and Ca²⁺ has 20 − 2 = 18. Na⁺ and Al³⁺ both have 10 electrons like neon, and Br⁻ has 36 like krypton, so matching the noble gas requires counting electrons, not just noting a full octet.

questions.q: Deuterium oxide (D₂O) undergoes the same types of chemical reactions as ordinary water. Why?
o: Isotopes have the same electron configuration
Correct: chemistry is set by electrons, which depend on Z, not neutron count.
Deuterium has no neutrons
Deuterium (²H) has one neutron; protium has none.
Neutrons are the particles involved in bonding
Bonds involve valence electrons, not nucleons.
Isotopes have identical masses
Deuterium is about twice as heavy as protium.
questions.note: Isotopes differ slightly in rates (kinetic isotope effect), not in reaction type.
questions.x: Chemical behavior depends on electrons, and the number of electrons in a neutral atom is set by Z. Isotopes share Z, so they share electron configurations and undergo the same reactions. Their extra neutrons change mass, which only alters rates slightly (the kinetic isotope effect), not the types of reactions.

questions.q: Bromine is about 50% ⁷⁹Br and 50% ⁸¹Br. In a mass spectrum of Br₂, what intensity ratio is expected for peaks at m/z 158, 160 and 162?
o: Ignores that ⁷⁹Br⁸¹Br can form two ways (79–81 and 81–79).
Correct: probabilities are ¼ (79,79), ½ (79,81 either order), ¼ (81,81).
Overcounts the mixed combination.
Inverts the result; the mixed pair is the most likely.
questions.x: Treat each Br atom as an independent 50:50 choice. The combinations are 79–79 (¼), 79–81 or 81–79 (½ total) and 81–81 (¼), giving peaks at 158, 160 and 162 in a 1:2:1 ratio. The key idea is that the mixed pair can form two ways, so it is twice as likely as either pure pair.

questions.q: What holds protons together in a nucleus despite their electrostatic repulsion?
o: Gravitational attraction
Gravity between nucleons is about 10³⁶ times too weak.
The weak nuclear force
The weak force drives beta decay, not nuclear binding.
Electrostatic attraction to neutrons
Neutrons are neutral and exert no electrostatic force.
The strong nuclear force
Correct: the strong force attracts all nucleons at very short range.
questions.x: The strong nuclear force is a very short-range attraction between all nucleons, protons and neutrons alike. Within about 1 fm it overwhelms proton–proton electrostatic repulsion. The weak force governs beta decay rather than binding, and gravity between nucleons is negligibly small.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the strong nuclear force?
o: It acts only over about 10⁻¹⁵ m, between protons and neutrons alike
Correct: it is very short-range and charge-independent.
It acts over long distances, like gravity
Its range is roughly the size of a nucleus.
It attracts protons to neutrons but not protons to protons
It acts between all nucleon pairs regardless of charge.
It is weaker than the Coulomb force at nuclear distances
If it were weaker, no nucleus with 2+ protons would be bound.
questions.x: The strong force is extremely powerful but acts only over roughly 10⁻¹⁵ m, about the size of a nucleus, and it is charge-independent: p–p, p–n and n–n pairs all attract. Its short range is why large nuclei struggle, since the long-range Coulomb repulsion reaches across the whole nucleus while the strong force reaches only neighbors.

questions.q: Stable heavy nuclei such as ²⁰⁸Pb have far more neutrons than protons. Why?
o: Neutrons repel each other less than electrons do
Electrons are outside the nucleus and irrelevant to nuclear stability.
Extra neutrons add strong-force binding without adding repulsion
Correct: long-range proton repulsion grows quickly, and neutrons offset it.
Neutrons carry a small negative charge that cancels protons
Neutrons are neutral.
Protons are converted to neutrons by gamma emission
Gamma emission changes neither Z nor N.
questions.x: Each proton repels every other proton through the long-range Coulomb force, while the strong force acts only between neighbors. Neutrons add strong-force attraction with no added repulsion, so heavy nuclei need N/Z well above 1 (about 1.5 for lead) to stay stable. Neutrons are neutral, so they do not cancel proton charge.

questions.q: A nuclide lies above the band of stability, with too many neutrons for its number of protons. Which decay mode is most likely?
o: Positron emission
Positron emission raises N/Z, the wrong direction here.
Electron capture
Electron capture also converts p → n, raising N/Z.
Beta-minus emission
Correct: n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino lowers N/Z toward stability.
Gamma emission
Gamma emission does not change N or Z.
questions.x: A neutron-rich nucleus moves toward stability by lowering N/Z. Beta-minus decay converts a neutron into a proton (n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino), doing exactly that. Positron emission and electron capture convert protons into neutrons, which is the fix for proton-rich nuclei below the band, and gamma emission changes neither N nor Z.

questions.q: In beta-minus decay, which change occurs in the nucleus?
o: A neutron becomes a proton, so Z rises by 1 and A is unchanged
Correct: n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino.
A proton becomes a neutron, so Z falls by 1
That describes β⁺ decay or electron capture.
Two protons and two neutrons leave, so A falls by 4
That describes alpha decay.
Z and A are both unchanged
That describes gamma emission.
questions.x: In β⁻ decay, a neutron converts into a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino. Z rises by 1 while A stays constant because the total nucleon count is unchanged. Lowering Z by 1 describes the opposite processes, positron emission and electron capture.

questions.q: Technetium-99m emits a 140 keV photon as it relaxes to technetium-99. How do Z and A change?
o: Z rises by 1; A is unchanged
That is β⁻ decay.
Neither Z nor A changes
Correct: a gamma photon only removes energy from an excited nucleus.
Z falls by 1; A is unchanged
That is β⁺ decay or electron capture.
Z falls by 2; A falls by 4
That is alpha decay.
questions.note: The 'm' means metastable: an excited nuclear state.
questions.x: The 'm' in ⁹⁹ᵐTc marks a metastable excited nuclear state. Relaxing to the ground state emits a gamma photon, which carries energy but no charge or mass number, so Z and A are unchanged and the element stays technetium. This is why Tc-99m is useful in imaging: it emits penetrating gamma rays without particle radiation.

questions.q: Uranium-238 (Z = 92) undergoes alpha decay. What is the daughter nucleus?
o: ²³⁴Pa (Z = 91)
Lowers Z by only 1; an alpha particle carries 2 protons.
²³⁸Np (Z = 93)
Alpha decay lowers A and Z; it does not raise them.
²³⁴Th (Z = 90)
Correct: removing ⁴He²⁺ lowers A by 4 and Z by 2.
²³⁴Ra (Z = 88)
Lowers Z by 4; only the mass number falls by 4.
questions.x: An alpha particle is a ⁴He nucleus with 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so alpha decay lowers A by 4 and Z by 2. For ²³⁸U (Z = 92), the daughter is ²³⁴Th (Z = 90). A common trap is lowering Z by 4 along with A, but only the mass number drops by 4.

questions.q: Phosphorus-32 (Z = 15) is a beta-minus emitter. What nucleus does it become?
o: ³²Si
Si (Z = 14) results from β⁺ decay, which lowers Z.
³¹P
Beta decay does not change the mass number.
²⁸Al
That would require alpha decay.
³²S
Correct: β⁻ raises Z from 15 to 16 (sulfur) with A = 32.
questions.x: Beta-minus decay turns a neutron into a proton, so Z rises by 1 and A is unchanged. Phosphorus-32 (Z = 15) therefore becomes sulfur-32 (Z = 16). Lowering Z to silicon would correspond to positron emission or electron capture, the opposite change.

questions.q: Which two decay modes produce the same daughter nucleus from a given parent?
o: Positron emission and electron capture
Correct: both convert one proton into a neutron, so Z − 1 and A unchanged.
Alpha decay and beta-minus decay
Alpha lowers A by 4; β⁻ leaves A unchanged and raises Z.
Beta-minus decay and electron capture
These change Z in opposite directions.
Gamma emission and positron emission
Gamma leaves Z unchanged; positron emission lowers it.
questions.x: Positron emission (p → n + e⁺ + neutrino) and electron capture (p + e⁻ → n + neutrino) both convert one proton into a neutron. Each lowers Z by 1 and leaves A unchanged, so from the same parent they give the same daughter. β⁻ decay does the reverse, raising Z, so it can never match electron capture.

questions.q: Potassium-40 (Z = 19) can decay by electron capture. What is the product?
o: ⁴⁰Ca
Calcium (Z = 20) is the β⁻ product, not the EC product.
⁴⁰Ar
Correct: e⁻ + p → n lowers Z to 18 (argon) and keeps A = 40.
³⁹K
Capturing an electron does not change the mass number.
⁴¹K
A captured electron does not add a nucleon.
questions.x: In electron capture, the nucleus absorbs an inner-shell electron, which combines with a proton to form a neutron. Z falls by 1 and A stays the same, so ⁴⁰K (Z = 19) becomes ⁴⁰Ar (Z = 18). Calcium-40 is the product of K-40's other route, β⁻ decay, which raises Z instead.

questions.q: Thorium-232 (Z = 90) decays through a series to stable lead-208 (Z = 82). How many alpha and beta-minus decays occur?
o: 6 α and 2 β⁻
Six alphas lower Z to 78, so 4 β⁻ are needed to reach 82.
4 α and 6 β⁻
Four alphas lower A by only 16; A must drop by 24.
6 α and 4 β⁻
Correct: ΔA = 24 gives 6 α (Z → 78); four β⁻ raise Z to 82.
8 α and 4 β⁻
Eight alphas would lower A by 32.
questions.note: Fix the alpha count from ΔA first, then use β⁻ to fix Z.
questions.x: Only alpha decay changes A, so count alphas first: ΔA = 232 − 208 = 24, which is 6 alpha decays. Six alphas lower Z by 12, from 90 to 78, but lead has Z = 82, so four β⁻ decays (each raising Z by 1) are needed. Fixing A first, then Z, avoids guessing.

questions.q: A nuclide undergoes two alpha decays followed by one beta-minus decay, producing bismuth-214 (Z = 83). What was the parent?
o: ²¹⁸Po (Z = 84)
Accounts for only one alpha decay.
²²²Fr (Z = 87)
Skips the β⁻ step: 83 + 4 = 87 ignores lowering Z by 1 when working backward.
²²⁶Ra (Z = 88)
Counts three alpha decays.
²²²Rn (Z = 86)
questions.x: Work backward by reversing each step. Undoing the β⁻ lowers Z by 1 (83 → 82, A = 214); undoing two alphas adds 8 to A and 4 to Z, giving A = 222 and Z = 86, which is radon-222. The usual error is reversing the β⁻ step in the wrong direction or skipping it.

questions.q: Which type of radiation is stopped by a single sheet of paper?
o: Alpha particles
Correct: their large mass and +2 charge make them interact strongly and stop quickly.
Beta particles
Beta particles need a few millimeters of aluminum to stop.
Gamma rays
Gamma rays need thick lead or concrete to attenuate.
X-rays
X-rays, like gamma rays, pass easily through paper.
questions.x: Penetrating power falls as charge and mass rise. Alpha particles are heavy and doubly charged, so they ionize intensely and lose energy within a few centimeters of air or a sheet of paper. Beta particles need millimeters of aluminum, and uncharged photons such as gamma rays and X-rays need dense shielding like lead.

questions.q: A beam of radiation passes between charged plates. One part bends slightly toward the negative plate, one bends sharply toward the positive plate, and one is undeflected. What is the sharply bent part?
o: Alpha particles
Alphas are positive and bend toward the negative plate, and only slightly because they are heavy.
Beta-minus particles
Correct: light, negatively charged electrons bend strongly toward the positive plate.
Gamma rays
Gamma rays are uncharged and pass undeflected.
Neutrons
Neutrons are uncharged and would not be deflected.
questions.x: Charged particles bend toward the oppositely charged plate, and lighter particles bend more for a given charge. Beta-minus particles are negative electrons, about 7000 times lighter than alphas, so they bend sharply toward the positive plate. Alphas bend only slightly toward the negative plate, and gamma rays pass undeflected.

questions.q: Complete the transmutation: ¹⁴N + ⁴He → ¹⁷O + ?
o: A neutron
A neutron would leave the charge unbalanced (Z: 9 vs 8).
An electron
An electron would add mass-number imbalance and the wrong charge.
A positron
A positron has A = 0, leaving the mass numbers unbalanced (18 vs 17).
A proton
Correct: A: 18 = 17 + 1 and Z: 9 = 8 + 1, so the product is ¹H.
questions.note: Balance both mass number and atomic number.
questions.x: In nuclear equations, both mass number and atomic number must balance. On the left A = 14 + 4 = 18 and Z = 7 + 2 = 9; ¹⁷O accounts for A = 17 and Z = 8, so the missing particle has A = 1 and Z = 1, a proton. A neutron balances the mass number but leaves the charge off by one.

questions.q: In one fission pathway, ²³⁵U + ¹n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + x ¹n. What is x?
o: Leaves two mass units unaccounted for.
Forgets to include the incoming neutron on the left.
Overcounts; 141 + 92 + 4 = 237.
questions.note: Extra neutrons are what sustain a chain reaction.
questions.x: Balance mass numbers including the incoming neutron: 235 + 1 = 236 on the left, and 141 + 92 = 233 on the right, so 3 neutrons are released. Protons also balance (92 = 56 + 36). Releasing more neutrons than are absorbed is what lets fission sustain a chain reaction.

questions.q: Fusing two deuterium nuclei releases energy, but fusing two iron-56 nuclei does not. Why?
o: Iron nuclei have more electrons
Electrons play no role in nuclear binding energy.
Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron
Correct: only reactions moving toward the iron peak release energy.
Iron is a solid at fusion temperatures
At fusion temperatures all matter is plasma.
Deuterium has fewer neutrons than protons
Deuterium has one of each.
questions.x: Binding energy per nucleon rises steeply for light nuclei and peaks near iron-56, then slowly falls. Fusing light nuclei or splitting heavy ones moves products toward the peak and releases energy. Iron already sits at the top, so fusing iron nuclei would consume energy rather than release it.

questions.q: Electrons emitted in beta-minus decay of a given nuclide have a continuous range of energies rather than one value. What explains this?
o: The nucleus recoils by a random amount
Nuclear recoil is tiny and fixed by momentum conservation in a two-body decay.
Electrons lose varying energy leaving the electron cloud
The spread is present at emission; it is not a shielding effect.
Each nucleus has a different decay energy
Every parent-to-daughter transition has the same Q value.
An antineutrino shares the decay energy
Correct: energy splits among three bodies, so the electron's share varies.
questions.note: This puzzle led Pauli to propose the neutrino.
questions.x: If beta decay produced only an electron and the daughter nucleus, momentum and energy conservation would force one fixed electron energy. The observed continuous spectrum means a third particle, the antineutrino, carries off a variable share of the fixed decay energy. Pauli proposed the neutrino for exactly this reason, and each decay of the same nuclide has the same total energy.

questions.q: After a nucleus decays by electron capture, which emission commonly follows from the atom?
o: X-rays
Correct: outer electrons drop into the inner-shell vacancy, emitting X-ray photons.
Alpha particles
Electron capture does not eject nucleons.
A positron
Positron emission is an alternative to EC, not a consequence of it.
A beta-minus particle
EC lowers Z; β⁻ would reverse that change.
questions.x: Electron capture pulls an inner-shell (usually K-shell) electron into the nucleus, leaving a vacancy. An outer electron drops into that vacancy and releases the energy difference as a characteristic X-ray (or an Auger electron). Nothing else leaves the nucleus besides a neutrino, so alpha or positron emission is not a consequence of capture.

questions.q: In PET imaging, a positron meets an electron and both are annihilated. What is produced?
o: One photon of 511 keV
A single photon cannot conserve momentum from a pair at rest.
Two 511 keV photons traveling in opposite directions
Correct: each photon carries one particle's rest energy, mc² = 511 keV.
A neutron and a neutrino
Annihilation converts mass to photons, not to nucleons.
Two 1.02 MeV photons in the same direction
Doubles the energy and violates momentum conservation.
questions.x: When a positron and electron annihilate nearly at rest, their total rest energy (2 × 511 keV) becomes photons. Since the initial momentum is about zero, the photons must carry equal and opposite momenta, so two 511 keV photons fly apart in opposite directions. PET scanners detect these coincident back-to-back photons to locate the source.

questions.q: In any balanced nuclear equation, which quantities are conserved?
o: Total mass and number of neutrons
Mass is not exactly conserved, and β decay changes neutron count.
Number of protons and number of electrons
Beta decay changes proton number.
Total charge and total nucleon (mass) number
Correct: Z sums and A sums balance on both sides.
Number of protons and total mass
Neither is strictly conserved in nuclear reactions.
questions.x: Nuclear equations balance total charge (sum of Z values, counting particles like e⁻ and e⁺) and total nucleon number A. Individual proton and neutron counts can change, as in beta decay, and rest mass is not strictly conserved because some converts to energy (E = mc²), producing the mass defect.

questions.q: Nuclear reactions release about a million times more energy per atom than chemical reactions. Why?
o: Nuclear reactions involve more electrons
Electrons govern chemistry, the low-energy case.
Nuclear reactions occur at higher temperatures
Temperature does not set the energy stored in bonds.
Gravity dominates at nuclear distances
Gravity is negligible inside nuclei.
The strong force binds nucleons in MeV-scale energies
Correct: nuclear binding is MeV per nucleon, chemical bonds only a few eV.
questions.x: Chemical reactions rearrange electrons, involving energies of a few eV per bond. Nuclear reactions rearrange nucleons held by the strong force, with binding energies of several MeV per nucleon, about a million times larger. Temperature and electron number do not set this scale; the force involved does.

questions.q: Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8 days. What fraction of a sample remains after 32 days?
o: That is two half-lives (16 days).
That is three half-lives (24 days).
Correct: 32/8 = 4 half-lives, and (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.
That is five half-lives (40 days).
questions.x: First find the number of half-lives (elapsed time divided by t½): 32/8 = 4. The fraction remaining is (1/2)ⁿ = (1/2)⁴ = 1/16. Each half-life halves what is left, not the original amount, so the fraction shrinks geometrically.

questions.q: An 80 mg sample of a radioisotope decays to 5 mg in 20 hours. What is its half-life?
o: 4 hours
Would give five half-lives: 80 → 2.5 mg.
5 hours
Correct: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 → 5 is 4 half-lives, so 20/4 = 5 h.
10 hours
Would leave 20 mg after 20 hours.
16 hours
Divides 80 by 5 instead of counting halvings.
questions.x: Count halvings: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 → 5 mg is 4 half-lives, so t½ = 20 h / 4 = 5 h. Equivalently, 5/80 = 1/16 = (1/2)⁴. Dividing the mass ratio by the time (80/5 = 16 hours) confuses a factor of 16 with a number of half-lives.

questions.q: A bone fragment contains 25% of the carbon-14 found in living tissue. The half-life of carbon-14 is about 5730 years. About how old is it?
o: 1430 years
Divides the half-life by 4 instead of counting halvings.
5730 years
One half-life leaves 50%, not 25%.
17,190 years
Three half-lives leaves 12.5%.
11,460 years
questions.x: 25% remaining equals (1/2)², so two half-lives have passed: 2 × 5730 ≈ 11,460 years. Radiocarbon dating works because living tissue keeps a steady ¹⁴C level that decays after death. A common error is assuming 25% means a quarter of one half-life rather than two full halvings.

questions.q: What percentage of a radioactive sample has decayed after five half-lives?
o: About 97%
Correct: (1/2)⁵ = 1/32 ≈ 3% remains, so about 97% has decayed.
About 3%
That is the fraction remaining, not the fraction decayed.
About 50%
That is the result after one half-life.
Exponential decay never reaches exactly zero remaining.
questions.note: Read carefully: remaining versus decayed.
questions.x: After n half-lives the fraction remaining is (1/2)ⁿ, so after five it is 1/32 ≈ 3%. The fraction decayed is 1 − 1/32 ≈ 97%. Read the question carefully: 3% is what remains, and exponential decay never reaches exactly 100% decayed.

questions.q: A radioisotope has a half-life of 10 minutes. What is its decay constant k? (ln 2 ≈ 0.7)
o: 0.007 min⁻¹
Off by a factor of 10.
0.07 min⁻¹
Correct: k = ln 2 / t½ = 0.7/10 = 0.07 min⁻¹.
7 min⁻¹
Multiplies ln 2 by t½ instead of dividing.
14 min⁻¹
Inverts the relationship (t½/ln 2) and mislabels units.
questions.x: For first-order decay, k = ln 2 / t½. With t½ = 10 min, k = 0.7/10 = 0.07 min⁻¹. The decay constant and half-life are inversely related, so a longer half-life means a smaller k; multiplying instead of dividing gives a value far too large.

questions.q: Samples of isotope A (t½ = 2 h) and isotope B (t½ = 4 h) start with equal numbers of nuclei. After 8 hours, what is the ratio of A to B remaining?
o: Compares half-life lengths rather than the fractions remaining.
A decays faster, so less A remains, not more.
Correct: A has gone through 4 half-lives (1/16), B through 2 (1/4); ratio 1:4.
Miscounts B as having gone through only one half-life.
questions.x: Convert time to half-lives for each isotope: A has 8/2 = 4 half-lives (1/16 left) and B has 8/4 = 2 half-lives (1/4 left). The ratio A:B is (1/16):(1/4) = 1:4. The shorter half-life decays faster, so A must be the smaller amount.

questions.q: A radioactive sample is heated from 25 °C to 500 °C. How does its half-life change?
o: It decreases because decay speeds up when hot
Treats nuclear decay like a chemical reaction with activation energy.
It increases because nuclei become more stable
Thermal energy is far too small to affect nuclear stability.
It doubles for every 10 °C rise
That rule of thumb applies loosely to some chemical reactions only.
It does not change
Correct: nuclear decay rates are independent of temperature and pressure.
questions.x: Radioactive decay depends on nuclear energy levels set by the strong and weak forces, measured in MeV. Thermal energy even at 500 °C is only about 0.1 eV per particle, far too small to affect nuclei, so the half-life stays constant. Temperature dependence via activation energy applies to chemical reactions, not nuclear decay.

questions.q: A sample with a half-life of 3 days has an activity of 400 counts/min today. What was its activity 9 days ago?
o: 3200 counts/min
Correct: 9 days is 3 half-lives back, so 400 × 2³ = 3200.
1200 counts/min
Multiplies by 3 instead of by 2³.
1600 counts/min
Counts only two half-lives.
50 counts/min
Runs time forward instead of backward.
questions.x: Running time backward, each half-life doubles activity. Nine days is 9/3 = 3 half-lives, so the earlier activity was 400 × 2³ = 3200 counts/min. Multiplying by 3 (1200) treats decay as linear, and dividing (50) runs time forward instead of backward.

questions.q: About how many half-lives must pass for a sample to fall to 10% of its original amount? (log 2 ≈ 0.3)
o: That is ln 10, not the number of half-lives.
Correct: (1/2)ⁿ = 0.1 gives n = 1/log 2 ≈ 3.3; between 1/8 and 1/16.
Five half-lives leaves about 3%.
Assumes 10% is lost per half-life, a linear misconception.
questions.x: Solve (1/2)ⁿ = 0.1: n = log 10 / log 2 = 1/0.3 ≈ 3.3 half-lives. A quick check: 3 half-lives leave 12.5% and 4 leave 6.25%, so 10% falls between them. Assuming 10% is lost per half-life treats exponential decay as linear.

questions.q: Which plot of radioactive decay data gives a straight line?
o: N versus t
Decay is exponential, so this curves downward.
1/N versus t
That is linear for second-order kinetics.
ln N versus t
Correct: ln N = ln N₀ − kt, a line of slope −k.
N versus 1/t
No standard rate law gives a line here.
questions.note: Radioactive decay is first-order kinetics.
questions.x: Radioactive decay is first-order: N = N₀e^(−kt). Taking the natural log gives ln N = ln N₀ − kt, a straight line with slope −k. A plot of N versus t curves, and 1/N versus t is linear only for second-order kinetics.

questions.q: A rock contains a parent isotope (t½ = 500 million years) and its stable daughter in a daughter-to-parent ratio of 7:1. If all daughter came from the parent, how old is the rock?
o: 500 million years
One half-life gives a 1:1 ratio.
1.0 billion years
Two half-lives gives a 3:1 ratio.
3.5 billion years
Multiplies the ratio 7 by 500 million years.
1.5 billion years
Correct: parent is 1/8 of the original, which is 3 half-lives = 1.5 billion years.
questions.note: Convert D:P to the fraction of parent remaining: P/(P + D).
questions.x: If every daughter atom came from a parent, the original parent count is P + D = 1 + 7 = 8, so 1/8 of the parent remains. That is (1/2)³, or 3 half-lives, giving 3 × 500 million = 1.5 billion years. Multiplying the ratio itself by the half-life skips converting it into a fraction remaining.

questions.q: What fraction of a radioisotope remains after half of one half-life has passed?
o: About 71%
Assumes linear decay during the half-life.
That is after a full half-life.
That is after two half-lives.
questions.note: Trap: decay is exponential, so the first half of a half-life removes more than 25%.
questions.x: Fraction remaining is (1/2)^(t/t½), so after half a half-life it is (1/2)^0.5 = 1/√2 ≈ 0.71. More than 25% decays in the first half of a half-life because decay is fastest when the most nuclei are present. Assuming linear decay gives 75%, which is the tempting trap.

questions.q: A hospital needs a tracer for diagnostic imaging that is detected outside the body. Which isotope property is most suitable?
o: Alpha emitter with a half-life of 10 years
Alphas do not escape the body, and a long half-life prolongs exposure.
Beta emitter with a half-life of 2 seconds
Betas are mostly absorbed in tissue, and 2 s is too short to use.
Gamma emitter with a half-life of several hours
Correct: gammas exit the body, and hours allows imaging with little lingering dose.
Stable isotope with no emission
A stable isotope gives no signal for an external detector.
questions.x: An imaging tracer must emit radiation that escapes the body to reach an external detector, which means gamma rays; alphas and betas are absorbed within tissue. Its half-life should be long enough to prepare, inject and image (hours) but short enough that dose does not linger. A 10-year alpha emitter fails both tests and would deposit damaging dose locally.

questions.q: A helium-4 nucleus has less mass than two free protons plus two free neutrons. What does this missing mass represent?
o: Mass carried off by electrons
Electrons are not part of the nucleus or this comparison.
Measurement error in nuclear masses
The difference is real and well measured.
Mass converted to the strong force carriers within the nucleus
The mass is not stored as extra particles inside the nucleus.
Energy released when the nucleons bound together
Correct: the mass defect equals binding energy divided by c².
questions.x: A bound nucleus weighs less than its separate nucleons because energy was released when they bound together. That missing mass, the mass defect, equals the binding energy divided by c² (E = Δmc²). It is not stored as extra particles; it left the system as energy, which is also how much energy it would take to pull the nucleus apart.

questions.q: A free proton has mass 1.0073 u and a free neutron 1.0087 u. A deuteron has mass 2.0136 u. What is the mass defect of the deuteron?
o: That is the neutron–proton mass difference, not the defect.
Uses only the decimal part of the nucleon sum.
That is the total mass of the free nucleons.
questions.note: 1 u ≈ 931 MeV, so this is about 2.2 MeV.
questions.x: Mass defect = (mass of separated nucleons) − (mass of nucleus) = (1.0073 + 1.0087) − 2.0136 = 0.0024 u. Using 1 u ≈ 931 MeV, that is about 2.2 MeV of binding energy. The neutron–proton mass difference (0.0014 u) is a different quantity that does not involve binding.

questions.q: Which nucleus has the highest binding energy per nucleon?
o: ⁴He
Tightly bound for its size, but about 7 MeV per nucleon.
¹²C
About 7.7 MeV per nucleon, below the iron peak.
⁵⁶Fe
Correct: nuclei near iron-56 sit at the peak, about 8.8 MeV per nucleon.
²³⁵U
About 7.6 MeV per nucleon; heavy nuclei fall off the peak.
questions.x: Binding energy per nucleon rises quickly for light nuclei, peaks near iron-56 at about 8.8 MeV, and declines slowly for heavy nuclei because Coulomb repulsion grows. That peak is why fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both release energy. Helium-4 is unusually stable for its size but still well below the iron peak.

questions.q: A nuclear reaction has a mass defect of 1 × 10⁻²⁹ kg. How much energy is released? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
o: Multiplies by c instead of c².
Correct: E = mc² = (1 × 10⁻²⁹)(9 × 10¹⁶) = 9 × 10⁻¹³ J.
Uses 10⁻¹⁶ instead of 10¹⁶ for c², flipping the sign of the exponent.
Squares the 10⁸ but not the 3.
questions.x: Mass-energy equivalence gives E = mc² = (1 × 10⁻²⁹ kg)(3 × 10⁸ m/s)² = (1 × 10⁻²⁹)(9 × 10¹⁶) = 9 × 10⁻¹³ J. Remember to square both the 3 and the 10⁸. Tiny mass changes give large energies because c² is enormous.

questions.q: A nucleus with A = 240 (7.6 MeV per nucleon) splits into two A = 120 fragments (8.5 MeV per nucleon each). About how much energy is released?
o: 0.9 MeV
That is the gain per nucleon, not the total.
108 MeV
Counts only one fragment's 120 nucleons.
2000 MeV
Uses the total binding energy of the products, not the change.
216 MeV
Correct: 240 nucleons × (8.5 − 7.6) MeV = 240 × 0.9 ≈ 216 MeV.
questions.note: Energy released = increase in total binding energy.
questions.x: Energy released equals the gain in total binding energy. Before: 240 × 7.6 = 1824 MeV; after: 240 × 8.5 = 2040 MeV; the difference is 240 × 0.9 ≈ 216 MeV. The total nucleon count stays 240, so the per-nucleon gain applies to all of them, not just one fragment.

questions.q: A gamma photon has an energy of 2 MeV. What is this energy in joules? (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
o: Correct: 2 × 10⁶ eV × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J/eV = 3.2 × 10⁻¹³ J.
Treats MeV as eV, dropping the 10⁶.
Divides by the conversion factor instead of multiplying, and drops the 10⁶.
Treats MeV as keV (10³).
questions.x: Convert MeV to eV first (2 MeV = 2 × 10⁶ eV), then multiply by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J/eV to get 3.2 × 10⁻¹³ J. The prefix M means 10⁶, so forgetting it gives an answer a million times too small. A joule is huge on the atomic scale, so photon energies in joules are always tiny numbers.

questions.q: In the Bohr model, an electron in hydrogen moves from n = 1 to n = 3. What must happen?
o: The atom emits a photon
Emission occurs when an electron drops to a lower level.
The atom absorbs energy
Correct: higher n is a higher (less negative) energy, so energy must be absorbed.
The atom loses a proton
Electronic transitions do not affect the nucleus.
No energy change occurs
Levels have different energies, Eₙ ∝ −1/n².
questions.x: Bohr energy levels are negative and rise toward zero as n increases (Eₙ ∝ −1/n²). Moving from n = 1 to n = 3 raises the electron's energy, so the atom must absorb energy, for example as a photon matching the gap exactly. Emission occurs only for downward transitions.

questions.q: Hydrogen levels follow Eₙ = −13.6 eV/n². How much energy is needed to ionize a hydrogen atom whose electron is in n = 2?
o: That is the ionization energy from the ground state, n = 1.
That is the 1 → 2 excitation energy.
3.4 eV
Correct: E₂ = −13.6/4 = −3.4 eV, so 3.4 eV brings it to E = 0.
6.8 eV
Divides by n instead of n².
questions.x: Ionization means raising the electron to E = 0 (n = ∞). For n = 2, E₂ = −13.6/2² = −3.4 eV, so 3.4 eV is needed. The 13.6 eV value is the ionization energy only from the ground state; an excited electron is already partway out.

questions.q: Using Eₙ = −13.6 eV/n², what is the energy of the photon emitted when hydrogen's electron drops from n = 3 to n = 2?
o: 1.9 eV
3.4 eV
That is the magnitude of E₂ alone.
That is the 2 → 1 transition.
That is the 3 → 1 transition.
questions.note: This is the red Balmer line near 656 nm.
questions.x: Photon energy equals the level gap: ΔE = 13.6(1/2² − 1/3²) = 13.6 × 5/36 ≈ 1.9 eV. This is the red Balmer line near 656 nm. Using E₂ alone (3.4 eV) forgets that the electron starts at n = 3, which is −1.5 eV, not zero.

questions.q: Which electron transition in hydrogen emits the photon with the shortest wavelength?
o: Small energy gap, long (red) wavelength.
Larger than 3 → 2 but much smaller than drops to n = 1.
A large gap, but 4 → 1 is larger still.
Correct: the largest energy drop gives the highest frequency and shortest λ.
questions.note: λ ∝ 1/ΔE.
questions.x: Photon wavelength is inversely proportional to energy (λ = hc/ΔE), so the shortest wavelength comes from the largest energy drop. Because levels crowd together at high n, drops to n = 1 are largest, and 4 → 1 beats 2 → 1. Drops ending at n = 2 (Balmer) are in the visible, much longer in wavelength.

questions.q: Hydrogen atoms are all excited to n = 4. As they relax by every possible downward path, how many distinct emission lines can appear?
o: Counts only single-step drops (4→3, 3→2, 2→1).
Counts the levels rather than the pairs of levels.
Correct: any pair of 4 levels can be joined, 4 × 3/2 = 6 lines.
That is the count for 5 levels.
questions.x: Each distinct line corresponds to a distinct pair of levels, and with atoms starting at n = 4 every pair among levels 1 to 4 can be reached. The number of pairs is 4 × 3 / 2 = 6: 4→3, 4→2, 4→1, 3→2, 3→1 and 2→1. Counting only single-step drops (3) misses transitions that skip levels.

questions.q: Why does excited hydrogen gas produce a line spectrum instead of a continuous rainbow?
o: Electron energy levels are quantized
Correct: only specific level differences, and so specific photon energies, are possible.
Hydrogen absorbs all visible light
Absorption of all colors would produce darkness, not discrete lines.
The nucleus emits light at fixed frequencies
Visible lines come from electron transitions, not nuclear ones.
Photons of other colors are too fast to detect
All photons travel at c.
questions.x: Electrons in atoms can occupy only discrete energy levels, so a transition can release only a photon whose energy equals a specific level gap. Each allowed gap gives one wavelength, producing bright lines rather than a continuum. A continuous spectrum comes from dense matter such as a hot solid, where energy states are effectively continuous.

questions.q: An atom emits a photon of energy 2.0 eV. What is its wavelength? (hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm)
o: 310 nm
Divides by 4 instead of 2.
Multiplies by 2 instead of dividing.
Forgets to divide by the energy.
620 nm
Correct: λ = hc/E = 1240/2.0 = 620 nm, orange-red light.
questions.x: Photon wavelength and energy are inversely related: λ = hc/E = 1240 eV·nm / 2.0 eV = 620 nm, which is orange-red visible light. The handy value hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm turns this into one division. Doubling instead of halving gives 2480 nm, a common inverse-relation slip.

questions.q: White light passes through cool sodium vapor and then a prism. What does the spectrum look like?
o: Bright lines on a dark background
That is an emission spectrum from a hot, excited gas.
A continuous spectrum with no features
Ignores that sodium absorbs specific wavelengths.
A continuous spectrum with dark lines at sodium's emission wavelengths
Correct: the gas absorbs exactly the photon energies matching its level gaps.
Dark lines at wavelengths different from sodium's emission lines
Absorption and emission share the same level gaps and so the same wavelengths.
questions.x: Cool gas absorbs exactly the photon energies that match its level gaps, removing those wavelengths from continuous white light. The result is an absorption spectrum: a rainbow with dark lines at the same wavelengths sodium emits when hot, since emission and absorption use the same level gaps. Bright lines on dark only appear when viewing the hot gas itself.

questions.q: In the Bohr model, orbit radius is proportional to n². How does the radius of the n = 3 orbit compare to the n = 1 orbit?
o: 9 times larger
Correct: r ∝ n², so 3² = 9.
3 times larger
Assumes r ∝ n.
1/9 as large
Inverts the relationship.
27 times larger
Uses n³.
questions.x: In the Bohr model, orbit radius scales as rₙ = n²a₀, so the n = 3 radius is 3² = 9 times the n = 1 radius. Energy, by contrast, scales as −1/n². Assuming a linear relation with n gives the tempting but wrong factor of 3.

questions.q: Sodium salts give a yellow color in a flame. What produces the light?
o: Sodium nuclei undergoing gamma decay
Gamma rays are not visible light, and sodium-23 is stable.
Combustion of the anion
The characteristic color is the same for many sodium salts, so the cation is responsible.
Excited electrons emitting photons as they drop to lower levels
Correct: the 3p → 3s transition in Na gives the yellow ~589 nm light.
Electrons being removed to form Na⁺
Ionization absorbs energy; it does not emit a fixed color.
questions.x: Flame heat excites sodium's outer electron from 3s to 3p; as it falls back, it emits a photon near 589 nm, which looks yellow. The color is characteristic of the element because it depends on that atom's level gaps, which is the basis of flame tests. The nucleus is not involved, and ionization absorbs energy rather than emitting a fixed color.

questions.q: Using Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV for one-electron species, what is the ionization energy of ground-state He⁺?
o: Ignores the nuclear charge Z = 2.
Uses Z instead of Z².
3.4 eV
Divides by Z² instead of multiplying.
Correct: 13.6 × 2² / 1² = 54.4 eV.
questions.x: For a one-electron ion, energy levels scale with Z²: Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV. He⁺ has Z = 2 and n = 1, so E₁ = −54.4 eV and the ionization energy is 54.4 eV. Greater nuclear charge pulls the lone electron in much more tightly; using Z instead of Z² gives only 27.2 eV.

questions.q: In hydrogen, how does the energy gap between n = 5 and n = 6 compare to the gap between n = 1 and n = 2?
o: It is the same
Levels are not evenly spaced; Eₙ ∝ −1/n².
It is much smaller
Correct: levels crowd together as n increases.
It is much larger
Higher levels converge toward E = 0.
It is exactly 5 times larger
No such linear relation exists.
questions.x: Because Eₙ ∝ −1/n², levels crowd together as n increases and converge at E = 0. The 1→2 gap is 13.6 × 3/4 = 10.2 eV, while the 5→6 gap is only 13.6(1/25 − 1/36) ≈ 0.17 eV. Assuming evenly spaced levels, like rungs on a ladder, is the main misconception.

questions.q: An atom absorbs a 500 nm photon, then relaxes in two steps. One emitted photon has a wavelength of 1000 nm. What is the wavelength of the other?
o: 500 nm
Subtracts wavelengths (1000 − 500) instead of energies.
Adds wavelengths (500 + 1000); wavelengths do not add, energies do.
333 nm
Adds 1/λ terms the wrong way; a cascade photon cannot exceed the absorbed energy.
questions.note: Energy (∝ 1/λ) is conserved, not wavelength.
questions.x: Energy is conserved, and photon energy is proportional to 1/λ, so 1/500 = 1/1000 + 1/λ. Solving gives 1/λ = 1/1000, so λ = 1000 nm: the 500 nm photon's energy splits into two equal halves. Wavelengths themselves do not add or subtract, which is the trap.

questions.q: Why does the Bohr model accurately predict the spectrum of H and He⁺ but fail for neutral helium?
o: Helium has a larger nucleus
Nuclear size is not the issue; He⁺ has the same nucleus and works.
Helium's electrons are not quantized
All atomic electrons have quantized energies.
Helium emits only ultraviolet light
Helium has many visible lines.
It ignores electron–electron repulsion
Correct: the model handles only one electron around a nucleus.
questions.x: The Bohr model treats a single electron moving around a nucleus, which fits H, He⁺, Li²⁺ and other one-electron species. Neutral helium has two electrons that repel and shield each other, an interaction the model has no way to include. He⁺ shares helium's nucleus and still works, so nuclear size is not the problem.

questions.q: A fluorescent dye absorbs violet light and emits green light. Why is the emitted photon lower in energy?
o: Some absorbed energy is lost nonradiatively before emission
Correct: vibrational relaxation drains energy, so emission has longer λ.
Green photons travel more slowly than violet ones
All photons travel at c in vacuum.
The dye's nucleus absorbs part of the energy
Fluorescence is an electronic process; the nucleus is not involved.
Emission always doubles the wavelength
No fixed doubling rule exists.
questions.x: In fluorescence, a molecule absorbs a photon and jumps to an excited electronic state, then loses some energy as heat through vibrational relaxation before emitting. The emitted photon therefore has less energy and longer wavelength than the absorbed one (the Stokes shift). All photons travel at c in vacuum, so speed is not the difference.

questions.q: In the photoelectric effect, light above the threshold frequency is made brighter. What changes?
o: The maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons rises
KE depends on frequency, not intensity.
The threshold frequency drops
Threshold depends on the metal's work function only.
The number of ejected electrons per second rises
Correct: more photons per second eject more electrons, each with the same max KE.
The work function of the metal decreases
The work function is a fixed property of the surface.
questions.x: Above threshold, each photon ejects at most one electron with KEmax = hf − φ, which depends only on frequency. Brighter light means more photons per second, so more electrons are ejected per second, but each has the same maximum energy. Intensity changes neither the threshold frequency nor the metal's work function.

questions.q: Photons of energy 6 eV strike a metal with a work function of 4 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons?
o: 10 eV
Adds the work function instead of subtracting it.
6 eV
Ignores the energy needed to free the electron.
4 eV
That is the work function itself.
2 eV
Correct: KEmax = hf − φ = 6 − 4 = 2 eV.
questions.x: Einstein's photoelectric equation is KEmax = hf − φ. The photon supplies 6 eV, 4 eV is spent freeing the electron from the metal, and at most 2 eV remains as kinetic energy. Adding the work function instead of subtracting it is the common slip.

questions.q: Very intense red light shines on a metal but ejects no electrons. Which change is most likely to cause emission?
o: Using ultraviolet light instead
Correct: higher-frequency photons can exceed the work function.
Increasing the red light's intensity further
More low-energy photons still cannot each free an electron.
Shining the red light for a longer time
Electrons cannot accumulate energy from several photons.
Using a metal with a larger work function
That would make emission even harder.
questions.x: Emission requires each individual photon to carry energy at least equal to the work function, since one photon frees one electron. Red photons are too low in energy, so more of them or longer exposure does not help. Higher-frequency light such as ultraviolet raises the energy per photon above the threshold.

questions.q: A metal has a work function of 2.48 eV. What is the longest wavelength of light that can eject electrons? (hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm)
o: 250 nm
Off by a factor of 2.
500 nm
Correct: λmax = hc/φ = 1240/2.48 = 500 nm.
620 nm
Uses 2.0 eV instead of 2.48 eV.
Multiplies hc by φ instead of dividing.
questions.note: Longest wavelength = lowest photon energy = threshold.
questions.x: The longest usable wavelength corresponds to the lowest photon energy that still equals the work function: λmax = hc/φ = 1240/2.48 = 500 nm. Longer wavelengths carry less energy per photon and eject nothing. Multiplying instead of dividing ignores the inverse relation between energy and wavelength.

questions.q: A plot of the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons versus light frequency is a straight line. What does its slope equal?
o: The work function
The work function is the magnitude of the y-intercept.
The threshold frequency
That is the x-intercept.
Planck's constant
Correct: KEmax = hf − φ, so the slope is h for every metal.
The speed of light
c does not appear in the KE versus frequency relation.
questions.x: Einstein's equation KEmax = hf − φ has the form y = mx + b with x = f. The slope is Planck's constant h, the same for every metal, while the y-intercept is −φ and the x-intercept is the threshold frequency. Different metals give parallel lines shifted by their work functions.

questions.q: Light with photon energy 4 eV ejects electrons with a maximum KE of 2 eV. If the light's frequency is doubled, what is the new maximum KE?
o: 4 eV
Assumes KE doubles; the work function is subtracted only once.
2 eV
KE does depend on frequency.
8 eV
That is the new photon energy, before subtracting φ.
6 eV
Correct: φ = 4 − 2 = 2 eV; new KE = 8 − 2 = 6 eV.
questions.x: First find the work function: φ = hf − KEmax = 4 − 2 = 2 eV. Doubling the frequency doubles the photon energy to 8 eV, so KEmax = 8 − 2 = 6 eV. KE does not simply double because the fixed work function is subtracted only once.

questions.q: Which aspect of light does the photoelectric effect most directly demonstrate?
o: Light is made of energy packets (photons)
Correct: each electron is ejected by one photon of energy hf.
Light diffracts around edges
Diffraction demonstrates wave behavior.
Light bends when entering glass
Refraction is explained by wave speed changes.
Light has a constant speed in vacuum
That is a relativity result, not shown here.
questions.x: The photoelectric effect shows that light delivers energy in discrete packets, photons of energy E = hf, each absorbed by a single electron. That explains why frequency, not intensity, sets the threshold and the maximum kinetic energy. Diffraction and refraction are explained by light's wave behavior, the opposite side of wave–particle duality.

questions.q: A lamp emits 2 W of light as photons that each carry 4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. About how many photons does it emit per second?
o: Multiplies power by photon energy instead of dividing.
Correct: (2 J/s) ÷ (4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J/photon) = 5 × 10¹⁸ photons/s.
Exponent slip: 1/10⁻¹⁹ is 10¹⁹, but 2/4 = 0.5 drops it to 10¹⁸.
Divides photon energy by power, inverting the ratio.
questions.note: Power is energy per second; divide by energy per photon.
questions.x: Light power is energy delivered per second, and each photon carries a fixed quantum of energy (E = hf). Dividing gives the photon rate: 2 J/s ÷ 4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 5 × 10¹⁸ photons per second. Even a dim lamp emits enormous numbers of photons, which is why light looks continuous; check units (J/s ÷ J = 1/s) to rule out multiplying.

questions.q: Electrons are accelerated to a higher speed. What happens to their de Broglie wavelength?
o: It increases
λ = h/p decreases as momentum rises.
It stays the same
Wavelength depends on momentum.
It decreases
Correct: λ = h/mv, so greater speed gives a shorter wavelength.
It becomes zero
λ shrinks but never reaches zero for finite momentum.
questions.x: The de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/p = h/mv, so it is inversely proportional to momentum. Speeding an electron up raises its momentum and shortens its wavelength, which is why higher-voltage electron microscopes resolve finer detail. The wavelength shrinks but never reaches zero for any finite momentum.

questions.q: What does the Heisenberg uncertainty principle state about an electron?
o: Its energy is always uncertain by 13.6 eV
No such fixed uncertainty exists.
Its charge cannot be measured precisely
Electron charge is known very precisely.
It occupies a fixed circular orbit
That is the Bohr picture, which the principle undermines.
Its position and momentum cannot both be known exactly
Correct: Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π.
questions.note: This is why orbitals are probability clouds.
questions.x: The uncertainty principle states Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π: the more precisely an electron's position is defined, the less precisely its momentum can be, and vice versa. This is a property of nature, not of imperfect instruments. It is why electrons are described by probability clouds (orbitals) rather than fixed Bohr orbits.

questions.q: Which quantum number primarily determines the shape of an orbital?
o: Azimuthal quantum number, l
Correct: l = 0, 1, 2, 3 gives s, p, d, f shapes.
Principal quantum number, n
n sets size and energy level.
Magnetic quantum number, mₗ
mₗ sets orientation in space.
Spin quantum number, mₛ
mₛ describes electron spin, not orbital shape.
questions.x: The azimuthal (angular momentum) quantum number l sets orbital shape: l = 0, 1, 2, 3 correspond to s, p, d and f. The principal number n sets size and energy, mₗ sets orientation in space, and mₛ is electron spin. Confusing n with shape is common because higher shells contain more shapes, but n alone does not set one.

questions.q: Which set of quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) is allowed for an electron?
o: l must be less than n, so l = 2 is not allowed when n = 2.
Correct: l < n, |mₗ| ≤ l, and mₛ = ±½ are all satisfied.
|mₗ| cannot exceed l = 1.
mₛ must be +½ or −½.
questions.x: The rules are l from 0 to n − 1, mₗ from −l to +l, and mₛ = +½ or −½. The set (2, 1, −1, +½) satisfies all three. The others fail one rule each: l = n is not allowed, |mₗ| cannot exceed l, and mₛ cannot be 0.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy the n = 3 shell?
o: Counts only 3s and 3p, ignoring 3d.
That is the number of orbitals (n²), not electrons.
Correct: 2n² = 18 (3s², 3p⁶, 3d¹⁰).
That is the capacity of n = 4.
questions.x: Shell n contains n² orbitals, each holding 2 electrons, for a capacity of 2n². For n = 3 that is 18 electrons: 3s² + 3p⁶ + 3d¹⁰. The count of 8 comes from the octet idea, which reflects how period 3 elements fill before 4s, not the shell's true capacity.

questions.q: How many orbitals make up a subshell with l = 3?
o: Equals l, but the count is 2l + 1.
That is a d subshell (l = 2).
That is the number of electrons an f subshell holds.
Correct: 2l + 1 = 7 orbitals in an f subshell.
questions.x: A subshell with azimuthal number l has 2l + 1 orbitals, one for each mₗ from −l to +l. For l = 3 (an f subshell), that is 7 orbitals holding up to 14 electrons. Answering 14 counts electrons instead of orbitals.

questions.q: How many electrons in an atom can have both n = 4 and mₗ = −1?
o: Correct: l = 1, 2, 3 each have one mₗ = −1 orbital; 3 orbitals × 2 = 6.
Counts only one orbital.
Includes l = 0, which has only mₗ = 0.
Confuses this with the capacity of a d subshell.
questions.x: For n = 4, l can be 0, 1, 2 or 3, and mₗ = −1 exists only when l ≥ 1. That gives three orbitals (4p, 4d and 4f each have one mₗ = −1 orbital), and each holds 2 electrons of opposite spin, for 6 total. Including l = 0 is the trap, since s orbitals have only mₗ = 0.

questions.q: Which subshell does not exist?
o: 1s
n = 1 allows l = 0, which is 1s.
2d
Correct: d requires l = 2, but l must be less than n = 2.
3p
n = 3 allows l = 0, 1, 2, so 3p exists.
4f
n = 4 allows l up to 3, so 4f exists.
questions.x: The azimuthal number l ranges from 0 to n − 1, so the n = 2 shell allows only l = 0 (2s) and l = 1 (2p). A d subshell needs l = 2, so 3d is the first that exists. Likewise, p first appears at n = 2 and f at n = 4.

questions.q: How many radial nodes does a 3p orbital have?
o: A 2p orbital has zero radial nodes, not 3p.
That is the total number of nodes (n − 1), including the angular one.
Correct: radial nodes = n − l − 1 = 3 − 1 − 1 = 1.
Uses n alone.
questions.note: Angular nodes = l; total nodes = n − 1.
questions.x: An orbital has n − 1 total nodes, of which l are angular and n − l − 1 are radial. For 3p (n = 3, l = 1), there are 2 total nodes: 1 angular (the nodal plane) and 1 radial. Answering 2 counts the angular node as radial.

questions.q: What is the ground-state electron configuration of sulfur (Z = 16)?
o: [Ne]3s²3p²
Accounts for only 14 electrons.
[Ne]3s¹3p⁵
3s fills completely before 3p.
[Ne]3p⁶
Skips the lower-energy 3s subshell.
[Ne]3s²3p⁴
Correct: 10 core electrons plus 6 valence electrons.
questions.x: Sulfur has 16 electrons: 10 in the neon core plus 6 valence electrons. By the Aufbau principle, 3s fills (2 electrons) before 3p receives the remaining 4, giving [Ne]3s²3p⁴. Sulfur sits in group 16, consistent with 6 valence electrons and two unpaired 3p electrons.

questions.q: What is the ground-state electron configuration of chromium (Z = 24)?
o: [Ar]4s¹3d⁵
Correct: two half-filled subshells are lower in energy than 4s²3d⁴.
[Ar]4s²3d⁴
That is the simple Aufbau prediction, but Cr is an exception.
[Ar]3d⁶
Moves both 4s electrons into 3d.
[Ar]4s²4p⁴
3d fills before 4p.
questions.x: Chromium is a classic Aufbau exception: [Ar]4s¹3d⁵ is lower in energy than the predicted 4s²3d⁴. Moving one 4s electron into 3d gives two half-filled subshells, reducing electron–electron repulsion and maximizing exchange stabilization. Copper shows the same pattern with a filled 3d¹⁰.

questions.q: What is the ground-state electron configuration of Cu⁺?
o: [Ar]4s²3d⁸
Ignores both copper's exception and the 4s-first removal rule.
[Ar]3d¹⁰
Correct: Cu is [Ar]4s¹3d¹⁰, and the 4s electron is removed first.
[Ar]4s¹3d⁹
Removes a 3d electron instead of the 4s electron.
[Ar]4s²3d⁹
That is the Aufbau-predicted configuration of neutral Cu, with no electron removed.
questions.x: Neutral copper is an exception, [Ar]4s¹3d¹⁰, because a filled d subshell is especially stable. When transition metals ionize, the 4s electrons leave before 3d, so Cu⁺ loses its single 4s electron to give [Ar]3d¹⁰. Removing from 3d instead is the common error, since 4s fills first but also empties first.

questions.q: How many unpaired electrons does a ground-state Mn²⁺ ion have?
o: Removes electrons from 3d rather than 4s.
Pairs d electrons in violation of Hund's rule.
Correct: Mn²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵, with one electron in each of five d orbitals.
Counts all valence electrons of neutral Mn.
questions.x: Neutral Mn is [Ar]4s²3d⁵, and transition-metal cations lose 4s electrons first, so Mn²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵. By Hund's rule the five d electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins, giving 5 unpaired electrons. Removing electrons from 3d instead would leave 3d³ and only 3 unpaired.

questions.q: Which element has the ground-state configuration [Kr]5s²4d¹⁰5p³?
o: Bi
Bismuth is the period 6 analog, [Xe]6s²4f¹⁴5d¹⁰6p³.
As
Arsenic is in period 4, [Ar]4s²3d¹⁰4p³.
In
Indium has 5p¹.
Sb
Correct: period 5, three p electrons, group 15 is antimony.
questions.x: Read the configuration as a map of the periodic table: the 5s/5p valence shell places the element in period 5, and p³ places it in group 15. That element is antimony (Sb, Z = 51). Arsenic and bismuth share the ns²np³ valence pattern but sit in periods 4 and 6, so the principal quantum number is what distinguishes them.

questions.q: Which neutral atom is diamagnetic in its ground state?
o: Fe
Fe ([Ar]4s²3d⁶) has four unpaired d electrons.
O
O (2p⁴) has two unpaired electrons.
Zn
Correct: [Ar]4s²3d¹⁰ has every electron paired.
N
N (2p³) has three unpaired electrons.
questions.x: A diamagnetic atom has every electron paired. Zinc, [Ar]4s²3d¹⁰, has completely filled 4s and 3d subshells, so it has no unpaired electrons. Fe (four unpaired 3d electrons), O (two) and N (three) all have partly filled subshells where Hund's rule leaves unpaired spins, making them paramagnetic.

questions.q: Which statement expresses Hund's rule?
o: No two electrons can share all four quantum numbers
That is the Pauli exclusion principle.
Electrons fill the lowest-energy subshells first
That is the Aufbau principle.
Position and momentum cannot both be known exactly
That is the Heisenberg uncertainty principle.
Degenerate orbitals each get one electron, same spin, before pairing
Correct: this minimizes repulsion and maximizes unpaired spins.
questions.x: Hund's rule says electrons entering a set of degenerate orbitals occupy them singly with parallel spins before any pairing. This lowers energy by reducing electron–electron repulsion and maximizing spin multiplicity. It is often confused with the Pauli principle, which limits each orbital to two electrons of opposite spin.

questions.q: An orbital diagram places two electrons with the same spin in one 2p orbital. Which principle does it violate?
o: Pauli exclusion principle
Correct: both electrons would have identical n, l, mₗ and mₛ.
Hund's rule
Hund's rule governs filling across orbitals, not spins within one orbital.
Aufbau principle
Aufbau concerns the order of subshell filling.
Heisenberg uncertainty principle
That concerns measurement limits, not orbital occupancy.
questions.x: The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in an atom can share all four quantum numbers. Two electrons in the same orbital already share n, l and mₗ, so they must have opposite spins. Hund's rule is about spreading electrons across degenerate orbitals, not about spins within one orbital.

questions.q: A student draws carbon's ground state with both 2p electrons paired in a single 2p orbital. Which rule is broken?
o: Pauli exclusion principle
Paired electrons with opposite spins satisfy Pauli.
Hund's rule
Correct: the electrons should occupy separate 2p orbitals with parallel spins.
Aufbau principle
1s, 2s and 2p are still filled in the right order.
Octet rule
The octet rule describes bonding, not orbital filling.
questions.x: Carbon's two 2p electrons should occupy separate 2p orbitals with parallel spins, as Hund's rule requires. Pairing them in one orbital with opposite spins is allowed by Pauli but is higher in energy because of added repulsion. The subshell order 1s, 2s, 2p is still correct, so the Aufbau principle is not violated.

questions.q: Which electron configuration represents an excited state of a neutral sodium atom?
o: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s¹
This is the ground state of sodium.
1s²2s²2p⁶
This is Na⁺, with only 10 electrons.
1s²2s²2p⁶3p¹
Correct: 11 electrons, with the valence electron promoted from 3s to 3p.
1s²2s²2p⁷3s⁰
A p subshell cannot hold more than 6 electrons.
questions.x: An excited state has the correct number of electrons but at least one in a higher subshell than the ground state places it. Neutral sodium has 11 electrons; moving its 3s electron to 3p gives 1s²2s²2p⁶3p¹. Configurations with 10 electrons describe Na⁺, and any p subshell holding more than 6 electrons is impossible.

questions.q: Which period 4 main-group element has three unpaired electrons in its ground state?
o: Ga
4p¹ has one unpaired electron.
Ge
4p² has two unpaired electrons.
Se
4p⁴ has two unpaired electrons.
As
Correct: 4p³ places one electron in each 4p orbital.
questions.x: Main-group elements in period 4 after the 3d block fill 4p. By Hund's rule, 4p¹ (Ga) has 1 unpaired electron, 4p² (Ge) has 2, 4p³ (As) has 3 and 4p⁴ (Se) has 2. Group 15 elements like arsenic have a half-filled p subshell, the maximum number of unpaired p electrons.

questions.q: How many electrons in a ground-state chlorine atom have l = 1?
o: Counts only the 3p electrons.
Correct: l = 1 means p electrons: 2p⁶ + 3p⁵ = 11.
Counts only the 2p electrons.
That is every electron in the atom.
questions.x: l = 1 identifies p orbitals, so count every p electron. Chlorine is 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁵, giving 6 (2p) + 5 (3p) = 11 electrons with l = 1. Counting only the valence 3p electrons (5) forgets the filled 2p subshell in the core.

questions.q: The highest-energy electron in a ground-state gallium atom (Z = 31) occupies which subshell?
o: 4s
4s is filled before 3d and 4p.
3d
3d is complete (3d¹⁰) before Ga's last electron.
4p
Correct: Ga is [Ar]4s²3d¹⁰4p¹.
5s
5s fills only after 4p is complete.
questions.x: Gallium (Z = 31) is [Ar]4s²3d¹⁰4p¹: after argon's 18 electrons, 4s takes 2, 3d takes 10, and the 31st electron enters 4p. Ga is the first p-block element of period 4, which places its highest-energy electron in 4p. 3d is already full, and 5s fills only after 4p is complete.

questions.q: In a hydrogen atom, the 2s and 2p orbitals have equal energy, but in lithium the 2s is lower. Why?
o: Lithium has more neutrons
Neutrons do not affect orbital energies.
The 2p orbitals in lithium hold more electrons
In ground-state Li the 2p orbitals are empty.
Lithium's nucleus is smaller
Lithium's nucleus is larger and its orbitals are not distorted by nuclear size.
2s penetrates the core, so it is shielded less than 2p
Correct: 2s density near the nucleus raises its Zeff in multi-electron atoms.
questions.x: In hydrogen, with one electron, orbital energy depends only on n. In multi-electron atoms, a 2s electron has some probability density close to the nucleus, inside the 1s core, so it is shielded less and feels a higher effective nuclear charge than a 2p electron. That penetration lowers the 2s energy, producing the familiar s < p < d ordering within a shell.

questions.q: The photoelectron spectrum of a neutral sodium atom shows how many peaks?
o: Correct: one peak per occupied subshell: 1s, 2s, 2p and 3s.
Counts shells rather than subshells.
Peaks correspond to subshells, not individual electrons.
PES detects core electrons too, not only the valence electron.
questions.note: Peak height is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell.
questions.x: Photoelectron spectroscopy shows one peak for each occupied subshell, at that subshell's binding energy. Sodium, 1s²2s²2p⁶3s¹, has four occupied subshells, so it gives four peaks, with heights of 2:2:6:1 reflecting electron counts. Counting shells (3) misses that 2s and 2p have different energies.

questions.q: A sample is pulled into a strong magnetic field. What does this indicate about its atoms or ions?
o: They have only paired electrons
Fully paired electrons give diamagnetism, a weak repulsion.
They have unpaired electrons
Correct: unpaired spins make a substance paramagnetic.
Their nuclei are radioactive
Magnetic attraction reflects electrons, not decay.
They carry a net positive charge
A static magnetic field does not attract stationary charges.
questions.x: Paramagnetic substances, which have unpaired electrons, are drawn into a magnetic field because their unpaired spins align with it. Species with all electrons paired are diamagnetic and are weakly repelled. Charge and radioactivity do not cause attraction to a static magnetic field.

questions.q: Iron forms Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺. Why is Fe³⁺ often especially stable?
o: It has a noble gas configuration
Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵, not [Ar].
It retains both 4s electrons
Both 4s electrons are lost first, in both ions.
It has a half-filled 3d subshell
Correct: [Ar]3d⁵ has five unpaired electrons and extra exchange stability.
It has a filled 3d subshell
A filled 3d subshell would be 3d¹⁰.
questions.x: Iron is [Ar]4s²3d⁶. Losing the two 4s electrons gives Fe²⁺ ([Ar]3d⁶), and losing one more 3d electron gives Fe³⁺ ([Ar]3d⁵). A half-filled d subshell has one electron in each orbital, minimizing repulsion and maximizing exchange energy, which is why Fe³⁺ is so stable. It is not a noble gas configuration.

questions.q: Which atom has the largest atomic radius?
o: Sr
Same period as Rb but one more proton pulls electrons closer.
I
Far right in period 5, so high Zeff makes it small.
Xe
Noble gases at the end of a period are small.
Rb
Correct: leftmost in period 5, with the lowest Zeff of the four.
questions.x: Atomic radius grows down a group and shrinks left to right across a period as effective nuclear charge increases. Rb, Sr, I and Xe are all in period 5, so the leftmost, Rb in group 1, has the lowest Zeff and the largest radius. Xe being a 'big' heavy atom is a trap; noble gases are among the smallest atoms in their period.

questions.q: Which ion in the isoelectronic series O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺ has the largest radius?
o: O²⁻
Correct: with the fewest protons (8) for 10 electrons, it is held least tightly.
F⁻
F⁻ has one more proton than O²⁻, so it is smaller.
Na⁺
Na⁺ has 11 protons pulling on 10 electrons.
Mg²⁺
Mg²⁺ has the most protons and is the smallest.
questions.x: In an isoelectronic series all species have the same number of electrons (10 here), so size depends on nuclear charge. O²⁻ has only 8 protons pulling on those 10 electrons, so it is held least tightly and is the largest. Radius then shrinks steadily through F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ as protons are added.

questions.q: Why is Na⁺ much smaller than a neutral Na atom?
o: Na⁺ has fewer protons
Ionization removes electrons, not protons.
Na⁺ has lost its entire n = 3 shell
Correct: its outermost electrons are now in n = 2, much closer to the nucleus.
Na⁺ gains neutrons when ionized
Ionization does not change the nucleus.
The remaining electrons repel each other more
Less repulsion, not more, would follow from removing an electron.
questions.x: Neutral sodium, [Ne]3s¹, has a lone valence electron in n = 3. Removing it leaves Na⁺ with the [Ne] configuration, whose outermost electrons are in n = 2, much closer to the nucleus, while 11 protons now pull on just 10 electrons. Ionization never changes the number of protons or neutrons.

questions.q: Nitrogen has a higher first ionization energy than oxygen. Why?
o: Nitrogen has more protons
Oxygen has more protons (8 vs 7).
Oxygen's valence electrons are in a higher shell
Both have valence electrons in n = 2.
Oxygen's paired 2p electron feels extra repulsion
Correct: the 2p⁴ pair is easier to remove than an electron from half-filled 2p³.
Nitrogen's atomic radius is smaller
N is slightly larger than O.
questions.x: Ionization energy generally rises across a period, but oxygen is an exception. Nitrogen's 2p³ has one electron in each p orbital, while oxygen's fourth 2p electron must pair, and the extra repulsion makes it easier to remove. Oxygen actually has more protons, which by itself would raise its IE.

questions.q: Boron has a lower first ionization energy than beryllium. Why?
o: Boron has fewer protons
Boron has 5 protons; beryllium has 4.
Boron has a half-filled subshell
Boron's 2p¹ is not half-filled.
Beryllium's electrons are paired and repel each other
Pairing repulsion would lower Be's IE, not raise it.
Boron's 2p electron is higher in energy and shielded by 2s
Correct: removing a 2p electron is easier than removing a 2s electron.
questions.x: Beryllium's first electron comes from 2s, while boron's comes from 2p. A 2p electron is higher in energy and partly shielded by the 2s pair, so it is easier to remove despite boron's extra proton. This dip, like the N to O dip, shows subshell structure in ionization trends.
