questions.q: An element has successive ionization energies of 738, 1451 and 7733 kJ/mol. To which group does it most likely belong?
o: Group 2
Correct: the huge jump after the 2nd electron means two valence electrons.
Group 1
Group 1 would show the big jump after the 1st electron.
Group 13
Group 13 would show the big jump after the 3rd electron.
Group 17
Halogens have high first IEs and no early large jump.
questions.note: The big jump marks the start of the core electrons.
questions.x: Successive ionization energies rise gradually until the first core electron is removed, where there is a huge jump. Here IE₃ is over five times IE₂, so the element has two valence electrons and belongs to group 2 (these are magnesium's values). Group 1 would show the jump between IE₁ and IE₂.

questions.q: Which atom has the largest second ionization energy?
o: Mg
Mg's 2nd electron is still a 3s valence electron.
Na
Correct: Na's 2nd electron comes from the stable [Ne] core.
Al
Al's 2nd electron is a 3s valence electron.
Si
Si's 2nd electron is a 3p valence electron.
questions.x: The second ionization energy is largest when the second electron must come from a noble gas core. Sodium, [Ne]3s¹, loses its 3s electron first, so its second electron comes from the tightly held 2p core. Mg, Al and Si still have valence electrons to remove for IE₂, so their values are much lower.

questions.q: Which pair of elements would form a bond with the greatest electronegativity difference?
o: C and O
Both are nonmetals in period 2; the difference is about 1.
H and Cl
A polar bond, but the difference is only about 1.
K and F
Correct: K is among the least electronegative and F is the most.
N and Cl
Their electronegativities are nearly equal.
questions.x: Electronegativity rises toward the upper right of the periodic table (excluding noble gases) and is lowest at the lower left. Potassium is near the low end (about 0.8) and fluorine is the highest (about 4.0), giving a difference above 3 and a strongly ionic bond. The other pairs are all nonmetals with differences of about 1 or less.

questions.q: Which element releases the most energy when a gaseous atom gains an electron?
o: F
Fluorine's small 2p shell crowds the added electron, so its EA is less than Cl's.
Br
Br is larger, so the added electron is held less strongly than in Cl.
O
Gaining one electron releases less energy for O than for halogens.
Cl
Correct: Cl has the most negative electron affinity of all elements.
questions.note: Trap: fluorine is the most electronegative but not the highest EA.
questions.x: Electron affinity generally becomes more exothermic toward the halogens, but chlorine, not fluorine, has the most negative value of any element. Fluorine's small 2p shell is crowded, so an added electron feels strong repulsion. Br is larger than Cl and holds the added electron less tightly, and O gains less energy by adding one electron.

questions.q: Adding an electron to which gaseous atom is energetically unfavorable (endothermic)?
o: Ne
Correct: the added electron must enter the much higher 3s subshell.
Cl
Cl releases a large amount of energy when completing its octet.
O
O's first electron affinity is exothermic.
C
C's electron affinity is exothermic.
questions.x: Neon's valence shell is full (2s²2p⁶), so an added electron would have to enter the much higher-energy 3s subshell, far from the nucleus and well shielded. That makes the process endothermic. Chlorine, oxygen and carbon all have room in their valence p subshells and release energy on gaining an electron.

questions.q: Atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period. What best explains this?
o: Electrons are added to higher shells
Electrons are added to the same shell across a period.
Effective nuclear charge increases
Correct: protons are added while shielding barely changes, pulling electrons inward.
Neutrons attract electrons more strongly
Neutrons have no charge.
Electron–electron repulsion increases
More repulsion would expand, not shrink, the atom.
questions.x: Across a period, each element adds one proton, while the added electron goes into the same shell and shields poorly. Effective nuclear charge on the valence electrons rises, pulling them closer and shrinking the atom. The added electron–electron repulsion is real but much smaller than the growing nuclear pull.

questions.q: Atomic radius increases down a group even though nuclear charge increases. Why?
o: Electrons are less negative in larger atoms
Every electron has the same charge.
Effective nuclear charge falls sharply down a group
Zeff on valence electrons stays roughly constant down a group.
Valence electrons occupy shells with higher n
Correct: each added shell is farther from the nucleus and shielded by inner shells.
Heavier nuclei have weaker attraction for electrons
More protons increase attraction; distance and shielding win out.
questions.x: Moving down a group, each element's valence electrons occupy a shell with a higher principal quantum number, farther from the nucleus. Inner shells shield most of the added nuclear charge, so effective nuclear charge on valence electrons stays roughly constant. Distance therefore wins, and the radius increases.

questions.q: Using Zeff ≈ Z − (number of core electrons), what is the approximate effective nuclear charge felt by a valence electron in chlorine?
o: Ignores shielding by the 10 core electrons.
That is the number of core electrons, not Zeff.
Subtracts all 16 other electrons.
Correct: 17 protons − 10 core electrons = +7.
questions.x: A simple estimate is Zeff ≈ Z − (core electrons), since core electrons shield valence electrons almost fully. Chlorine has Z = 17 and 10 core electrons (1s²2s²2p⁶), so Zeff ≈ +7, matching its 7 valence electrons. Subtracting all other electrons (giving +1) wrongly treats same-shell electrons as fully shielding.

questions.q: Zirconium (period 5) and hafnium (period 6) have almost the same atomic radius. What explains this?
o: Lanthanide contraction from poorly shielding 4f electrons
Correct: 14 protons added with weakly shielding 4f electrons offset the new shell.
Hafnium has fewer protons than zirconium
Hafnium (Z = 72) has far more protons than Zr (Z = 40).
Both lack d electrons
Both are d-block metals with d electrons.
Relativistic expansion of hafnium's 6s orbital
Relativity contracts, not expands, heavy-atom s orbitals, and is not the main cause here.
questions.x: Between Zr and Hf, the 4f subshell fills with 14 electrons across the lanthanides. f electrons shield poorly, so the 14 added protons raise effective nuclear charge and contract the atom, offsetting the size gain from the new shell. This lanthanide contraction makes Hf almost the same size as Zr, which is why they are hard to separate chemically.

questions.q: Which species in the isoelectronic set Ne, Na⁺, F⁻, O²⁻ has the highest first ionization energy?
o: Ne
Ne has fewer protons (10) than Na⁺ (11) for the same 10 electrons.
F⁻
Anions hold their extra electrons loosely.
Na⁺
Correct: the most protons pulling on 10 electrons makes removal hardest.
O²⁻
O²⁻ has the fewest protons and the lowest IE.
questions.x: All four species have 10 electrons in the neon configuration, so the one with the most protons holds its electrons most tightly. Na⁺ has 11 protons, more than Ne (10), F⁻ (9) or O²⁻ (8), so removing an electron from it is hardest. Neon being the 'stable noble gas' is the tempting trap.

questions.q: Which lists the iron species in order of increasing radius?
o: Fe < Fe²⁺ < Fe³⁺
Reverses the order; removing electrons shrinks an atom.
Fe²⁺ < Fe³⁺ < Fe
Fe³⁺ has fewer electrons than Fe²⁺, so it is smaller.
Fe³⁺ < Fe < Fe²⁺
Fe²⁺ has fewer electrons than Fe and so is smaller.
Fe³⁺ < Fe²⁺ < Fe
Correct: fewer electrons for the same 26 protons means a smaller species.
questions.x: All three iron species have 26 protons, so the one with fewer electrons is smaller: fewer electrons means less repulsion and a stronger pull per electron. Fe³⁺ (23 electrons) is smaller than Fe²⁺ (24), which is smaller than neutral Fe (26), which also loses its 4s shell when ionized. Cations are always smaller than their parent atoms.

questions.q: Which property describes an atom's tendency to attract shared electrons in a covalent bond?
o: Electronegativity
Correct: it measures pull on bonding electrons, not isolated-atom energies.
Ionization energy
That is the energy to remove an electron from a gaseous atom.
Electron affinity
That is the energy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron.
Atomic radius
Radius is a size, though it correlates with electronegativity.
questions.x: Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom pulls on electrons shared in a covalent bond, a property of bonded atoms. Ionization energy and electron affinity are energy changes for isolated gaseous atoms losing or gaining an electron. They correlate with electronegativity but measure different things.

questions.q: Potassium metal is dropped into water. What are the products?
o: K₂O and H₂
The oxide reacts with water; the products in solution are hydroxide and H₂.
KOH and H₂
Correct: 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂.
KH and O₂
Water is reduced to H₂, not oxidized to O₂.
KOH and O₂
Potassium is oxidized, so water must be reduced, giving H₂.
questions.x: Alkali metals reduce water: 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂. Potassium is oxidized to K⁺, and water's hydrogen is reduced to H₂ gas, leaving hydroxide in solution. Oxygen gas cannot form, because that would require oxidizing water at the same time as the metal is oxidized.

questions.q: Cesium reacts with water far more violently than lithium. What best explains this?
o: Cesium has more valence electrons
All alkali metals have one valence electron.
Cesium has a higher electronegativity
Cesium has one of the lowest electronegativities.
Cesium's valence electron is farther from the nucleus and easier to remove
Correct: lower ionization energy makes Cs a stronger reducing agent.
Cesium has a higher electron affinity
The reaction depends on losing electrons, not gaining them.
questions.x: Alkali metal reactivity with water depends on how easily the single valence electron is lost. Down group 1, the valence electron is in a higher shell, farther from the nucleus and better shielded, so ionization energy falls and cesium reacts far more vigorously. Every alkali metal has one valence electron, so that count cannot explain the difference.

questions.q: Which reaction occurs spontaneously?
o: I₂ + 2KCl → 2KI + Cl₂
I₂ is a weaker oxidizer than Cl₂ and cannot oxidize Cl⁻.
Br₂ + 2KCl → 2KBr + Cl₂
Br₂ cannot oxidize Cl⁻, a halogen above it.
I₂ + 2KBr → 2KI + Br₂
I₂ cannot oxidize Br⁻.
Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂
Correct: halogen oxidizing strength falls down the group, so Cl₂ oxidizes Br⁻.
questions.x: Halogen oxidizing strength decreases down the group: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. A halogen can oxidize the halide ion of any halogen below it, so Cl₂ oxidizes Br⁻ to Br₂ while being reduced to Cl⁻. The reverse reactions, where a lower halogen tries to oxidize a higher one's halide, are not spontaneous.

questions.q: Why are noble gases so chemically unreactive?
o: They have filled valence shells
Correct: a full ns²np⁶ shell gives very high IE and no drive to gain electrons.
They have no electrons in p orbitals
All but helium have filled p subshells.
Their nuclei are especially stable
Nuclear stability does not govern chemical reactivity.
They are always gases at room temperature
Physical state is a result of weak forces, not the cause of inertness.
questions.x: Noble gases have filled valence shells (ns²np⁶, or 1s² for helium). They have very high ionization energies and gain nothing by accepting electrons, so they have little drive to form bonds. Being gases is a consequence of weak intermolecular forces, not the reason they are unreactive.

questions.q: What is the formula of the ionic compound formed between calcium and nitrogen?
o: CaN
Charges of +2 and −3 do not balance 1:1.
Ca₃N₂
Correct: three Ca²⁺ (+6) balance two N³⁻ (−6).
Ca₂N₃
Gives +4 and −9; the subscripts are swapped.
CaN₂
Treats nitrogen as forming N⁻.
questions.x: Calcium (group 2) forms Ca²⁺ and nitrogen (group 15) forms N³⁻. The formula must be neutral, so the least common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6: three Ca²⁺ (+6) balance two N³⁻ (−6), giving Ca₃N₂. Swapping the subscripts gives Ca₂N₃, which carries a net charge of −5.

questions.q: Which aqueous ion is most likely to give a colorless solution?
o: Cu²⁺
Cu²⁺ (3d⁹) has a partly filled d subshell and is blue.
Ni²⁺
Ni²⁺ (3d⁸) allows d–d transitions and is green.
Zn²⁺
Correct: Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so no d–d transitions absorb visible light.
Fe³⁺
Fe³⁺ (3d⁵) solutions are typically yellow to brown.
questions.x: Transition-metal ion color usually comes from d–d transitions, in which a d electron absorbs visible light and moves between split d orbitals. Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so every d orbital is full and no d–d transition is possible, leaving the solution colorless. Cu²⁺ (3d⁹), Ni²⁺ (3d⁸) and Fe³⁺ (3d⁵) have partly filled d subshells and are colored.

questions.q: Which oxide dissolves in water to form a basic solution?
o: Na₂O
Correct: metal oxides form hydroxides, Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH.
SO₃
Nonmetal oxide; it forms H₂SO₄.
CO₂
Nonmetal oxide; it forms carbonic acid.
P₄O₁₀
Nonmetal oxide; it forms phosphoric acid.
questions.x: Metal oxides are basic: Na₂O reacts with water to form NaOH, raising the pH. Nonmetal oxides such as SO₃, CO₂ and P₄O₁₀ are acidic anhydrides, forming H₂SO₄, H₂CO₃ and H₃PO₄. The key distinction is metal versus nonmetal, not how many oxygen atoms the oxide has.

questions.q: In sodium hydride (NaH), what is the oxidation state of hydrogen?
o: Hydrogen is +1 with more electronegative partners, not with Na.
Correct: Na is less electronegative, so hydrogen gains an electron as hydride, H⁻.
H is bonded, not elemental.
Hydrogen has only one electron to lose.
questions.x: In metal hydrides, hydrogen is more electronegative than the metal partner, so it takes the electron and becomes hydride, H⁻. In NaH, sodium is +1 and hydrogen is −1. The usual +1 for hydrogen applies only when it is bonded to more electronegative atoms, such as in H₂O or HCl.

questions.q: Element X readily forms X²⁻ ions. In which group is X most likely found?
o: Group 2
Group 2 elements form 2+ ions.
Group 14
Group 14 elements rarely form simple 2− ions.
Group 16
Correct: ns²np⁴ gains two electrons to complete an octet.
Group 17
Halogens form 1− ions.
questions.x: Group 16 elements have ns²np⁴ valence configurations, two electrons short of a noble gas octet, so they readily gain two electrons to form 2− ions such as O²⁻ and S²⁻. Group 17 gains one electron to form 1− ions, and group 2 loses two to form 2+ ions. Group 14 elements typically share electrons rather than forming simple anions.

questions.q: Which halogen is a liquid at room temperature?
o: Fluorine
F₂ is a gas.
Chlorine
Cl₂ is a gas.
Iodine
I₂ is a solid.
Bromine
Correct: dispersion forces grow with size, making Br₂ a liquid.
questions.x: Halogens are nonpolar diatomic molecules held together only by London dispersion forces, which grow with molecular size and polarizability. Moving down the group, fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid at room temperature. Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature, along with mercury.

questions.q: Xenon forms compounds such as XeF₄, but neon forms none. What best explains the difference?
o: Xenon's valence electrons are farther out and have a lower ionization energy
Correct: Xe's outer electrons are easier to share with a very electronegative atom like F.
Xenon has unpaired electrons in its ground state
Xenon's ground state has all electrons paired.
Neon is radioactive
Neon's common isotopes are stable.
Neon has a higher electron affinity
Noble gases have unfavorable electron affinities, and bonding to F requires Xe to share electrons, not gain them.
questions.x: Xenon's valence electrons are in n = 5, far from the nucleus and well shielded, so its ionization energy is low enough for it to share electrons with very electronegative atoms like fluorine. Neon's n = 2 electrons are held extremely tightly. Ground-state xenon has all electrons paired, so bonding is not due to unpaired electrons.

questions.q: Transition metals often show several oxidation states, unlike alkali metals. Why?
o: They have more protons
Proton count alone does not create multiple oxidation states.
Their ns and (n−1)d electrons are close in energy
Correct: varying numbers of s and d electrons can be lost.
They have filled p subshells
Many main-group elements do too, without multiple states.
They are always paramagnetic
Some transition metal species are diamagnetic, and magnetism is unrelated.
questions.x: In transition metals, the ns and (n−1)d orbitals are close in energy, so different numbers of electrons can be removed at similar cost, giving several stable oxidation states (for example Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺). Alkali metals have one valence electron above a noble-gas core, so removing a second electron is far too costly. Proton count and magnetism do not explain this.

questions.q: An unknown solid is shiny, conducts electricity, reacts with water to release H₂, and has a first IE far below its second. Which element fits best?
o: Mg
Mg's first and second IEs are close; the jump is after the second.
Al
Al shows its big jump after the third electron.
Sr
Sr would show its big jump after the second electron.
Na
Correct: a single valence electron gives a large jump after IE1.
questions.x: All four metals are shiny conductors, so the decisive clue is ionization energy. A first IE far below the second means the atom has just one valence electron, and the second must come from a noble-gas core, as in a group 1 metal like sodium, which also reacts with water to release H₂. Group 2 metals (Mg, Sr) show their large jump after IE₂, and Al after IE₃.

questions.q: Water (molar mass 18) boils at 100 °C, while H₂S (molar mass 34) boils near −60 °C. What best explains the difference?
o: Stronger London dispersion forces in water
H₂S has more electrons, so its dispersion forces are larger, not smaller.
Extensive hydrogen bonding between water molecules
Correct: O–H···O hydrogen bonds require far more energy to break than the weak dipole forces in H₂S.
Stronger covalent O–H bonds within each molecule
Boiling breaks intermolecular attractions, not intramolecular covalent bonds.
Water's lower molar mass
Lower mass alone would predict a lower boiling point, the opposite of what is observed.
questions.note: Boiling point reflects intermolecular forces, not bond strength inside the molecule.
questions.x: Boiling point measures how hard it is to pull molecules apart from each other, so it reflects intermolecular forces. Water's O–H bonds are highly polar and oxygen is small and electronegative, so each molecule can hydrogen bond to several neighbors. Sulfur is less electronegative and larger, so H₂S has only weak dipole and dispersion forces. Dispersion actually favors H₂S (more electrons), so it cannot explain water's higher boiling point.

questions.q: Why does ice float on liquid water?
o: Ice contains trapped air bubbles that lower its density
Pure, bubble-free ice still floats; the effect is structural.
Water molecules in ice have fewer hydrogen bonds than in the liquid
Ice has more, and more ordered, hydrogen bonds per molecule than liquid water.
Hydrogen bonds lock ice into an open hexagonal lattice that is less dense
Correct: the rigid H-bonded lattice spaces molecules farther apart than in the liquid.
Ice has a higher molar mass than liquid water
Molar mass of H₂O is the same in both phases.
questions.x: In ice, each water molecule hydrogen bonds to four neighbors in a fixed tetrahedral arrangement, building an open hexagonal lattice with a lot of empty space. When ice melts, some hydrogen bonds break and molecules pack more closely, so the liquid is denser. The tempting idea that ice has fewer hydrogen bonds is backwards: it has more, and their rigid geometry is exactly what lowers the density.

questions.q: Coastal cities have milder temperature swings than inland cities. Which property of water is most responsible?
o: Its high surface tension
Surface tension affects droplets and capillarity, not heat storage.
Its low viscosity
Viscosity relates to flow, not to how much heat is stored per degree.
Its maximum density at 4 °C
This explains lake stratification, not daily temperature buffering.
Its high specific heat capacity
Correct: water absorbs or releases much heat with little temperature change, buffering the climate.
questions.x: Specific heat is the energy needed to raise 1 g of a substance by 1 °C, and water's is unusually high (about 4.18 J/g·°C) because added energy must first disrupt hydrogen bonds. Large bodies of water therefore absorb heat by day and release it by night with small temperature changes, buffering nearby air. The 4 °C density maximum matters for lakes freezing from the top, not for moderating daily air temperature.

questions.q: When NaCl dissolves in water, how are the water molecules nearest a Na⁺ ion oriented?
o: Oxygen atoms point toward the Na⁺ ion
Correct: the partially negative oxygen is attracted to the cation (ion–dipole interaction).
Hydrogen atoms point toward the Na⁺ ion
Partially positive hydrogens would be repelled by a cation; they face anions like Cl⁻.
Water molecules form covalent bonds to Na⁺
Hydration is an ion–dipole attraction, not covalent bonding.
Orientation is random because Na⁺ is nonpolar
An ion carries full charge and strongly orders surrounding dipoles.
questions.x: Water is a polar molecule: oxygen carries a partial negative charge and the hydrogens partial positive charges. Around a cation, water molecules turn their oxygen ends inward, forming a hydration shell held by ion–dipole attraction. Around an anion like Cl⁻ the orientation flips and the hydrogens point inward. These are electrostatic attractions, not covalent bonds.

questions.q: Which substance is most soluble in hexane?
o: Sodium chloride
Ionic lattices need polar solvents to stabilize separated ions.
Octane
Correct: nonpolar octane mixes with nonpolar hexane through dispersion forces (like dissolves like).
Glucose
Glucose's many –OH groups make it highly polar and water-soluble, not hexane-soluble.
Potassium nitrate
An ionic salt cannot be solvated by a nonpolar solvent.
questions.x: Solubility follows 'like dissolves like': a solute dissolves well when the solute–solvent attractions resemble those it gives up. Hexane is nonpolar and interacts only through London dispersion forces, so another alkane like octane mixes freely. Ionic salts and polar glucose depend on strong ion–dipole or hydrogen-bond interactions that hexane cannot provide, so they stay undissolved.

questions.q: Dissolving NH₄NO₃ in water makes the beaker feel cold, yet the salt dissolves spontaneously. What drives the dissolution?
o: A negative enthalpy of solution
The beaker cools, so heat is absorbed and ΔH is positive.
A decrease in entropy as ions become hydrated
Ordering would oppose dissolution; the net entropy change must be positive here.
A large increase in entropy
Correct: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative because the positive TΔS term outweighs the positive ΔH.
Release of heat from forming ion–dipole bonds
Net heat is absorbed, so lattice breaking costs more than hydration releases.
questions.note: Endothermic but spontaneous means entropy-driven.
questions.x: Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not on ΔH alone. Here the cold beaker shows ΔH > 0, so dissolution can only be spontaneous if ΔS is large and positive, making TΔS bigger than ΔH. Breaking up the ordered crystal into freely moving hydrated ions provides that entropy gain. Any answer claiming the process releases heat contradicts the observed cooling.

questions.q: In the stepwise model of dissolution, which step is exothermic?
o: Separating solute particles from one another
Breaking solute–solute attractions requires energy.
Separating solvent molecules to make cavities
Breaking solvent–solvent attractions requires energy.
Breaking the crystal lattice of an ionic solute
Overcoming lattice energy is endothermic.
Solute particles interacting with solvent particles
Correct: forming new solute–solvent attractions releases energy.
questions.x: Dissolution can be split into three steps: separating solute particles, separating solvent particles to make room, and letting solute and solvent attract each other. The first two break attractions and always cost energy; only the third forms new attractions and releases energy. The overall ΔH of solution is the sum, so its sign depends on whether step three outweighs the first two.

questions.q: A fish kill occurs in a lake during an unusually hot summer. Which solution property best explains low dissolved O₂?
o: Gas solubility in water decreases as temperature rises
Correct: warmer water holds less dissolved gas, so O₂ levels fall.
Gas solubility in water increases as temperature rises
This reverses the trend; heating drives gases out of solution.
O₂ reacts with water at high temperature
O₂ does not chemically react with water under these conditions.
Warm water has a higher Henry's law solubility constant for O₂
A higher solubility constant would mean more O₂ dissolves, not less.
questions.x: Dissolving a gas in water is exothermic, so by Le Châtelier's principle raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the gas escaping. Warm water therefore holds less O₂ than cold water, which can suffocate fish. This is opposite to most solid solutes, whose solubility usually rises with temperature, a common source of confusion.

questions.q: At constant temperature, the partial pressure of O₂ above a water sample is tripled. According to Henry's law, the dissolved O₂ concentration will:
o: Stay the same
Henry's law says concentration tracks partial pressure.
Triple
Correct: dissolved gas concentration is directly proportional to its partial pressure (C = kP).
Increase by a factor of 9
The relationship is linear, not squared.
Decrease to one-third
Higher pressure pushes more gas into solution, not less.
questions.x: Henry's law states that the concentration of a dissolved gas is directly proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid: C = kP. Tripling P at constant temperature therefore triples C. The relationship is linear, so there is no squaring, and raising pressure always drives more gas into solution.

questions.q: Why is the hydration enthalpy of Li⁺ more negative than that of Cs⁺?
o: Li⁺ has a larger charge than Cs⁺
Both are +1 ions.
Cs⁺ forms hydrogen bonds with water
Metal cations do not donate hydrogen bonds; they interact by ion–dipole forces.
Li⁺ is smaller, giving it a higher charge density
Correct: same charge on a smaller ion attracts water dipoles more strongly.
Li⁺ is more polarizable than Cs⁺
Larger ions like Cs⁺ are more polarizable; this does not explain stronger hydration.
questions.x: Hydration enthalpy reflects how strongly an ion attracts the water dipoles around it, which depends on charge density (charge divided by size). Li⁺ and Cs⁺ have the same +1 charge, but Li⁺ is far smaller, so water molecules can approach its nucleus more closely and are held more tightly, releasing more energy. Polarizability rises with size, so it favors Cs⁺ and cannot explain the trend.

questions.q: Which statement describes an ideal solution?
o: ΔH of mixing is strongly negative
Strongly favorable mixing gives negative deviation from Raoult's law, not ideality.
The solute must be an ionic compound
Ideal behavior depends on similar intermolecular forces, not ionic character.
The vapor pressure is higher than Raoult's law predicts
That is positive deviation, a non-ideal case.
ΔH of mixing is zero and each component obeys Raoult's law
Correct: solute–solvent forces equal the pure-component forces, so no heat change.
questions.x: An ideal solution forms when the attractions between unlike molecules are the same as those between like molecules. Then mixing releases or absorbs no heat (ΔH mix = 0) and each component's vapor pressure equals its mole fraction times its pure vapor pressure (Raoult's law). Strongly exothermic mixing signals stronger A–B attractions, which lowers vapor pressure and is a negative deviation.

questions.q: Mixing liquids A and B gives a solution whose vapor pressure is higher than Raoult's law predicts. What is true of this mixture?
o: A–B attractions are weaker than A–A and B–B attractions, so mixing is endothermic
Correct: weaker cross attractions let molecules escape more easily and require heat to mix.
A–B attractions are stronger than A–A and B–B attractions
Stronger cross attractions would lower vapor pressure (negative deviation).
Mixing is exothermic
Exothermic mixing accompanies negative deviation, not positive.
The mixture behaves ideally
An ideal mixture follows Raoult's law exactly.
questions.note: Positive deviation: weaker A–B forces, ΔH(mix) > 0, higher vapor pressure.
questions.x: Raoult's law assumes A–B attractions match A–A and B–B attractions. If the cross attractions are weaker, molecules escape the liquid more easily, so the vapor pressure exceeds the prediction (positive deviation), and mixing must absorb heat because more is broken than formed. Stronger cross attractions do the opposite: lower vapor pressure and exothermic mixing.

questions.q: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 4.0 g of NaOH (molar mass 40 g/mol) in enough water to make 500 mL?
o: Divided grams by milliliters without converting to moles and liters.
This is the number of moles, not divided by the 0.5 L volume.
Correct: 0.10 mol ÷ 0.500 L = 0.20 M.
Decimal slip: 0.10 mol ÷ 0.500 L is 0.20, not 2.0.
questions.x: Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution. First convert mass to moles: 4.0 g ÷ 40 g/mol = 0.10 mol NaOH. Then divide by volume in liters: 0.10 mol ÷ 0.500 L = 0.20 M. The most common slip is stopping at moles or forgetting to convert mL to L.

questions.q: 50 mL of 6.0 M HCl is diluted with water to a final volume of 300 mL. What is the new concentration?
o: Used 600 mL as the final volume.
Correct: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ → (6.0)(50) = M₂(300), so M₂ = 1.0 M.
Treated 250 mL of added water as the final volume.
Multiplied the dilution factor instead of dividing; dilution lowers concentration.
questions.x: Dilution adds solvent but not solute, so moles stay constant and M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. Here 6.0 M × 50 mL = 300 mmol, spread through 300 mL total, giving 1.0 M. The key is to use the final total volume (300 mL), not the volume of water added (250 mL).

questions.q: What is the molality of a solution containing 117 g of NaCl (molar mass 58.5 g/mol) dissolved in 500 g of water?
o: Divided by 2 kg instead of 0.5 kg.
This is moles of solute, not divided by kilograms of solvent.
Correct: 2.0 mol NaCl ÷ 0.500 kg water = 4.0 mol/kg.
Counted both ions; molality of the formula unit is 4.0 m (particle molality would be 8).
questions.x: Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, not per liter of solution. 117 g ÷ 58.5 g/mol = 2.0 mol NaCl, and 500 g water = 0.500 kg, so m = 2.0 ÷ 0.500 = 4.0 mol/kg. Counting dissociated ions (8 m of particles) matters for colligative properties, but the molality of NaCl itself is 4.0 m.

questions.q: A researcher wants a concentration unit for freezing-point experiments that does not change as the solution is cooled. Which unit should be used?
o: Molality
Correct: molality uses kilograms of solvent, and mass does not change with temperature.
Molarity
Molarity uses volume, which contracts or expands with temperature.
Mass per volume (g/L)
This also depends on solution volume, which changes with temperature.
Normality
Normality is volume-based like molarity, so it varies with temperature.
questions.x: Liquids expand when warmed and contract when cooled, so any unit based on solution volume (molarity, normality, g/L) shifts slightly with temperature. Molality uses the mass of solvent, and mass does not change with temperature. That is why freezing-point depression and boiling-point elevation equations use molality.

questions.q: A solution contains 1.0 mol ethanol and 4.0 mol water. What is the mole fraction of ethanol?
o: Divided by moles of water only (1/4) rather than total moles.
This is the mole fraction of water.
Inverted ratio of water to ethanol; mole fractions cannot exceed 1.
questions.x: Mole fraction is the moles of one component divided by the total moles of all components. For ethanol, 1.0 ÷ (1.0 + 4.0) = 0.20, and water's mole fraction is 0.80; the two must sum to 1. Dividing by water's moles alone gives a mole ratio (0.25), not a mole fraction.

questions.q: A 1.0 L water sample (density 1.0 g/mL) contains 5.0 mg of dissolved lead. What is the lead concentration in parts per million?
o: Mixed up mg and g; 1 mg/L equals 1 ppm in dilute aqueous solution.
5.0 ppm
Correct: 5.0 mg per 1.0 × 10⁶ mg of solution = 5.0 ppm (1 mg/L ≈ 1 ppm in water).
50 ppm
Off by a factor of 10 in the unit conversion.
5000 ppm
That would be 5.0 g per liter, a thousand times too high.
questions.x: Parts per million is the mass of solute per million units of mass of solution. A liter of dilute aqueous solution weighs about 1.0 kg, which is 1.0 × 10⁶ mg, so 1 mg/L equals 1 ppm. Thus 5.0 mg in 1.0 L is 5.0 ppm. This shortcut works only when the solution's density is close to 1 g/mL.

questions.q: What is the normality of 0.50 M H₂SO₄ in a reaction where both protons are neutralized?
o: Divided by the number of protons instead of multiplying.
Normality equals molarity only for monoprotic acids.
Correct: each mole supplies 2 equivalents of H⁺, so N = 2 × 0.50 = 1.0.
Multiplied by 4; H₂SO₄ has only two acidic protons.
questions.x: Normality counts equivalents per liter, where an equivalent of acid is the amount that donates one mole of H⁺ in the reaction considered. When both protons of H₂SO₄ react, each mole provides 2 equivalents, so N = 2 × 0.50 M = 1.0 N. Normality is always molarity times the number of equivalents per formula unit, never molarity divided by it.

questions.q: 20 g of sucrose is dissolved in 80 g of water. What is the mass percent of sucrose?
o: Arithmetic slip; 20/100 is 20%.
Correct: 20 g ÷ (20 + 80) g total × 100 = 20%.
Divided by the mass of water only rather than total solution mass.
This is the mass percent of water.
questions.x: Mass percent is solute mass divided by total solution mass, times 100. The solution weighs 20 g + 80 g = 100 g, so sucrose is 20 g ÷ 100 g = 20%. Dividing by the mass of water alone (25%) is the classic error, because the denominator must include the solute.

questions.q: 100 mL of 0.20 M NaCl is mixed with 300 mL of 0.60 M NaCl. What is the final NaCl concentration?
o: Used the wrong weighting toward the smaller volume.
Simple average of 0.20 and 0.60 ignores the different volumes.
Correct: (20 + 180) mmol ÷ 400 mL = 0.50 M.
Added concentrations directly; concentrations are not additive.
questions.note: Mix solutions by adding moles, then divide by total volume.
questions.x: When solutions of the same solute are mixed, moles add and volumes add, but concentrations do not. Moles: 0.100 L × 0.20 M = 0.020 mol and 0.300 L × 0.60 M = 0.180 mol, total 0.200 mol in 0.400 L, giving 0.50 M. The answer lies closer to 0.60 M because that solution contributes three times the volume, so a simple average (0.40 M) is wrong.

questions.q: What is the sulfate ion concentration in 0.10 M Al₂(SO₄)₃, assuming complete dissociation?
o: Ignored the subscript 3 on sulfate.
Used the aluminum subscript (2) instead of the sulfate subscript (3).
Correct: each formula unit releases 3 SO₄²⁻, so 3 × 0.10 = 0.30 M.
This is the total ion concentration (2 Al³⁺ + 3 SO₄²⁻).
questions.x: A strong electrolyte dissociates into its component ions in the ratio given by its formula. Al₂(SO₄)₃ → 2 Al³⁺ + 3 SO₄²⁻, so 0.10 M of the salt gives 0.20 M Al³⁺ and 0.30 M SO₄²⁻. Total ion concentration would be 0.50 M, but the question asks only for sulfate.

questions.q: A 2.0 M stock solution undergoes three successive 1:10 dilutions. What is the final concentration?
o: Divided by 30; serial dilutions multiply, they do not add.
Applied only one 1:10 dilution.
2.0 mM
Correct: overall dilution is 10³, so 2.0 M ÷ 1000 = 2.0 × 10⁻³ M.
20 mM
Applied only two 1:10 dilutions.
questions.x: In a serial dilution, each step divides the concentration by its dilution factor, so the overall factor is the product of the steps. Three 1:10 dilutions give 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000-fold, so 2.0 M becomes 0.0020 M, or 2.0 mM. Adding the factors (30-fold) is the common mistake.

questions.q: What volume of 12 M HCl stock is needed to prepare 600 mL of 2.0 M HCl?
o: 50 mL
Arithmetic slip; 1200 ÷ 12 = 100.
100 mL
200 mL
Used 6 M as the stock concentration.
Multiplied 12 × 600 ÷ 2; this inverts the dilution equation.
questions.x: Use M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ because the moles of HCl taken from the stock equal the moles in the final solution. The target holds 2.0 M × 0.600 L = 1.2 mol, and 1.2 mol ÷ 12 M = 0.100 L = 100 mL of stock, then diluted to 600 mL. A sanity check: concentrated stock should need a small volume, so 3600 mL is impossible.

questions.q: What is the osmolarity of 0.15 M NaCl, assuming complete dissociation?
o: 0.075 osmol/L
Divided by the number of ions instead of multiplying.
0.15 osmol/L
Ignores dissociation into two ions.
0.30 osmol/L
Correct: NaCl gives two particles (Na⁺ + Cl⁻), so 2 × 0.15 = 0.30 osmol/L.
0.45 osmol/L
Assumed three particles per formula unit.
questions.x: Osmolarity counts the total moles of dissolved particles per liter, because colligative effects depend on particle number, not identity. NaCl dissociates into Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so the van 't Hoff factor is 2 and 0.15 M becomes 0.30 osmol/L, close to body fluid osmolarity. Using 0.15 osmol/L forgets that each formula unit becomes two particles.

questions.q: A 10% (w/w) NaOH solution has a density of 1.1 g/mL. What is its molarity? (NaOH = 40 g/mol)
o: Decimal error; 110 g ÷ 40 g/mol = 2.75 mol.
Ignored density and assumed 1 L weighs 1000 g.
Correct: 1 L weighs 1100 g, contains 110 g NaOH = 2.75 mol, so 2.75 M.
Divided 1100 g by 250 instead of using 10% of the mass.
questions.note: w/w → molarity: use density to get grams of solution per liter.
questions.x: To convert mass percent to molarity, pick 1 L of solution and use density to find its mass: 1000 mL × 1.1 g/mL = 1100 g. Ten percent of that is NaOH: 110 g ÷ 40 g/mol = 2.75 mol, so 2.75 M. Assuming 1 L weighs 1000 g ignores the density and gives 2.5 M.

questions.q: A plasma sample contains 2.5 mmol/L of Ca²⁺. Expressed in milliequivalents per liter, this is:
o: 1.25 mEq/L
Divided by the charge instead of multiplying.
2.5 mEq/L
Equivalents equal moles only for singly charged ions.
5.0 mEq/L
Correct: each Ca²⁺ carries 2 charges, so 2 × 2.5 = 5.0 mEq/L.
10 mEq/L
Multiplied by 4; the ion's charge is 2.
questions.x: An equivalent of an ion is the amount carrying one mole of charge, so mEq = mmol × |charge|. Ca²⁺ carries two charges, so 2.5 mmol/L × 2 = 5.0 mEq/L. Only for singly charged ions like Na⁺ or Cl⁻ are millimoles and milliequivalents numerically equal.

questions.q: Which species is a Lewis acid but not a Brønsted–Lowry acid?
o: HCl
HCl donates H⁺, so it is a Brønsted acid (and also a Lewis acid).
NH₃
NH₃ donates its lone pair, so it is a Lewis base.
H₂O
Water can donate H⁺, so it can be a Brønsted acid.
BF₃
Correct: boron has an empty orbital to accept an electron pair but no H⁺ to donate.
questions.x: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair, while a Brønsted–Lowry acid donates a proton. BF₃ has only six valence electrons around boron and an empty p orbital, so it readily accepts a lone pair (for example from NH₃), yet it has no H⁺ to give. HCl and H₂O can donate protons, so they qualify as Brønsted acids, and NH₃ is a base.

questions.q: Which acid–base definition is the most inclusive?
o: Arrhenius
Arrhenius is the narrowest, limited to H⁺ and OH⁻ in water.
Brønsted–Lowry
Brønsted requires proton transfer, so it excludes reactions like BF₃ + NH₃.
Arrhenius and Brønsted are equally inclusive
Brønsted includes non-aqueous proton transfer that Arrhenius excludes.
Lewis
Correct: every Brønsted or Arrhenius acid–base reaction also involves electron-pair transfer.
questions.x: Arrhenius acids make H⁺ in water; Brønsted–Lowry acids donate H⁺ in any medium; Lewis acids accept an electron pair. Every proton transfer involves a base donating a lone pair to H⁺, so every Brønsted reaction is also a Lewis reaction, but Lewis also covers reactions with no proton at all, like BF₃ + NH₃. Thus Lewis is the broadest and Arrhenius the narrowest.

questions.q: What is the conjugate base of H₂PO₄⁻?
o: H₃PO₄
This is the conjugate acid, formed by adding H⁺.
PO₄³⁻
This removes two protons, not one.
H₂PO₄²⁻
Removing H⁺ must also remove an H atom from the formula.
HPO₄²⁻
Correct: removing one H⁺ from H₂PO₄⁻ gives HPO₄²⁻.
questions.x: A conjugate base is what remains after an acid loses exactly one H⁺: one fewer hydrogen and one more negative charge. Removing H⁺ from H₂PO₄⁻ gives HPO₄²⁻. Adding H⁺ instead gives the conjugate acid H₃PO₄, and PO₄³⁻ is two steps away, not the direct conjugate.

questions.q: What is the conjugate acid of HCO₃⁻?
o: H₂CO₃
Correct: adding H⁺ to HCO₃⁻ gives carbonic acid.
CO₃²⁻
This is the conjugate base, formed by losing H⁺.
CO₂
CO₂ is the dehydration product of H₂CO₃, not the conjugate acid.
H₃O⁺
Hydronium is water's conjugate acid.
questions.x: A conjugate acid is formed by adding one H⁺ to a base: one more hydrogen and one less negative charge. HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂CO₃, carbonic acid. CO₂ is related to H₂CO₃ through dehydration (as in the blood buffer system), but it is not the conjugate acid because it differs by H₂O, not by H⁺.

questions.q: In the reaction HSO₄⁻ + CO₃²⁻ ⇌ SO₄²⁻ + HCO₃⁻, which species acts as a Brønsted acid in the forward direction?
o: HSO₄⁻
Correct: HSO₄⁻ donates a proton and becomes SO₄²⁻.
CO₃²⁻
Carbonate accepts the proton; it is the base.
SO₄²⁻
Sulfate is the conjugate base formed in the forward reaction.
HCO₃⁻
HCO₃⁻ is a product; it acts as an acid only in the reverse direction.
questions.x: In a Brønsted–Lowry reaction, find which species loses H⁺ and which gains it. HSO₄⁻ becomes SO₄²⁻ (lost a proton), so it is the acid; CO₃²⁻ becomes HCO₃⁻ (gained a proton), so it is the base. The products form the conjugate pairs that act as acid and base only in the reverse reaction.

questions.q: For HF + CN⁻ ⇌ F⁻ + HCN, pKa(HF) = 3.2 and pKa(HCN) = 9.2. What is the equilibrium constant?
o: 10⁻¹²
Wrong exponent; Ka values are divided, giving 10 to the pKa difference (6), not 10⁻¹².
Inverted the ratio; equilibrium favors the weaker acid (HCN).
Correct: K = Ka(HF)/Ka(HCN) = 10⁻³·²/10⁻⁹·² = 10⁶; products favored.
10¹²
Doubled the pKa difference; K = 10^(ΔpKa) = 10⁶, not 10¹².
questions.note: Acid–base equilibria favor the side with the weaker acid.
questions.x: For an acid–base reaction, K equals Ka of the reactant acid divided by Ka of the product acid. Here K = 10⁻³·²/10⁻⁹·² = 10⁶, so K = 10 raised to the pKa difference (9.2 − 3.2 = 6). A large K makes sense because the reaction converts the stronger acid (HF, lower pKa) into the weaker acid (HCN); equilibrium always favors the weaker acid side.

questions.q: An aqueous solution of Fe(NO₃)₃ is acidic. What best explains this?
o: NO₃⁻ is a strong base that pulls H⁺ from water
Nitrate is the conjugate of a strong acid and is essentially neutral.
Fe³⁺ donates its own protons
Fe³⁺ has no protons; acidity comes from coordinated water.
Nitrate ions combine with water to form HNO₃
Nitrate does not significantly protonate in water.
Fe³⁺ polarizes bound water molecules, which release H⁺
Correct: the hydrated Fe(H₂O)₆³⁺ ion is a Brønsted acid because Fe³⁺ withdraws electron density.
questions.x: Small, highly charged metal ions like Fe³⁺ bind six water molecules and pull electron density from the O–H bonds, weakening them. A bound water then releases H⁺: Fe(H₂O)₆³⁺ ⇌ Fe(H₂O)₅(OH)²⁺ + H⁺, making the solution acidic. Nitrate is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so it is too weak a base to affect pH.

questions.q: Which species cannot act as a Lewis base?
o: NH₃
Nitrogen's lone pair makes NH₃ a classic Lewis base.
H₂O
Oxygen has two lone pairs available to donate.
Cl⁻
Chloride has four lone pairs and can donate one.
CH₄
Correct: methane has no lone pairs to donate.
questions.x: A Lewis base must have a lone pair of electrons it can donate to an electron-pair acceptor. NH₃, H₂O and Cl⁻ all have lone pairs on N, O or Cl. In CH₄, carbon's four valence electrons are all used in C–H bonds, so there is no lone pair to donate.

questions.q: Which species is amphiprotic, able to both donate and accept a proton?
o: H₂PO₄⁻
Correct: it can lose H⁺ (→ HPO₄²⁻) or gain H⁺ (→ H₃PO₄).
PO₄³⁻
Phosphate has no protons left to donate.
H₃O⁺
Hydronium can only donate a proton under normal conditions.
NH₄⁺
Ammonium has no lone pair to accept another proton.
questions.x: An amphiprotic species can both lose and gain a proton, so it must contain an ionizable H and have a site to accept H⁺. Intermediate forms of polyprotic acids, like H₂PO₄⁻, HPO₄²⁻ and HCO₃⁻, fit this pattern. PO₄³⁻ has no proton left, while NH₄⁺ and H₃O⁺ have used their lone pairs and can only donate.

questions.q: Solid Al(OH)₃ dissolves in both 1 M HCl and 1 M NaOH. This behavior shows that Al(OH)₃ is:
o: A strong base
A strong base would not react with NaOH.
Amphoteric
Correct: it reacts as a base with acid and as an acid with base (forming Al(OH)₄⁻).
A strong acid
A strong acid would not dissolve in HCl by neutralization.
A neutral salt
A neutral salt would not react with both acid and base.
questions.x: An amphoteric substance can react as either an acid or a base. Al(OH)₃ neutralizes HCl as a base (forming Al³⁺ and water) and reacts with NaOH as an acid (forming soluble Al(OH)₄⁻). A strong base would dissolve in acid but not react further with NaOH, so dissolving in both points to amphoterism.

questions.q: In the reaction NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, water acts as:
o: A Brønsted base
Water accepts a proton only when reacting with an acid stronger than itself.
A Lewis base
Here water gives up a proton; NH₃ is the electron-pair donor.
A spectator
Water is a reactant that is converted to OH⁻.
A Brønsted acid
Correct: water donates H⁺ to NH₃ and becomes OH⁻.
questions.x: Identify roles by tracking the proton: water gives H⁺ to NH₃ and becomes OH⁻, so water is the Brønsted acid and NH₃ is the base. Water is amphoteric, acting as a base toward stronger acids (like HCl) and as an acid toward bases (like NH₃). Since NH₃ donates its lone pair to the proton, NH₃, not water, is the Lewis base here.

questions.q: Zn(OH)₂ precipitates when a little NaOH is added to Zn²⁺(aq), but redissolves in excess NaOH. What species forms in excess base?
o: [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻
Correct: amphoteric Zn(OH)₂ accepts more OH⁻ to form a soluble hydroxo complex.
Zn metal
No reducing agent is present; zinc stays +2.
ZnO(s)
Forming the oxide requires dehydration by heating; excess base dissolves the solid instead.
Zn²⁺(aq)
Free Zn²⁺ forms in excess acid, not excess base.
questions.x: Zn(OH)₂ is amphoteric. With a little OH⁻, Zn²⁺ precipitates as the neutral hydroxide, but excess OH⁻ lets it act as a Lewis acid and bind more hydroxide: Zn(OH)₂ + 2 OH⁻ → [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻, a soluble complex ion. Free Zn²⁺ would only reappear if acid were added.

questions.q: Glycine exists mainly as a zwitterion at pH 6. Which description is correct?
o: –NH₂ and –COOH are both present
This neutral form is negligible in water; pKa values favor the charged groups.
–NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻ are both present, giving net charge 0
Correct: the amine is protonated and the carboxyl is deprotonated near the pI.
–NH₃⁺ and –COOH, giving net charge +1
This cationic form dominates below pH ≈ 2.3.
–NH₂ and –COO⁻, giving net charge −1
This anionic form dominates above pH ≈ 9.6.
questions.x: Glycine's carboxyl group has a pKa near 2.3 and its amino group a pKa near 9.6. At pH 6, above the first pKa and below the second, the carboxyl is mostly deprotonated (–COO⁻) and the amine mostly protonated (–NH₃⁺). Net charge is zero, the zwitterion. The uncharged –NH₂/–COOH form never dominates because no pH lets both groups be neutral at once.

questions.q: Which reaction illustrates the autoionization of water?
o: H₂O ⇌ H₂ + ½O₂
This is decomposition (electrolysis), not autoionization.
2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻
Correct: one water donates H⁺ to another, showing water's amphoterism.
H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺
This shows only water acting as a base.
H₂O ⇌ 2H⁺ + O²⁻
Oxide ion does not form in water; it would immediately be protonated.
questions.x: Autoionization is a proton transfer between two water molecules: one acts as an acid and the other as a base, giving H₃O⁺ and OH⁻. At 25 °C, Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴. Splitting water into H₂ and O₂ is a redox decomposition that requires energy input, not an acid–base equilibrium.

questions.q: Which of the following is a weak acid in water?
o: HCl
HCl ionizes completely in water.
HNO₃
Nitric acid is a strong acid.
HClO₄
Perchloric acid is one of the strongest common acids.
HF
Correct: the strong H–F bond and small F⁻ make HF only partially ionized.
questions.x: The common strong acids are HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, HClO₄ and H₂SO₄ (first proton); they ionize essentially completely in water. HF is weak despite fluorine's electronegativity because the H–F bond is very strong and the small F⁻ ion is tightly solvated, which makes ionization less favorable. Electronegativity alone would wrongly predict HF to be the strongest.

questions.q: Which hydrohalic acid is the strongest in a solvent that does not level their strengths?
o: HI
Correct: the long, weak H–I bond and large, stable I⁻ make HI the strongest.
HF
HF is the weakest; its short H–F bond is very strong.
HCl
HCl is weaker than HBr and HI because its H–X bond is stronger.
HBr
HBr is strong but its bond is shorter and stronger than H–I.
questions.note: Down a group, bond strength and anion size dominate over electronegativity.
questions.x: Acid strength depends on how easily H–X breaks and how stable X⁻ is. Going down group 17, the halogen atom grows, so the H–X bond gets longer and weaker and the negative charge of X⁻ spreads over a larger volume. HI therefore gives up H⁺ most easily. Electronegativity would wrongly predict HF to be strongest; down a group, size and bond strength dominate.

questions.q: Rank the oxyacids HClO, HClO₂, HClO₃ and HClO₄. Which is the strongest acid?
o: HClO₄
Correct: more oxygens withdraw electron density and delocalize the anion's charge.
HClO
With one oxygen, ClO⁻ is the least stabilized conjugate base.
HClO₂
Two oxygens give less stabilization than four.
HClO₃
Strong, but HClO₄'s extra oxygen stabilizes its anion further.
questions.x: In oxyacids with the same central atom, each extra oxygen pulls electron density away from the O–H bond by induction and adds resonance forms that spread the anion's negative charge. ClO₄⁻ distributes its charge over four oxygens, making it the most stable conjugate base, so HClO₄ is the strongest acid. HClO, with only one oxygen, is a weak acid (pKa ≈ 7.5).

questions.q: Trichloroacetic acid (pKa ≈ 0.7) is far more acidic than acetic acid (pKa ≈ 4.8). The main reason is:
o: Cl atoms donate electrons to the carboxyl group
Chlorine is electron-withdrawing, not donating.
Electron-withdrawing Cl atoms stabilize the carboxylate by induction
Correct: Cl pulls electron density away, spreading the negative charge of the anion.
Trichloroacetic acid has more ionizable protons
Both have only one acidic carboxyl proton.
Cl atoms form hydrogen bonds that release H⁺
The effect is inductive stabilization of the conjugate base.
questions.x: Acidity rises when the conjugate base is stabilized. Chlorine is electronegative, so three Cl atoms on the α-carbon pull electron density through the sigma bonds (inductive effect), spreading out the carboxylate's negative charge. That makes ionization far more favorable, dropping the pKa by about 4 units. Both acids have just one acidic proton, so proton count cannot explain the difference.

questions.q: Four acids have pKa values of 2.0, 4.5, 7.0 and 9.5. Which acid has the strongest conjugate base?
o: The acid with pKa 2.0
The strongest acid has the weakest conjugate base.
The acid with pKa 4.5
A lower pKa than 9.5 means a weaker conjugate base.
The acid with pKa 7.0
pKb = 7.0 here, still weaker than the base with pKb 4.5.
The acid with pKa 9.5
Correct: the weakest acid (highest pKa) has the strongest conjugate base.
questions.x: For a conjugate pair, Ka × Kb = Kw, so pKa + pKb = 14 at 25 °C. The weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base. The acid with pKa 9.5 holds its proton most tightly, so its conjugate base has pKb 4.5, the lowest of the four, and is the strongest base. A strong acid like pKa 2.0 has a very weak conjugate base.

questions.q: Acetic acid has Ka = 2 × 10⁻⁵. What is Kb for acetate?
o: Multiplied Ka by Kw instead of dividing.
Correct: Kb = Kw/Ka = 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ (2 × 10⁻⁵) = 5 × 10⁻¹⁰.
Multiplied Ka by 10⁻⁴; Kb = Kw ÷ Ka, which is 5 × 10⁻¹⁰.
Took 1/Ka without multiplying by Kw.
questions.x: For any conjugate acid–base pair in water, Ka × Kb = Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C. So Kb = 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ (2 × 10⁻⁵) = 0.5 × 10⁻⁹ = 5 × 10⁻¹⁰. The tiny Kb confirms acetate is a weak base. Multiplying instead of dividing by Kw gives an absurdly small value, a quick sign of the error.

questions.q: NH₃ has pKb = 4.75 at 25 °C. What is the pKa of NH₄⁺?
o: Conjugate pairs share pKa + pKb = 14, not equal values.
Neutral pH is unrelated to this pair's pKa.
Correct: pKa + pKb = 14, so pKa = 14 − 4.75 = 9.25.
Added 14 instead of subtracting.
questions.x: Because Ka × Kb = Kw, taking negative logs gives pKa + pKb = pKw = 14 at 25 °C. For the NH₄⁺/NH₃ pair, pKa = 14 − 4.75 = 9.25. This means an ammonia buffer works best near pH 9.25. Conjugate partners never share the same pK value unless both equal 7.

questions.q: In water, HCl and HClO₄ appear equally strong, but in glacial acetic acid HClO₄ is clearly stronger. What explains this?
o: HCl decomposes in acetic acid
HCl does not decompose; it simply ionizes less in a weaker base solvent.
Acetic acid is a stronger base than water
Acetic acid is a weaker base, which is why differences emerge.
HClO₄ gains extra protons in acetic acid
Strength depends on donating H⁺, not gaining protons.
Water levels both acids to H₃O⁺ because both ionize completely
Correct: in water the strongest acid present is H₃O⁺; a less basic solvent reveals differences.
questions.note: Leveling effect: no acid stronger than the solvent's conjugate acid survives in it.
questions.x: In water, any acid stronger than H₃O⁺ transfers its proton to water essentially completely, so HCl and HClO₄ both appear as 100% H₃O⁺; water levels them. Acetic acid is a much weaker base than water, so neither acid ionizes completely in it, and the greater intrinsic strength of HClO₄ shows up as more ionization. A less basic solvent differentiates strong acids.

questions.q: A 0.10 M weak acid solution is diluted to 0.010 M. How do the percent ionization and pH change?
o: Percent ionization increases and pH increases
Correct: dilution shifts HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ right, but [H⁺] still drops overall.
Percent ionization decreases and pH increases
By Le Châtelier, dilution favors the side with more particles, so percent ionization rises.
Percent ionization increases and pH decreases
The fraction ionized rises, but total [H⁺] falls, so pH rises.
Both stay the same
Ka is constant, but percent ionization depends on concentration.
questions.x: For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, dilution lowers all concentrations, and Le Châtelier's principle shifts equilibrium toward the side with more dissolved particles, so the fraction ionized rises. Using x ≈ √(Ka·C), percent ionization ∝ 1/√C, so a 10-fold dilution raises it about 3-fold, while [H⁺] itself falls about 3-fold and pH rises by about 0.5. Higher percent ionization does not mean more H⁺.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.0050 M Ba(OH)₂ at 25 °C?
o: This is the pOH, not the pH.
Computed pOH using only one hydroxide per formula unit.
Ignored the second hydroxide; [OH⁻] is 0.010 M, not 0.0050 M.
questions.x: Ba(OH)₂ is a strong base that releases two OH⁻ per formula unit, so [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.0050 M = 0.010 M. Then pOH = −log(10⁻²) = 2 and pH = 14 − 2 = 12. Forgetting the second hydroxide gives pOH 2.3 and pH 11.7, the most common trap.

questions.q: Why does dissolving NaCl in water not change the pH?
o: Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid and Na⁺ is a negligible acid
Correct: neither ion reacts appreciably with water.
Cl⁻ is a strong base that cancels Na⁺
Cl⁻ is an extremely weak base.
NaCl reacts to form HCl and NaOH in equal amounts
No measurable hydrolysis occurs.
Na⁺ is a strong acid
Na⁺ is a spectator ion with negligible acidity.
questions.x: A salt changes pH only if one of its ions reacts with water (hydrolysis). Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of the strong acid HCl, so it has essentially no tendency to take H⁺ back. Na⁺ is a large, singly charged ion from a strong base and does not polarize water enough to release H⁺. Salts of a strong acid and strong base give neutral solutions.

questions.q: Across period 2, which binary hydride is the strongest acid?
o: CH₄
Carbon is least electronegative; CH₃⁻ is very unstable.
HF
Correct: within a period, more electronegative atoms better stabilize the negative charge of the conjugate base.
NH₃
N is less electronegative than O and F; NH₂⁻ is a very strong base.
H₂O
O is less electronegative than F, so OH⁻ is a stronger base than F⁻.
questions.note: Across a period electronegativity rules; down a group size rules.
questions.x: Across a period the atoms are similar in size, so the deciding factor is electronegativity: the more electronegative the atom, the better it holds the negative charge left behind when H⁺ leaves. Acidity rises CH₄ < NH₃ < H₂O < HF. Down a group the trend flips to size (HI strongest), which is why HF is the strongest period 2 hydride yet a weak acid among the hydrohalic acids.

questions.q: What is the pH of 1.0 × 10⁻³ M NaOH at 25 °C?
o: This is the pOH.
Off by one; pOH = 3 gives pH 11.
Correct: pOH = 3, so pH = 14 − 3 = 11.
Mistook the concentration as 10⁻¹ M.
questions.x: NaOH is a strong base, so [OH⁻] equals its concentration, 1.0 × 10⁻³ M, and pOH = 3. At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14, so pH = 11. Reporting 3 is the common slip of giving pOH instead of pH for a base.

questions.q: A solution at 25 °C has pH 4.5. What is its pOH?
o: pH and pOH are equal only in neutral water.
Correct: pOH = 14 − 4.5 = 9.5.
Subtraction slip; 14 − 4.5 = 9.5.
Added rather than subtracted.
questions.x: At 25 °C, Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴, so pH + pOH = 14. With pH 4.5, pOH = 14 − 4.5 = 9.5. The solution is acidic, so pOH must be larger than 7; pH and pOH are equal only at neutrality.

questions.q: What is [H⁺] in a solution of pH 3.3? (log 2 ≈ 0.3)
o: Correct: 10⁻³·³ = 10⁰·⁷ × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁴ M.
Used 10⁻³ × 2; that would be pH ≈ 2.7.
Treated the pH digits as the coefficient.
Exponent error; pH 2.3 corresponds to 5 × 10⁻³.
questions.x: [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ. Split the exponent into an integer and a positive decimal: 10⁻³·³ = 10⁰·⁷ × 10⁻⁴. Since log 5 ≈ 0.7 (because log 2 ≈ 0.3 and log 10 = 1), 10⁰·⁷ ≈ 5, giving 5 × 10⁻⁴ M. A quick check: pH 3.3 lies between pH 3 (10⁻³) and pH 4 (10⁻⁴), so the answer must fall between them.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.10 M weak acid HA with Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵?
o: Treated HA as a strong acid.
Correct: [H⁺] = √(Ka·C) = √(10⁻⁶) = 10⁻³ M.
Used pKa as the pH; that applies only to a half-neutralized buffer.
Forgot to take the square root of Ka·C.
questions.x: For a weak acid with small Ka, only a small amount x ionizes, so Ka ≈ x²/C and x = [H⁺] = √(Ka·C). Here √(1.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.10) = √(10⁻⁶) = 10⁻³ M, so pH = 3. The approximation holds because 10⁻³ is only 1% of 0.10 M. pH equals pKa only when [HA] = [A⁻], as in a half-neutralized buffer.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.040 M HA with Ka = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶? (log 4 ≈ 0.6)
o: Treated HA as fully ionized.
Added 0.6 instead of subtracting it from 4.
Did not take the square root of Ka·C.
questions.x: For a weak acid, [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C). Ka·C = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.040 = 1.6 × 10⁻⁷ = 16 × 10⁻⁸, whose square root is 4 × 10⁻⁴ M. Then pH = 4 − log 4 = 4 − 0.6 = 3.4. The coefficient of 4 makes [H⁺] larger than 10⁻⁴, so the pH must be lower than 4, not higher.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.10 M NH₃ if Kb = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵?
o: This is the pOH, not the pH.
Used pKa of the conjugate acid as the pH.
Correct: [OH⁻] = √(10⁻⁶) = 10⁻³ M, pOH = 3, pH = 11.
Treated NH₃ as a strong base.
questions.x: A weak base works like a weak acid but produces OH⁻: [OH⁻] ≈ √(Kb·C) = √(1.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.10) = 10⁻³ M. That gives pOH = 3 and pH = 14 − 3 = 11. Stopping at 3 reports pOH, and a basic solution must have pH above 7.

questions.q: HA has Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁹. What is the pH of 0.10 M NaA?
o: Used pKb (5) as the pH; A⁻ is a base, so the pH must be above 7.
Used pKa = 9 as the pH.
Correct: Kb = 10⁻⁵, [OH⁻] = √(10⁻⁶) = 10⁻³ M, pH = 11.
Assumed A⁻ fully reacts as a strong base.
questions.note: Salt of a weak acid: convert Ka to Kb first.
questions.x: NaA dissolves to give A⁻, the conjugate base of a weak acid, which makes the solution basic. First convert: Kb = Kw/Ka = 10⁻¹⁴/10⁻⁹ = 10⁻⁵. Then [OH⁻] ≈ √(Kb·C) = √(10⁻⁶) = 10⁻³ M, so pOH = 3 and pH = 11. The weaker the parent acid, the stronger and more basic its salt's anion.

questions.q: Which 0.1 M salt solution is acidic?
o: NaCH₃COO
Acetate is a weak base, making the solution basic.
KNO₃
Both ions come from a strong acid/strong base; neutral.
Na₂CO₃
Carbonate is a fairly strong weak base; basic.
NH₄Cl
Correct: NH₄⁺ is a weak acid; Cl⁻ is a negligible base.
questions.x: Predict salt pH by asking which ion reacts with water. NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of the weak base NH₃, so it donates H⁺ to water and lowers pH, while Cl⁻ from strong HCl is inert. Acetate and carbonate are conjugate bases of weak acids and raise pH, and KNO₃ contains only spectator ions.

questions.q: Which 0.1 M aqueous solution has a pH closest to 7?
o: NaHCO₃
Bicarbonate is mildly basic in water (pH ≈ 8.3).
NH₄NO₃
NH₄⁺ makes the solution acidic.
Na₃PO₄
Phosphate is a strong-ish base; pH well above 7.
KBr
Correct: K⁺ and Br⁻ come from a strong base and strong acid, so neither hydrolyzes.
questions.x: A salt is neutral when both ions come from a strong acid and a strong base, because neither ion hydrolyzes. K⁺ (from KOH) and Br⁻ (from HBr) are such ions, so KBr gives pH ≈ 7. The others contain an ion from a weak partner: NH₄⁺ is acidic, and HCO₃⁻ and PO₄³⁻ are basic.

questions.q: What is the approximate pH of 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ M HCl?
o: Slightly below 7
Correct: water's 10⁻⁷ M H⁺ dominates; added acid lowers pH only slightly (≈ 6.98).
An acid cannot make water basic; water's own H⁺ must be included.
Exactly 7
The added H⁺, though tiny, still lowers pH a little.
Confused the concentration with 10⁻¹ M.
questions.note: Very dilute strong acid: include water's autoionization.
questions.x: Normally [H⁺] from a strong acid equals its concentration, but 10⁻⁸ M is ten times smaller than the 10⁻⁷ M H⁺ already supplied by water's autoionization. Total [H⁺] is therefore slightly above 10⁻⁷ M (about 1.05 × 10⁻⁷ M), giving pH ≈ 6.98. Simply writing pH = 8 ignores water and absurdly makes an acid solution basic.

questions.q: At 50 °C, Kw ≈ 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ and pure water has pH ≈ 6.6. Which statement is true?
o: The water is neutral because [H⁺] = [OH⁻]
Correct: neutrality means equal concentrations; the neutral pH shifts with temperature.
The water is acidic because pH < 7
pH 7 marks neutrality only at 25 °C.
Kw decreased because autoionization is exothermic
Kw rose, which shows autoionization is endothermic.
[OH⁻] is greater than [H⁺]
Pure water always produces H⁺ and OH⁻ in a 1:1 ratio.
questions.x: Neutrality is defined by [H⁺] = [OH⁻], not by pH 7. Pure water always forms H⁺ and OH⁻ in a 1:1 ratio, so it is neutral at any temperature. Because Kw rises on heating (autoionization is endothermic), [H⁺] = √Kw ≈ 2.3 × 10⁻⁷ M at 50 °C, giving a neutral pH near 6.6. A pH below 7 here does not mean acidic.

questions.q: A strong acid solution has pH 2. It is diluted 100-fold with water. What is the new pH?
o: Dilution lowers [H⁺], so pH must change.
A 100-fold dilution adds 2 pH units, not 1.
Correct: [H⁺] drops from 10⁻² to 10⁻⁴ M.
pH is logarithmic; each 10-fold dilution adds 1.
questions.x: pH is −log[H⁺], so every 10-fold change in [H⁺] shifts pH by 1 unit. A strong acid at pH 2 has [H⁺] = 10⁻² M; a 100-fold dilution gives 10⁻⁴ M, so pH 4. A 100-fold dilution is two factors of ten, so it adds 2 units, not 1. This holds as long as [H⁺] stays well above water's 10⁻⁷ M.

questions.q: Equal volumes of 0.20 M HCl and 0.10 M NaOH are mixed. What is the resulting pH? (log 5 ≈ 0.7)
o: Took the pH of 0.20 M HCl alone.
Forgot that mixing doubles the volume.
Correct: excess H⁺ = 0.10 M before mixing, halved by doubling volume to 0.050 M; pH ≈ 1.3.
The acid is in excess, so the solution is not neutral.
questions.x: For strong acid–strong base mixtures, neutralize moles first, then divide by the total volume. Per liter of each, 0.20 mol H⁺ reacts with 0.10 mol OH⁻, leaving 0.10 mol H⁺ in 2 L, so [H⁺] = 0.050 M. pH = −log(5 × 10⁻²) = 2 − 0.7 = 1.3. Forgetting the doubled volume gives 0.10 M and pH 1.0.

questions.q: What is [OH⁻] in a solution of pH 9 at 25 °C?
o: pH is not a coefficient; use pOH = 14 − pH.
This is [H⁺], not [OH⁻].
This applies only to neutral water.
Correct: pOH = 5, so [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁵ M.
questions.x: At 25 °C, pOH = 14 − pH, and [OH⁻] = 10⁻ᵖᴼᴴ. At pH 9, pOH = 5, so [OH⁻] = 1 × 10⁻⁵ M. The value 10⁻⁹ M is [H⁺]; a basic solution must have [OH⁻] greater than 10⁻⁷ M, so that choice cannot be right.

questions.q: How many times greater is [H⁺] at pH 3 than at pH 6?
o: Divided the pH values; pH is logarithmic.
Subtracted pH values but did not convert from log scale.
Three units correspond to 10³, not 10².
Correct: each pH unit is a 10-fold change; 3 units = 10³.
questions.x: pH is a base-10 logarithmic scale, so each 1-unit drop in pH means [H⁺] is 10 times higher. From pH 6 to pH 3 is 3 units: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000-fold. Here [H⁺] goes from 10⁻⁶ M to 10⁻³ M. Treating the pH difference as a linear ratio (2 or 3) ignores the log scale.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.050 M H₂SO₄, assuming both protons fully dissociate?
o: Assumed four protons per molecule.
Counted only one proton ([H⁺] = 0.050 M).
Mistook 0.050 M for 0.010 M.
questions.x: With both protons dissociated, each H₂SO₄ releases 2 H⁺, so [H⁺] = 2 × 0.050 = 0.10 M and pH = 1.0. Counting only one proton gives 0.050 M and pH 1.3. In reality the second dissociation is not complete (Ka₂ ≈ 10⁻²), but the stem states to assume full dissociation.

questions.q: A 0.10 M solution of a monoprotic weak acid has pH 3.0. What is Ka?
o: Forgot to divide by the 0.10 M concentration.
Correct: Ka = [H⁺]²/C = (10⁻³)² ÷ 0.10 = 10⁻⁵.
This is [H⁺], not Ka.
Divided [H⁺] by C without squaring.
questions.x: pH 3.0 means [H⁺] = [A⁻] = 10⁻³ M at equilibrium, and [HA] stays about 0.10 M because so little ionized. So Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] = (10⁻³)²/0.10 = 10⁻⁶/10⁻¹ = 10⁻⁵. Forgetting to divide by [HA] gives 10⁻⁶, and forgetting to square [H⁺] gives 10⁻².

questions.q: A 0.20 M monoprotic weak acid has [H⁺] = 2.0 × 10⁻³ M at equilibrium. What is its percent ionization?
o: Divided by 2.0 M instead of 0.20 M.
Divided by 0.10 M instead of the given 0.20 M initial concentration.
Decimal error by a factor of 10.
questions.x: Percent ionization is the amount ionized divided by the initial acid concentration, times 100. For a monoprotic acid, [H⁺] at equilibrium equals the amount ionized, so (2.0 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.20) × 100 = 1.0%. Weak acids typically ionize only a few percent, which is why approximations like √(Ka·C) work.

questions.q: At 25 °C a solution has [H⁺] = 2.0 × 10⁻³ M. What is [OH⁻]?
o: Multiplied by 2 instead of dividing by 2.
Exponent error in dividing by 10⁻³.
[H⁺] equals [OH⁻] only in neutral water.
questions.x: At 25 °C, [H⁺][OH⁻] = Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, so [OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻³). Divide coefficients (1 ÷ 2 = 0.5) and exponents (10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 10⁻³ = 10⁻¹¹), giving 0.5 × 10⁻¹¹ = 5.0 × 10⁻¹² M. Since the solution is acidic, [OH⁻] must be far below 10⁻⁷ M.

questions.q: The autoionization of water is endothermic. When pure water is heated from 25 °C to 60 °C, what happens?
o: Kw decreases and pH increases
An endothermic process is favored by heating, so Kw rises.
Kw stays constant at 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴
Kw is an equilibrium constant and changes with temperature.
The water becomes acidic
[H⁺] still equals [OH⁻], so it is neutral.
Kw increases and pH decreases, but the water stays neutral
Correct: heat shifts equilibrium right, raising both [H⁺] and [OH⁻] equally.
questions.x: For an endothermic equilibrium, heat acts like a reactant, so heating shifts 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ to the right and Kw increases. Both [H⁺] and [OH⁻] rise equally, so pH falls below 7 while the water remains neutral. pH 7 is the neutral point only at 25 °C, so a lower pH in hot pure water does not mean it is acidic.

questions.q: Which statement about pH + pOH = 14 is correct?
o: It holds only at 25 °C, where Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴
Correct: pH + pOH = pKw, and pKw changes with temperature.
It holds at all temperatures
Kw varies with temperature, so the sum varies.
It holds only for strong acids
It applies to any aqueous solution at 25 °C.
It holds only for buffered solutions
Buffering is irrelevant to Kw.
questions.x: Taking −log of Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] gives pH + pOH = pKw. Only at 25 °C is Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ and pKw = 14. Because Kw changes with temperature (rising on heating), the sum is smaller at higher temperature. The relationship applies to every aqueous solution regardless of what solute is present.

questions.q: Which is the stronger acid, phenol (pKa 10) or ethanol (pKa 16), and why?
o: Ethanol, because its O–H bond is weaker
Ethanol's higher pKa shows it is the weaker acid.
Phenol, because it has more hydrogen atoms
Number of H atoms does not determine acidity.
Ethanol, because ethoxide is resonance-stabilized
Ethoxide has no resonance; its charge is localized.
Phenol, because its conjugate base is resonance-stabilized
Correct: phenoxide's charge delocalizes into the ring.
questions.x: Lower pKa means stronger acid, so phenol (pKa 10) is about a million times more acidic than ethanol (pKa 16). The reason is conjugate base stability: phenoxide's negative charge is delocalized by resonance into the aromatic ring, while ethoxide's charge is stuck on one oxygen and is further destabilized by the electron-donating alkyl group. Ethoxide has no resonance to help.

questions.q: A student measures the pH of 0.1 M solutions of HCl and CH₃COOH. Which result is expected?
o: HCl has the lower pH
Correct: HCl ionizes fully, giving higher [H⁺] at the same concentration.
CH₃COOH has the lower pH
Acetic acid ionizes only about 1%, giving less H⁺.
Both have pH 1
Only the strong acid reaches pH 1 at 0.1 M.
Both have pH 7
Both are acids, so neither is neutral.
questions.x: At equal concentration, a strong acid gives more H⁺ than a weak acid because it ionizes completely. 0.1 M HCl gives [H⁺] = 0.1 M and pH 1, while 0.1 M acetic acid (Ka ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) gives [H⁺] ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻³ M and pH about 2.9. Strength describes extent of ionization, not concentration.

questions.q: A 0.10 M solution of HX has pH 1.0, and a 0.10 M solution of HY has pH 3.0. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: HY is stronger because its pH is higher
Higher pH means less H⁺, so HY is weaker.
HX is a strong acid and HY is a weak acid with Ka ≈ 10⁻⁵
Correct: [H⁺] = C for HX; for HY, Ka = (10⁻³)²/0.10 = 10⁻⁵.
Both are weak acids with equal Ka
Their very different pH values show different strengths.
HX is weak with Ka ≈ 10⁻¹
[H⁺] = 0.10 M equals C, meaning complete ionization.
questions.x: Compare [H⁺] with the acid's concentration. HX at 0.10 M has [H⁺] = 10⁻¹ M, equal to C, so it is fully ionized and strong. HY gives only 10⁻³ M, so it ionizes about 1%, and Ka ≈ (10⁻³)²/0.10 = 10⁻⁵. Higher pH at the same concentration means less H⁺ and therefore a weaker acid.

questions.q: Which aqueous solution is basic?
o: 0.1 M KCl
Cl⁻ is the conjugate of a strong acid; neutral.
0.1 M NH₄Br
NH₄⁺ is a weak acid; the solution is acidic.
0.1 M KF
Correct: F⁻ is the conjugate base of the weak acid HF and pulls H⁺ from water.
0.1 M AlCl₃
Hydrated Al³⁺ is acidic.
questions.x: A salt is basic when its anion is the conjugate base of a weak acid and its cation is a spectator. F⁻ comes from HF (weak), so F⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HF + OH⁻ raises the pH, while K⁺ is inert. NH₄⁺ and hydrated Al³⁺ are acidic, and KCl contains only spectator ions.

questions.q: Which change makes a weak acid HA ionize to a greater percentage in water?
o: Adding NaA
A common ion shifts equilibrium left, reducing ionization.
Adding HCl
Extra H⁺ suppresses ionization of HA.
Concentrating the solution
Higher concentration lowers percent ionization.
Adding a small amount of strong base
Correct: OH⁻ removes H⁺, pulling HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ to the right.
questions.x: Percent ionization of HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ rises when equilibrium is pulled to the right. A small amount of strong base consumes H⁺ (H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O), so more HA ionizes to replace it. Adding H⁺ or A⁻ (the common-ion effect) pushes equilibrium left, and concentrating the acid lowers the ionized fraction.

questions.q: Which expression correctly defines Ka for HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ in water?
o: Correct: products over reactants; water is omitted as a pure liquid.
This is 1/Ka, the association constant.
Pure liquids like water do not appear in K expressions.
Equilibrium expressions multiply concentrations, not add them.
questions.x: Equilibrium constants are products over reactants, each concentration raised to its coefficient, so Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. Pure liquids and solids, including the water solvent, have activity 1 and are left out. The inverted ratio is the association constant (1/Ka) for the reverse reaction.

questions.q: A solution with pOH 3 at 25 °C is best described as:
o: Acidic, pH 3
Confused pOH with pH.
Basic, pH 11
Correct: pH = 14 − 3 = 11.
Neutral, pH 7
pOH 3 means [OH⁻] = 10⁻³ M, far above neutral.
Acidic, pH 11
pH above 7 is basic, not acidic.
questions.x: At 25 °C, pH = 14 − pOH, so pOH 3 gives pH 11. That means [OH⁻] = 10⁻³ M, far above [H⁺] = 10⁻¹¹ M, so the solution is basic. Mistaking pOH for pH would wrongly label it acidic.

questions.q: Acid HA (pKa 4) and acid HB (pKa 8) are each prepared at 0.10 M. Compared with the HB solution, the HA solution has [H⁺] that is:
o: 10,000 times greater
Ka differs by 10⁴, but [H⁺] scales with its square root.
10 times greater
Treated the 4-unit pKa gap as a single factor of 10.
100 times greater
Correct: [H⁺] ∝ √Ka, and √(10⁴) = 100.
2 times greater
Divided the pKa values (8/4); pKa is logarithmic.
questions.x: For weak acids at the same concentration, [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C), so [H⁺] scales with the square root of Ka. HA's Ka (10⁻⁴) is 10⁴ times HB's (10⁻⁸), so its [H⁺] is √(10⁴) = 100 times greater: about 3 × 10⁻³ M versus 3 × 10⁻⁵ M. Equivalently, the pH differs by half the pKa difference, 2 units.

questions.q: Which pair of substances, dissolved together in water, forms a buffer?
o: HCl and NaCl
Cl⁻ is too weak a base to neutralize added acid.
NaOH and NaCl
A strong base and a neutral salt cannot absorb added base.
HNO₃ and KNO₃
A strong acid and its negligible conjugate base do not buffer.
CH₃COOH and CH₃COONa
Correct: a weak acid with its conjugate base resists pH change.
questions.x: A buffer needs both a weak acid to neutralize added OH⁻ and its conjugate base to neutralize added H⁺, in comparable amounts. Acetic acid and acetate fit: CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH and CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O. Strong acids like HCl or HNO₃ fail because their conjugate bases (Cl⁻, NO₃⁻) are too weak to take up added H⁺.

questions.q: A buffer contains a weak acid with pKa 4.7 and [A⁻]/[HA] = 0.1. What is the pH?
o: Subtracted 0.1 instead of log(0.1).
This would require equal amounts of A⁻ and HA.
Added 1 instead of subtracting; log 0.1 = −1.
questions.x: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), links buffer pH to the base-to-acid ratio. With a ratio of 0.1, log(0.1) = −1, so pH = 4.7 − 1 = 3.7. When there is more acid than base (ratio below 1), the pH must fall below the pKa, which rules out 5.7.

questions.q: Which conjugate pair would make the best buffer at pH 9.2?
o: CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻ (pKa 4.76)
Its pKa is more than 4 units away from 9.2.
NH₄⁺/NH₃ (pKa 9.25)
Correct: the best buffer has pKa within about 1 unit of the target pH.
H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻ (pKa 6.35)
Its pKa is nearly 3 units too low.
HSO₄⁻/SO₄²⁻ (pKa 1.99)
Its pKa is far too low for pH 9.2.
questions.x: A buffer works best when [HA] ≈ [A⁻], which happens when pH ≈ pKa; its useful range is about pKa ± 1. NH₄⁺/NH₃ has pKa 9.25, nearly matching the target of 9.2. The other pairs have pKa values several units away, so at pH 9.2 almost all of their acid form would already be converted to base, leaving little capacity.

questions.q: For buffers of the same total concentration, which composition gives the greatest capacity against both added acid and added base?
o: Lots of base means little capacity against added base.
Lots of acid means little capacity against added acid.
Correct: equal amounts let the buffer absorb either H⁺ or OH⁻ equally; pH = pKa.
Only HA, no A⁻
With no conjugate base, added acid cannot be neutralized.
questions.x: Buffer capacity against added acid depends on how much A⁻ is present, and against added base on how much HA is present. For a fixed total, the best two-way capacity comes from equal amounts, which also makes pH = pKa. A 10:1 ratio in either direction leaves the buffer weak on one side, and pure HA cannot neutralize added acid at all.

questions.q: A buffer is diluted tenfold with pure water. What happens?
o: pH drops by 1 unit
Henderson–Hasselbalch depends on the ratio, which dilution does not change.
pH rises by 1 unit
Both components dilute equally, so the ratio is constant.
Capacity increases because ionization rises
Capacity depends on concentration, which falls.
pH stays nearly the same, but buffer capacity decreases
Correct: the [A⁻]/[HA] ratio is unchanged, but fewer moles per liter are available.
questions.x: Buffer pH depends on the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] (Henderson–Hasselbalch), and dilution lowers both concentrations by the same factor, so the ratio and pH barely change. Capacity, however, depends on the absolute amount of HA and A⁻ per liter, so a tenfold dilution leaves a tenth as much to neutralize added acid or base. That is why dilute buffers are easily overwhelmed.

questions.q: 1.0 L of buffer contains 0.10 mol HA and 0.10 mol NaA (pKa 5.0). After 0.050 mol HCl is added, what is the pH? (log 3 ≈ 0.48)
o: Treated HCl as if no buffer were present.
Ignored the reaction of H⁺ with A⁻.
Used log(3) with the wrong sign; acid lowers pH.
questions.x: First do the stoichiometry: added H⁺ converts A⁻ to HA completely, so A⁻ goes from 0.10 to 0.05 mol and HA from 0.10 to 0.15 mol. Then apply Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = 5.0 + log(0.05/0.15) = 5.0 − log 3 = 5.0 − 0.48 = 4.52. Adding acid must lower the pH, but only modestly, because the buffer absorbs most of the H⁺.

questions.q: Blood pH is 7.4, and the pKa of the H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻ system is about 6.4. What is the ratio [HCO₃⁻]/[H₂CO₃]?
o: Correct: 7.4 = 6.4 + log(ratio), so ratio = 10¹ = 10.
Inverted the ratio; pH above pKa means more base form.
That would require pH = pKa.
That would correspond to pH = 8.4.
