questions.x: Rearranging Henderson–Hasselbalch gives log([HCO₃⁻]/[H₂CO₃]) = pH − pKa = 7.4 − 6.4 = 1, so the ratio is 10:1. Because blood pH sits above the pKa, the base form must dominate. Even though this ratio makes the buffer stronger against acid than base, the lungs and kidneys adjust CO₂ and HCO₃⁻ to keep pH stable.

questions.q: A patient hyperventilates, blowing off CO₂. What happens to blood pH, using CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻?
o: It falls, because more H₂CO₃ forms
Removing CO₂ shifts equilibrium away from H₂CO₃.
It is unchanged because the buffer is perfect
Buffers resist but do not eliminate pH changes.
It rises, because lost CO₂ pulls the equilibrium left and consumes H⁺
Correct: this is respiratory alkalosis.
It falls, because HCO₃⁻ is exhaled
Bicarbonate is not exhaled; CO₂ is.
questions.x: Hyperventilation removes CO₂, so by Le Châtelier the equilibria shift left to replace it: H⁺ combines with HCO₃⁻ to form H₂CO₃, which breaks down into CO₂ and water. Consuming H⁺ raises blood pH, producing respiratory alkalosis. The key is that CO₂ acts as an acid in blood; removing it removes acid, so pH rises, not falls.

questions.q: Phosphoric acid has pKa values 2.1, 7.2 and 12.3. Which pair is best for a buffer at pH 7.0?
o: H₃PO₄ and H₂PO₄⁻
This pair buffers near pH 2.1.
HPO₄²⁻ and PO₄³⁻
This pair buffers near pH 12.3.
H₃PO₄ and PO₄³⁻
These are not a conjugate pair; they differ by three protons.
H₂PO₄⁻ and HPO₄²⁻
Correct: this pair corresponds to pKa₂ = 7.2.
questions.x: Each pKa of a polyprotic acid defines a conjugate pair that buffers near that pH. To buffer at pH 7.0, choose the pair whose pKa is closest: pKa₂ = 7.2, which corresponds to H₂PO₄⁻/HPO₄²⁻. This phosphate pair is a major buffer inside cells. H₃PO₄ and PO₄³⁻ differ by three protons, so they are not a conjugate pair at all.

questions.q: 0.20 mol of a weak acid (pKa 6.0) is mixed with 0.10 mol NaOH in water. What is the pH of the resulting solution?
o: The acid is half neutralized, so the pH is pKa, not that of the free acid.
Correct: half the acid is converted to A⁻, so [HA] = [A⁻] and pH = pKa.
The mixture is a buffer, not a neutral solution.
NaOH is fully consumed, so it does not set the pH.
questions.note: Half-neutralizing a weak acid makes a buffer with pH = pKa.
questions.x: NaOH reacts completely with the weak acid: 0.10 mol OH⁻ converts 0.10 mol HA to A⁻, leaving 0.10 mol HA and 0.10 mol A⁻. With equal amounts, log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 0, so pH = pKa = 6.0, regardless of the volume. This is the half-equivalence point of a titration, and the mixture is a buffer, not a neutral solution.

questions.q: A weak acid has pKa 5.0. At pH 4.0, approximately what fraction of the acid is in the protonated form?
o: This is the deprotonated fraction.
This applies only when pH = pKa.
This would need pH 2 units below pKa.
questions.x: Henderson–Hasselbalch gives log([A⁻]/[HA]) = pH − pKa = 4.0 − 5.0 = −1, so [A⁻]/[HA] = 1/10. Out of 11 total parts, 10 are HA, so about 91% is protonated and 9% is deprotonated. Rule of thumb: one pH unit below pKa is about 91% protonated, two units below is about 99%.

questions.q: Aspirin is a weak acid (pKa ≈ 3.5). In the stomach (pH 1.5), which form predominates, and how does it affect absorption across lipid membranes?
o: The neutral protonated form, which crosses membranes readily
Correct: pH is 2 units below pKa, so about 99% is uncharged HA.
The anionic form, which crosses membranes readily
Below pKa the protonated form dominates, and ions cross lipids poorly.
The neutral form, which cannot cross membranes
Uncharged molecules pass through lipid bilayers more easily.
Equal amounts of both forms
That requires pH = pKa.
questions.x: When pH is below the pKa, the protonated form of an acid dominates; at 2 units below, the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] is 10⁻², so about 99% of aspirin is the neutral HA form. Uncharged molecules dissolve in the lipid bilayer and diffuse across it far more easily than ions, which are held back by their hydration shells. So a weak acid drug is well suited to cross membranes in an acidic environment.

questions.q: What is the pH of a solution that is 0.20 M NH₃ and 0.20 M NH₄Cl? (pKb of NH₃ = 4.75)
o: This is the pOH, not the pH.
A weak base buffer is not neutral.
Correct: equal concentrations give pH = pKa(NH₄⁺) = 14 − 4.75.
Off by one unit; pKa(NH₄⁺) = 14 − 4.75 = 9.25.
questions.x: Equal concentrations of a weak base and its conjugate acid form a buffer with pH = pKa of the acid form. For NH₄⁺, pKa = 14 − pKb = 14 − 4.75 = 9.25. Equivalently, pOH = pKb = 4.75, and pH = 14 − 4.75. Reporting 4.75 confuses the pOH with the pH; an ammonia buffer must be basic.

questions.q: How does an acetate buffer neutralize a small amount of added HCl?
o: Acetate ions react with H⁺ to form acetic acid
Correct: the conjugate base consumes added acid.
Acetic acid reacts with H⁺ to form acetate
Acetic acid is the component that neutralizes added base.
Na⁺ ions bind the Cl⁻ ions
Spectator ions do not affect pH.
Water reacts with H⁺ to form OH⁻
Water does not convert H⁺ into OH⁻.
questions.x: Each buffer component handles one kind of threat: the conjugate base neutralizes added acid, and the weak acid neutralizes added base. Added H⁺ reacts with acetate, CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH, turning a strong acid into a weak one, so pH changes only slightly. Acetic acid itself cannot take up more H⁺; it is the part that reacts with OH⁻.

questions.q: In a buffer, the pH is 2 units above the pKa. What is [A⁻]/[HA]?
o: Inverted the ratio; pH above pKa favors A⁻.
Forgot to take the antilog.
The antilog of 2 is 100, not 20.
Correct: log(ratio) = 2, so ratio = 10².
questions.x: From Henderson–Hasselbalch, log([A⁻]/[HA]) = pH − pKa = +2, so the ratio is 10² = 100. Each pH unit above the pKa multiplies the base-to-acid ratio by 10. A positive difference means more base form, so a ratio of 0.01 has the direction backwards.

questions.q: 1.0 L of buffer contains 0.50 mol HA and 0.50 mol NaA (pKa 7.0). After 0.10 mol NaOH is added, what is the pH? (log 1.5 ≈ 0.18)
o: Used the inverse ratio; added base raises pH.
Ignored the reaction of OH⁻ with HA.
Treated the NaOH as if no buffer were present.
questions.x: Stoichiometry first: 0.10 mol OH⁻ converts 0.10 mol HA into A⁻, giving 0.40 mol HA and 0.60 mol A⁻. Then pH = 7.0 + log(0.60/0.40) = 7.0 + log 1.5 = 7.18. Added base must raise the pH, and the large buffer amounts keep the rise small, so 6.82 and 13.0 are both ruled out.

questions.q: What is the pH at the equivalence point when a strong acid is titrated with a strong base at 25 °C?
o: Below 7
Only a weak base titration gives an acidic equivalence point.
Above 7
Only a weak acid titration gives a basic equivalence point.
Equal to the pKa of the acid
pH = pKa at the half-equivalence point of a weak acid.
Correct: the products are water and a neutral salt.
questions.x: At the equivalence point all the acid and base have reacted, so pH depends on what is left in solution. Strong acid plus strong base gives water and a salt whose ions (like Na⁺ and Cl⁻) do not hydrolyze, so pH = 7 at 25 °C. Equivalence pH is above 7 only when a weak acid is titrated (its conjugate base remains) and below 7 for a weak base.

questions.q: When NH₃ is titrated with HCl, the pH at the equivalence point is:
o: Below 7, because NH₄⁺ is a weak acid
Correct: the conjugate acid formed hydrolyzes to release H⁺.
Exactly 7
A neutral equivalence point requires a strong acid and strong base.
Above 7, because NH₃ remains
At equivalence, essentially all NH₃ has been converted to NH₄⁺.
Above 7, because Cl⁻ is basic
Cl⁻ is a negligible base.
questions.x: At equivalence, all NH₃ has been converted to NH₄⁺ by the reaction NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺. NH₄⁺ is a weak acid (pKa 9.25) and partially donates H⁺ to water, while Cl⁻ is a negligible base, so the solution is acidic. A weak base titrated with a strong acid always has an equivalence point below 7.

questions.q: In a titration of 50 mL of a weak acid, the equivalence point occurs at 25 mL of NaOH. At 12.5 mL of NaOH the pH is 4.8. What is the acid's pKa?
o: Halved the pH; the volume, not the pH, is halved.
Correct: at half-equivalence, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.
Subtracted 4.8 from 14; that gives pKb of the conjugate base.
Doubled the pH; pKa equals the half-equivalence pH directly.
questions.x: At the half-equivalence point, exactly half the weak acid has been converted to A⁻, so [HA] = [A⁻] and Henderson–Hasselbalch gives pH = pKa. Half of 25 mL is 12.5 mL, so the measured pH of 4.8 equals the pKa. Volume is halved to locate this point, but the pH is read directly with no halving or doubling.

questions.q: What volume of 0.10 M NaOH is needed to neutralize 25 mL of 0.20 M HCl?
o: Inverted the concentration ratio.
25 mL
Equal volumes work only for equal concentrations.
50 mL
Correct: 5.0 mmol HCl requires 5.0 mmol NaOH = 50 mL.
100 mL
Doubled twice; 5.0 mmol ÷ 0.10 M = 50 mL.
questions.x: At neutralization, moles of H⁺ equal moles of OH⁻. HCl provides 0.025 L × 0.20 M = 5.0 mmol, so NaOH must supply 5.0 mmol: 5.0 mmol ÷ 0.10 M = 50 mL. Because the base is half as concentrated as the acid, twice the volume is needed.

questions.q: How many mL of 0.10 M NaOH are required to fully neutralize 20 mL of 0.10 M H₂SO₄?
o: 10 mL
Divided by 2 instead of multiplying.
20 mL
Ignored the second acidic proton.
40 mL
Correct: 2.0 mmol H₂SO₄ supplies 4.0 mmol H⁺.
80 mL
Counted four acidic protons.
questions.x: Neutralization matches moles of H⁺ with moles of OH⁻, so count acidic protons. 20 mL × 0.10 M = 2.0 mmol H₂SO₄, and each releases 2 H⁺, giving 4.0 mmol H⁺. That requires 4.0 mmol OH⁻, or 4.0 mmol ÷ 0.10 M = 40 mL. Ignoring the second proton gives only 20 mL.

questions.q: 30 mL of 0.10 M NaOH neutralizes 20 mL of an acetic acid solution. What is the acetic acid concentration?
o: Inverted the volume ratio.
Assumed equal concentrations despite unequal volumes.
Correct: 3.0 mmol NaOH = 3.0 mmol acid, ÷ 20 mL = 0.15 M.
Decimal error; 3.0 mmol ÷ 20 mL = 0.15 M.
questions.x: Acetic acid is monoprotic, so at equivalence moles of acid equal moles of OH⁻ added: 30 mL × 0.10 M = 3.0 mmol. Dividing by the acid's volume gives 3.0 mmol ÷ 20 mL = 0.15 M. It took more base volume than acid volume, so the acid must be more concentrated than the base, ruling out 0.067 M.

questions.q: A weak acid is titrated with NaOH, and the equivalence point is at pH 8.8. Which indicator is best?
o: Methyl orange (transition pH 3.1–4.4)
It would change color long before equivalence.
Phenolphthalein (transition pH 8.2–10)
Correct: its color change brackets the equivalence pH.
Methyl red (transition pH 4.4–6.2)
Its range is well below the equivalence pH.
Bromothymol blue (transition pH 6.0–7.6)
It changes before the weak acid is fully neutralized.
questions.x: An indicator changes color over a range of about pKa ± 1, so the best choice is one whose transition range includes the equivalence-point pH. Weak acid–strong base titrations have basic equivalence points (here 8.8) because the conjugate base remains. Phenolphthalein (8.2–10) fits; methyl orange, methyl red and bromothymol blue would all change color too early, before the acid is fully neutralized.

questions.q: An indicator has pKa 5.0. Over approximately what pH range will its color change be visible?
o: Too broad; color change spans about 2 pH units.
Correct: the visible transition is roughly pKa ± 1.
The range is centered on the pKa, not starting at it.
Used pKb (14 − 5) instead of pKa.
questions.x: An indicator's color depends on the ratio [In⁻]/[HIn]. The eye sees mostly one color when that ratio is beyond about 10:1 either way, which by Henderson–Hasselbalch is pH = pKa ± 1. So an indicator with pKa 5.0 changes visibly between about pH 4 and 6, centered on its pKa.

questions.q: An indicator HIn is red and In⁻ is blue, with pKa = 6.0. What color is a solution at pH 3?
o: Blue
Blue (In⁻) dominates at pH above about 7.
Purple
A mixed color appears only near pH 6.
Colorless
Both forms are colored; one must dominate.
Red
Correct: pH is well below pKa, so the protonated HIn form dominates.
questions.x: An indicator is a weak acid whose two forms have different colors. When pH is below the pKa, the protonated form HIn dominates; at pH 3, 3 units below pKa 6, [In⁻]/[HIn] = 10⁻³, so the solution looks red. Blue would appear only well above pH 6, and a mixed purple only near pH 6.

questions.q: Why should only a few drops of indicator be used in an acid–base titration?
o: The indicator is itself a weak acid and consumes titrant
Correct: a large amount of indicator would shift the volume needed to reach the endpoint.
Indicators catalyze the neutralization reaction
Indicators do not act as catalysts.
Indicators raise the equivalence-point pH by 2 units
A few drops have negligible effect; the issue is consuming titrant.
More indicator makes the color change slower
Color change speed is not the concern.
questions.x: Indicators are weak acids or bases, so they react with titrant just like the analyte. A large amount of indicator would use up measurable base or acid and shift the endpoint volume away from the true equivalence volume. A few drops supply so little indicator that its consumption is negligible while the color is still visible.

questions.q: When a diprotic acid H₂A is titrated with NaOH, how many buffer regions (half-equivalence points) appear on the curve?
o: One
Each acidic proton gives its own buffer region.
Three
A diprotic acid has only two ionizable protons.
Four
There are two half-equivalence points and two equivalence points, not four buffer regions.
Two
Correct: one for H₂A/HA⁻ and one for HA⁻/A²⁻.
questions.x: Each ionizable proton gives a separate buffer region with its own half-equivalence point, where pH = pKa for that step. A diprotic acid has two: one where [H₂A] = [HA⁻] (pH = pKa₁) and one where [HA⁻] = [A²⁻] (pH = pKa₂). It also shows two equivalence points, but those are steep jumps, not buffer regions.

questions.q: 0.10 M HCl and 0.10 M CH₃COOH are titrated with the same NaOH solution. Which is true at the start of each titration?
o: The acetic acid solution has a higher initial pH
Correct: acetic acid ionizes only partially, giving less H⁺.
The HCl solution has a higher initial pH
Full ionization gives HCl more H⁺, so lower pH.
Both start at pH 1
Only the strong acid starts at pH 1.
Both start at pH 7
Both are acids.
questions.x: At equal concentration, a strong acid produces more H⁺ than a weak acid. 0.10 M HCl is fully ionized and starts at pH 1, while 0.10 M acetic acid ionizes only about 1%, starting near pH 2.9. So the weak acid's curve begins higher and has a buffer region, even though both need the same volume of base to reach equivalence.

questions.q: 25 mL each of 0.10 M HCl and 0.10 M CH₃COOH are titrated with 0.10 M NaOH. How do the volumes needed to reach equivalence compare?
o: HCl requires more NaOH
Both contain 2.5 mmol of acidic protons.
Acetic acid requires more NaOH
Weak acids do not need extra base; the equilibrium shifts as base is added.
Acetic acid cannot be fully neutralized
OH⁻ reacts essentially completely with weak acids.
They are equal
Correct: equivalence depends only on moles of acid, not on acid strength.
questions.note: Trap: acid strength changes the equivalence pH, not the equivalence volume.
questions.x: The equivalence point is reached when moles of OH⁻ added equal moles of acid initially present, regardless of acid strength. Both solutions contain 25 mL × 0.10 M = 2.5 mmol of monoprotic acid, so both need 25 mL of 0.10 M NaOH. As OH⁻ removes H⁺, the weak acid keeps ionizing until it is fully consumed. Strength affects the pH curve, not the equivalence volume.

questions.q: 0.10 mol of weak acid HA (Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵) is titrated to equivalence with NaOH, giving 1.0 L total. What is the pH at equivalence?
o: This is pKa, the half-equivalence pH.
A⁻ is a weak base, so the solution is basic.
Used Kb = 10⁻⁵ instead of Kw/Ka.
questions.x: At equivalence, all HA has become A⁻, so the solution is 0.10 M A⁻, a weak base. Convert first: Kb = Kw/Ka = 10⁻¹⁴/10⁻⁵ = 10⁻⁹. Then [OH⁻] ≈ √(Kb·C) = √(10⁻¹⁰) = 10⁻⁵ M, so pOH = 5 and pH = 9. A weak acid–strong base titration always has a basic equivalence point.

questions.q: What distinguishes the endpoint from the equivalence point in a titration?
o: They are always identical
Indicator choice can make the endpoint deviate from equivalence.
Endpoint is the color change; equivalence is where moles match
Correct: equivalence is stoichiometric; a well-chosen indicator makes the endpoint nearly coincide.
The endpoint always occurs at pH 7
Endpoint pH depends on the indicator.
Equivalence occurs at half the endpoint volume
That describes the half-equivalence point.
questions.x: The equivalence point is a stoichiometric fact: the moment when moles of added titrant exactly match moles of analyte. The endpoint is an observation: when the indicator changes color. A good indicator is chosen so its color change occurs at nearly the equivalence pH, making the two almost coincide, but they are not identical by definition.

questions.q: Glycine has pKa values of 2.3 (carboxyl) and 9.7 (amino). What is its isoelectric point?
o: Subtracted pKa values and halved them.
Physiological pH is not the same as the pI.
Added the pKa values without dividing by 2.
questions.x: The isoelectric point is the pH at which the molecule has no net charge. For an amino acid without an ionizable side chain, pI is the average of the two pKa values on either side of the zwitterion: (2.3 + 9.7)/2 = 6.0. At pI, small amounts of + and − forms balance out. pI is a property of the molecule, while 7.4 is just physiological pH.

questions.q: 20 mL of 0.10 M HCl is mixed with 30 mL of 0.10 M NaOH. What is the pH? (log 2 ≈ 0.3)
o: This is the pOH.
Base is in excess, so it is past equivalence.
Correct: excess OH⁻ = 1.0 mmol in 50 mL = 0.020 M; pOH 1.7, pH 12.3.
Used the stock 0.10 M NaOH; only the excess OH⁻ diluted into 50 mL sets the pH.
questions.x: For strong acid–strong base mixtures, neutralize moles, then divide the excess by the total volume. H⁺ = 2.0 mmol and OH⁻ = 3.0 mmol, so 1.0 mmol OH⁻ remains in 50 mL: [OH⁻] = 0.020 M. pOH = 2 − log 2 = 1.7, so pH = 14 − 1.7 = 12.3. Reporting 1.7 gives the pOH, not the pH.

questions.q: Why is the second acid dissociation constant of H₃PO₄ much smaller than the first?
o: Removing H⁺ from the negative H₂PO₄⁻ ion is harder than from neutral H₃PO₄
Correct: electrostatic attraction holds the proton more tightly to an anion.
H₂PO₄⁻ has fewer oxygen atoms
Both species have four oxygens.
The second proton is bonded to phosphorus
All acidic protons are on oxygen.
The first dissociation is endothermic
The trend arises from charge, not from this claim.
questions.x: Each successive proton is harder to remove because it must leave an increasingly negative ion. Pulling H⁺ off neutral H₃PO₄ leaves H₂PO₄⁻, but pulling the next H⁺ off H₂PO₄⁻ requires separating a positive proton from an anion, which electrostatically attracts it. That is why Ka values drop by roughly 10⁵ per step (pKa 2.1, 7.2, 12.3). All acidic protons sit on oxygen atoms.

questions.q: Phosphoric acid has pKa values 2.1, 7.2 and 12.3. Which species predominates at pH 10?
o: H₂PO₄⁻
This dominates between pH 2.1 and 7.2.
PO₄³⁻
This dominates only above pH 12.3.
H₃PO₄
This dominates only below pH 2.1.
HPO₄²⁻
Correct: pH 10 lies between pKa₂ and pKa₃.
questions.x: For a polyprotic acid, each species dominates in the pH window between the pKa values that form and remove it. H₃PO₄ dominates below 2.1, H₂PO₄⁻ from 2.1 to 7.2, HPO₄²⁻ from 7.2 to 12.3, and PO₄³⁻ above 12.3. pH 10 falls in the HPO₄²⁻ window. Above a pKa the deprotonated partner of that pair wins, so at pH 10 HPO₄²⁻ beats H₂PO₄⁻.

questions.q: Carbonic acid has pKa₁ = 6.4 and pKa₂ = 10.3. Which species predominates at pH 12?
o: CO₃²⁻
Correct: pH is above pKa₂, so the fully deprotonated form dominates.
HCO₃⁻
Bicarbonate dominates between pH 6.4 and 10.3.
H₂CO₃
Carbonic acid dominates below pH 6.4.
CO₂(g)
CO₂ is favored in acidic conditions.
questions.x: Above a given pKa, the deprotonated member of that conjugate pair predominates. At pH 12, the solution is above both pKa₁ (6.4) and pKa₂ (10.3), so carbonic acid is converted all the way to CO₃²⁻. Bicarbonate dominates only between 6.4 and 10.3, and CO₂/H₂CO₃ only in acidic solution.

questions.q: For a diprotic acid with Ka₁ = 10⁻⁴ and Ka₂ = 10⁻⁹, the pH of a 0.1 M solution is determined mainly by:
o: The second dissociation only
The second step contributes far less H⁺.
The sum of Ka₁ and Ka₂ equally
The two steps contribute very unequal amounts.
The product Ka₁ × Ka₂
The product governs overall H₂A → A²⁻, not the pH here.
The first dissociation only
Correct: Ka₂ is 10⁵ times smaller, so the second step adds negligible H⁺.
questions.x: When successive Ka values differ by a large factor, the first ionization supplies essentially all the H⁺. Here Ka₁ = 10⁻⁴ gives [H⁺] ≈ √(10⁻⁴ × 0.1) ≈ 3 × 10⁻³ M, while HA⁻ (Ka₂ = 10⁻⁹) ionizes so little in that already acidic solution that it adds a negligible amount. So you can treat the acid as monoprotic using Ka₁ only.

questions.q: Carbonic acid has pKa₁ = 6.4 and pKa₂ = 10.3. What is the approximate pH of a NaHCO₃ solution?
o: This is pKa₁, the pH of an H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻ buffer.
Bicarbonate is not neutral; it is mildly basic.
Correct: for an amphiprotic species, pH ≈ (pKa₁ + pKa₂)/2.
This is pKa₂, the pH of an HCO₃⁻/CO₃²⁻ buffer.
questions.x: HCO₃⁻ is amphiprotic: it can lose H⁺ (governed by pKa₂) or gain H⁺ (governed by pKa₁). Its competing reactions balance at a pH that is the average of the two pKa values: (6.4 + 10.3)/2 ≈ 8.35. So baking soda solutions are mildly basic. pKa₁ or pKa₂ alone would apply only to buffers containing both members of one conjugate pair.

questions.q: Which statement about sulfuric acid in water is correct?
o: Both ionizations are complete at all concentrations
HSO₄⁻ ionization is incomplete, especially at higher concentration.
The first ionization is complete; the second is partial (Ka₂ ≈ 10⁻²)
Correct: HSO₄⁻ is a moderately weak acid.
Neither ionization is complete
The first proton is lost completely.
The second ionization is stronger than the first
Removing H⁺ from an anion is harder.
questions.x: Sulfuric acid's first proton ionizes essentially completely, making H₂SO₄ a strong acid. The second proton must leave the negatively charged HSO₄⁻ ion, which holds it more tightly, so HSO₄⁻ is only a moderately weak acid with Ka₂ ≈ 10⁻². Many simple problems assume both protons come off, but strictly the second ionization is partial.

questions.q: Citric acid is triprotic. How many moles of NaOH fully neutralize 1 mole of citric acid?
o: This neutralizes only the first proton.
Ignores the third acidic proton.
Correct: one OH⁻ per acidic proton.
Doubled the number of protons.
questions.x: Full neutralization requires one OH⁻ for every acidic proton. Citric acid is triprotic (three carboxylic acid groups), so 1 mol of acid needs 3 mol NaOH. This is why polyprotic acids show one equivalence point per acidic proton in a titration.

questions.q: In a phosphoric acid solution at pH equal to pKa₂, which relationship holds?
o: [H₂PO₄⁻] = [HPO₄²⁻]
Correct: pH = pKa means the two forms of that conjugate pair are equal.
[H₃PO₄] = [H₂PO₄⁻]
That occurs at pH = pKa₁.
[HPO₄²⁻] = [PO₄³⁻]
That occurs at pH = pKa₃.
[H₃PO₄] = [PO₄³⁻]
These are not a conjugate pair; equality has no simple pKa rule.
questions.x: At pH = pKa for any step, the acid and base forms of that conjugate pair are present in equal amounts, because log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 0. pKa₂ belongs to the H₂PO₄⁻ ⇌ HPO₄²⁻ + H⁺ step, so those two are equal. pKa₁ and pKa₃ refer to different conjugate pairs.

questions.q: What is the Ksp expression for Ca₃(PO₄)₂?
o: [Ca²⁺]³[PO₄³⁻]²
Correct: each ion is raised to its stoichiometric coefficient; the solid is omitted.
[Ca²⁺]²[PO₄³⁻]³
The exponents are swapped.
3[Ca²⁺] × 2[PO₄³⁻]
Coefficients become exponents, not multipliers.
[Ca²⁺]³[PO₄³⁻]² / [Ca₃(PO₄)₂]
Pure solids are excluded from equilibrium expressions.
questions.x: Ksp is the equilibrium constant for a solid dissolving into its ions: Ca₃(PO₄)₂(s) ⇌ 3 Ca²⁺ + 2 PO₄³⁻. Each ion concentration is raised to its coefficient, giving Ksp = [Ca²⁺]³[PO₄³⁻]². The solid is left out because a pure solid's activity is 1. Coefficients become exponents, never multipliers.

questions.q: The molar solubility of AgBr in pure water is 7 × 10⁻⁷ M. What is its Ksp?
o: Correct: Ksp = s² = (7 × 10⁻⁷)² = 4.9 × 10⁻¹³.
Used 4s²; that form is not correct for a 1:1 salt.
This is the molar solubility, not Ksp.
Doubled s instead of squaring it.
questions.x: For a 1:1 salt like AgBr, dissolving s mol/L gives [Ag⁺] = s and [Br⁻] = s, so Ksp = s·s = s². Squaring 7 × 10⁻⁷ gives 49 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 4.9 × 10⁻¹³. The 4s³ form applies only to salts that release one ion of one type and two of another, like CaF₂.

questions.q: A salt MX₂ has Ksp = 4 × 10⁻⁹. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
o: Used Ksp = s², which applies only to 1:1 salts.
Correct: Ksp = (s)(2s)² = 4s³, so s³ = 10⁻⁹ and s = 10⁻³ M.
Took the cube root of 4 × 10⁻⁹ without first dividing by 4.
This is [X⁻] = 2s, not the molar solubility of the salt.
questions.x: Set up the dissolution with an ICE approach: MX₂(s) ⇌ M²⁺ + 2 X⁻, so [M²⁺] = s and [X⁻] = 2s. Then Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³; with 4s³ = 4 × 10⁻⁹, s³ = 10⁻⁹ and s = 10⁻³ M. Molar solubility is moles of salt dissolved per liter, so it equals [M²⁺], not the doubled [X⁻].

questions.q: Ag₂CrO₄ has Ksp = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
o: Used s² = Ksp as for a 1:1 salt.
Correct: 4s³ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹, s³ = 8 × 10⁻¹², s = 2 × 10⁻⁴ M.
Took a cube root of 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ without dividing by 4.
This is [Ag⁺] = 2s.
questions.x: Ag₂CrO₄ ⇌ 2 Ag⁺ + CrO₄²⁻, so [Ag⁺] = 2s and [CrO₄²⁻] = s, giving Ksp = (2s)²(s) = 4s³. Then s³ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ ÷ 4 = 8 × 10⁻¹², and the cube root is 2 × 10⁻⁴ M. Remember the factor of 4 comes from squaring the 2s, and molar solubility refers to the salt, not to [Ag⁺].

questions.q: Salt AB has Ksp = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰, and salt AB₂ has Ksp = 4 × 10⁻¹². Which is more soluble in pure water (mol/L)?
o: AB, because its Ksp is larger
Ksp can compare solubility only for salts of the same ion ratio.
They are equally soluble
Their computed solubilities differ by a factor of 10.
AB, with s = 1 × 10⁻⁵ M
That value is correct for AB, but it is smaller than AB₂'s.
AB₂, with s = 1 × 10⁻⁴ M
Correct: AB has s = 10⁻⁵ M; AB₂ has 4s³ = 4 × 10⁻¹², s = 10⁻⁴ M.
questions.note: Trap: compare Ksp directly only for salts with the same stoichiometry.
questions.x: Ksp values can rank solubility directly only when salts have the same ion ratio, because the Ksp expression has different forms. For AB, Ksp = s², so s = √(10⁻¹⁰) = 10⁻⁵ M. For AB₂, Ksp = 4s³, so s³ = 10⁻¹² and s = 10⁻⁴ M. Despite its smaller Ksp, AB₂ is ten times more soluble.

questions.q: Equal volumes of 2 × 10⁻⁴ M AgNO₃ and 2 × 10⁻⁴ M NaCl are mixed. Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. What happens?
o: No precipitate forms because Q < Ksp
Q = 10⁻⁸ is far larger than 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰.
No precipitate forms because both salts are soluble
Soluble reactants can still form an insoluble product.
Precipitation occurs only if Q equals exactly Ksp
Q = Ksp means saturated; Q > Ksp means precipitation.
AgCl precipitates because Q = 1 × 10⁻⁸ exceeds Ksp
Correct: after mixing each ion is 1 × 10⁻⁴ M; Q = 10⁻⁸ > Ksp.
questions.x: Mixing equal volumes halves each concentration, so [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = 1 × 10⁻⁴ M right after mixing. The ion product Q = (10⁻⁴)(10⁻⁴) = 10⁻⁸, which is far larger than Ksp = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰, so AgCl precipitates until Q falls to Ksp. Both starting salts are soluble, but their ions can still combine into an insoluble product.

questions.q: Which compound is least soluble in water?
o: NaNO₃
Sodium and nitrate salts are soluble.
KCl
Potassium salts are soluble.
NH₄Br
Ammonium salts are soluble.
BaSO₄
Correct: barium sulfate is a classic insoluble sulfate.
questions.x: Solubility rules: salts of Group 1 cations (Na⁺, K⁺), ammonium and nitrate are essentially always soluble. Sulfates are usually soluble, with major exceptions such as BaSO₄, PbSO₄ and SrSO₄. BaSO₄ is so insoluble (Ksp ≈ 10⁻¹⁰) that it is used as a safe X-ray contrast agent even though Ba²⁺ is toxic.

questions.q: Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. What is the molar solubility of AgCl in 0.10 M NaCl?
o: Multiplied Ksp by 0.10 instead of dividing.
Correct: s = Ksp/[Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 0.10.
This is the solubility in pure water, ignoring the common ion.
This is [Cl⁻] from NaCl, not dissolved AgCl.
questions.x: The common-ion effect: Cl⁻ from NaCl shifts AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ to the left, lowering solubility. Because [Cl⁻] ≈ 0.10 M from NaCl and the AgCl contribution is negligible, Ksp = s(0.10), so s = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M. That is roughly 10,000 times lower than the 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M solubility in pure water.

questions.q: CaF₂ has Ksp = 4 × 10⁻¹¹. What is its molar solubility in 0.10 M NaF?
o: Did not square [F⁻].
Divided Ksp by 4 as in the pure-water case.
Correct: Ksp = s(0.10)², so s = 4 × 10⁻¹¹ ÷ 10⁻² = 4 × 10⁻⁹ M.
Ignored the common ion.
questions.x: With a common ion, the added F⁻ dominates: [F⁻] ≈ 0.10 M while [Ca²⁺] = s. Ksp = [Ca²⁺][F⁻]² = s(0.10)², so s = 4 × 10⁻¹¹ ÷ 10⁻² = 4 × 10⁻⁹ M. Because F⁻ is squared in the Ksp expression, the common ion suppresses solubility even more strongly than for a 1:1 salt.

questions.q: How does lowering the pH affect the solubility of Mg(OH)₂?
o: Solubility increases because H⁺ removes OH⁻
Correct: consuming OH⁻ shifts Mg(OH)₂ ⇌ Mg²⁺ + 2OH⁻ to the right.
Solubility decreases because H⁺ is a common ion
H⁺ is not part of the dissolution equilibrium.
Solubility is unchanged because Ksp is constant
Ksp is constant, but removing OH⁻ lets more solid dissolve.
Solubility decreases because Mg²⁺ is protonated
Mg²⁺ does not accept protons.
questions.x: Mg(OH)₂(s) ⇌ Mg²⁺ + 2 OH⁻. Adding acid removes OH⁻ by forming water, so by Le Châtelier the equilibrium shifts right and more solid dissolves. Ksp itself is unchanged; only the ion concentrations rearrange. This is why antacids like milk of magnesia dissolve in stomach acid. Any salt with a basic anion becomes more soluble at low pH.

questions.q: Which salt's solubility is least affected by adding strong acid?
o: CaCO₃
Carbonate is protonated, so acid strongly increases solubility.
Ca₃(PO₄)₂
Phosphate is a strong-ish base; acid dissolves it.
Mg(OH)₂
Hydroxide is neutralized by acid, increasing solubility.
AgCl
Correct: Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid and is not protonated.
questions.note: Salts with basic anions dissolve better in acid.
questions.x: Acid raises a salt's solubility only if the salt's anion is basic enough to be protonated, which removes it from the dissolution equilibrium. Carbonate, phosphate and hydroxide all react with H⁺, so their salts dissolve more in acid. Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of the strong acid HCl and does not take up H⁺, so AgCl's solubility barely changes.

questions.q: For a salt whose dissolution is endothermic, what happens to its Ksp as temperature increases?
o: Ksp increases
Correct: Le Châtelier treats heat as a reactant, so heating favors dissolution.
Ksp decreases
That is true for exothermic dissolution.
Ksp stays constant
Equilibrium constants change with temperature.
Ksp depends only on pressure
Ksp for solids depends on temperature, not pressure.
questions.x: For an endothermic dissolution, heat acts like a reactant: heat + solid ⇌ ions. Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the ions, so Ksp increases. Unlike Q or concentrations, equilibrium constants change only with temperature. If dissolution were exothermic, heating would instead lower Ksp.

questions.q: Solid NaCl is added to a saturated PbCl₂ solution at constant temperature. Which quantity remains unchanged?
o: Molar solubility of PbCl₂
The common ion lowers solubility.
Ksp of PbCl₂
Correct: Ksp depends only on temperature.
[Pb²⁺] in solution
Pb²⁺ precipitates as PbCl₂ when Cl⁻ is added.
[Cl⁻] in solution
Added NaCl raises [Cl⁻].
questions.x: Ksp is an equilibrium constant, so at a fixed temperature it does not change no matter what is added. Adding NaCl raises [Cl⁻], making Q larger than Ksp, so PbCl₂ precipitates and [Pb²⁺] falls until [Pb²⁺][Cl⁻]² again equals Ksp. The molar solubility of PbCl₂ drops (common-ion effect), but the constant stays the same.

questions.q: NaCl is slowly added to a solution containing 0.01 M Ag⁺ and 0.01 M Pb²⁺. Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰; Ksp(PbCl₂) = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵. Which precipitates first?
o: PbCl₂
It needs a much higher [Cl⁻] to reach its Ksp.
AgCl
Correct: AgCl needs only [Cl⁻] ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁸ M; PbCl₂ needs [Cl⁻] ≈ 4 × 10⁻² M.
Both precipitate at the same [Cl⁻]
Their required [Cl⁻] differ by about 10⁶.
Neither, because chlorides are soluble
AgCl and PbCl₂ are exceptions to chloride solubility.
questions.x: Each salt starts to precipitate when its ion product reaches Ksp, so find the [Cl⁻] each one needs. AgCl: [Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 0.01 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁸ M. PbCl₂: [Cl⁻]² = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 0.01, so [Cl⁻] ≈ 0.04 M. AgCl needs far less chloride, so it precipitates first, which allows selective precipitation.

questions.q: In a solution of a sparingly soluble salt, the ion product Q is less than Ksp. The solution is:
o: Saturated
Saturation corresponds to Q = Ksp.
Supersaturated
Supersaturation corresponds to Q > Ksp.
Unsaturated, so more solid can dissolve
Correct: Q < Ksp means the system has not reached equilibrium with the solid.
About to precipitate
Precipitation occurs when Q exceeds Ksp.
questions.x: Compare the ion product Q with Ksp to predict what a solution will do. Q < Ksp means the solution is unsaturated, so more solid can dissolve; Q = Ksp means saturated and at equilibrium; Q > Ksp means supersaturated, and precipitation is expected. This mirrors the general Q-versus-K test for any equilibrium.

questions.q: Fe(OH)₃ has Ksp = 1 × 10⁻³⁶. At what pH will it begin to precipitate from 1 × 10⁻³ M Fe³⁺?
o: pH 11
This is the pOH.
pH 7
Fe(OH)₃ is so insoluble it precipitates even in acid.
pH 2
Did not take the cube root properly; [OH⁻] = 10⁻¹¹ M.
pH 3
Correct: [OH⁻]³ = 10⁻³⁶/10⁻³ = 10⁻³³, [OH⁻] = 10⁻¹¹, pOH 11, pH 3.
questions.x: Precipitation begins when Q = [Fe³⁺][OH⁻]³ reaches Ksp. Solve for [OH⁻]: [OH⁻]³ = 10⁻³⁶ ÷ 10⁻³ = 10⁻³³, so [OH⁻] = 10⁻¹¹ M. That gives pOH = 11 and pH = 3. Fe(OH)₃ is so insoluble that it forms even in quite acidic solution; 11 is the pOH, not the pH.

questions.q: More solid AgCl is added to a saturated AgCl solution at constant temperature. What happens to [Ag⁺]?
o: It stays the same
Correct: a saturated solution is already at equilibrium; extra solid simply sits undissolved.
It increases
The solution cannot hold more dissolved ions.
It decreases
Adding solid does not remove ions from solution.
It doubles
Solids do not appear in Ksp, so adding solid does not shift equilibrium.
questions.x: In a saturated solution, dissolution and precipitation are already balanced, so [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = Ksp. Adding more solid does not change the ion concentrations, because pure solids do not appear in the equilibrium expression; the extra solid simply remains undissolved. Only temperature or another added ion would change [Ag⁺].

questions.q: Mg(OH)₂ has Ksp = 4 × 10⁻¹². What is the pH of a saturated solution? (log 2 ≈ 0.3)
o: This is the pOH.
Used Ksp = s², giving [OH⁻] = 2 × 10⁻⁶ M and pOH 5.7.
Used [OH⁻] = s rather than 2s.
questions.x: Mg(OH)₂ ⇌ Mg²⁺ + 2 OH⁻, so Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³ = 4 × 10⁻¹², giving s = 10⁻⁴ M. Then [OH⁻] = 2s = 2 × 10⁻⁴ M, so pOH = 4 − log 2 = 3.7 and pH = 14 − 3.7 = 10.3. Using [OH⁻] = s gives pH 10.0, because it forgets that each formula unit releases two hydroxides.

questions.q: PbI₂ dissolves to give a molar solubility s. Which expressions are correct?
o: [Pb²⁺] = s, [I⁻] = s, Ksp = s²
Each formula unit releases two iodide ions.
[Pb²⁺] = 2s, [I⁻] = s, Ksp = 4s³
The 2 belongs to iodide, not lead.
[Pb²⁺] = s, [I⁻] = 2s, Ksp = 4s³
Correct: (s)(2s)² = 4s³.
[Pb²⁺] = s, [I⁻] = 2s, Ksp = 2s²
(2s)² must be squared: Ksp = s·4s².
questions.x: PbI₂(s) ⇌ Pb²⁺ + 2 I⁻. If s mol/L dissolves, [Pb²⁺] = s and [I⁻] = 2s, so Ksp = (s)(2s)² = 4s³. The coefficient 2 goes on iodide and is both multiplied into the concentration and used as the exponent. Forgetting to square the 2 gives the wrong 2s² form.

questions.q: AgCl is barely soluble in water but dissolves when aqueous NH₃ is added. Why?
o: Ag⁺ forms the complex ion [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺, pulling the equilibrium toward dissolution
Correct: complexation removes free Ag⁺.
NH₃ raises the pH and protonates Cl⁻
Cl⁻ is not protonated, and higher pH would not do that anyway.
NH₃ is a common ion with AgCl
NH₃ is not part of the AgCl equilibrium.
NH₃ oxidizes Ag⁺ to a soluble form
No redox reaction occurs; Ag stays +1.
questions.x: NH₃ is a Lewis base that binds Ag⁺ to form the stable complex [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺. This removes free Ag⁺ from solution, so by Le Châtelier the dissolution AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ shifts right and more solid dissolves. Complex-ion formation is a general way to increase the solubility of salts whose cation can accept lone pairs.

questions.q: A metal–ligand complex has a formation constant Kf = 10²⁰. What does this indicate?
o: The complex dissociates almost completely
That would correspond to a very small Kf.
The complex is very stable and forms nearly completely
Correct: a huge Kf means equilibrium lies far toward the complex.
The complex forms very slowly
K describes equilibrium position, not rate.
The metal ion is a Lewis base
In complexes, the metal accepts electron pairs as a Lewis acid.
questions.x: A formation constant Kf describes M + nL ⇌ MLₙ. A value as large as 10²⁰ means the equilibrium lies overwhelmingly toward the complex, so nearly all metal ions are bound and the complex is very stable. Like all equilibrium constants, Kf says nothing about how fast the complex forms. The metal acts as a Lewis acid, accepting lone pairs from the ligands.

questions.q: In the complex [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺, the roles of Cu²⁺ and NH₃ are:
o: Cu²⁺ is a Lewis base; NH₃ is a Lewis acid
Roles are reversed; ligands donate electron pairs.
Cu²⁺ is a Lewis acid; NH₃ is a Lewis base
Correct: each NH₃ donates a lone pair into an empty orbital on Cu²⁺.
Both are Brønsted acids
No proton transfer occurs.
Cu²⁺ is a Brønsted base
Cu²⁺ accepts electron pairs, not protons.
questions.x: In a coordination complex, ligands donate lone pairs into empty orbitals of the metal ion, forming coordinate covalent bonds. That makes the ligand (NH₃, with its nitrogen lone pair) the Lewis base and the metal cation (Cu²⁺) the Lewis acid. No protons are transferred, so Brønsted labels do not apply.

questions.q: What is the coordination number of iron in [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻?
o: This is the magnitude of the complex's charge.
Common for some complexes, but six ligands are bonded here.
Correct: six cyanide ligands each donate one pair.
Added the ligand count to the charge.
questions.x: The coordination number is the number of donor atoms bonded directly to the central metal. In [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ there are six monodentate cyanide ligands, each binding through carbon, so the coordination number is 6, typically octahedral. The 3− is the overall charge of the complex and has nothing to do with ligand count.

questions.q: What is the oxidation state of cobalt in [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺?
o: Sign error in the bookkeeping; x + 2(−1) = +1 gives x = +3, not −1.
Equated the metal's charge to the overall complex charge.
Counted only one chloride.
Correct: NH₃ is neutral, each Cl⁻ is −1: x − 2 = +1, so x = +3.
questions.x: The metal's oxidation state x plus all ligand charges equals the overall charge of the complex. NH₃ is neutral, and each chloride is −1, so x + 4(0) + 2(−1) = +1, giving x = +3. Equating the metal's oxidation state with the complex's overall charge ignores the charged ligands.

questions.q: EDTA (hexadentate) binds Ca²⁺ far more strongly than six separate monodentate ligands with similar donor atoms. The main reason is:
o: A favorable entropy change, since one EDTA releases several water ligands
Correct: the chelate effect is largely entropic.
EDTA forms covalent bonds while monodentate ligands do not
All ligands form coordinate covalent bonds.
EDTA is a stronger Brønsted acid
Binding strength here is not about proton donation.
Each EDTA donor atom is far more basic
Donor atoms are similar; the gain is entropic.
questions.note: Chelate effect: fewer particles bound, more released, ΔS > 0.
questions.x: The chelate effect is mainly entropic. When one hexadentate EDTA replaces six water ligands, the number of free particles rises from 2 (complex + EDTA) to 7 (complex + 6 H₂O), so ΔS is positive. Six monodentate ligands replacing six waters give no change in particle count. Since the donor atoms and bonds are similar, ΔH is similar, and the entropy gain makes ΔG more negative.

questions.q: AgCl(s) + 2NH₃ ⇌ [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + Cl⁻. If Ksp(AgCl) = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ and Kf([Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺) = 1 × 10⁷, what is K for this reaction?
o: Squared Ksp; the 2 NH₃ do not change how Ksp and Kf combine.
Divided Ksp by Kf instead of multiplying.
Correct: adding reactions multiplies K: 10⁻¹⁰ × 10⁷ = 10⁻³.
Divided Kf by Ksp instead of multiplying.
questions.x: When reactions are added, their equilibrium constants multiply. AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ (Ksp) plus Ag⁺ + 2 NH₃ ⇌ [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ (Kf) gives the overall reaction, so K = Ksp × Kf = 10⁻¹⁰ × 10⁷ = 10⁻³. This K is 10 million times larger than Ksp alone, showing how complexation boosts solubility.

questions.q: EDTA is added to hard water containing Ca²⁺ before soap is used. What is its effect?
o: It precipitates Ca²⁺ as CaCO₃
EDTA keeps calcium dissolved as a complex.
It oxidizes Ca²⁺ to Ca³⁺
Calcium does not form a +3 ion.
It raises [Ca²⁺] by dissolving pipes
Its purpose is to bind free Ca²⁺.
It chelates Ca²⁺, preventing insoluble calcium salts from precipitating
Correct: the stable Ca–EDTA complex keeps free [Ca²⁺] very low.
questions.x: EDTA is a hexadentate chelating agent that wraps around Ca²⁺ to form a very stable, water-soluble complex. This keeps free [Ca²⁺] extremely low, so calcium cannot combine with soap anions or carbonate to form insoluble scum or scale. The calcium is not removed or precipitated; it is sequestered in solution.

questions.q: Colligative properties depend primarily on:
o: The number of dissolved solute particles
Correct: identity matters only through how many particles form.
The chemical identity of the solute
Glucose and urea at the same molality give the same effect.
The molar mass of the solute
Mass matters only in converting to moles.
The color of the solution
Color has no effect on colligative properties.
questions.x: Colligative properties (vapor pressure lowering, boiling point elevation, freezing point depression and osmotic pressure) depend on the number of solute particles per amount of solvent, not on what the particles are. That is why the van 't Hoff factor matters: 1 m NaCl gives about twice the effect of 1 m glucose. Molar mass matters only for converting grams to moles.

questions.q: What is the ideal van't Hoff factor for CaCl₂?
o: This applies to nonelectrolytes.
Counted only one chloride.
Correct: CaCl₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ gives three particles.
Counted the charge of Ca²⁺ as particles.
questions.x: The ideal van 't Hoff factor i is the number of particles each formula unit produces on complete dissociation. CaCl₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2 Cl⁻ gives three ions, so i = 3. The ion's charge does not add particles; only the count of separate ions matters.

questions.q: The measured van't Hoff factor for 0.05 m MgSO₄ is about 1.3 rather than 2. What best explains this?
o: MgSO₄ is a covalent nonelectrolyte
MgSO₄ is ionic and does dissociate.
Ion pairing between Mg²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ reduces the number of free particles
Correct: strongly attracted ions behave partly as single units.
The solution contains extra water molecules
Solvent amount does not change i.
Sulfate ions react to form three particles
This would raise i, not lower it.
questions.x: Ideal i counts ions assuming they move independently, but real ions attract each other. Mg²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ each carry a double charge, so the attraction is strong and some ions spend time as ion pairs that act as one particle. That lowers the effective particle count and i. Ion pairing grows with ion charge and concentration, so i falls furthest below ideal for salts like MgSO₄.

questions.q: What is the freezing point of 0.50 m aqueous NaCl, assuming complete dissociation? (Kf of water = 1.86 °C/m)
o: Used m = 1.0 or i = 4.
Ignored the van't Hoff factor (i = 2).
Freezing point is depressed, not elevated.
questions.x: Freezing point depression is ΔTf = i·Kf·m. NaCl gives two particles (i = 2), so ΔTf = 2 × 1.86 × 0.50 = 1.86 °C, and the solution freezes at 0 − 1.86 = −1.86 °C. Leaving out i gives only 0.93 °C, and solutes always lower freezing points, never raise them.

questions.q: What is the boiling point of 1.0 m aqueous glucose? (Kb of water = 0.51 °C/m)
o: Boiling point is elevated, not lowered.
Any nonvolatile solute raises the boiling point.
Correct: ΔTb = 1 × 0.51 × 1.0 = 0.51 °C above 100 °C.
Used i = 2; glucose does not dissociate.
questions.x: Boiling point elevation is ΔTb = i·Kb·m. Glucose is a nonelectrolyte (i = 1), so ΔTb = 1 × 0.51 × 1.0 = 0.51 °C, and the solution boils at 100.51 °C. Any nonvolatile solute lowers the vapor pressure, so the liquid must be heated more to reach atmospheric pressure. Using i = 2 wrongly treats glucose as if it dissociated.

questions.q: Which aqueous solution has the highest boiling point: 0.30 m glucose, 0.10 m Na₂SO₄, 0.20 m KCl, or 0.10 m MgCl₂?
o: 0.20 m KCl
Correct: KCl gives 0.40 m particles; the others give 0.30 m.
0.30 m glucose
Nonelectrolyte: 0.30 m particles.
0.10 m Na₂SO₄
Three ions per unit: 0.30 m particles.
0.10 m MgCl₂
Three ions per unit: 0.30 m particles.
questions.x: Boiling point elevation depends on total particle molality, i × m. Glucose: 1 × 0.30 = 0.30 m; Na₂SO₄: 3 × 0.10 = 0.30 m; MgCl₂: 3 × 0.10 = 0.30 m; KCl: 2 × 0.20 = 0.40 m. KCl has the most dissolved particles, so it has the highest boiling point. Higher formal molality alone (glucose) is not enough if the solute does not dissociate.

questions.q: 10 g of a nonelectrolyte dissolved in 100 g of water lowers the freezing point by 1.86 °C. What is its molar mass? (Kf = 1.86 °C/m)
o: 10 g/mol
Assumed 1.0 mol of solute rather than 0.10 mol.
100 g/mol
Correct: m = 1.0 mol/kg, so 0.100 kg holds 0.10 mol; 10 g ÷ 0.10 mol = 100 g/mol.
186 g/mol
Multiplied by Kf instead of using it to find molality.
200 g/mol
Assumed i = 2; a nonelectrolyte has i = 1.
questions.x: Use ΔTf = i·Kf·m to find molality, then moles and molar mass. With i = 1, m = 1.86 ÷ 1.86 = 1.0 mol/kg. The solution has 0.100 kg water, so it holds 0.10 mol solute, and 10 g ÷ 0.10 mol = 100 g/mol. Forgetting to scale molality to 0.100 kg of solvent is the common slip.

questions.q: What is the osmotic pressure of 0.10 M glucose at 300 K? (R = 0.082 L·atm/(mol·K))
o: 0.25 atm
Decimal error by a factor of 10.
2.5 atm
4.9 atm
Used i = 2 for a nonelectrolyte.
25 atm
Used M = 1.0 M.
questions.x: Osmotic pressure is π = iMRT. For glucose, i = 1, so π = 1 × 0.10 mol/L × 0.082 L·atm/(mol·K) × 300 K ≈ 2.5 atm. Even this modest concentration creates a sizable pressure, which is why osmotic water movement is powerful in cells. Using i = 2 would double the value, but glucose does not dissociate.

questions.q: Which solution is approximately isotonic with 0.15 M NaCl?
o: 0.15 M glucose
Glucose does not dissociate, so this is only 0.15 osmol/L.
0.15 M CaCl₂
This gives 0.45 osmol/L.
0.30 M NaCl
This gives 0.60 osmol/L.
0.30 M glucose
Correct: both are about 0.30 osmol/L.
questions.x: Isotonic solutions have equal osmolarity, which is i × M. 0.15 M NaCl gives 2 × 0.15 = 0.30 osmol/L, close to body fluids. 0.30 M glucose (i = 1) also gives 0.30 osmol/L. 0.15 M glucose is only half as concentrated in particles, while CaCl₂ (i = 3) and 0.30 M NaCl would be hypertonic.

questions.q: A red blood cell is placed in distilled water. What happens?
o: Water enters the cell, which swells and may lyse
Correct: the cell interior is hypertonic to pure water.
Water leaves the cell, which shrinks
That happens in a hypertonic solution.
Nothing, because pure water is isotonic
Pure water has zero osmolarity.
Salt leaves the cell to equalize concentration
The membrane limits solute flow; water moves.
questions.x: Water moves by osmosis from lower to higher solute concentration across a semipermeable membrane. Distilled water has essentially zero osmolarity, while the red blood cell's interior is about 0.3 osmol/L, so the outside is hypotonic and water rushes in. With no rigid wall to resist, the cell swells and may burst (hemolysis). The membrane largely blocks the solutes, so water, not salt, moves.

questions.q: Pure solvent has a vapor pressure of 100 torr. A nonvolatile solute is added so that the solvent mole fraction is 0.90. What is the solution's vapor pressure?
o: 10 torr
Used the solute's mole fraction.
90 torr
Correct: Raoult's law: P = x(solvent)·P° = 0.90 × 100.
100 torr
A nonvolatile solute lowers vapor pressure.
110 torr
Vapor pressure decreases, not increases.
questions.x: Raoult's law states that a solution's vapor pressure from the solvent equals the solvent's mole fraction times its pure vapor pressure: P = x(solvent)·P°. Here P = 0.90 × 100 torr = 90 torr. A nonvolatile solute contributes no vapor of its own, so it can only lower the vapor pressure, never raise it.

questions.q: Adding a nonvolatile solute to a liquid lowers its vapor pressure. What happens to its boiling point?
o: It decreases
Lower vapor pressure delays boiling.
It is unchanged
Vapor pressure lowering always shifts boiling point.
It increases only for ionic solutes
Any nonvolatile solute elevates boiling point.
It increases, because a higher temperature is needed to reach atmospheric pressure
Correct: lower vapor pressure means more heating is required to boil.
questions.x: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the external pressure. A nonvolatile solute lowers the solvent's vapor pressure at every temperature, so the solution must be heated to a higher temperature to reach atmospheric pressure. This boiling point elevation is colligative, so it happens for any nonvolatile solute, ionic or not.

questions.q: Liquids A (P° = 200 torr) and B (P° = 100 torr) form an ideal solution with x_A = 0.50. What is the mole fraction of A in the vapor?
o: This is B's mole fraction in the vapor.
The vapor is enriched in the more volatile component.
Divided 150 torr by A's pure vapor pressure (200); y_A is P_A ÷ P_total.
questions.note: The vapor is richer in the more volatile component.
questions.x: For an ideal solution, each partial pressure follows Raoult's law: P_A = 0.50 × 200 = 100 torr and P_B = 0.50 × 100 = 50 torr, for a total of 150 torr. By Dalton's law, the vapor mole fraction of A is P_A/P_total = 100/150 ≈ 0.67. The vapor is enriched in the more volatile liquid, which is the principle behind distillation.

questions.q: To purify seawater by reverse osmosis, the pressure applied to the seawater side must be:
o: Greater than the seawater's osmotic pressure
Correct: overcoming π forces water from the salty side to the fresh side.
Less than the osmotic pressure
Then water would flow into the seawater by normal osmosis.
Exactly equal to the osmotic pressure
Equal pressure stops net flow.
Zero, as the membrane does the work
Without pressure, osmosis moves water the wrong way.
questions.x: Normal osmosis moves water from fresh water into seawater, toward the higher solute concentration. Osmotic pressure is the pressure that just stops this flow. To reverse it and push water out of the seawater through the membrane, the applied pressure must exceed the seawater's osmotic pressure. Equal pressure gives no net flow.

questions.q: Per mole dissolved, why is CaCl₂ more effective than NaCl at melting ice on roads?
o: It has a higher molar mass
Colligative effects depend on particle count, not mass.
It reacts chemically with ice
No chemical reaction is involved.
It raises the freezing point of water
Solutes lower the freezing point.
It produces more particles in solution
Correct: three ions per formula unit versus two.
questions.x: Freezing point depression is colligative: ΔTf = i·Kf·m, so it depends on the number of particles. Each mole of CaCl₂ gives three ions (i = 3), while NaCl gives two (i = 2), so per mole dissolved CaCl₂ lowers the freezing point about 1.5 times as much. The extra effect comes from particle count, not from molar mass or any chemical reaction with ice.

questions.q: Why does a nonvolatile solute lower the freezing point of a solvent?
o: It forms strong bonds with the solid solvent
Solutes are generally excluded from the pure solid solvent.
It increases the vapor pressure of the liquid
Nonvolatile solutes lower vapor pressure.
It increases the entropy of the liquid phase, stabilizing the liquid relative to the solid
Correct: the solvent's chemical potential falls in solution.
It increases the enthalpy of fusion
The enthalpy of fusion is unrelated here.
questions.x: Dissolving a solute increases the entropy of the liquid phase and lowers the solvent's chemical potential (free energy), while the pure solid that freezes out is unaffected because solutes are excluded from the crystal. The liquid is therefore more stable relative to the solid, and the system must be cooled further before freezing becomes favorable. The same idea explains vapor pressure lowering.

questions.q: A 0.10 m aqueous solution of an unknown solute freezes at −0.37 °C (Kf = 1.86 °C/m). Which solute is it most likely?
o: Sucrose
A nonelectrolyte would give ΔTf ≈ 0.19 °C.
MgCl₂
Three ions would give ΔTf ≈ 0.56 °C.
AlCl₃
Four ions would give ΔTf ≈ 0.74 °C.
KBr
Correct: i = 0.37 ÷ (1.86 × 0.10) ≈ 2, matching two ions.
questions.x: Rearrange ΔTf = i·Kf·m to find i: i = 0.37 ÷ (1.86 × 0.10) ≈ 2.0. A factor of 2 means each formula unit gives two particles, matching KBr → K⁺ + Br⁻. Sucrose (i = 1) would depress only about 0.19 °C, and MgCl₂ (i = 3) or AlCl₃ (i = 4) would give larger depressions.

questions.q: A weak acid HA is 10% ionized in a solution. What is its effective van't Hoff factor?
o: Ignores the partial ionization.
Correct: 0.90 HA + 0.10 H⁺ + 0.10 A⁻ = 1.10 particles per formula unit.
Counted extra particles beyond the 0.10 ionized.
Assumed complete ionization.
questions.x: The van 't Hoff factor equals total particles per formula unit of solute added. If 10% of HA ionizes, then from 1 unit you get 0.90 HA left plus 0.10 H⁺ and 0.10 A⁻, for 1.10 particles, so i = 1.1. In general for a weak acid, i = 1 + α, where α is the fraction ionized.

questions.q: A membrane permeable only to water separates 0.1 M glucose (side A) from 0.3 M glucose (side B). Which way does water move?
o: From A to B
Correct: water moves toward higher solute concentration.
From B to A
Water moves toward the more concentrated side, B.
No net movement
Concentrations differ, so there is net flow.
Glucose moves from B to A
The membrane is impermeable to glucose.
questions.x: Across a membrane permeable only to water, water flows by osmosis from the side with lower solute concentration (higher water concentration) to the side with higher solute concentration. Side B has 0.3 M glucose, so water moves from A to B, diluting B. Glucose cannot cross, so only the water moves.

questions.q: Ethanol is added to water. Unlike adding glucose, the solution's vapor pressure increases. Why?
o: Ethanol increases water's mole fraction
Adding ethanol lowers water's mole fraction.
Ethanol is an electrolyte
Ethanol does not ionize.
Ethanol is volatile and contributes its own vapor pressure
Correct: Raoult's law adds each volatile component's partial pressure.
Ethanol reacts with water to form a gas
No chemical reaction occurs.
questions.x: Raoult's law gives the total vapor pressure as the sum of each volatile component's partial pressure: P = x_water·P°_water + x_ethanol·P°_ethanol. Ethanol is more volatile than water, so adding it raises the total even while lowering water's mole fraction. Glucose, by contrast, is nonvolatile and only dilutes the water, lowering vapor pressure.

questions.q: Which pair of elements is most likely to bond covalently rather than ionically?
o: Na and Cl
A Group 1 metal and a halogen differ greatly in electronegativity: ionic.
K and F
This is the classic large-ΔEN metal–nonmetal pair: ionic.
C and O
Correct: two nonmetals with a moderate ΔEN share electrons in polar covalent bonds.
Mg and O
A Group 2 metal and oxygen form the ionic solid MgO.
questions.note: Two nonmetals → covalent; metal + nonmetal with big ΔEN → ionic.
questions.x: Bond type tracks the electronegativity difference between atoms. A metal paired with a strongly electronegative nonmetal (Na–Cl, K–F, Mg–O) transfers electrons and forms ions. Carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals with only a moderate difference, so neither can strip an electron from the other; they share pairs instead, giving polar covalent bonds.

questions.q: Which carbon–carbon bond is both the shortest and the strongest?
o: The C–C bond in ethane
Bond order 1 gives the longest, weakest C–C bond.
The C=C bond in ethene
Bond order 2 is shorter than a single bond but longer than a triple.
A C–C bond in benzene
Benzene's bond order of 1.5 lies between single and double.
The C≡C bond in ethyne
Correct: bond order 3 gives the shortest, strongest C–C bond.
questions.note: Higher bond order → shorter and stronger bond.
questions.x: Each additional bond between two atoms adds shared electron density between the nuclei, pulling them closer and requiring more energy to separate. A triple bond (order 3) is therefore shorter and stronger than a double (2), aromatic (1.5) or single (1) bond. Benzene is tempting as 'special', but its 1.5 bond order puts it between single and double, not above triple.

questions.q: A C=C bond (≈610 kJ/mol) is strong, but not twice as strong as a C–C bond (≈350 kJ/mol). Why?
o: The π bond is weaker than the σ bond because side-on p overlap is less effective
Correct: sideways p–p overlap concentrates less density between nuclei than head-on σ overlap.
A double bond is longer than a single bond, so it is weaker per bond
Double bonds are shorter than single bonds, not longer.
Adding a π bond partially breaks the existing σ bond
The σ bond remains intact; the π bond is simply a weaker second bond.
Carbons in a double bond are sp³ hybridized, which weakens overlap
Double-bonded carbons are sp² hybridized, not sp³.
questions.note: σ bonds are stronger than π bonds.
questions.x: A double bond is one σ bond plus one π bond. The σ bond forms by head-on overlap that puts density directly between the nuclei; the π bond forms by weaker side-on overlap of parallel p orbitals. So the second bond adds only about 260 kJ/mol, not another 350. Double bonds are actually shorter than single bonds, so length cannot explain the shortfall.

questions.q: In a coordinate covalent bond, such as the N–B bond in H₃N–BF₃, the shared electron pair:
o: Is transferred completely to the more electronegative atom
Complete transfer describes ionic bonding, not a shared pair.
Comes entirely from one atom, here the nitrogen lone pair
Correct: the Lewis base (N) donates both electrons to the electron-poor boron.
Comes one electron from each atom, as in any covalent bond
That describes an ordinary covalent bond, not a coordinate one.
Is delocalized over all the fluorine atoms
The pair is localized between N and B; fluorines are not the donor.
questions.note: Coordinate (dative) bond = Lewis base donates both electrons to a Lewis acid.
questions.x: A coordinate (dative) covalent bond forms when a Lewis base donates both electrons of a lone pair to an electron-deficient Lewis acid. In H₃N–BF₃, nitrogen's lone pair fills boron's empty p orbital. Once formed, the bond behaves like any covalent bond, but its electrons originated from one atom rather than one from each, which is the key distinction from an ordinary covalent bond.

questions.q: As two isolated hydrogen atoms approach and form an H₂ molecule, how does the potential energy of the system change?
o: It rises steadily until the bond forms, then stays constant
Bond formation releases energy, so potential energy falls rather than rises.
It stays constant because no electrons are gained or lost
Sharing electrons stabilizes the system; the energy changes.
It decreases continuously the closer the nuclei get
At very short distances nuclear repulsion makes energy rise sharply.
It falls to a minimum at the bond length, then rises sharply if the nuclei get closer
Correct: the minimum marks the equilibrium bond length; its depth is the bond energy.
questions.note: The well depth of the energy curve equals the bond dissociation energy.
questions.x: Two H atoms far apart have zero interaction energy. As they approach, each electron is attracted to both nuclei, lowering the energy until a minimum is reached at the bond length (about 74 pm). Closer than that, nucleus–nucleus repulsion dominates and energy climbs steeply. The depth of this well equals the bond dissociation energy, so energy does not simply keep falling.

questions.q: Which statement about breaking a covalent bond is always true?
o: It requires an input of energy
Correct: bond breaking is always endothermic; bond formation releases energy.
It releases energy stored in the bond
Misconception: energy is released when bonds form, not when they break.
It releases energy only if the bond is weak
Even weak bonds require energy to break.
It requires energy only for π bonds
Breaking any bond, σ or π, requires energy.
questions.note: Trap: 'energy stored in bonds' is released only when stronger bonds form.
questions.x: Atoms in a bond sit in an energy well, so pulling them apart always requires energy: bond breaking is endothermic and bond formation is exothermic. When a reaction such as ATP hydrolysis releases energy, it is because the new bonds formed are stronger than the ones broken, not because breaking a bond liberates stored energy.

questions.q: In which molecule does the central atom have fewer than eight valence electrons in its Lewis structure?
o: NF₃
N has three bonds plus one lone pair: a full octet.
BF₃
Correct: boron forms three bonds and has only six valence electrons.
CF₄
C forms four bonds: eight electrons.
OF₂
O has two bonds plus two lone pairs: eight electrons.
questions.note: B and Be compounds are the common incomplete-octet exceptions.
questions.x: Boron has only three valence electrons, so in BF₃ it forms three bonds and is left with six electrons and an empty p orbital. This electron deficiency makes BF₃ a strong Lewis acid. Nitrogen, carbon and oxygen reach eight electrons by combining bonds with lone pairs, so NF₃, CF₄ and OF₂ all obey the octet rule.

questions.q: Which of these molecules does NOT exist because its central atom cannot expand its octet?
o: PCl₅
Phosphorus is in period 3 and can hold more than eight electrons.
SF₄
Sulfur is in period 3 and can expand its octet.
NCl₅
Correct: nitrogen is in period 2 and has no accessible d orbitals, so it cannot exceed an octet.
XeF₂
Xe is in period 5, so it can hold ten electrons (two bonds plus three lone pairs).
questions.note: Only period 3 and lower atoms can have expanded octets.
questions.x: Only atoms in period 3 or below can hold more than eight electrons around them; the usual explanation is that they are larger and have empty d orbitals in their valence shell. Nitrogen is in period 2 with only 2s and 2p orbitals, so it cannot accommodate five bonds and NCl₅ does not exist, though its period-3 analog PCl₅ does. S and Xe, being larger, routinely expand their octets.

questions.q: Which species has an odd number of valence electrons and is therefore a radical?
o: NO
Correct: 5 + 6 = 11 valence electrons, so one electron must be unpaired.
CO
4 + 6 = 10 electrons: all paired.
CN⁻
4 + 5 + 1 = 10 electrons: all paired.
N₂
5 + 5 = 10 electrons: all paired.
questions.note: Count valence electrons; an odd total guarantees a radical.
questions.x: A species with an odd total of valence electrons cannot pair them all, so at least one electron is unpaired and the species is a radical. NO has 5 + 6 = 11 valence electrons. CO, N₂ and CN⁻ each have 10, an even number that pairs completely; they are isoelectronic with one another, which is why they share a triple-bonded structure.

questions.q: Using bond energies H–H = 440, Cl–Cl = 240 and H–Cl = 430 kJ/mol, what is ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl?
o: Sign flipped: that is bonds formed minus bonds broken.
Counts only one H–Cl bond formed; two form.
Counts only the two H–Cl bonds formed and ignores the energy needed to break H–H and Cl–Cl.
Correct: ΔH = broken − formed = (440 + 240) − 2(430) = −180 kJ.
questions.note: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
questions.x: Reaction enthalpy can be estimated as energy absorbed breaking bonds minus energy released forming bonds. Breaking one H–H and one Cl–Cl costs 440 + 240 = 680 kJ; forming two H–Cl bonds releases 2 × 430 = 860 kJ. ΔH = 680 − 860 = −180 kJ, exothermic. Reversing the subtraction gives the tempting +180 kJ with the wrong sign.

questions.q: What is the formal charge on nitrogen in the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺?
o: N with four bonds and no lone pairs has one fewer electron than its 5 valence electrons.
Correct: FC = 5 − 0 − ½(8) = +1.
A −1 nitrogen would have two bonds and two lone pairs.
Confuses formal charge with the number of bonds.
questions.note: FC = valence e⁻ − nonbonding e⁻ − ½(bonding e⁻).
questions.x: Formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − half the bonding electrons. In NH₄⁺, nitrogen has four N–H bonds (8 bonding electrons) and no lone pairs, so it 'owns' 4 electrons versus its usual 5, giving +1. The total of all formal charges must equal the ion's charge, and each H is 0, so +1 on nitrogen accounts for the whole charge.

questions.q: In the best Lewis structure of carbon monoxide, :C≡O:, what is the formal charge on carbon?
o: Correct: FC(C) = 4 − 2 − ½(6) = −1, balanced by +1 on oxygen.
Zero would require carbon to own four electrons; it owns five.
That is oxygen's formal charge, not carbon's.
Overcounts: carbon has one lone pair, not two.
questions.note: Formal charge can put a negative sign on the less electronegative atom when octets demand it.
questions.x: In :C≡O:, carbon has one lone pair (2 electrons) and shares a triple bond (6 electrons), so it owns 2 + 3 = 5 electrons versus its 4 valence electrons: −1. Oxygen owns 2 + 3 = 5 of its 6: +1. This structure is still the best one because it gives both atoms octets, which outranks putting the negative charge on the more electronegative atom.

questions.q: In the Lewis structure of ozone, O=O–O, what is the formal charge on the central oxygen?
o: The central O has three bonds and one lone pair, owning only five electrons.
That is the charge on the singly bonded terminal oxygen.
Correct: FC = 6 − 2 − ½(6) = +1.
Would require the central O to own only four electrons; it owns five (two lone-pair electrons plus three bonding).
questions.note: Ozone is neutral overall but has separated formal charges.
questions.x: The central oxygen of ozone has one double bond, one single bond and one lone pair. It owns 2 nonbonding electrons plus half of 6 bonding electrons = 5, one fewer than its 6 valence electrons, so its formal charge is +1. The singly bonded terminal O owns 7 and is −1, so the charges sum to zero for the neutral molecule.

questions.q: Which Lewis structure contributes most to the cyanate ion, OCN⁻ (C central)?
o: O=C=N with −1 on nitrogen
Reasonable, but the negative charge sits on N rather than the more electronegative O.
O≡C–N with +1 on O and −2 on N
Large, separated formal charges make this a minor contributor.
O=C=N with no formal charges
Impossible: the ion has an overall −1 charge that must appear somewhere.
O–C≡N with −1 on oxygen
Correct: smallest formal charges, with the −1 on the most electronegative atom.
questions.note: Best structure: minimal formal charges, negative charge on the most electronegative atom.
questions.x: Rank resonance contributors by octets first, then by the smallest formal charges, then by placing negative charge on the most electronegative atom. Both O=C=N⁻ (−1 on N) and ⁻O–C≡N (−1 on O) satisfy octets with minimal charge, but oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen and better stabilizes the negative charge. The O≡C–N form with +1 and −2 charges is a minor contributor.

questions.q: How many valence electrons are in the Lewis structure of the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻?
o: Subtracts the two charge electrons instead of adding them.
Correct: 6 (S) + 4 × 6 (O) + 2 (charge) = 32.
Adds an extra pair beyond the 2− charge.
Counts a full octet of eight electrons for each of the five atoms instead of valence electrons.
questions.note: Anions add electrons equal to the charge; cations subtract.
questions.x: To count Lewis-structure electrons, add each atom's valence electrons and then adjust for charge: add one per negative charge, subtract one per positive charge. Sulfate has 6 from sulfur, 4 × 6 = 24 from oxygen, and 2 more for the 2− charge, totaling 32. Subtracting the charge electrons instead of adding them is the common error that gives 30.

questions.q: How many lone pairs are on the central xenon atom in XeF₄?
o: Xe has 8 valence electrons; only 4 are used in bonds.
Leaves two electrons unaccounted for.
Correct: 8 − 4 bonding electrons from Xe = 4 electrons = 2 lone pairs.
Three lone pairs are on Xe in XeF₂, not XeF₄.
questions.x: Xenon brings 8 valence electrons. In XeF₄ it forms four single bonds, contributing one electron to each, so 4 of its electrons are used and 4 remain as two lone pairs. That gives six electron domains around Xe, which is why XeF₄ is square planar. In XeF₂, only 2 electrons bond, leaving 6 electrons, or three lone pairs.

questions.q: In any one resonance structure of the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻, what is the formal charge on nitrogen?
o: Correct: N has four bonds and no lone pairs: 5 − 0 − 4 = +1.
Would require N to own five electrons; it owns four.
The −1 charges sit on the singly bonded oxygens.
Confuses formal charge with nitrogen's oxidation state.
questions.note: Formal charge ≠ oxidation state.
questions.x: In each resonance structure of NO₃⁻, nitrogen has one double bond and two single bonds and no lone pairs: it owns half of 8 bonding electrons = 4, versus 5 valence electrons, so its formal charge is +1. The two singly bonded oxygens each carry −1, summing to the ion's −1 charge. The oxidation state of +5 uses a different bookkeeping that assigns bonding electrons to oxygen.

questions.q: In the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺, how many lone pairs does oxygen have, and what is its formal charge?
o: Two lone pairs; +1
Two lone pairs plus three bonds would give O ten electrons.
One lone pair; +1
Correct: three bonds and one lone pair: FC = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1.
One lone pair; −1
Owning five electrons, oxygen is one short of six: positive, not negative.
Two lone pairs; 0
That describes neutral water, not hydronium.
questions.x: In H₃O⁺, oxygen forms three O–H bonds and keeps one lone pair, giving four electron domains and a full octet. It owns 2 nonbonding electrons plus half of 6 bonding electrons = 5, one less than its 6 valence electrons, so its formal charge is +1. Water's oxygen, by contrast, has two bonds and two lone pairs and owns 6, giving 0.

questions.q: Why do many textbooks draw SO₄²⁻ with two S=O bonds rather than four S–O single bonds?
o: It gives sulfur a complete octet, which the single-bond structure lacks
The all-single structure already gives S an octet; the double-bond form expands it.
It reduces the formal charge on sulfur from +2 to 0
Correct: with four single bonds S is +2; two double bonds bring it to 0 and lower charge separation.
It makes the four S–O bonds unequal, as measured experimentally
All four S–O bonds are measured to be equal in length.
It reduces the total number of valence electrons to 30
Electron count is fixed at 32 regardless of the drawing.
questions.note: Formal-charge minimization is the MCAT rationale for expanded octets.
questions.x: With four S–O single bonds, sulfur owns only 4 electrons and has formal charge +2, while every oxygen is −1. Converting two bonds to S=O lets sulfur expand its octet and drops its formal charge to 0, which minimizes charge separation; that is the textbook rationale. The single-bond structure already gives S an octet, so the double bonds do not complete one.

questions.q: A carbon atom has three bonds and one lone pair. What is its formal charge?
o: That is a carbocation: three bonds and no lone pairs.
Neutral carbon has four bonds and no lone pairs.
Correct: FC = 4 − 2 − 3 = −1, a carbanion.
Overcounts the nonbonding electrons.
questions.note: Carbanion: 3 bonds + 1 lone pair; carbocation: 3 bonds + empty orbital.
questions.x: Neutral carbon has four bonds and no lone pairs. A carbon with three bonds and one lone pair owns 2 + 3 = 5 electrons, one more than its 4 valence electrons, so it is −1: a carbanion. A carbon with three bonds and an empty orbital owns only 3 and is +1: a carbocation. Telling these apart depends on counting the lone pair.

questions.q: How does the bookkeeping for formal charge differ from that for oxidation state?
o: Formal charge gives all bonding electrons to the more electronegative atom
That is the oxidation-state convention.
Formal charge treats bonding electrons as shared equally between the two atoms
Correct: each atom gets half of each bonding pair, ignoring electronegativity.
Formal charge ignores lone pairs
Lone pairs are counted fully toward the atom that holds them.
Formal charge applies only to ions
Neutral molecules such as CO and O₃ have nonzero formal charges.
questions.x: Formal charge assumes perfectly covalent bonds: each atom gets all its lone-pair electrons plus exactly half of every bonding pair, regardless of electronegativity. Oxidation state assumes perfectly ionic bonds: all bonding electrons go to the more electronegative atom. That is why nitrogen in NO₃⁻ has formal charge +1 but oxidation state +5, and why neutral molecules can still carry formal charges.

questions.q: In the Lewis structure of hydrogen cyanide (HCN), how are carbon and nitrogen connected?
o: Single bond; three lone pairs on N
Leaves carbon with only four electrons.
Double bond; two lone pairs on N
Leaves carbon with only six electrons.
Double bond; one lone pair on C and one on N
Uses all 10 electrons but leaves nitrogen with only six (one double bond plus one lone pair).
Triple bond; one lone pair on N
Correct: H–C≡N: uses all 10 electrons and gives C and N octets.
questions.x: HCN has 1 + 4 + 5 = 10 valence electrons. Placing an H–C bond and a C≡N triple bond uses 8, and the last 2 go as a lone pair on nitrogen. Carbon then has 2 + 6 = 8 electrons and nitrogen 6 + 2 = 8, so every heavy atom has an octet with zero formal charges. Single- or double-bond versions leave carbon or nitrogen short of an octet.

questions.q: Resonance structures of the same species differ only in:
o: The positions of the atoms
Moving atoms produces isomers, not resonance structures.
The placement of π electrons and lone pairs
Correct: the atomic skeleton and σ framework stay fixed; only electrons move.
The total number of valence electrons
All resonance structures must have the same electron count.
The overall charge of the species
The net charge is identical in every resonance structure.
questions.x: Resonance structures are different ways of placing electrons on one fixed arrangement of atoms. Only π electrons and lone pairs are moved; the nuclei, the σ framework, the electron count and the net charge stay the same. If an atom such as hydrogen changes position, the drawings represent different compounds (isomers or tautomers), not resonance forms.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the true structure of benzene?
o: It rapidly alternates between two Kekulé structures
Resonance forms are not in equilibrium; the molecule does not flip.
It has three short and three long C–C bonds
All six C–C bonds are measured to be identical.
It is a single hybrid with π electrons delocalized evenly around the ring
Correct: the real molecule is one structure, a blend of the contributors.
It is a mixture of two molecules present in equal amounts
There is only one kind of benzene molecule.
questions.note: Trap: resonance is not a rapid back-and-forth.
questions.x: Benzene's real structure is a single resonance hybrid: its six π electrons are delocalized evenly over the ring, so all six C–C bonds are the same length (about 140 pm), between a single and a double bond. The Kekulé drawings are only limiting pictures. The molecule never flips between them, and there is no mixture of two kinds of benzene.

questions.q: Experimentally, all three C–O bonds in the carbonate ion are the same length. What is the average C–O bond order?
o: Ignores the double bond that is shared among the three positions.
1⅓
Correct: four bonds spread over three C–O positions = 4/3.
1½
That is the bond order for a two-oxygen system like carboxylate.
Only one of three C–O bonds is double in any single structure.
questions.note: Bond order = total bonds between the atoms ÷ number of positions.
questions.x: Carbonate's three resonance structures each have one C=O and two C–O bonds, so four bonds are spread over three positions and the average bond order is 4/3, about 1.33. That is why all three bonds have identical length, intermediate between a single and a double bond. A bond order of 1.5 applies to two-oxygen systems such as carboxylate.

questions.q: Which species has the longest N–O bonds?
o: NO₂⁺
O=N=O has bond order 2: short bonds.
NO₂⁻
Two resonance structures give bond order 1.5.
NO₃⁻
Correct: three resonance structures give bond order 1⅓, the lowest, so the longest bonds.
NO
Nitric oxide has a bond order above 2: very short.
questions.note: Lower average bond order → longer bond.
questions.x: Bond length increases as bond order decreases. Average bond orders: NO (about 2.5), NO₂⁺ (2, linear O=N=O), NO₂⁻ (1.5 over two resonance structures), NO₃⁻ (4/3, one double bond shared among three oxygens). Nitrate has the lowest bond order and so the longest N–O bonds; nitrite is the tempting choice because it also has resonance, but its bond order is higher.

questions.q: Acetic acid (pKa ≈ 4.8) is far more acidic than ethanol (pKa ≈ 16). Which factor best explains this?
o: Acetate's negative charge is delocalized over two oxygens by resonance
Correct: resonance stabilizes the conjugate base, so the acid gives up H⁺ more readily.
The O–H bond in acetic acid is a stronger bond
A stronger O–H bond would make the acid weaker, not stronger.
Ethanol has more hydrogen atoms to lose
Acidity depends on conjugate base stability, not the number of hydrogens.
Ethoxide is stabilized by resonance with the methyl group
Ethoxide has no resonance; its charge is localized on one O.
questions.note: More stable conjugate base → stronger acid.
questions.x: Acid strength depends on how stable the conjugate base is. When acetic acid loses H⁺, acetate's negative charge is shared equally between two oxygens by resonance, which strongly stabilizes it. Ethoxide's charge stays localized on one oxygen with no resonance, so ethanol is a much weaker acid. A stronger O–H bond would make an acid weaker, not stronger.

questions.q: Which pair are NOT resonance structures of each other?
o: The two Kekulé structures of benzene
Only π electrons shift: valid resonance.
The two structures of the acetate ion
