Only electrons move between the two oxygens: valid resonance.
The keto and enol forms of acetone
Correct: a hydrogen atom moves, so these are tautomers (constitutional isomers).
The two structures of ozone
Only electrons move between terminal oxygens: valid resonance.
questions.note: If an atom moves, it's not resonance.
questions.x: Resonance structures differ only in where electrons are drawn; the atoms stay put. The keto and enol forms of acetone differ by the position of a hydrogen atom (C–H versus O–H), so they are tautomers: real, distinct constitutional isomers that interconvert by a chemical reaction. Benzene's Kekulé structures, acetate and ozone differ only in π electron placement.

questions.q: The C–N bond in an amide is shorter than a typical C–N single bond, and rotation about it is restricted. What is the best explanation?
o: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl, giving the C–N bond partial double-bond character
Correct: resonance makes the amide planar and the C–N bond partly π.
Nitrogen is sp³ hybridized, which holds substituents rigidly
sp³ nitrogen would allow free rotation; amide N is effectively sp².
Hydrogen bonding between N–H and C=O locks the bond
Restricted rotation exists even in tertiary amides with no N–H.
The carbonyl oxygen sterically blocks rotation
Sterics cannot explain the shortened bond length.
questions.note: This planarity underlies the rigid peptide bond.
questions.x: In an amide, the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the C=O π system, so one resonance contributor has a C=N double bond with negative charge on oxygen. This partial double-bond character shortens the C–N bond, makes the group planar with sp²-like nitrogen, and creates a rotation barrier. Hydrogen bonding cannot be the cause, since tertiary amides with no N–H are equally rigid.

questions.q: For protonated acetone, which resonance contributor is more important: (CH₃)₂C=OH⁺ or (CH₃)₂C⁺–OH?
o: (CH₃)₂C⁺–OH, because the positive charge rests on the less electronegative carbon
Charge placement matters less than complete octets; this carbon has only six electrons.
Both contribute equally because they have the same charge
Equal net charge does not mean equal stability.
(CH₃)₂C=OH⁺, because every atom has a full octet
Correct: full octets outrank placing charge on the less electronegative atom.
Neither, because protonated acetone has no resonance
Moving the π pair onto oxygen gives a valid second structure.
questions.note: Priority: full octets first, then minimal formal charge, then charge on the right atom.
questions.x: When judging resonance contributors, complete octets come first. In (CH₃)₂C=OH⁺ every atom has an octet, and the +1 sits on oxygen. In (CH₃)₂C⁺–OH the positive charge rests on less electronegative carbon, but that carbon has only six electrons. The octet criterion outranks charge placement, so the oxonium form is the major contributor, though the carbocation form explains why the carbon is electrophilic.

questions.q: What is the O–C–O bond angle in carbon dioxide?
o: That is the tetrahedral angle for four electron domains.
That is the trigonal planar angle for three domains.
That is water's bent angle, not CO₂'s.
Correct: two electron domains and no lone pairs on carbon give a linear molecule.
questions.x: VSEPR geometry depends on the number of electron domains around the central atom, with each double bond counting as one domain. Carbon in CO₂ has two double bonds and no lone pairs, so the two domains lie opposite each other at 180°, giving a linear molecule. 109.5° and 120° would require four or three domains, and water's 104.5° comes from lone pairs carbon lacks.

questions.q: The H–O–H angle in water is about 104.5°, smaller than the ideal tetrahedral 109.5°. Why?
o: Hydrogen atoms attract each other
Hydrogens bear partial positive charges and repel slightly.
Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, compressing the bond angle
Correct: lone pairs occupy more space near O and push the O–H bonds together.
Oxygen is sp² hybridized
Water's oxygen is treated as sp³ with four electron domains.
Hydrogen bonding between molecules bends each molecule
The angle is a property of an isolated molecule, even in the gas phase.
questions.note: Repulsion: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.
questions.x: Water's oxygen has four electron domains (two bonds, two lone pairs), so its ideal electron geometry is tetrahedral at 109.5°. Lone pairs are held only by one nucleus and spread out closer to the central atom, repelling more strongly than bonding pairs. They squeeze the H–O–H angle to about 104.5°. The angle is the same in isolated gas-phase molecules, so hydrogen bonding is not the cause.

questions.q: What is the molecular geometry of BF₃?
o: Trigonal planar
Correct: three bonding domains and no lone pairs on B give 120° angles in a plane.
Trigonal pyramidal
That requires a lone pair on the central atom, which boron lacks.
T-shaped
T-shaped requires five domains with two lone pairs.
Tetrahedral
Boron has only three electron domains.
questions.x: Boron in BF₃ has three bonding domains and no lone pairs, so the three B–F bonds spread as far apart as possible in one plane at 120°: trigonal planar. Trigonal pyramidal geometry, as in NH₃, requires a fourth domain that is a lone pair. The absence of that lone pair is why BF₃ is flat and nonpolar, unlike NF₃.

questions.q: What is the molecular geometry of SF₄?
o: Tetrahedral
Ignores the lone pair on sulfur; there are five domains.
Square planar
Square planar needs six domains with two lone pairs.
Seesaw
Correct: four bonds plus one lone pair = five domains, trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry.
Trigonal pyramidal
That shape comes from four domains with one lone pair.
questions.x: Sulfur in SF₄ has four bonds and one lone pair, giving five electron domains and a trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry. The lone pair takes an equatorial position, where it has fewer 90° neighbors, leaving the four F atoms in a seesaw shape. Calling it tetrahedral is the tempting error of ignoring the lone pair, which is only correct for four-domain molecules like CF₄.

questions.q: Chlorine trifluoride, ClF₃, has two lone pairs on chlorine. What is its molecular geometry?
o: Trigonal planar
Ignores the two lone pairs; Cl has five domains, not three.
Trigonal pyramidal
That needs four domains with one lone pair.
Seesaw
Seesaw has one lone pair, not two.
T-shaped
Correct: five domains, two equatorial lone pairs, leaving three F atoms in a T.
questions.x: Chlorine in ClF₃ has three bonds and two lone pairs, five domains in total, so its electron geometry is trigonal bipyramidal. Both lone pairs occupy equatorial positions to minimize 90° repulsions, leaving one equatorial and two axial fluorines in a T shape with F–Cl–F angles near 90°. Trigonal planar would require only three domains with no lone pairs.

questions.q: What is the molecular geometry of XeF₂?
o: Bent
Bent shapes come from three or four domains with lone pairs; Xe here has five domains.
Linear
Correct: five domains; the three lone pairs fill the equatorial positions, leaving F–Xe–F at 180°.
Trigonal planar
XeF₂ has five domains, not three.
T-shaped
T-shaped needs three bonded atoms.
questions.note: Three equatorial lone pairs on a trigonal bipyramid → linear.
questions.x: Xenon in XeF₂ has two bonds and three lone pairs, five domains with trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry. The three lone pairs occupy the three equatorial positions, 120° apart, which minimizes repulsion. That leaves the two fluorines in the axial positions, directly opposite each other, so the molecule is linear at 180°. Having lone pairs does not always make a molecule bent.

questions.q: What is the molecular geometry of XeF₄?
o: Tetrahedral
Ignores Xe's two lone pairs; there are six domains.
Seesaw
Seesaw comes from five domains with one lone pair.
Square planar
Correct: six domains; the two lone pairs sit opposite each other, leaving four F in a square.
Square pyramidal
Square pyramidal has five bonded atoms and one lone pair.
questions.x: Xenon in XeF₄ has four bonds and two lone pairs, six domains with octahedral electron geometry. The two lone pairs sit trans to each other (180° apart) to minimize their strong mutual repulsion, so the four fluorines lie in one plane at 90°: square planar. Square pyramidal is the shape for six domains with only one lone pair, as in BrF₅.

questions.q: PCl₅ has a trigonal bipyramidal shape. Which set of Cl–P–Cl bond angles does it contain?
o: Correct: axial–equatorial 90°, equatorial–equatorial 120°, axial–axial 180°.
Only 109.5°
That is the tetrahedral angle for four domains.
Only 90° and 180°
Those are the octahedral angles; the equatorial plane gives 120°.
Only 120°
Misses the axial positions.
questions.note: In a trigonal bipyramid, axial and equatorial positions are not equivalent.
questions.x: A trigonal bipyramid has two kinds of positions. The three equatorial atoms lie in a plane 120° apart; the two axial atoms sit above and below that plane, 90° from each equatorial atom and 180° from each other. PCl₅ therefore contains 90°, 120° and 180° angles. Only 90° and 180° describes an octahedron, where all six positions are equivalent.

questions.q: BrF₅ has five Br–F bonds and one lone pair on bromine. What is its molecular geometry?
o: Trigonal bipyramidal
Ignores the lone pair; there are six domains.
Octahedral
Octahedral requires six bonded atoms.
Seesaw
Seesaw has only four bonded atoms.
Square pyramidal
Correct: six domains, one occupied by a lone pair, leave a square pyramid.
questions.x: Bromine in BrF₅ has five bonds and one lone pair, six domains with octahedral electron geometry. Removing one vertex of an octahedron for the lone pair leaves four fluorines in a square base and one at the apex: square pyramidal. Molecular geometry names only the positions of atoms, so this is not octahedral even though the electron geometry is.

questions.q: What are the electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry of SO₂?
o: Trigonal planar; bent
Correct: two bonding domains plus one lone pair on S = three domains, bent shape.
Linear; linear
Unlike CO₂, sulfur in SO₂ carries a lone pair.
Tetrahedral; bent
S has three domains, not four.
Trigonal planar; trigonal planar
Molecular shape counts only atoms; one domain is a lone pair.
questions.x: Sulfur in SO₂ has two bonds to oxygen plus one lone pair, giving three electron domains and trigonal planar electron geometry. Because molecular geometry describes only atom positions, the shape is bent with an angle a bit under 120°. CO₂ is linear because carbon has no lone pair, which is the key difference that makes SO₂ bent and polar.

questions.q: Which species is trigonal pyramidal?
o: NO₃⁻
Nitrogen has three domains and no lone pair: trigonal planar.
SO₃
Sulfur has three domains and no lone pair: trigonal planar.
BF₃
Boron has three bonds and no lone pair: trigonal planar.
ClO₃⁻
Correct: Cl has three bonded O atoms plus one lone pair = four domains.
questions.note: Three atoms + one lone pair → trigonal pyramidal.
questions.x: Trigonal pyramidal geometry needs four electron domains: three bonded atoms plus one lone pair. In ClO₃⁻, chlorine bonds to three oxygens and keeps a lone pair, so the oxygens sit at the base of a pyramid. NO₃⁻, SO₃ and BF₃ also have three bonded atoms, but their central atoms carry no lone pair, so all three are flat trigonal planar.

questions.q: Which ranking of bond angles is correct?
o: H₂O > NH₃ > CH₄
Reversed: more lone pairs compress the angle more.
CH₄ > NH₃ > H₂O
Correct: 109.5° > ≈107° > ≈104.5°, as lone pairs increase from 0 to 2.
NH₃ > CH₄ > H₂O
Methane, with no lone pairs, has the largest angle.
All three are 109.5°
Only CH₄ has the ideal angle; lone pairs compress the others.
questions.x: CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O all have four electron domains, so each starts from the 109.5° tetrahedral angle. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so each lone pair squeezes the remaining bonds closer. With 0, 1 and 2 lone pairs, the angles fall from 109.5° to about 107° to about 104.5°. Having the same electron geometry does not mean having the same bond angle.

questions.q: What is the electron-domain geometry around oxygen in a water molecule?
o: Bent
Bent is the molecular geometry, which ignores lone pairs.
Linear
Oxygen has four domains, not two.
Tetrahedral
Correct: two bonds plus two lone pairs = four domains arranged tetrahedrally.
Trigonal planar
That requires three domains.
questions.note: Electron geometry counts lone pairs; molecular geometry does not.
questions.x: Electron-domain geometry counts every region of electron density around the central atom, bonding or nonbonding. Oxygen in water has two O–H bonds and two lone pairs, four domains, so its electron geometry is tetrahedral. Molecular geometry describes only where the atoms are, and with two lone pairs invisible to that description, the molecular shape is bent.

questions.q: In SF₄, the lone pair on sulfur occupies an equatorial rather than an axial position. Why?
o: Equatorial positions are closer to the nucleus
Position-to-nucleus distances differ only slightly; the deciding factor is the number of 90° neighbors.
Axial positions are reserved for the most electronegative atoms only
Electronegative atoms tend to favor axial sites, but nothing reserves them; lone-pair placement is set by 90° repulsions.
An equatorial lone pair is perpendicular to the π system
SF₄ placement is a VSEPR effect, not a π effect.
An equatorial site has only two 90° neighbors versus three for an axial site
Correct: fewer 90° repulsions minimize energy for the bulky lone pair.
questions.x: In a trigonal bipyramid, repulsions at 90° are far stronger than at 120°. An axial position has three equatorial neighbors at 90°, while an equatorial position has only two (the axial atoms). Lone pairs are bulky and repel most strongly, so they go where they face the fewest 90° contacts: equatorial. That rule produces the seesaw, T-shaped and linear shapes.

questions.q: What is the molecular geometry of the triiodide ion, I₃⁻?
o: Bent
Bent would result from three or four domains with lone pairs, not five.
Trigonal planar
The central I has five domains, not three.
Linear
Correct: central I has two bonds and three lone pairs, which sit equatorially.
T-shaped
T-shaped needs three bonded atoms.
questions.note: I₃⁻ is isoelectronic in shape logic with XeF₂.
questions.x: The central iodine in I₃⁻ has 7 valence electrons plus 1 for the charge. Two go into bonds and six remain as three lone pairs, giving five domains with trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry. The three lone pairs take the equatorial sites, leaving the two terminal iodines axial at 180°, so the ion is linear. Lone pairs do not automatically mean a bent shape.

questions.q: What is the molecular geometry of SF₆?
o: Octahedral
Correct: six bonding domains and no lone pairs give 90° angles.
Hexagonal planar
VSEPR places six domains in three dimensions, not a flat hexagon.
Trigonal bipyramidal
That geometry has five domains.
Square pyramidal
That requires one of the six domains to be a lone pair.
questions.x: Sulfur in SF₆ has six bonding domains and no lone pairs. The arrangement that keeps six domains as far apart as possible in three dimensions is an octahedron, with all F–S–F angles of 90° or 180°. A flat hexagon would put neighboring bonds only 60° apart, so VSEPR never predicts it; square pyramidal applies only if one domain is a lone pair.

questions.q: What is the hybridization of sulfur in SF₆?
o: sp³
sp³ gives only four hybrid orbitals.
sp³d
That gives five orbitals, for trigonal bipyramidal molecules.
sp³d²
Correct: six electron domains require six hybrid orbitals.
sp²
sp² gives only three orbitals.
questions.note: Number of domains = number of hybrid orbitals.
questions.x: Hybridization is matched to the number of electron domains: two → sp, three → sp², four → sp³, five → sp³d, six → sp³d². Sulfur in SF₆ has six bonding domains, so it needs six equivalent hybrid orbitals, described as sp³d². This is the conventional MCAT model for expanded octets; sp³d would provide only five orbitals.

questions.q: What is the hybridization of phosphorus in PCl₅?
o: sp³d
Correct: five electron domains need five hybrid orbitals.
sp³
sp³ gives four orbitals, one short.
sp³d²
That gives six orbitals, one too many.
sp²
sp² gives three orbitals.
questions.x: Phosphorus in PCl₅ has five bonding domains and no lone pairs. Five hybrid orbitals are needed, so the conventional description is sp³d (one s, three p and one d orbital), matching the trigonal bipyramidal geometry. Counting domains, not just bonds or valence electrons, is the reliable way to assign hybridization; sp³d² would supply one orbital too many.

questions.q: What is the hybridization of carbon in methane?
o: sp
sp gives two orbitals for linear geometry.
sp²
sp² gives three orbitals for trigonal planar geometry.
sp³d
Carbon cannot expand its octet.
sp³
Correct: four σ bonds in a tetrahedron use four sp³ orbitals.
questions.x: Carbon in methane forms four equivalent σ bonds arranged tetrahedrally at 109.5°. Mixing one 2s and three 2p orbitals gives four equivalent sp³ hybrids that point to the corners of a tetrahedron. sp² and sp carbons leave p orbitals unhybridized for π bonds, which methane has none of. Carbon, in period 2, cannot use d orbitals, ruling out sp³d.

questions.q: In pyridine, nitrogen is part of the aromatic ring. What is the hybridization of N, and where is its lone pair?
o: sp³; in an orbital above the ring
Ring atoms in an aromatic system are sp², not sp³.
sp²; in an sp² orbital in the plane of the ring
Correct: the lone pair is not part of the π system, which is why pyridine is basic.
sp²; in the p orbital as part of the aromatic π system
That describes pyrrole; pyridine's N already contributes one p electron.
sp; along the C–N axis
N has three domains, not two.
questions.note: Pyridine's lone pair is available for protonation; pyrrole's is not.
questions.x: Pyridine's nitrogen has three domains (two ring bonds and a lone pair), so it is sp². Its p orbital holds one electron that completes the six-electron aromatic π system, and its lone pair sits in an sp² orbital in the ring plane, pointing outward. Because that pair is not needed for aromaticity, pyridine is basic. In pyrrole, the N lone pair is in the p orbital, so protonating it would destroy aromaticity.

questions.q: In acetaldehyde, CH₃–CHO, what are the hybridizations of the methyl carbon and the carbonyl carbon?
o: sp² and sp²
The methyl carbon has four σ bonds: sp³.
sp³ and sp³
The carbonyl carbon has three domains: sp².
sp³ and sp²
Correct: CH₃ has four single bonds; C=O carbon has three electron domains.
sp³ and sp
sp requires two domains, as in a triple bond or allene center.
questions.x: Count electron domains around each carbon. The methyl carbon has four σ bonds (three C–H, one C–C): four domains, sp³, tetrahedral. The carbonyl carbon has a C–H bond, a C–C bond and a C=O double bond counting as one domain: three domains, sp², trigonal planar. A double bond does not make a carbon sp; that requires two domains, as in a triple bond.

questions.q: Which C–H bond is the shortest?
o: The C–H bond in ethyne
Correct: the sp carbon (50% s character) holds bonding electrons closer to the nucleus.
The C–H bond in ethene
sp² (33% s) bonds are longer than sp (50% s) bonds.
The C–H bond in ethane
sp³ (25% s) C–H bonds are the longest of these.
All are identical in length
C–H length varies with the carbon's hybridization.
questions.note: More s character → shorter, stronger bond and more electronegative carbon.
questions.x: s orbitals hold electrons closer to the nucleus than p orbitals, so hybrids with more s character form shorter, stronger bonds. An sp carbon (50% s) in ethyne forms a shorter C–H bond than an sp² carbon (33%) in ethene, which is shorter than an sp³ carbon (25%) in ethane. This same effect makes the sp carbon more electronegative and terminal alkyne C–H more acidic.

questions.q: In allene, H₂C=C=CH₂, what is the hybridization of the central carbon, and how are the two CH₂ planes oriented?
o: sp²; the two CH₂ groups are coplanar
The central carbon forms two σ bonds and two π bonds: sp.
sp; the two CH₂ groups are coplanar
The two π bonds use perpendicular p orbitals, which twists the ends.
sp²; the two CH₂ groups are perpendicular
sp² would give the central carbon three σ bonds; it has two.
sp; the two CH₂ groups are perpendicular
Correct: the perpendicular p orbitals of the sp carbon force the terminal planes to be at 90°.
questions.x: The central carbon of allene forms two σ bonds, so it is sp and linear. Its two remaining p orbitals are perpendicular: one π bond uses one p orbital with the left carbon, the other uses the second p orbital with the right carbon. Each terminal CH₂ plane must lie perpendicular to the p orbital it overlaps, so the two CH₂ planes end up twisted 90° from each other.

questions.q: What is the hybridization of the carbon atom in CO₂?
o: sp³
Carbon in CO₂ has two domains, not four.
sp
Correct: two σ bonds in a linear arrangement use two sp orbitals.
sp²
sp² needs three electron domains.
sp³d
Carbon cannot expand its octet.
questions.note: Count domains, not bonds: each double bond is one domain.
questions.x: Hybridization depends on electron domains, and a double bond counts as one domain. Carbon in CO₂ has two double bonds and no lone pairs, so two domains: sp hybridization with a linear geometry. The sp orbitals form the two σ bonds, and carbon's two leftover p orbitals form the two π bonds. Counting four bonds and choosing sp³ is the common mistake.

questions.q: How many unhybridized p orbitals does an sp²-hybridized carbon have, and how are they oriented?
o: Two, both in the plane of the hybrid orbitals
sp² uses two of the three p orbitals, leaving one.
None; all orbitals are hybridized
Only three of the four valence orbitals hybridize.
One, in the plane of the hybrid orbitals
The leftover p orbital is perpendicular to the plane.
One, perpendicular to the plane of the three hybrid orbitals
Correct: this p orbital forms the π bond.
questions.x: In sp² hybridization, the 2s orbital mixes with two of the three 2p orbitals, producing three hybrids in a plane at 120°. One p orbital remains unhybridized, oriented perpendicular to that plane. Side-by-side overlap of this p orbital with a neighbor's forms a π bond, which is why sp² carbons are found in double bonds and planar systems.

questions.q: How many σ and π bonds are in ethene, H₂C=CH₂?
o: 5 σ, 1 π
Correct: four C–H σ bonds, one C–C σ, and one C–C π.
6 σ, 0 π
Treats the double bond as two σ bonds.
4 σ, 2 π
A double bond contains one σ and one π.
4 σ, 1 π
Misses the σ component of the C=C bond.
questions.x: Every bond between two atoms contains exactly one σ bond; any additional bonds are π bonds. Ethene has four C–H single bonds (4 σ) and one C=C double bond (1 σ + 1 π). That gives 5 σ and 1 π. Forgetting that a double bond also contains a σ component leads to the tempting 4 σ, 1 π answer.

questions.q: How many σ and π bonds are in acrylonitrile, H₂C=CH–C≡N?
o: 6 σ, 2 π
The C≡N triple bond has two π bonds, plus one more in C=C.
6 σ, 3 π
Correct: 3 C–H + C=C σ + C–C + C≡N σ = 6 σ; 1 π (C=C) + 2 π (C≡N) = 3 π.
9 σ, 0 π
Counts every bond line as σ.
5 σ, 3 π
Misses one σ bond, likely the central C–C single bond.
questions.note: Every bond has exactly one σ; extras are π.
questions.x: Each bonded pair of atoms has one σ bond; extra bonds are π. In H₂C=CH–C≡N, there are three C–H σ bonds, one σ in C=C, one C–C single σ and one σ in C≡N, totaling 6 σ. The C=C adds 1 π and the C≡N adds 2 π, totaling 3 π. Forgetting that a triple bond holds two π bonds gives the tempting 6 σ, 2 π.

questions.q: Why is rotation about a C=C double bond restricted at room temperature?
o: The σ bond is too short to rotate
σ bonds alone allow free rotation regardless of length.
Rotation would require breaking the π bond, whose p orbitals must stay parallel
Correct: twisting 90° destroys p–p overlap, which costs too much energy.
The substituents are too large to pass each other
Even ethene, with only hydrogens, does not rotate freely.
Double-bonded carbons are sp³ hybridized
Double-bonded carbons are sp².
questions.note: Restricted rotation is why cis/trans isomers exist.
questions.x: A π bond depends on side-by-side overlap of p orbitals that are parallel. Rotating one end of a C=C by 90° makes the p orbitals perpendicular, eliminating overlap and effectively breaking the π bond, which costs roughly 260 kJ/mol, far above thermal energy at room temperature. That is why cis and trans alkenes do not interconvert. Even ethene, with tiny H substituents, is rigid.

questions.q: A π bond forms from:
o: Head-on overlap of two hybrid orbitals
That forms a σ bond.
Overlap of an s orbital with a p orbital along the bond axis
Any end-on overlap forms a σ bond.
Side-by-side overlap of parallel p orbitals
Correct: π density lies above and below the bond axis.
Transfer of an electron from one atom to another
Electron transfer describes ionic bonding.
questions.x: Bonds are classified by how orbitals overlap. Any head-on overlap along the internuclear axis, whether s–s, s–p, p–p or hybrid–hybrid, forms a σ bond. A π bond forms only when two parallel p orbitals overlap side by side, placing density above and below the axis. Because side-on overlap is less effective, π bonds are weaker than σ bonds.

questions.q: Where is the electron density of a π bond located?
o: Concentrated directly along the internuclear axis
That describes a σ bond.
Mostly on the more electronegative atom only
Polarity shifts density, but π density still has two lobes off the axis.
In a spherical cloud around one nucleus
That describes an s orbital, not a bond.
Above and below the internuclear axis, with a node along the axis
Correct: the p orbital nodal plane contains the bond axis.
questions.x: A π bond is built from two parallel p orbitals, each of which has a nodal plane containing the bond axis. When they overlap side by side, the resulting π bond keeps that node: there is zero density along the internuclear axis and two lobes above and below it. Density concentrated on the axis is the defining feature of a σ bond, not a π bond.

questions.q: How many σ and π bonds are in benzene, C₆H₆?
o: Correct: 6 C–C σ + 6 C–H σ = 12 σ; three π bonds (delocalized) from the alternating doubles.
9 σ, 3 π
Misses three σ bonds; each of six C–C links has a σ bond.
6 σ, 6 π
Ignores the C–H bonds and doubles the π count.
Six π electrons form three π bonds, not six.
questions.note: Count π bonds as pairs of π electrons.
questions.x: Benzene has six C–C links and six C–H bonds, each with one σ bond: 12 σ bonds. Its six π electrons fill three π bonding orbitals, so it is counted as having three π bonds, even though they are delocalized over the whole ring rather than fixed between particular carbons. Counting six π bonds confuses six π electrons with six bonds.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide contains two C=O π bonds. How are they oriented relative to each other?
o: In the same plane, on opposite sides of carbon
The sp carbon's two p orbitals are perpendicular, so the π bonds cannot share a plane.
In perpendicular planes
Correct: carbon uses its two remaining p orbitals, which are at 90° to each other.
Both along the molecular axis
π bonds never lie along the internuclear axis.
They merge into one delocalized π bond
The two π systems are orthogonal and do not overlap.
questions.x: The carbon in CO₂ is sp, using its 2s and one 2p orbital for the two σ bonds. Its two remaining p orbitals are perpendicular to each other and to the molecular axis. One forms a π bond with the left oxygen and the other with the right oxygen, so the two π bonds lie in perpendicular planes. This is the same orbital logic that twists the ends of allene.

questions.q: A carbon–nitrogen triple bond consists of:
o: Three σ bonds
Only one σ bond can form between two atoms.
Two σ bonds and one π bond
There is only one σ bond per bonded pair.
Three π bonds
Every bond needs a σ component first.
One σ bond and two π bonds
Correct: one head-on overlap plus two perpendicular side-on overlaps.
questions.x: Two atoms can form only one σ bond, by head-on overlap along the axis between them. Any further bonding must use side-on overlap of p orbitals. In a C≡N triple bond, the sp carbon and nitrogen each contribute two perpendicular p orbitals, giving two π bonds at right angles to each other. So every triple bond is one σ plus two π bonds.

questions.q: Which bond is the most polar?
o: C–H
C and H have nearly equal electronegativity.
C–N
N is less electronegative than F.
C–O
O is electronegative, but less so than F.
C–F
Correct: fluorine is the most electronegative element, so ΔEN is largest.
questions.x: Bond polarity grows with the electronegativity difference between the two atoms. Electronegativity increases across a period toward fluorine: C (2.5) < N (3.0) < O (3.5) < F (4.0). With carbon as the common partner, C–F has the largest difference and is the most polar. C–H is nearly nonpolar because hydrogen and carbon have similar electronegativities.

questions.q: Which molecule has polar bonds but no net dipole moment?
o: CCl₄
Correct: four identical C–Cl dipoles in a tetrahedron cancel.
CHCl₃
Replacing one Cl with H breaks the symmetry: polar.
CH₂Cl₂
The unequal substituents leave a net dipole.
CH₃Cl
A single C–Cl dipole is not canceled.
questions.note: Symmetry can cancel polar bonds.
questions.x: A molecule's net dipole is the vector sum of its bond dipoles. In CCl₄, four identical polar C–Cl bonds point to the corners of a regular tetrahedron, so they cancel exactly and the molecule is nonpolar. Replacing any Cl with H, as in CHCl₃, CH₂Cl₂ or CH₃Cl, breaks that symmetry and leaves a net dipole. Polar bonds do not guarantee a polar molecule.

questions.q: Which molecule is polar?
o: SF₆
Octahedral symmetry cancels all bond dipoles.
XeF₄
Square planar symmetry cancels the dipoles.
SF₄
Correct: the seesaw shape is asymmetric, so bond dipoles do not cancel.
BF₃
Trigonal planar symmetry cancels the three B–F dipoles.
questions.x: Whether bond dipoles cancel depends on molecular symmetry. SF₆ (octahedral), XeF₄ (square planar) and BF₃ (trigonal planar) have identical bonds arranged symmetrically, so their dipoles sum to zero. SF₄ is seesaw shaped because of its lone pair; its S–F dipoles do not point in balanced directions, leaving a net dipole. XeF₄ is tempting because it has lone pairs, but they sit opposite each other and cancel.

questions.q: Which isomer of 1,2-dichloroethene has a net dipole moment of zero?
o: cis-1,2-Dichloroethene
Both Cl atoms on the same side add their dipoles.
trans-1,2-Dichloroethene
Correct: the C–Cl dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.
Both isomers
Only the trans isomer is centrosymmetric.
Neither isomer
The trans isomer's dipoles do cancel.
questions.x: In trans-1,2-dichloroethene the two C–Cl bonds point in exactly opposite directions across the rigid C=C bond, so their dipoles cancel and the net moment is zero. In the cis isomer both chlorines lie on the same side, so their dipoles add to a net moment. Because the double bond prevents rotation, these geometries are fixed, which is why the isomers differ in polarity and boiling point.

questions.q: Dipole moment is μ = q × d. Two bonds have equal partial charges, but bond X is twice as long as bond Y. How does μ(X) compare with μ(Y)?
o: Half as large
Inverts the relationship; μ is proportional to d.
The same
Ignores the dependence on separation.
Four times as large
μ depends linearly on d, not on d².
Twice as large
Correct: μ scales directly with charge separation.
questions.x: The dipole moment equals charge magnitude times separation, μ = q × d, a direct linear proportion. With q held constant, doubling d doubles μ. Unlike Coulomb's law force, which falls off with 1/r², the dipole moment does not involve a square, so neither four times nor half as large is correct. Larger dipoles usually come from larger charge separation or larger partial charges.

questions.q: NH₃ has a dipole moment of about 1.5 D, but NF₃ has only about 0.2 D, even though N–F bonds are more polar than N–H bonds. Why?
o: In NF₃ the N–F bond dipoles point away from N and oppose the lone-pair dipole
Correct: in NH₃ bond and lone-pair dipoles reinforce; in NF₃ they largely cancel.
NF₃ is trigonal planar, so its dipoles cancel
NF₃ is trigonal pyramidal like NH₃.
Fluorine is less electronegative than nitrogen
Fluorine is more electronegative than nitrogen.
NF₃ has no lone pair on nitrogen
N in NF₃ still has one lone pair.
questions.note: Net dipole = vector sum of bond dipoles and lone-pair contributions.
questions.x: A molecule's dipole is the vector sum of bond dipoles and the lone-pair contribution. In NH₃, nitrogen is more electronegative than H, so the bond dipoles point toward N, the same way as the lone pair; they add up. In NF₃, fluorine is more electronegative, so the N–F dipoles point away from N, opposing the lone-pair dipole and nearly canceling it. Both molecules are trigonal pyramidal.

questions.q: CO₂ is nonpolar, whereas SO₂ is polar. What accounts for the difference?
o: C–O bonds are nonpolar, while S–O bonds are polar
Both bond types are polar.
CO₂ is linear so its dipoles cancel; SO₂ is bent so they do not
Correct: geometry, driven by S's lone pair, determines the net dipole.
Sulfur is more electronegative than oxygen
Oxygen is more electronegative than sulfur.
SO₂ contains π bonds and CO₂ does not
Both molecules contain π bonds.
questions.x: C=O and S=O bonds are both polar because oxygen is more electronegative than carbon and sulfur. The difference is shape. Carbon in CO₂ has no lone pair, so the molecule is linear and the two bond dipoles point opposite ways and cancel. Sulfur in SO₂ has a lone pair, making the molecule bent, so the dipoles add to a net moment. Molecular geometry, not bond polarity, decides here.

questions.q: Which bond is best described as nonpolar covalent?
o: O–H
ΔEN ≈ 1.2: strongly polar.
N–H
ΔEN ≈ 0.9: polar.
C–O
ΔEN ≈ 0.9: polar.
C–H
Correct: ΔEN ≈ 0.4, small enough that the bond is treated as nonpolar.
questions.note: C–H bonds make hydrocarbons nonpolar.
questions.x: Bond polarity depends on the electronegativity difference. Using Pauling values H 2.2, C 2.5, N 3.0, O 3.4: O–H differs by about 1.2, N–H about 0.9, C–O about 0.9 and C–H only about 0.4. A difference below roughly 0.5 is treated as nonpolar covalent, so C–H qualifies. This is why hydrocarbons are nonpolar and dissolve in nonpolar solvents.

questions.q: BF₃ has no net dipole moment, but NF₃ does. Which feature explains this?
o: NF₃ has a lone pair on N that makes it trigonal pyramidal
Correct: BF₃ is planar and symmetric; the lone pair puckers NF₃.
B–F bonds are nonpolar
B–F bonds are highly polar; they cancel by symmetry.
NF₃ has more fluorine atoms
Both have three fluorines.
Boron is more electronegative than fluorine
Fluorine is far more electronegative than boron.
questions.x: BF₃ has three bonds and no lone pair on boron, so it is trigonal planar; its three polar B–F dipoles sit 120° apart and cancel. NF₃ has three bonds plus a lone pair on nitrogen, so it is trigonal pyramidal, and its N–F dipoles do not cancel, leaving a net dipole. Both have polar bonds; the lone pair changes the geometry and therefore the net polarity.

questions.q: A charged rod is held near thin falling streams of four liquids. Which stream is deflected most strongly toward the rod?
o: Hexane
Nonpolar hydrocarbon: no net dipole to align with the field.
Carbon disulfide
Linear S=C=S: bond dipoles cancel.
Dichloromethane
Correct: CH₂Cl₂ has a net dipole, so molecules orient and are pulled toward the charge.
Benzene
Planar and symmetric: no net dipole.
questions.note: Polar molecules align in an electric field; nonpolar ones barely respond.
questions.x: Molecules with a permanent dipole rotate in an electric field so their oppositely charged end faces the rod, and the nonuniform field then pulls them in. Dichloromethane is tetrahedral with two Cl and two H, so its bond dipoles do not cancel. Hexane, CS₂ and benzene have no net dipole, so they respond only weakly through induced dipoles. Polarity comes from symmetry, not just from polar bonds.

questions.q: Which compound can form hydrogen bonds with other molecules of itself?
o: CH₃OCH₃
Its hydrogens are bonded only to carbon, so it cannot donate.
CH₃OH
Correct: the O–H hydrogen can donate to another molecule's oxygen.
CH₃F
H is bonded to C, not to F, so there is no donor.
H₂C=O
Can accept H-bonds, but has no H on N, O or F to donate.
questions.note: A donor needs H covalently bonded to N, O or F.
questions.x: A hydrogen bond needs a donor, a hydrogen covalently bonded to N, O or F, and an acceptor, a lone pair on N, O or F. Methanol has an O–H group, so each molecule can both donate and accept. Dimethyl ether, formaldehyde and fluoromethane contain O or F acceptors, but their hydrogens are all on carbon, so they cannot donate to each other.

questions.q: Pure acetone cannot hydrogen bond with itself, yet it is fully miscible with water. Why?
o: Acetone's methyl hydrogens donate hydrogen bonds to water
C–H hydrogens are not H-bond donors.
Acetone ionizes in water
Acetone is a neutral molecule that does not ionize appreciably.
Only London forces are needed to mix with water
Dispersion alone cannot overcome water's H-bond network.
Its carbonyl oxygen accepts hydrogen bonds from water
Correct: acetone is an H-bond acceptor even though it cannot donate.
questions.note: Acceptors without donors still mix with water.
questions.x: Hydrogen bonding with water needs a donor on one partner and an acceptor on the other. Acetone has no O–H, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself, but its carbonyl oxygen has lone pairs that accept hydrogen bonds from water's O–H groups. Those strong solute–solvent interactions make acetone miscible with water. Its C–H hydrogens are not donors.

questions.q: What intermolecular force holds molecules together in liquid nitrogen, N₂?
o: Hydrogen bonding
N₂ has no hydrogen atoms.
Dipole–dipole forces
N₂ is nonpolar, with no permanent dipole.
London dispersion forces
Correct: temporary induced dipoles are the only attractions between nonpolar molecules.
Ion–dipole forces
There are no ions present.
questions.x: N₂ is a nonpolar homonuclear molecule with no permanent dipole and no hydrogen. The only attractions between N₂ molecules are London dispersion forces, which come from momentary fluctuations in electron distribution that induce dipoles in neighbors. Because N₂ has few electrons, these forces are very weak, which is why it boils at about −196 °C.

questions.q: At room temperature, I₂ is a solid while F₂ is a gas. What is the best explanation?
o: I₂ is polar and F₂ is not
Both are homonuclear diatomics with no dipole.
I₂ forms hydrogen bonds
Neither halogen has hydrogen.
The I–I covalent bond is stronger than the F–F bond
Phase changes do not break covalent bonds; intermolecular forces matter.
I₂ has a larger, more polarizable electron cloud, giving stronger dispersion forces
Correct: more electrons → larger induced dipoles → stronger London forces.
questions.note: Trap: melting and boiling molecular substances never break covalent bonds.
questions.x: F₂ and I₂ are both nonpolar, so only London dispersion forces hold their molecules together. Iodine has far more electrons in a larger, loosely held cloud, so it is much more polarizable and forms much larger temporary dipoles, making dispersion forces strong enough to keep I₂ solid. Melting or boiling a molecular substance separates molecules without breaking covalent bonds, so bond strength is irrelevant.

questions.q: n-Pentane (bp 36 °C) and neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane, bp 10 °C) have the same formula. Why does n-pentane boil higher?
o: Its elongated shape allows more surface contact, so dispersion forces are stronger
Correct: compact, branched molecules touch less, weakening London forces.
It has more electrons
Isomers have identical electron counts.
It is polar while neopentane is not
Both alkanes are essentially nonpolar.
It forms hydrogen bonds
Alkanes cannot hydrogen bond.
questions.note: Branching lowers boiling point.
questions.x: Dispersion forces depend on how much surface area neighboring molecules can share. n-Pentane is a long chain that can lie alongside its neighbors with extensive contact, while neopentane is nearly spherical and touches neighbors over a small area. Same formula, same electron count, but weaker dispersion forces in the branched isomer, so neopentane boils about 26 °C lower.

questions.q: When NaCl dissolves in water, what is the main interaction between a Na⁺ ion and the surrounding water?
o: Ion–dipole attraction with the hydrogen atoms pointed toward Na⁺
The partially positive hydrogens would repel a cation.
Hydrogen bonding between Na⁺ and water's oxygen
Na⁺ has no H; hydrogen bonding requires an H donor.
Ion–dipole attraction with water's oxygen oriented toward Na⁺
Correct: the partially negative oxygen faces the cation.
Covalent bonding between Na and O
Hydration is noncovalent.
questions.note: Cations are hydrated by O; anions by H.
questions.x: When ionic solids dissolve in water, each ion is surrounded by water molecules oriented by charge, an ion–dipole interaction. Water's oxygen carries a partial negative charge, so it faces cations such as Na⁺, while the partially positive hydrogens face anions such as Cl⁻. Hydrogen bonding is not involved, because Na⁺ has no hydrogen and is not N, O or F.

questions.q: For molecules of comparable size, which ranking of interaction strengths is typical, from strongest to weakest?
o: Hydrogen bond > ion–dipole > dipole–dipole > London dispersion
Ion–dipole interactions involve full charges and are stronger than H-bonds.
Ion–dipole > hydrogen bond > dipole–dipole > London dispersion
Correct: full charges beat partial ones; H-bonds are especially strong dipole–dipole forces.
Dipole–dipole > hydrogen bond > ion–dipole > London dispersion
Places dipole–dipole above both; H-bonds are the strongest dipole–dipole forces and ion–dipole beats them.
London dispersion > dipole–dipole > hydrogen bond > ion–dipole
This reverses the usual ranking for similar-sized species.
questions.note: Caveat: dispersion can dominate for very large molecules.
questions.x: Interaction strength scales with the charges involved. Ion–dipole forces involve a full ionic charge and are strongest. Hydrogen bonds are especially strong dipole–dipole interactions because H on N, O or F is highly exposed and positive. Ordinary dipole–dipole forces come next, and London dispersion is weakest for molecules of similar size. Very large molecules can still have dispersion forces that dominate.

questions.q: Which hydrogen halide has the lowest boiling point?
o: HF
HF hydrogen bonds and has the highest boiling point of the four.
HCl
Correct: it lacks H-bonding and has the fewest electrons of HCl, HBr and HI, so the weakest dispersion forces.
HBr
More electrons than HCl give stronger dispersion forces.
HI
The largest electron cloud gives the strongest dispersion among HCl–HI.
questions.note: HF is the anomaly; otherwise boiling point rises down the group.
questions.x: Among HCl, HBr and HI, the only attractions are dipole–dipole and dispersion forces, and dispersion grows with the number of electrons, so boiling point rises from HCl (−85 °C) to HI (−35 °C). HF breaks the trend: its H–F bond lets it form strong hydrogen bonds, so it boils near 20 °C despite being the lightest. HCl is therefore lowest.

questions.q: Water (molar mass 18) boils at 100 °C, but H₂S (molar mass 34) boils at about −60 °C. What best explains this?
o: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds; H₂S molecules do not form significant ones
Correct: O is electronegative enough for strong H-bonding; S is not.
H₂S has stronger dispersion forces than water
True but irrelevant: it would make H₂S boil higher, not lower.
Water's O–H covalent bonds are stronger than S–H bonds
Boiling does not break covalent bonds.
H₂S is nonpolar
H₂S is bent and slightly polar.
questions.x: Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom (N, O or F). Water's O–H bonds give strong hydrogen bonds that must be overcome to boil it. Sulfur is larger and much less electronegative, so H₂S forms only weak dipole–dipole and dispersion attractions. Although heavier H₂S has more dispersion, water's hydrogen bonding dominates, giving it a boiling point about 160 °C higher.

questions.q: Small amounts of O₂ dissolve in water. Which interaction mainly accounts for this?
o: Hydrogen bonding
O₂ has no hydrogens and is a very poor acceptor.
Ion–dipole forces
O₂ is not an ion.
Dipole–dipole forces
O₂ has no permanent dipole.
Dipole–induced dipole forces
Correct: water's dipole distorts O₂'s electron cloud, creating a weak attraction.
questions.x: O₂ is nonpolar, so it cannot form ion–dipole, dipole–dipole or hydrogen-bond interactions with water. A polar water molecule can, however, distort O₂'s electron cloud and induce a temporary dipole, giving a weak dipole–induced dipole attraction (plus dispersion). Because this attraction is weak compared with water–water hydrogen bonds, O₂ solubility in water is low.

questions.q: o-Nitrophenol boils at a much lower temperature than p-nitrophenol. What is the best explanation?
o: The ortho isomer has a lower molar mass
The isomers have identical molar masses.
The ortho isomer forms an intramolecular H-bond, leaving fewer intermolecular H-bonds
Correct: the OH and NO₂ groups bond within one molecule, weakening attractions between molecules.
The para isomer is nonpolar
The para isomer has a large dipole and H-bonds intermolecularly.
The ortho isomer cannot hydrogen bond at all
It does hydrogen bond, but internally.
questions.note: Intramolecular H-bonds lower boiling points relative to isomers.
questions.x: In o-nitrophenol, the OH and NO₂ groups are adjacent, so the OH hydrogen bonds to a nitro oxygen within the same molecule, forming a six-membered ring. With its donor tied up internally, the molecule forms few hydrogen bonds to neighbors, so it is more volatile. In p-nitrophenol the groups are too far apart, so OH hydrogen bonds to other molecules, raising the boiling point. Both isomers have identical mass.

questions.q: DNA with a higher fraction of G–C base pairs has a higher melting temperature. What is the classic explanation based on intermolecular forces?
o: G–C pairs are joined by covalent bonds
Base pairs are held by noncovalent hydrogen bonds.
G–C pairs form ionic bonds with the phosphate backbone
Base pairing does not involve the phosphates.
G–C pairs form three hydrogen bonds, versus two for A–T pairs
Correct: more hydrogen bonds per pair require more energy to separate.
G and C are more hydrophobic than A and T
Hydrophobicity is not the standard explanation.
questions.x: Melting DNA means separating the two strands, which requires breaking the noncovalent interactions between them. The classic explanation is that a G–C pair is joined by three hydrogen bonds while an A–T pair has two, so GC-rich DNA needs more energy to separate. Base-stacking interactions, also stronger for G–C, contribute too. No covalent bonds are broken when DNA melts.

questions.q: Ethanol and dimethyl ether both have the formula C₂H₆O, yet ethanol boils about 100 °C higher. Why?
o: Ethanol has a higher molar mass
They are isomers with identical molar mass.
Dimethyl ether is nonpolar
The ether is bent at O and is polar.
Ethanol has stronger covalent bonds
Covalent bonds are not broken on boiling.
Ethanol's O–H group lets it hydrogen bond with itself
Correct: the ether has no O–H and cannot donate H-bonds.
questions.x: Ethanol and dimethyl ether have the same formula and mass, so their dispersion forces are similar. Ethanol's O–H group makes it both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, so its molecules hydrogen bond strongly to each other. Dimethyl ether has an oxygen acceptor but all its hydrogens are on carbon, so it only has weaker dipole–dipole attractions. That is why ethanol boils near 78 °C and the ether near −24 °C.

questions.q: In liquid water, what is the maximum number of hydrogen bonds a single water molecule can take part in?
o: Correct: it can donate two through its H atoms and accept two through its lone pairs.
Counts only donations or only acceptances.
Misses one of the two lone pairs or one of the two hydrogens.
Water is a multiple donor and acceptor.
questions.x: A water molecule has two O–H hydrogens, each able to donate one hydrogen bond, and two lone pairs on oxygen, each able to accept one. That allows up to four hydrogen bonds per molecule, arranged tetrahedrally. This is the basis of ice's lattice; in the liquid, molecules average somewhat fewer at any instant because bonds constantly break and re-form.

questions.q: Ice floats on liquid water. What is the molecular explanation?
o: Ice contains trapped air bubbles
Even bubble-free ice is less dense than water.
Covalent bonds lengthen when water freezes
O–H covalent bond lengths barely change.
Molecules in ice move faster and spread apart
Molecules move slower in the solid.
Hydrogen bonds lock molecules into an open hexagonal lattice with more empty space
Correct: the rigid H-bond network holds molecules farther apart than in the liquid.
questions.x: As water freezes, each molecule locks into four hydrogen bonds arranged tetrahedrally, producing an open hexagonal lattice. This rigid network holds molecules farther apart than in the liquid, where hydrogen bonds constantly break and molecules can pack more closely. So ice is about 9% less dense than liquid water and floats. Molecules actually move more slowly in the solid, not faster.

questions.q: Glycerol (HOCH₂–CHOH–CH₂OH) is far more viscous than 1-propanol, a molecule of similar size. Why?
o: Glycerol has three OH groups, so each molecule forms many more hydrogen bonds
Correct: an extensive H-bond network resists flow.
Glycerol is nonpolar
Glycerol is highly polar.
1-Propanol has stronger dispersion forces
Their sizes are similar, and dispersion is not the deciding factor.
Glycerol forms ionic bonds
Glycerol is a neutral molecule.
questions.x: Viscosity reflects how strongly molecules resist sliding past one another. Glycerol has three OH groups per molecule, so each molecule hydrogen bonds to several neighbors, creating an extensive network that must be continually broken for flow. 1-Propanol, with one OH, forms far fewer hydrogen bonds. Their sizes and dispersion forces are similar, so hydrogen bonding is what makes glycerol syrupy.

questions.q: Propane (C₃H₈), acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO) and ethanol (C₂H₅OH) have similar molar masses (44–46 g/mol). Which order lists them by increasing boiling point?
o: Ethanol < acetaldehyde < propane
Reversed: stronger intermolecular forces raise boiling point.
Acetaldehyde < propane < ethanol
Propane, with only dispersion forces, boils lowest.
Propane < acetaldehyde < ethanol
Correct: dispersion only < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding.
Propane < ethanol < acetaldehyde
Acetaldehyde cannot donate H-bonds, so it boils below ethanol.
questions.note: At similar mass, rank by the strongest IMF available.
questions.x: At similar molar mass, dispersion forces are comparable, so boiling point is set by the strongest additional interaction. Propane is nonpolar with only dispersion forces and boils near −42 °C. Acetaldehyde has a polar C=O and adds dipole–dipole attraction, boiling near 20 °C. Ethanol can donate and accept hydrogen bonds and boils at 78 °C. Acetaldehyde has an oxygen but no O–H, so it cannot match ethanol.

questions.q: In ethane, H₃C–CH₃, each C–H σ bond forms from the overlap of which orbitals?
o: A carbon 2p orbital and a hydrogen 1s orbital
Unhybridized p orbitals cannot give four equivalent bonds at 109.5°.
A carbon sp² orbital and a hydrogen 1s orbital
sp² carbons have three domains; each ethane carbon has four σ bonds.
A carbon sp³ orbital and a hydrogen 1s orbital
Correct: each tetrahedral carbon uses sp³ hybrids, and hydrogen uses its only valence orbital, 1s.
A carbon sp³ orbital and a hydrogen sp³ orbital
Hydrogen has only a 1s orbital and does not hybridize.
questions.x: Each carbon in ethane forms four σ bonds arranged tetrahedrally, so it is sp³ hybridized. Every C–H bond is head-on overlap of one carbon sp³ hybrid with hydrogen's 1s orbital, and the C–C bond is sp³–sp³ overlap. Hydrogen has only one valence orbital, 1s, so it never hybridizes. Pure p orbitals would give 90° bonds, not the observed 109.5°.

questions.q: Ethanol is miscible with water, but 1-hexanol is only slightly soluble. Why?
o: 1-Hexanol cannot hydrogen bond
It has an OH group and can hydrogen bond.
1-Hexanol is ionic
Alcohols are molecular, not ionic.
Ethanol has a higher molar mass
1-Hexanol is heavier, not lighter.
1-Hexanol's long hydrocarbon chain disrupts water's hydrogen-bond network
Correct: the larger nonpolar portion outweighs the single OH group.
questions.note: Water solubility falls as the nonpolar chain grows.
questions.x: An alcohol's OH group hydrogen bonds with water, but its hydrocarbon chain cannot, and inserting a nonpolar chain forces nearby water into ordered cages, which is entropically unfavorable. In ethanol the small ethyl group is outweighed by the OH, so it mixes completely. In 1-hexanol the six-carbon chain dominates, so solubility drops to a few grams per liter. 1-Hexanol still hydrogen bonds; it is simply outweighed.

questions.q: At 25 °C, which liquid has the highest vapor pressure?
o: Water
Strong hydrogen bonding keeps molecules in the liquid.
Diethyl ether
Correct: no H-bond donors, so weak IMFs let molecules escape easily.
Ethanol
Ethanol hydrogen bonds, lowering its vapor pressure.
Glycerol
Three OH groups make glycerol's vapor pressure very low.
questions.note: Weaker IMFs → higher vapor pressure → lower boiling point.
questions.x: Vapor pressure measures how easily molecules escape from the liquid, so weaker intermolecular forces mean higher vapor pressure. Diethyl ether has no O–H, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself and is held only by weak dipole and dispersion forces, giving it very high vapor pressure (bp 35 °C). Ethanol, water and glycerol all hydrogen bond, with glycerol's three OH groups giving the lowest vapor pressure.

questions.q: Liquids X and Y have similar molar masses. X has ΔH_vap = 40 kJ/mol and Y has ΔH_vap = 25 kJ/mol. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: X has stronger intermolecular attractions and a higher boiling point
Correct: more energy to vaporize means stronger forces holding the liquid together.
X has a higher vapor pressure at a given temperature
Stronger IMFs lower vapor pressure.
Y has stronger covalent bonds
Vaporization does not break covalent bonds.
Y is more likely to hydrogen bond
H-bonding would raise Y's ΔH_vap, not lower it.
questions.x: The enthalpy of vaporization is the energy needed to pull molecules out of the liquid into the gas, so it directly measures the strength of intermolecular attractions. X needs 40 kJ/mol versus 25 for Y, so X's attractions are stronger; at similar molar mass that means X has the lower vapor pressure and the higher boiling point. Vaporization separates molecules without breaking covalent bonds.

questions.q: Acetic acid (60 g/mol, bp 118 °C) boils higher than 1-propanol (60 g/mol, bp 97 °C). What is the best explanation?
o: Acetic acid has more electrons, so stronger dispersion forces
The molar masses and electron counts are nearly equal.
1-Propanol cannot hydrogen bond
1-Propanol has an OH group and does hydrogen bond.
Acetic acid ionizes completely in the pure liquid
Pure acetic acid is barely ionized.
Acetic acid pairs form two hydrogen bonds each (dimers) and the C=O adds strong polarity
Correct: the carboxyl group both donates and accepts, forming strongly H-bonded dimers.
questions.note: Carboxylic acids boil higher than alcohols of similar mass.
questions.x: Both compounds have the same molar mass and can hydrogen bond. The carboxyl group of acetic acid contains both an O–H donor and a C=O acceptor, so two molecules pair into a cyclic dimer held by two hydrogen bonds, and the polar C=O adds strong dipole attraction. These interactions exceed those of 1-propanol's single OH, so the acid boils about 20 °C higher. Pure acetic acid is barely ionized.

questions.q: KBr dissolves readily in water but not in hexane. Why?
o: Hexane reacts with KBr
There is no reaction; the issue is solvation.
Hexane molecules cannot provide ion–dipole interactions to offset the lattice energy
Correct: water's dipoles stabilize K⁺ and Br⁻; nonpolar hexane cannot.
KBr is a covalent compound
KBr is ionic.
Water breaks the covalent K–Br bonds
K–Br is ionic; water separates ions, not covalent bonds.
questions.x: Dissolving an ionic solid requires replacing the strong ion–ion attractions of the lattice with ion–solvent attractions. Water's polar molecules orient around K⁺ and Br⁻, and these ion–dipole interactions release enough energy to offset the lattice energy. Hexane is nonpolar and offers only weak dispersion forces, so it cannot stabilize separated ions. KBr is ionic, so no covalent bonds are broken.

questions.q: NaCl melts at 801 °C, while Cl₂ melts at −101 °C. What best explains the difference?
o: Melting Cl₂ breaks the Cl–Cl covalent bond, which is weak
Melting a molecular solid breaks no covalent bonds.
NaCl contains hydrogen bonds
NaCl has no hydrogen atoms.
Melting NaCl requires overcoming strong ionic attractions, while Cl₂ molecules are held only by dispersion forces
Correct: ionic lattices are far stronger than London forces.
Cl₂ is lighter than NaCl
Mass alone cannot explain a 900 °C difference.
questions.x: Melting point reflects the forces that hold the solid's particles in place. Solid NaCl is a lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by strong electrostatic attractions that must be overcome to melt it. Solid Cl₂ consists of nonpolar molecules held by weak London dispersion forces. Melting Cl₂ separates intact molecules without breaking the Cl–Cl covalent bond, which is why it melts at such a low temperature.

questions.q: SiO₂ melts above 1600 °C, but CO₂ sublimes at −78 °C. What explains this difference?
o: SiO₂ is ionic and CO₂ is covalent
SiO₂ is covalently bonded, not ionic.
Si–O bonds are polar and C=O bonds are not
Both bond types are polar.
CO₂ is linear, so it has no intermolecular forces at all
CO₂ still has dispersion forces, just weak ones.
SiO₂ is a network solid whose melting breaks covalent bonds; CO₂ is held only by weak intermolecular forces
Correct: melting quartz requires breaking Si–O bonds throughout the lattice.
questions.note: Network covalent solids (diamond, quartz) have the highest melting points.
questions.x: Despite similar formulas, SiO₂ and CO₂ have very different structures. Silicon does not form stable π bonds with oxygen, so each Si bonds to four O atoms in a continuous three-dimensional network; melting quartz requires breaking strong Si–O covalent bonds. CO₂ is a discrete linear molecule held to its neighbors only by weak dispersion forces, so it sublimes at −78 °C. Both contain polar covalent bonds.

questions.q: Sodium stearate (a soap) forms micelles in water. How are the molecules arranged?
o: Nonpolar tails point inward and charged heads face the water
Correct: tails avoid water while carboxylate heads interact with it.
Charged heads point inward and tails face the water
That is a reverse micelle, which forms in nonpolar solvents.
Molecules stack in a flat bilayer sheet
Single-tailed soaps favor spherical micelles, not bilayers.
Molecules dissolve individually with no organization
Above the critical concentration they aggregate.
questions.note: The hydrophobic effect drives micelle formation.
questions.x: Soap molecules are amphipathic: a long nonpolar hydrocarbon tail and a charged carboxylate head. In water, the tails cluster inside a sphere, away from water, while the heads face outward and interact with water through ion–dipole forces. The hydrophobic effect drives this, because it frees water from ordering around tails. Reversed arrangements form only in nonpolar solvents, and double-tailed lipids prefer bilayers.

questions.q: Which compound is held together primarily by ionic bonding?
o: CF₄
Two nonmetals: covalent.
SiO₂
A covalent network solid.
HF
A polar covalent molecule.
CaF₂
Correct: a metal cation and a nonmetal anion held by electrostatic attraction.
questions.x: Ionic bonding occurs when a metal transfers electrons to a nonmetal and the resulting ions are held by electrostatic attraction. Calcium, a Group 2 metal, gives two electrons to form Ca²⁺, and each fluorine gains one to form F⁻, giving the ionic lattice CaF₂. CF₄, SiO₂ and HF are all bonds between nonmetals, which share electrons covalently even when the bonds are polar.

questions.q: Which ionic compound has the largest lattice energy?
o: NaCl
Ions of charge +1 and −1 give a modest lattice energy.
MgO
Correct: +2 and −2 charges and small ions give the strongest attraction.
KBr
+1/−1 charges and larger ions than NaCl.
CsI
Large +1/−1 ions give the smallest lattice energy here.
questions.note: Lattice energy ∝ (q₁q₂)/r: charge matters most, then size.
questions.x: Lattice energy follows Coulomb's law: it is proportional to the product of the ion charges and inversely proportional to the distance between them. MgO combines +2 and −2 charges, a charge product of 4, with small ions, so its lattice energy is about four times that of the +1/−1 salts. Among NaCl, KBr and CsI, all +1/−1, lattice energy falls as the ions get larger, making CsI the smallest.

questions.q: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, and why: NaF or NaI?
o: NaI, because iodide has more electrons
More electrons do not strengthen ionic attraction; larger size weakens it.
NaI, because I⁻ is more polarizable
Polarizability matters for dispersion, not lattice energy here.
NaF, because the smaller F⁻ lets the ions get closer
Correct: smaller interionic distance means stronger Coulomb attraction.
They are equal, because both ions have the same charges
Same charges, but different ion sizes change the distance.
questions.x: NaF and NaI have the same ion charges, so lattice energy depends on interionic distance. Fluoride is much smaller than iodide, so Na⁺ and F⁻ sit closer together, and Coulomb attraction, proportional to 1/r, is stronger. NaF therefore has the larger lattice energy and a higher melting point. Iodide's greater size and polarizability do not strengthen ionic attraction.

questions.q: Under which condition does sodium chloride conduct electricity?
o: When melted or dissolved in water
Correct: ions become mobile and can carry current.
As a dry crystalline solid
Ions are locked in the lattice and cannot move.
When cooled to very low temperature
Cooling further immobilizes the ions.
Never, because it has no free electrons
Current can be carried by moving ions, not only electrons.
questions.x: Electric current needs mobile charged particles. In solid NaCl, the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are fixed in the lattice and there are no free electrons, so it is an insulator. Melting the solid or dissolving it in water frees the ions to move, and they carry current toward the electrodes. Conduction by ions, not only by electrons, is what rules out the 'never' answer.

questions.q: Why are ionic crystals brittle, shattering when struck?
o: Their covalent bonds are weak
Ionic crystals are held by ionic attractions, not covalent bonds.
Electrons flow away from the impact site
Ionic solids have no mobile electrons.
Ions are only weakly attracted to each other
Ionic attractions are strong; that is why melting points are high.
Shifting a layer brings like charges side by side, and they repel
Correct: displacement aligns cations with cations and anions with anions.
questions.note: Contrast: metals deform because their electron sea moves with the ions.
questions.x: In an ionic crystal, each ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge. A sharp blow that shifts one layer by half an ion spacing places cations next to cations and anions next to anions; these like charges repel strongly and the crystal cleaves along that plane. Ionic attractions are strong, which is why melting points are high; brittleness comes from the geometry of repulsion, not weak bonding.

questions.q: A hypothetical salt M²⁺X²⁻ has the same interionic distance as Na⁺Cl⁻. By Coulomb's law, its lattice energy should be about how many times that of NaCl?
o: 2 times
Only one charge is accounted for; both are doubled.
4 times
Correct: energy ∝ q₁q₂/r, and (2)(2) = 4 at the same r.
8 times
Overcounts; the distance is unchanged.
½ as much
Larger charges increase attraction.
questions.x: Coulomb's law gives lattice energy proportional to q₁q₂/r. For Na⁺Cl⁻, the charge product is (1)(1) = 1; for M²⁺X²⁻ it is (2)(2) = 4. With the same interionic distance, the lattice energy is about four times greater. Doubling only one charge would double it, which is the tempting error. This explains why MgO melts near 2850 °C while NaCl melts at 801 °C.

questions.q: What is the formula of the ionic compound formed between aluminum and oxygen?
o: AlO
Charges of Al³⁺ and O²⁻ would not balance.
Al₃O₂
Swaps the subscripts: gives +9 and −4.
AlO₃
Gives +3 and −6: not neutral.
Al₂O₃
questions.x: An ionic formula must be electrically neutral. Aluminum, in Group 13, forms Al³⁺, and oxygen, in Group 16, forms O²⁻. The smallest whole numbers that balance the charges are 2 Al and 3 O: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0, giving Al₂O₃. A quick check is to cross the charge magnitudes into subscripts, then reduce if possible.

questions.q: Which bond has the greatest ionic character?
o: Cs–F
Correct: the least electronegative metal with the most electronegative nonmetal gives the largest ΔEN.
Li–I
Small Li⁺ and large I⁻ have a smaller ΔEN and significant covalent character.
Na–Cl
Ionic, but ΔEN is smaller than for Cs–F.
Be–Cl
Beryllium chloride is largely covalent.
questions.x: Ionic character increases with the electronegativity difference between the two atoms. Cesium is among the least electronegative elements (about 0.8) and fluorine is the most electronegative (4.0), so Cs–F has the largest difference, above 3. Na–Cl is also ionic but has a smaller difference, while small, highly polarizing cations such as Li⁺ and Be²⁺ give Li–I and Be–Cl substantial covalent character.

questions.q: Butane and 2-methylpropane (isobutane), both C₄H₁₀, are best described as:
o: Enantiomers
Enantiomers have the same connectivity and are mirror images.
Diastereomers
Diastereomers have the same connectivity.
Conformers
Conformers interconvert by bond rotation; these require bond breaking.
Constitutional (structural) isomers
Correct: same formula, different atom connectivity.
questions.x: Butane (a straight four-carbon chain) and isobutane (three carbons with a methyl branch on the middle carbon) share the formula C₄H₁₀ but connect their atoms differently, making them constitutional isomers. Stereoisomers, which include enantiomers and diastereomers, share connectivity and differ only in 3-D arrangement. Conformers interconvert by single-bond rotation, while turning butane into isobutane requires breaking bonds.

questions.q: Which compound contains a chiral carbon?
o: 2-Propanol
C2 bears two identical CH₃ groups.
2-Butanol
Correct: C2 bears H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃, four different groups.
3-Pentanol
C3 bears two identical ethyl groups.
1-Butanol
No carbon bears four different groups.
questions.note: A chiral carbon has four different substituents.
questions.x: A chiral carbon (stereocenter) is an sp³ carbon bonded to four different groups. In 2-butanol, C2 carries H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃, all different, so the molecule exists as R and S enantiomers. 2-Propanol and 3-pentanol each have an OH carbon flanked by two identical groups, and in 1-butanol the OH carbon has two hydrogens, so none of those is chiral.

questions.q: A molecule has three stereocenters and no internal symmetry. What is the maximum number of stereoisomers?
o: Adds rather than multiplies the possibilities.
Uses 2n instead of 2ⁿ.
Correct: 2³ = 8.
Uses 3² instead of 2³.
questions.note: Max stereoisomers = 2ⁿ; meso forms reduce the count.
questions.x: Each stereocenter can independently be R or S, so n stereocenters give at most 2ⁿ stereoisomers: 2³ = 8 for three centers. The number can only fall below this when internal symmetry creates meso compounds, which the stem rules out. Adding (3), doubling (6) or squaring (9) ignore that each center's two choices multiply with every other center's.

questions.q: (2R,3R)-2,3-dibromopentane and (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromopentane are:
o: Diastereomers
Correct: they differ at one but not all stereocenters, so they are not mirror images.
Enantiomers
Enantiomers differ at every stereocenter.
Identical
The configurations at C3 differ.
Constitutional isomers
Their connectivity is the same.
questions.x: Compare the configurations center by center. Here C2 is R in both, but C3 is R in one and S in the other. Stereoisomers that differ at some but not all stereocenters are not mirror images, so they are diastereomers with different physical properties. Enantiomers must be inverted at every center, which would make (2S,3S) the enantiomer of (2R,3R). Pentane's unequal ends rule out a meso form.

questions.q: Which method can separate a racemic mixture into its two enantiomers?
o: Simple distillation
Enantiomers have identical boiling points.
Extraction with water
Enantiomers have identical solubility in achiral solvents.
Reaction with a single enantiomer of a chiral acid, then crystallization
Correct: this forms diastereomeric salts with different physical properties.
Standard silica gel chromatography
An achiral stationary phase cannot distinguish enantiomers.
questions.note: Resolution converts enantiomers into separable diastereomers.
questions.x: Enantiomers have identical physical properties in an achiral environment, so distillation, extraction and ordinary chromatography cannot separate them. Reacting the racemic acid or base with one pure enantiomer of a chiral resolving agent converts the pair into diastereomeric salts, such as (R,R) and (S,R), which differ in solubility and can be separated by crystallization. The resolving agent is then removed to recover each enantiomer.

questions.q: What is the observed optical rotation of a racemic mixture?
o: Twice that of the pure (+) enantiomer
Equal amounts of opposite rotations do not add.
Zero
Correct: equal amounts of enantiomers cancel each other's rotations.
Equal to that of the pure (+) enantiomer
The (−) enantiomer cancels the (+) rotation.
It depends on which enantiomer is R
Cancellation occurs regardless of R/S labels.
questions.x: A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of two enantiomers. Each enantiomer rotates plane-polarized light by the same amount in opposite directions, so the contributions cancel and the observed rotation is zero. This is true no matter which enantiomer is labeled R, since R/S describes spatial arrangement and does not predict the sign of rotation.

questions.q: cis-2-Butene and trans-2-butene are best classified as:
o: Enantiomers
Neither isomer is chiral, so they cannot be enantiomers.
Constitutional isomers
They have the same connectivity.
Diastereomers
Correct: stereoisomers that are not mirror images; geometric isomers are diastereomers.
Conformers
They cannot interconvert by single-bond rotation.
questions.note: Cis/trans isomers are diastereomers.
questions.x: cis- and trans-2-butene have the same atom connectivity but differ in the spatial arrangement of groups around the rigid C=C bond, so they are stereoisomers. They are not mirror images of each other, and both are achiral, so they cannot be enantiomers. Stereoisomers that are not enantiomers are diastereomers, which is why cis/trans isomers have different boiling points and stabilities.

questions.q: Looking down the C2–C3 bond of butane, which conformation has the lowest energy?
o: Eclipsed, with methyls aligned (totally eclipsed)
This is the highest-energy conformation.
Gauche
Staggered, but the 60° methyl–methyl contact adds strain.
Eclipsed, with methyls aligned with hydrogens
Eclipsing creates torsional strain.
Anti
Correct: staggered with the methyls 180° apart minimizes torsional and steric strain.
questions.x: Rotating about the C2–C3 bond of butane creates conformations with different strain. Staggered conformations avoid the torsional strain of eclipsed bonds. Among them, anti places the two methyl groups 180° apart, minimizing steric repulsion, while gauche puts them 60° apart with some steric strain. The fully eclipsed conformation, with methyls directly aligned, is the highest in energy.

questions.q: A pure enantiomer has specific rotation +20°. A mixture of it and its enantiomer has specific rotation +6°. What percentage of the mixture is the (+) enantiomer?
o: That is the enantiomeric excess, not the percentage of (+).
That is the racemic portion of the mixture.
That is the percentage of the (−) enantiomer.
questions.note: ee = observed ÷ pure rotation; major = ee + (100 − ee)/2.
questions.x: Enantiomeric excess equals observed rotation divided by the pure enantiomer's rotation: 6/20 = 0.30, or 30%. That means 30% of the sample is excess (+) and the other 70% is racemic, split evenly as 35% (+) and 35% (−). So (+) = 30% + 35% = 65% and (−) = 35%. Reporting 30% confuses the excess with the actual percentage of the major enantiomer.

questions.q: Rank these substituents by Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priority, highest first: –CH₃, –OH, –H, –CH₂OH.
o: –OH > –CH₂OH > –CH₃ > –H
Correct: O beats C; between carbons, the one bearing O wins; H is lowest.
–CH₂OH > –OH > –CH₃ > –H
Compare the first attached atom: O (8) outranks C (6).
–OH > –CH₃ > –CH₂OH > –H
At the first point of difference, CH₂OH has (O,H,H) versus CH₃'s (H,H,H).
–CH₃ > –CH₂OH > –OH > –H
Priority depends on atomic number, not group size.
questions.x: Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priorities are assigned by atomic number of the atom directly attached to the stereocenter. Oxygen (8) beats carbon (6), which beats hydrogen (1), so –OH is first and –H is last. For the two carbon groups, compare the sets of atoms attached to each carbon: –CH₂OH has (O, H, H) versus –CH₃'s (H, H, H), so –CH₂OH wins at the first point of difference.

questions.q: An R enantiomer is found to be dextrorotatory (+). Which statement must be true?
o: All R compounds are dextrorotatory
R/S labels do not predict the sign of rotation.
Its S enantiomer rotates light to the same extent in the opposite direction
Correct: enantiomers have equal magnitude, opposite sign of specific rotation.
Its S enantiomer is also dextrorotatory
Enantiomers always rotate light in opposite directions.
Its S enantiomer is optically inactive
A single enantiomer of a chiral compound is optically active.
questions.note: Trap: R/S and (+)/(−) are unrelated conventions.
questions.x: Enantiomers have identical physical properties except their interaction with plane-polarized light: they rotate it by exactly the same magnitude in opposite directions. If the R enantiomer is (+), its S enantiomer must be (−) by the same amount. The R/S label is a naming convention based on priorities and gives no information about the sign of rotation of other compounds.

questions.q: On a single stereocenter, swapping the positions of any two substituents produces:
o: The same configuration
One swap always inverts the configuration.
A constitutional isomer
Connectivity is unchanged; only spatial arrangement changes.
A conformer of the original
Swapping requires breaking bonds, not rotation.
The opposite configuration at that center (R ↔ S)
Correct: one swap inverts; two swaps restore the original.
questions.note: Useful trick when the lowest priority group is not pointing back.
questions.x: Exchanging any two substituents on a stereocenter changes its spatial arrangement into the mirror-image arrangement, inverting R to S or S to R; a second swap restores the original. This is a useful trick for assigning configuration when the lowest-priority group points toward the viewer. A swap of positions requires breaking and re-forming bonds, so it never gives a mere conformer.

questions.q: Which alkene can exist as cis and trans isomers?
o: Propene
C1 carries two hydrogens, so no cis/trans isomers are possible.
1-Butene
The terminal CH₂ carbon has two identical hydrogens.
2-Methyl-2-butene
C2 carries two identical methyl groups.
2-Pentene
Correct: each alkene carbon bears two different groups (H/CH₃ and H/C₂H₅).
questions.note: Each sp² carbon must have two different substituents.
questions.x: Cis/trans isomerism requires that each carbon of the C=C bond carry two different groups; if either carbon has two identical groups, swapping sides gives the same molecule. In 2-pentene, C2 carries H and CH₃, and C3 carries H and CH₂CH₃, so cis and trans forms exist. Propene and 1-butene have a CH₂ terminal carbon, and 2-methyl-2-butene has two methyls on C2.

questions.q: Liquid–liquid extraction separates compounds mainly on the basis of differences in what property?
o: Boiling point
Boiling point differences are exploited by distillation, not extraction.
Molecular size
Size is the basis of size-exclusion chromatography or dialysis.
Solubility in two immiscible solvents
Correct: solutes partition between two immiscible phases according to relative solubility.
Migration in an electric field
That describes electrophoresis.
questions.x: Extraction relies on a solute partitioning between two immiscible liquids, usually water and an organic solvent, according to where it is more soluble. Changing a solute's charge (for example, by acid or base) changes which layer it prefers. Boiling point is the basis of distillation, a separate technique that uses volatility instead.

questions.q: Diethyl ether (density 0.71 g/mL) is shaken with water in a separatory funnel. Where is the ether layer?
o: On top, because it is less dense than water
Correct: immiscible layers stack by density, and ether is less dense than water.
On the bottom, because organic layers always sink
Organic layers sink only when denser than water, as with dichloromethane.
On top, because it is more polar than water
Layer position depends on density, and ether is far less polar than water.
Mixed evenly through the water as one phase
Ether and water are largely immiscible and form two layers.
questions.x: In a separatory funnel, two immiscible liquids stack by density: the less dense one floats. Diethyl ether (0.71 g/mL) is lighter than water (1.00 g/mL), so it is the top layer. Polarity decides whether liquids mix, not which one sits on top, and many organic solvents (ether, hexane, ethyl acetate) float, while halogenated ones sink.

questions.q: A product is extracted from water into dichloromethane (density 1.33 g/mL). Which layer should be drained and kept?
o: The top layer, which is the organic phase
Assumes all organic solvents float; dichloromethane is denser than water.
The bottom layer, which is the aqueous phase
Water (1.00 g/mL) is less dense than dichloromethane, so it sits on top.
Either layer, since the product splits evenly
A neutral organic product partitions strongly into the organic layer.
The bottom layer, which is the organic phase
Correct: dichloromethane is denser than water, so the organic layer is on the bottom.
questions.note: Trap: halogenated solvents like CH₂Cl₂ and CHCl₃ sink below water.
