questions.x: Layer position depends only on density. Dichloromethane (1.33 g/mL) is denser than water, so the organic layer is on the bottom and is drained out through the stopcock. A neutral organic product partitions into that layer. The tempting mistake is assuming the organic layer is always on top, which holds only for solvents less dense than water.

questions.q: An ether solution contains p-cresol (a phenol, pKa ≈ 10) and naphthalene. Which aqueous wash moves p-cresol into the water layer?
o: Saturated NaHCO₃
Bicarbonate (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 6.4) is too weak a base to deprotonate a phenol.
1 M NaOH
Correct: hydroxide fully deprotonates the phenol to a water-soluble phenoxide.
1 M HCl
Acid keeps the phenol neutral, so it stays in the ether.
Saturated NaCl
Brine removes water from the organic layer; it does not ionize the phenol.
questions.note: NaHCO₃ removes carboxylic acids only; NaOH removes carboxylic acids and phenols.
questions.x: A base moves an acid into water only if it is strong enough to deprotonate it: the base's conjugate acid must have a higher pKa than the acid being removed. Hydroxide (conjugate acid water, pKa ≈ 15.7) easily deprotonates a phenol (pKa ≈ 10), making a charged phenoxide that dissolves in water. Bicarbonate (pKa ≈ 6.4) is too weak for phenols and removes only carboxylic acids.

questions.q: To move aniline from an ether solution into an aqueous layer, the ether should be washed with:
o: Dilute NaOH
Base leaves the amine neutral, so it stays in the organic layer.
Dilute HCl
Correct: the amine is protonated to a water-soluble anilinium chloride salt.
Aqueous NaHCO₃
Bicarbonate is basic and will not protonate an amine.
Pure water
Neutral aniline is only slightly water-soluble and mostly stays in ether.
questions.x: Amines are bases, so an acid wash protonates them into ammonium salts. These salts are ionic and dissolve in water, which pulls the amine out of the organic layer. A basic wash such as NaOH or NaHCO₃ leaves the amine neutral, and neutral aniline stays mostly in the ether.

questions.q: Benzoic acid has been extracted from ether into aqueous NaOH as sodium benzoate. How is the neutral acid recovered?
o: Add more NaOH and collect the precipitate
More base keeps it as the soluble benzoate anion.
Distill off the water to leave pure benzoic acid
Evaporation leaves the sodium benzoate salt plus excess NaOH, not the free acid.
Add brine to salt out the neutral acid
Brine does not protonate benzoate, so the anion stays dissolved.
Acidify with HCl, then filter the precipitate or extract it into fresh ether
Correct: protonation regenerates neutral, poorly water-soluble benzoic acid.
questions.x: Once an acid has been extracted as its water-soluble salt, adding a stronger acid such as HCl protonates the anion back to the neutral acid. Neutral benzoic acid is poorly water-soluble, so it precipitates or can be extracted back into ether. Simply evaporating the water would leave the sodium salt, not the free acid.

questions.q: An ether solution of benzoic acid, 2-naphthol and naphthalene is washed with NaHCO₃ and then with NaOH. Which compound remains in the ether?
o: Naphthalene
Correct: a neutral hydrocarbon has no acidic proton and stays in the organic layer.
Benzoic acid
Bicarbonate deprotonates the carboxylic acid in the first wash.
2-Naphthol
The NaOH wash deprotonates the phenol into the aqueous layer.
Both acids, since ether favors aromatics
Both acids become water-soluble salts with the appropriate base.
questions.x: Acid–base extraction only moves compounds that can be ionized. NaHCO₃ deprotonates the carboxylic acid, and NaOH then deprotonates the phenol, and each becomes a water-soluble salt. Naphthalene is a neutral hydrocarbon with no acidic or basic group, so it stays in the ether through both washes.

questions.q: In the sequence NaHCO₃ wash then NaOH wash of an ether solution of benzoic acid, 2-naphthol and naphthalene, what is in the NaOH extract?
o: Benzoic acid as sodium benzoate
Benzoic acid was removed by the earlier bicarbonate wash.
Naphthalene
Naphthalene has no acidic proton and stays in ether.
2-Naphthol as its sodium salt
Correct: the carboxylic acid was already removed by bicarbonate, leaving only the phenol for NaOH.
Both benzoate and naphthoxide
Possible only if NaOH were used first; the weak base went first here.
questions.note: Use the weaker base first to separate a carboxylic acid from a phenol.
questions.x: Using bases in order of increasing strength separates acids by pKa. Bicarbonate is strong enough for a carboxylic acid (pKa ≈ 4 to 5) but not a phenol (pKa ≈ 10), so the first wash removes only benzoic acid. The later NaOH wash then takes the 2-naphthol as sodium naphthoxide. If NaOH were used first, it would remove both acids together.

questions.q: For a fixed total volume of extracting solvent, which approach recovers the most solute from water?
o: One extraction with the whole volume
One large extraction leaves more solute behind than several smaller ones.
Either approach, since total solvent volume is equal
Partitioning is not linear in volume; splitting it improves recovery.
One extraction followed by heating the funnel
Heating a closed funnel with volatile solvent is hazardous and does not aid partitioning.
Several extractions with smaller portions
Correct: each portion removes a fraction of what remains, so repeated small extractions beat one large one.
questions.x: In each extraction, a fixed fraction of the remaining solute moves into the fresh solvent. Several small portions apply that fraction repeatedly, so the amount left behind shrinks geometrically and total recovery beats one large portion of the same total volume. Partitioning is not linear in solvent volume, which is why splitting the volume helps.

questions.q: A solute has K = [organic]/[aqueous] = 4. If 1.0 g is dissolved in 100 mL of water and extracted once with 100 mL of organic solvent, how much is extracted?
o: This is the amount left in the water, not the amount extracted.
Uses 1/K rather than K/(K + 1).
Uses 3/4 instead of 4/5 of the solute.
Correct: with equal volumes, fraction extracted = K/(K + 1) = 4/5, so 0.80 g.
questions.x: With K = [org]/[aq], the fraction extracted is K·Vorg/(K·Vorg + Vaq). With equal 100 mL volumes this is K/(K + 1) = 4/5, so 0.80 g moves to the organic layer and 0.20 g stays in water. The tempting 0.20 g is the amount left behind, not the amount extracted.

questions.q: Same solute (K = 4), 1.0 g in 100 mL of water, but now extracted twice with 50 mL organic portions. About how much is extracted in total?
o: This is only the first 50 mL extraction (2/3 of the solute).
That is the single 100 mL extraction result; two portions do better.
Correct: each 50 mL pass leaves 1/3 behind, so (1/3)² = 1/9 remains and 8/9 ≈ 0.89 g is extracted.
Partitioning never removes all solute in a finite number of extractions.
questions.x: The fraction left in water after each extraction is Vaq/(Vaq + K·Vorg) = 100/(100 + 4×50) = 1/3. After two extractions (1/3)² = 1/9 of the solute remains, so about 8/9 ≈ 0.89 g is extracted, more than the 0.80 g from one 100 mL portion. Recovery approaches but never reaches 100% in a finite number of extractions.

questions.q: Why is an organic layer often washed with saturated NaCl (brine) near the end of a workup?
o: To protonate any remaining amines
NaCl is neutral and cannot protonate bases.
To draw dissolved water out of the organic layer
Correct: the highly ionic brine pulls water from the organic phase and reduces emulsions.
To neutralize residual acids
Brine has no meaningful acid-neutralizing capacity.
To make the organic solvent more polar
Brine does not change the organic solvent itself; it removes water.
questions.x: Water dissolves slightly in organic solvents such as ether. Saturated NaCl has a very high ionic strength, so water moves from the organic layer into the brine, which pre-dries the solution and also helps break emulsions. Brine is neutral, so it does not protonate bases or neutralize acids; that takes acidic or basic washes.

questions.q: After an extraction, anhydrous MgSO₄ is added to the organic layer. What is its purpose?
o: To precipitate the desired product
Drying agents absorb water; they do not precipitate organic products.
To neutralize acidic impurities
MgSO₄ is a neutral drying agent, not a base.
To remove trace water from the organic solution
Correct: anhydrous salts bind water as hydrates and are then filtered off.
To increase the density of the organic layer
Its job is drying, and it is removed by filtration.
questions.x: Anhydrous salts such as MgSO₄ or Na₂SO₄ bind trace water as hydrates, removing it from the organic solution. The hydrated solid is then filtered off and the dry solution is evaporated to give the product. MgSO₄ is not a base and does not neutralize acids or precipitate the product.

questions.q: Washing an ether solution of a carboxylic acid with aqueous NaHCO₃ requires frequent venting of the funnel mainly because:
o: CO₂ gas forms as bicarbonate neutralizes the acid
Correct: HCO₃⁻ + RCOOH → RCOO⁻ + H₂O + CO₂, and the gas builds pressure.
The reaction releases H₂ gas
Acid–bicarbonate reactions release CO₂, not hydrogen.
Water boils from the heat of neutralization
The heat released is small and does not boil water.
Ether reacts with bicarbonate to form gas
Ether is unreactive toward bicarbonate; the acid is what reacts.
questions.x: Bicarbonate reacts with a carboxylic acid to give the carboxylate, water and carbon dioxide gas. The CO₂ builds pressure in the closed separatory funnel, so the funnel must be vented often. The gas is CO₂, not H₂; hydrogen comes from active metals reacting with acid, not from a carbonate.

questions.q: Which solvent is NOT suitable for extracting an organic product out of an aqueous solution?
o: Ethanol
Correct: ethanol is fully miscible with water, so no second layer forms.
Ethyl acetate
Ethyl acetate is only slightly water-soluble and forms a separate layer.
Dichloromethane
Dichloromethane is immiscible with water and commonly used for extraction.
Hexane
Hexane is immiscible with water and suitable for nonpolar products.
questions.x: An extraction solvent must be immiscible with water so that two layers form. Ethanol is fully miscible with water because it hydrogen bonds strongly, so it cannot form a separate phase. Ethyl acetate, dichloromethane and hexane all form distinct layers with water, although ethyl acetate is slightly water-soluble.

questions.q: A carboxylic acid (pKa 4.2) is to be extracted into water as its anion. What is the minimum aqueous pH that ionizes about 99% of it?
o: At pH = pKa only half the acid is ionized.
One unit above pKa gives about 91% ionized, not 99%.
Correct: pH = pKa + 2 gives [A⁻]/[HA] = 100, or about 99% ionized.
Two units below pKa leaves the acid about 99% protonated.
questions.note: Henderson–Hasselbalch: each pH unit above pKa multiplies [A⁻]/[HA] by 10.
questions.x: Henderson–Hasselbalch says pH − pKa = log([A⁻]/[HA]). For about 99% ionized, the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] must be about 100, so pH must be 2 units above the pKa: 4.2 + 2 = 6.2. At pH = pKa the acid is only 50% ionized, and one unit above gives about 91%.

questions.q: Distillation separates the components of a liquid mixture primarily on the basis of differences in:
o: Polarity toward a stationary phase
Adsorption to a stationary phase is the basis of chromatography.
Solubility in an immiscible solvent
That is the basis of extraction.
Volatility (vapor pressure)
Correct: the more volatile component vaporizes preferentially and is collected first.
Net electric charge
Charge is exploited in ion exchange or electrophoresis.
questions.x: Distillation separates liquids by volatility: the component with the higher vapor pressure (lower boiling point) enriches the vapor and condenses first. Chromatography separates by interactions with a stationary phase, and extraction by solubility between immiscible solvents. Each technique exploits a different physical property.

questions.q: Which separation is best accomplished by simple distillation?
o: Separating two liquids that boil 5 °C apart
Close-boiling liquids need fractional distillation.
Recovering water from a sodium chloride solution
Correct: simple distillation easily separates a volatile liquid from a nonvolatile solute.
Purifying a compound that decomposes below its boiling point
Heat-sensitive compounds call for vacuum distillation.
Separating a pair of enantiomers
Enantiomers have identical boiling points and cannot be distilled apart.
questions.x: Simple distillation works well when the components differ greatly in volatility, roughly by more than 25 °C, or when a volatile liquid is separated from a nonvolatile solute such as salt. Close-boiling liquids need a fractionating column, heat-sensitive compounds need vacuum distillation, and enantiomers have identical boiling points.

questions.q: How does a fractionating column improve separation compared with simple distillation?
o: It raises the boiling point of the less volatile component
A column does not change intrinsic boiling points.
It cools the vapor so it condenses faster
Condensing is the condenser's job; the column's job is repeated equilibration.
It filters nonvolatile impurities from the vapor
Nonvolatile impurities never vaporize; the column enriches volatile components.
It provides many successive vaporization–condensation cycles
Correct: each cycle (theoretical plate) further enriches the vapor in the more volatile component.
questions.x: A fractionating column offers a large surface on which vapor repeatedly condenses and re-vaporizes. Each cycle is like a separate simple distillation (a theoretical plate), enriching the vapor further in the more volatile component. The column does not change any compound's boiling point; it multiplies the separation.

questions.q: A compound boils at 280 °C at 1 atm but decomposes near 250 °C. Why is vacuum distillation used to purify it?
o: The vacuum raises its vapor pressure at every temperature
Vapor pressure at a given temperature is an intrinsic property, unaffected by the applied vacuum.
The vacuum removes oxygen, which is the only cause of decomposition
Thermal decomposition can occur without oxygen; the key is the lower temperature.
Lowering the pressure lowers its boiling point below the decomposition temperature
Correct: a liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the external pressure, so less pressure means a lower bp.
Reduced pressure increases the difference between boiling points
The main purpose is to lower the boiling temperature.
questions.x: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the external pressure. Lowering the pressure with a vacuum means the compound reaches that vapor pressure at a lower temperature, so it can be distilled below 250 °C without decomposing. The vacuum does not change the compound's vapor pressure at a given temperature; it lowers the pressure the vapor must match.

questions.q: Why are boiling chips added to a distillation flask?
o: To provide nucleation sites that prevent bumping
Correct: bubbles form smoothly on the porous chips instead of superheating then erupting.
To raise the boiling point of the mixture
Chips are inert and do not change boiling points.
To absorb water from the mixture
Boiling chips are not drying agents.
To catalyze vaporization of the less volatile component
Chips promote smooth boiling, not selective vaporization.
questions.x: Bubbles need nucleation sites to form. Without them, a liquid can superheat above its boiling point and then boil violently all at once, which is called bumping. Porous boiling chips trap air and provide many nucleation sites for smooth boiling. They are inert and do not change the boiling point or the composition.

questions.q: During a distillation, the thermometer bulb sits well above the side arm of the distillation head. How will the recorded temperature compare with the true boiling point?
o: It will read higher
A misplaced bulb receives less hot vapor, not more.
It will read the same
Accurate readings require the bulb just below the side arm, in the vapor stream.
It will read the temperature of the pot liquid
The bulb is in the head, nowhere near the boiling liquid.
It will read lower
Correct: the vapor does not fully bathe a bulb placed too high, so it reads low.
questions.x: The thermometer bulb must sit just below the side arm so it is fully bathed in vapor that is about to pass into the condenser, giving the true boiling temperature. If the bulb is too high, the vapor does not fully surround it, and the reading is lower than the actual boiling point. A misplaced bulb cannot read higher than the vapor actually is.

questions.q: Fractional distillation of dilute aqueous ethanol stops enriching at about 95.6% ethanol no matter how efficient the column. Why?
o: Ethanol and water have identical boiling points
Ethanol boils at 78 °C and water at 100 °C.
The mixture forms an azeotrope whose vapor and liquid have the same composition
Correct: at the azeotrope, vaporization no longer changes composition, so distillation cannot enrich further.
The column runs out of theoretical plates
Even unlimited plates cannot pass an azeotropic composition.
Water reacts with ethanol at its boiling point
No reaction occurs; the limit is a vapor–liquid equilibrium effect.
questions.x: Ethanol and water form a minimum-boiling azeotrope at about 95.6% ethanol. At that composition the vapor has the same composition as the liquid, so further vaporization–condensation cycles cannot enrich it. More theoretical plates do not help; getting past an azeotrope needs a different method, such as a drying agent or adding a third component.

questions.q: A mixture of hexane (bp 69 °C) and heptane (bp 98 °C) undergoes fractional distillation. What is the first distillate enriched in?
o: Heptane
Heptane has the higher boiling point and lower vapor pressure.
Hexane
Correct: the lower-boiling, more volatile component enriches the vapor first.
Equal amounts of both
Fractionation enriches the vapor in the more volatile component.
Neither, since alkanes form an azeotrope
Hexane and heptane form a nearly ideal mixture, not an azeotrope.
questions.x: In fractional distillation, the more volatile component (lower boiling point, higher vapor pressure) enriches the vapor and comes over first. Hexane boils at 69 °C and heptane at 98 °C, so the early distillate is mostly hexane. Similar alkanes form nearly ideal mixtures, so no azeotrope stops this separation.

questions.q: An ideal 50:50 (mole) liquid mixture has P°A = 300 torr and P°B = 100 torr. What is the mole fraction of A in the vapor?
o: The vapor is enriched in the more volatile component, not equal to the liquid.
Computes 300/(300 + 150) or another mix-up; use the partial pressures 150 and 50 torr.
Overestimates enrichment; Raoult's law gives 150/200.
questions.note: Raoult's law: Pᵢ = xᵢP°ᵢ, then yᵢ = Pᵢ/P(total).
questions.x: Raoult's law gives each partial pressure as Pᵢ = xᵢP°ᵢ: PA = 0.5 × 300 = 150 torr and PB = 0.5 × 100 = 50 torr. The vapor mole fraction is yA = PA/Ptotal = 150/200 = 0.75. The vapor is always richer than the liquid in the more volatile component, which is the basis of distillation.

questions.q: During fractional distillation of a two-liquid mixture, the head temperature holds steady, then rises sharply before leveling off again. What does the sharp rise indicate?
o: The column has flooded and must be emptied
Flooding disrupts flow; it does not produce a clean plateau-to-plateau transition.
An azeotrope has formed in the pot
An azeotrope would distill at a constant temperature, not cause a jump.
The higher-boiling component is decomposing
Decomposition is not indicated by a clean transition to a new plateau.
The lower-boiling component has largely distilled over
Correct: once the volatile component is depleted, the vapor temperature climbs toward the second boiling point.
questions.note: Change receivers during the temperature jump to keep fractions pure.
questions.x: A temperature plateau at the head means one component is distilling at its boiling point. When that lower-boiling component is used up, the vapor temperature rises until the higher-boiling component begins to distill at a new plateau. Changing receivers during the rise keeps each fraction pure. An azeotrope would distill at one constant temperature.

questions.q: What is the most important property of a good recrystallization solvent?
o: It dissolves the compound well when hot but poorly when cold
Correct: a steep solubility–temperature curve lets the compound crystallize on cooling.
It dissolves the compound well at all temperatures
The compound would stay dissolved and never crystallize.
It dissolves the compound poorly at all temperatures
The compound could not be dissolved to free it from impurities.
It boils above the compound's melting point
This favors oiling out; the solvent's bp should usually be below the solid's mp.
questions.x: Recrystallization relies on a solubility that changes steeply with temperature: the compound dissolves in hot solvent, then crystallizes as it cools, while impurities stay in solution. A solvent that dissolves the compound well even when cold gives little or no recovery, and one that never dissolves it cannot purify it.

questions.q: Why is a hot recrystallization solution allowed to cool slowly rather than being plunged into ice?
o: Slow cooling makes the compound more soluble
Solubility falls as temperature falls regardless of rate.
Rapid cooling decomposes most organic compounds
Cooling does not decompose compounds; it reduces purity by trapping impurities.
Slow crystal growth excludes impurities from the lattice
Correct: slow, ordered growth rejects impurities; rapid crashing traps them.
Slow cooling evaporates the impurities
Impurities remain in the mother liquor; they do not evaporate.
questions.x: Slow cooling lets molecules join the growing crystal lattice in an orderly way, and impurity molecules that do not fit are rejected into the solution. Rapid cooling makes the solid crash out quickly, trapping impurities and solvent within small, imperfect crystals. Cooling rate affects purity and crystal size, not the final solubility.

questions.q: A student dissolves a crude solid in far more hot solvent than needed. What is the most likely result after cooling?
o: A higher yield of crystals
More solvent dissolves more product, so less crystallizes.
Crystals with more impurities
Extra solvent tends to keep impurities dissolved too; the main cost is yield.
Crystals with a higher melting point than the pure compound
A pure compound's melting point cannot be exceeded by recrystallizing.
A low yield of crystals
Correct: excess solvent keeps more product dissolved in the cold mother liquor.
questions.note: Use the minimum amount of hot solvent.
questions.x: Some compound always stays dissolved in the cold mother liquor, and the amount lost grows with solvent volume. Using far more hot solvent than needed means much more product stays in solution after cooling, so the yield drops. That is why the minimum amount of hot solvent is used to just dissolve the solid.

questions.q: How does the melting point of a recrystallized product typically show that purification worked?
o: It becomes broader and lower
Broad, depressed melting indicates impurities.
It becomes sharp and close to the literature value
Correct: pure solids melt over a narrow range at the expected temperature.
It rises well above the literature value
Purification approaches, but does not exceed, the true melting point.
It disappears because the solid sublimes
Recrystallization does not change whether a solid melts.
questions.x: Impurities disrupt the crystal lattice, which lowers the melting point and broadens the melting range (melting point depression). A purified solid melts sharply, over 1 to 2 °C, near its literature value. Recrystallization can bring the melting point up to the true value but never above it.

questions.q: A hot recrystallization solution contains insoluble dust particles. What should be done next?
o: Cool the solution in ice, then vacuum-filter the mixture
The dust would be collected along with the crystals.
Add more solvent until the dust dissolves
Insoluble impurities will not dissolve, and excess solvent lowers yield.
Gravity-filter the solution while hot, then cool the filtrate
Correct: hot gravity filtration removes insolubles while keeping the product dissolved.
Add activated charcoal to dissolve the dust
Charcoal adsorbs colored impurities; it does not dissolve particles.
questions.x: Insoluble impurities are removed by filtering the solution while it is still hot, so the desired compound stays dissolved and passes through. Gravity filtration with fluted paper is used, because vacuum would cool the solution and cause early crystallization in the funnel. If the solution were cooled first, the dust would be collected along with the crystals.

questions.q: Activated charcoal is added to a hot recrystallization solution. What does it remove?
o: Colored, highly conjugated impurities
Correct: charcoal's large surface adsorbs large colored molecules, then it is filtered out hot.
Dissolved water
Water is removed by drying agents, not charcoal.
Inorganic salts
Salts are not adsorbed effectively by charcoal.
Excess recrystallization solvent
Charcoal does not reduce solvent volume.
questions.x: Activated charcoal has a huge porous surface area that adsorbs large, flat, highly conjugated molecules, which are often the colored impurities. It is added to the hot solution and then removed by hot gravity filtration. It does not remove water or salts, and too much charcoal can also adsorb some of the product.

questions.q: A clear solution is cooled in ice but no crystals form even though the compound should be supersaturated. What is a good next step?
o: Scratch the flask with a glass rod or add a seed crystal
Correct: both provide nucleation sites that start crystal growth.
Add much more hot solvent
Extra solvent makes the solution less saturated.
Reheat the solution to boiling
Heating raises solubility and moves away from crystallization.
Add a drying agent
Water is not what prevents nucleation here.
questions.x: A supersaturated solution may fail to crystallize because crystals need a nucleation site to start growing. Scratching the glass makes rough surfaces and tiny glass fragments, and a seed crystal gives a ready-made lattice to build on. Adding solvent or reheating would raise solubility and move the solution further from crystallization.

questions.q: For a two-solvent recrystallization, the compound is dissolved in a hot 'good' solvent and a 'poor' solvent is added until cloudy. Which pair is appropriate?
o: Hexane (good) and water (poor)
Hexane and water are immiscible and would form two layers.
Diethyl ether (good) and water (poor)
Ether and water are largely immiscible.
Ethanol (good) and water (poor)
Correct: the pair must be miscible, and ethanol and water mix in all proportions.
Dichloromethane (good) and water (poor)
Dichloromethane and water are immiscible.
questions.x: In a mixed-solvent recrystallization the two solvents must be miscible, so the poor solvent can be added steadily to lower the compound's solubility until it reaches the cloud point. Ethanol and water mix in all proportions, which makes them a classic pair. Hexane, ether and dichloromethane are immiscible with water and would form separate layers instead.

questions.q: Compound X dissolves to 20 g/100 mL at 80 °C and 2 g/100 mL at 0 °C. If 10 g of X is dissolved in 50 mL of hot solvent and cooled to 0 °C, what is the maximum recovery?
o: 8 g
Uses 2 g lost per 50 mL; at 2 g/100 mL, 50 mL holds only 1 g.
9 g
Correct: 50 mL holds 1 g at 0 °C, so 10 − 1 = 9 g can crystallize.
Some compound always remains dissolved in the cold solvent.
5 g
Halves the mass without using the cold solubility data.
questions.x: At 0 °C the solvent holds 2 g per 100 mL, so 50 mL keeps 1 g dissolved. The rest, 10 − 1 = 9 g, can crystallize, which is the maximum recovery. First check that all 10 g dissolve hot: 50 mL holds 10 g at 80 °C, so it does. Using 2 g as the loss ignores that only 50 mL of solvent is present.

questions.q: Purified crystals are usually collected after recrystallization by:
o: Simple distillation
Distillation separates liquids by volatility, not solids from liquids.
Vacuum filtration with a Büchner funnel
Correct: suction quickly pulls off mother liquor and partly dries the crystals.
Gravity filtration through fluted paper
Gravity filtration is slower and used when the filtrate is wanted or the solution is hot.
Liquid–liquid extraction
Extraction partitions solutes between liquids; it does not collect solids.
questions.x: Vacuum filtration through a Büchner funnel quickly separates crystals from the mother liquor and pulls air through the solid to partly dry it. It is the standard method when the solid is the product. Gravity filtration is slower and is used when the liquid is the desired part or the solution must stay hot.

questions.q: Why is gravity rather than vacuum filtration used to remove MgSO₄ from a diethyl ether solution of a product?
o: MgSO₄ dissolves under vacuum
Applying vacuum does not dissolve the drying agent.
Vacuum filtration cannot separate solids from liquids
It does separate solids, but it is meant for collecting a solid.
Gravity filtration removes dissolved water as well
Water is removed by the MgSO₄ itself, not by the filtration method.
Suction would evaporate the volatile solvent and possibly product
Correct: the filtrate is the product here, and vacuum rapidly boils off volatile ether.
questions.x: Choose the filtration method by which part is wanted. When removing a drying agent, the filtrate holds the product, and suction would rapidly evaporate a low-boiling solvent like diethyl ether, possibly carrying off some product. Gravity filtration avoids this. Vacuum filtration is the choice when the solid is what you want to keep.

questions.q: On a TLC plate, a spot travels 2.4 cm while the solvent front travels 8.0 cm from the baseline. What is the Rf?
o: Correct: Rf = spot distance / solvent front distance = 2.4/8.0 = 0.30.
Divides by 10 cm rather than the actual solvent front distance.
Inverts the ratio; Rf cannot exceed 1.
Gives the fraction of the distance not traveled.
questions.x: Rf is the distance the spot travels divided by the distance the solvent front travels, both measured from the baseline: 2.4/8.0 = 0.30. Because a spot can never move farther than the solvent, Rf is always between 0 and 1. Use the actual solvent front distance, not the plate length.

questions.q: On silica TLC, the eluent is changed from 10% to 40% ethyl acetate in hexane. What happens to the Rf values of the spots?
o: They all decrease
A more polar eluent displaces compounds from silica, so they move farther.
They stay the same
Rf depends strongly on the eluent composition.
They all increase
Correct: a more polar eluent competes better for the polar silica, moving all compounds farther.
Polar spots decrease and nonpolar spots increase
A stronger eluent increases mobility of all compounds.
questions.x: On silica, compounds compete with the eluent for the polar stationary phase. A more polar eluent binds silica better and displaces the analytes, so every compound spends more time in the mobile phase and moves farther. The order of the spots generally stays the same; only how far they travel changes.

questions.q: On a reverse-phase (C18-coated) TLC plate developed with water–methanol, which compound has the highest Rf?
o: The most polar compound
Correct: the nonpolar stationary phase retains nonpolar compounds, so polar ones travel farthest.
The least polar compound
That is the normal-phase (silica) pattern, reversed here.
The highest-molecular-weight compound
TLC separates by polarity, not mass.
All compounds have equal Rf
The C18 phase discriminates by polarity.
questions.note: Reverse phase flips the elution order: polar moves first.
questions.x: In reverse-phase chromatography the stationary phase is nonpolar (C18 hydrocarbon chains) and the mobile phase is polar. Nonpolar compounds stick to the C18 coating, while polar compounds stay in the polar mobile phase and travel farthest. This is the opposite of normal-phase silica, where nonpolar compounds have the highest Rf.

questions.q: A spot of cyclohexanol is invisible under a 254 nm UV lamp but appears after dipping the plate in KMnO₄ stain. Why?
o: It evaporated before the UV check
It was still present for the stain to detect.
UV light only detects ionic compounds
UV detects chromophores such as aromatic rings, not ions specifically.
Its Rf was too high for the lamp
Spot position does not affect UV visibility.
It lacks a UV-absorbing chromophore but is oxidized by the stain
Correct: UV shows conjugated or aromatic compounds; permanganate reacts with oxidizable groups like alcohols.
questions.x: A 254 nm UV lamp shows only compounds with a chromophore, such as aromatic rings or conjugated π systems, which absorb UV and darken the fluorescent plate. Cyclohexanol has no such group, so it is invisible under UV. Permanganate oxidizes alcohols, alkenes and other oxidizable groups, turning brown where the compound sits, so the stain reveals it.

questions.q: An alcohol (Rf 0.25 on silica) is oxidized to a ketone. After 1 hour, the reaction lane shows spots at Rf 0.25 and 0.55. What is the best interpretation?
o: The reaction is complete, and the ketone is the lower spot
The lower spot matches the starting alcohol.
The reaction is incomplete, and the less polar ketone is the upper spot
Correct: the ketone loses the O–H and moves farther, while remaining alcohol stays at 0.25.
The ketone is more polar than the alcohol and runs at 0.25
Losing hydrogen bonding makes the ketone less polar, giving it a higher Rf.
Two side products formed and no starting material remains
The spot at 0.25 matches the starting material.
questions.x: On silica, more polar compounds have lower Rf. An alcohol can hydrogen bond to silica through its O–H, while the ketone product cannot donate a hydrogen bond, so the ketone is less polar and runs higher (Rf 0.55). The spot remaining at 0.25 matches the starting alcohol, so the reaction is not yet complete.

questions.q: A TLC lane shows a long smear from the baseline upward rather than a compact spot. What is the most likely cause?
o: The eluent was too nonpolar
A weak eluent keeps spots low; it does not usually cause streaks by itself.
Too much sample was applied
Correct: overloading saturates the stationary phase and causes streaking.
The chamber was covered
Covering the chamber improves results by saturating it with vapor.
The plate was viewed under UV
Visualization does not change the shape of a spot.
questions.x: Applying too much sample overloads the stationary phase at the origin, so the compound cannot form a compact band and smears up the lane. Diluting the sample or spotting less fixes it. Eluent polarity mainly moves spots up or down, and covering the chamber improves results by saturating it with vapor.

questions.q: An unknown and an authentic sample give identical Rf values in one solvent system. What is the best additional evidence that they are the same compound?
o: Rerunning both in the same eluent gives the same Rf again
Repeating the same conditions cannot distinguish compounds with coincidentally equal Rf.
Both spots appear under UV light
Many different compounds absorb UV.
Both spots have the same size
Spot size reflects amount applied, not identity.
A co-spot gives a single spot in a second, different eluent
Correct: matching in multiple solvent systems and co-spotting rules out coincidental Rf matches.
questions.x: Different compounds can have the same Rf in one solvent by coincidence, so one match is weak evidence. Co-spotting puts the unknown and the authentic sample in the same lane, where two different compounds would usually show two spots or an elongated spot. Repeating this in a second, different eluent makes a coincidental match much less likely.

questions.q: In normal-phase TLC, what is the stationary phase?
o: Polar silica gel
Correct: silica's surface Si–OH groups strongly retain polar compounds.
A nonpolar hydrocarbon coating
That describes reverse-phase plates.
The organic eluent
The eluent is the mobile phase.
An inert carrier gas
Carrier gas is the mobile phase in gas chromatography.
questions.x: Normal-phase TLC uses polar silica gel as the stationary phase, with a less polar organic eluent as the mobile phase. Silica's surface Si–OH groups hydrogen bond to polar compounds, which therefore move slowly and have low Rf. A nonpolar hydrocarbon coating is reverse phase, the opposite arrangement.

questions.q: In paper chromatography, what acts as the stationary phase?
o: The organic developing solvent
The developing solvent is the mobile phase.
Silica gel coated on the paper
Silica is used for TLC plates, not ordinary chromatography paper.
Water bound to the cellulose fibers
Correct: hydrated cellulose holds a polar water layer that retains polar solutes.
The ink pigments being separated
Pigments are the analytes, not a phase.
questions.x: Cellulose fibers in chromatography paper bind a thin layer of water, and that bound water acts as the polar stationary phase. The developing solvent moving up the paper is the mobile phase. Polar solutes partition into the bound water and move slowly, while less polar solutes travel farther with the solvent.

questions.q: A mixture is loaded onto a silica gel column and eluted with hexane, then increasingly polar solvent. Which component elutes first?
o: The most polar component
Polar compounds adhere to silica and elute last.
The largest component
Adsorption chromatography separates by polarity, not size.
The component present in greatest amount
Elution order is set by polarity, not quantity.
The least polar component
Correct: nonpolar compounds interact weakly with silica and are carried out first.
questions.x: On a silica column, compounds adsorb to the polar surface in proportion to their polarity. With a nonpolar eluent like hexane, the least polar compound interacts weakest with silica and is washed out first. More polar compounds stay bound until the eluent polarity is increased. Elution order depends on polarity, not on size or amount.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of gradient elution, gradually increasing eluent polarity during a silica column?
o: To make nonpolar compounds elute after polar ones
Elution order on silica stays nonpolar first.
To elute strongly retained polar compounds in reasonable time
Correct: early weak eluent separates nonpolar compounds; later strong eluent moves polar ones off.
To keep all compounds bound until the end
Raising polarity releases compounds progressively.
To convert normal phase into size exclusion
The separation mechanism remains adsorption.
questions.x: In gradient elution, a weak (nonpolar) eluent first separates the less polar compounds, then gradually more polar eluent displaces the strongly retained polar compounds. This gives good resolution early without waiting a very long time for polar compounds to elute. The elution order stays nonpolar first; the gradient only speeds up the later compounds.

questions.q: On silica TLC, a target compound has Rf 0.00 in pure hexane and 0.95 in pure ethyl acetate. What is the best eluent for column purification?
o: Pure hexane
The compound would never leave the column.
Pure ethyl acetate
The compound would race through near the solvent front with poor separation.
A hexane/ethyl acetate mixture giving the target Rf ≈ 0.3
Correct: moderate Rf gives enough retention to separate from impurities while still eluting.
Water
Water is not a practical silica eluent and would deactivate the silica.
questions.x: A good column eluent puts the target at an Rf of about 0.2 to 0.4 on TLC. That gives enough retention to separate the target from impurities but still elutes it in a reasonable volume. At Rf 0 it never leaves the column, and near Rf 1 it runs with the solvent front and separates poorly, so a hexane/ethyl acetate mix in between is best.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of column chromatography over TLC?
o: It can isolate larger amounts of pure compound
Correct: column chromatography is preparative, while TLC is mainly analytical.
It uses no stationary phase
Column chromatography uses a packed stationary phase such as silica.
It separates compounds by boiling point
Separation is by adsorption and polarity.
It always runs faster than TLC
Columns usually take longer than a quick TLC.
questions.x: TLC and column chromatography use the same principle, adsorption to a stationary phase such as silica, but at different scales. TLC is analytical, using micrograms to check purity or follow a reaction. Column chromatography is preparative, using larger amounts of stationary phase to isolate milligrams to grams of pure compound.

questions.q: In gas chromatography, what is the mobile phase?
o: An inert carrier gas such as helium
Correct: the carrier gas sweeps vaporized analytes through the column.
A liquid solvent pumped at high pressure
That describes HPLC.
Silica gel
Silica is a stationary phase in TLC or column chromatography.
A buffered aqueous solution
Aqueous buffers are used in ion exchange and electrophoresis.
questions.x: In gas chromatography, an inert carrier gas such as helium or nitrogen is the mobile phase, carrying vaporized analytes through a column coated with a liquid stationary phase. Analytes separate based on volatility and interaction with that coating. A liquid pumped at high pressure is the mobile phase in HPLC, not GC.

questions.q: On a nonpolar GC column, which compound has the longest retention time?
o: Butane
Butane is the most volatile and elutes first.
2-Methylbutane
Branched pentane is quite volatile and elutes early.
Hexane
Correct: hexane has the highest boiling point of these, so it spends the most time in the stationary phase.
Pentane
Pentane boils lower than hexane and elutes before it.
questions.x: On a nonpolar GC column, retention depends mainly on volatility: higher-boiling compounds spend more time dissolved in the stationary phase and elute later. Boiling points rise with chain length and fall with branching, so hexane (six carbons) boils highest and has the longest retention time. Butane, the smallest, elutes first.

questions.q: Which sample is least suitable for direct analysis by gas chromatography?
o: Toluene
Toluene is volatile and thermally stable.
Sucrose
Correct: sucrose is nonvolatile and decomposes on heating, so it cannot be vaporized intact.
Ethyl acetate
Ethyl acetate is volatile and well suited to GC.
Limonene
Limonene is a volatile terpene often analyzed by GC.
questions.x: GC requires that the sample vaporize without decomposing at the injector and column temperatures. Sucrose is a large, highly hydrogen-bonded sugar with negligible volatility, and it chars on heating instead of vaporizing. Small organic molecules such as toluene, ethyl acetate and limonene are volatile and thermally stable, so they suit GC well.

questions.q: The oven temperature of a GC column is raised while all else is held constant. What happens to retention times?
o: They increase
Heating favors the gas phase and shortens retention.
They are unchanged
Retention is strongly temperature dependent.
Only polar compounds change
Temperature affects the partitioning of all analytes.
They decrease
Correct: higher temperature raises vapor pressures, so analytes spend more time in the gas phase.
questions.x: GC retention reflects how analytes partition between the gas phase and the stationary phase. Raising the oven temperature raises every analyte's vapor pressure, shifting the partition toward the gas, so compounds move through the column faster and retention times decrease. This is why temperature programs are used to elute high-boiling compounds.

questions.q: A GC trace shows peaks for A and B with areas in a 3:1 ratio. Assuming equal detector response per mole, what is the mole percent of A?
o: Inverts the ratio to 1:3.
Ignores the different peak areas.
Uses 2/3 rather than 3/4.
Correct: 3/(3 + 1) = 0.75, so A is 75 mol%.
questions.x: When the detector responds equally per mole, peak area is proportional to the amount of each compound. A 3:1 area ratio means A makes up 3 of every 4 parts, so A is 3/(3 + 1) = 75 mol%. The tempting 67% wrongly uses 2/3; always divide one part by the total of all parts.

questions.q: What is the main reason HPLC achieves higher resolution than gravity column chromatography?
o: It uses a gas mobile phase
HPLC uses a liquid mobile phase; GC uses gas.
It separates compounds only by boiling point
HPLC separates by interactions with the stationary phase, not boiling point.
High pressure drives liquid through very small, uniform particles
Correct: small particles give more surface area and theoretical plates, so pressure is needed for flow.
It requires no stationary phase
HPLC columns are packed with a stationary phase.
questions.x: Resolution improves as stationary-phase particles get smaller and more uniform, because that gives more surface area and more theoretical plates. Small particles resist flow strongly, so HPLC uses high pressure to push the liquid mobile phase through the column. Gravity columns must use larger particles to allow flow, giving lower resolution.

questions.q: A mixture of ethanol, 1-butanol, 1-hexanol and 1-octanol is analyzed by reverse-phase HPLC (C18, water/acetonitrile). Which elutes first?
o: Ethanol
Correct: the most polar, least hydrophobic alcohol interacts least with the C18 phase.
1-Butanol
Butanol is more hydrophobic than ethanol and is retained longer.
1-Hexanol
Longer chains increase retention on C18.
1-Octanol
Octanol is the most hydrophobic and elutes last.
questions.x: In reverse-phase HPLC, retention increases with hydrophobicity because nonpolar molecules stick to the C18 chains. In a series of straight-chain alcohols, each added CH₂ makes the molecule more hydrophobic, so ethanol (shortest chain) elutes first and 1-octanol last. On normal-phase silica, the polarity-based order would run the opposite way.

questions.q: In reverse-phase HPLC, the percentage of acetonitrile in a water/acetonitrile mobile phase is increased. What happens to retention times?
o: They increase
That would happen if the mobile phase became more polar.
They are unchanged
Mobile phase strength strongly affects retention.
Elution order reverses completely
Retention shortens, but the polarity-based order generally holds.
They decrease
Correct: a less polar mobile phase competes better with C18 and elutes hydrophobic analytes faster.
questions.x: In reverse phase, water is the weak solvent and organic solvents like acetonitrile are the strong solvent. Raising the acetonitrile fraction makes the mobile phase less polar, so hydrophobic analytes are drawn off the C18 phase more easily and all retention times decrease. The polarity-based order of the analytes usually stays the same.

questions.q: A carboxylic acid (pKa 4.5) is analyzed by reverse-phase HPLC. The mobile phase pH is lowered from 7 to 2.5. What happens to its retention time?
o: It decreases, because the acid becomes ionized
At pH 2.5 the acid is mostly protonated, not ionized.
It increases, because the neutral acid binds the C18 phase more strongly
Correct: below its pKa the acid is mostly protonated and less polar, so it is retained longer.
It is unchanged, because pH does not affect reverse phase
Ionization state strongly affects hydrophobic retention.
It decreases, because the C18 phase becomes charged
C18 chains carry no ionizable groups.
questions.note: Neutral forms are retained longer in reverse phase than ionized forms.
questions.x: Reverse-phase retention depends on hydrophobicity, and ionized molecules are much more polar than neutral ones. At pH 7, well above the pKa of 4.5, the acid is mostly a polar carboxylate that elutes early. At pH 2.5, two units below the pKa, it is about 99% neutral RCOOH, which binds C18 more strongly, so its retention time increases.

questions.q: In size-exclusion (gel filtration) chromatography, which proteins elute first?
o: The smallest
Small proteins enter pores and are delayed.
The largest
Correct: large proteins are excluded from bead pores and travel the shortest path.
The most negatively charged
Charge is the basis of ion exchange, not gel filtration.
The most hydrophobic
Hydrophobicity is the basis of reverse phase.
questions.x: Gel filtration beads have pores of a set size. Large proteins cannot enter the pores, so they pass only through the space between beads and elute first. Small proteins diffuse into the pores, enter a larger volume, and elute later. This is the opposite of a sieving gel, where small molecules move fastest.

questions.q: Why do small molecules elute later than large ones from a gel filtration column?
o: They bind covalently to the beads
Gel filtration involves no binding; separation is by pore access.
They carry more charge per mass
Charge does not determine gel filtration behavior.
They are denser and sink through the column
Flow, not density, moves molecules through the column.
They enter the bead pores and so access a larger volume
Correct: diffusing into pores lengthens their path through the column.
questions.x: In size-exclusion chromatography, molecules small enough to enter the bead pores can explore the volume inside the beads as well as the volume between them. That longer path delays them, so they elute after larger molecules that are excluded. No binding occurs, so separation depends only on size and shape.

questions.q: Which method quickly removes ammonium sulfate from a protein sample without denaturing the protein?
o: A gel filtration desalting column
Correct: the protein elutes in the void volume while small salt ions are delayed in the pores.
SDS-PAGE
SDS-PAGE denatures the protein and does not recover it for use.
Isoelectric focusing
IEF separates by pI and is incompatible with high salt.
Adding more ammonium sulfate
That increases salt and precipitates protein.
questions.x: A desalting column is a gel filtration column with small pores. The protein is too large to enter the pores and elutes quickly in the void volume, while small salt ions enter the pores and elute much later. The method is gentle and nondenaturing. SDS-PAGE would denature the protein and not recover it in usable form.

questions.q: A protein runs as a single 50 kDa band on SDS-PAGE but elutes from a calibrated gel filtration column at about 200 kDa. What is the best interpretation?
o: The protein is degraded during gel filtration
Degradation would make it appear smaller, not larger.
SDS adds 150 kDa of mass to the protein
SDS binding does not change the apparent mass on gel filtration.
The native protein is a tetramer of identical subunits
Correct: SDS-PAGE gives subunit mass, gel filtration gives native size: 200/50 = 4.
The protein is a monomer with four disulfide bonds
Disulfides within one chain do not quadruple native size.
questions.x: SDS-PAGE denatures proteins and breaks apart noncovalent subunits, so it reports the mass of a single polypeptide (50 kDa). Gel filtration is run under native conditions and measures the size of the intact assembly (about 200 kDa). The ratio 200/50 = 4 shows a tetramer of identical subunits. Disulfides within one chain cannot change the total mass.

questions.q: Two proteins are both larger than the exclusion limit of a gel filtration resin. How do they elute?
o: The larger one first, well resolved
Above the exclusion limit, size differences are no longer distinguished.
The smaller one first
Neither protein enters the pores, so neither is delayed.
They stay bound until salt is added
Gel filtration has no binding step.
Together in the void volume, unseparated
Correct: neither enters the pores, so both take the same path.
questions.x: The exclusion limit is the size above which molecules cannot enter any of the resin's pores. Two proteins both above that limit take the same path between the beads and elute together in the void volume, unresolved. To separate them, choose a resin with larger pores so at least one can enter.

questions.q: Ion-exchange chromatography separates proteins mainly on the basis of:
o: Molecular size
Size is the basis of gel filtration.
Net surface charge
Correct: proteins bind oppositely charged groups on the resin.
Specific ligand binding
That is affinity chromatography.
Volatility
Volatility is the basis of distillation and GC.
questions.x: Ion-exchange resins carry fixed charged groups that bind proteins with the opposite net charge. A protein's net charge depends on the buffer pH relative to its pI. Proteins are then eluted by raising salt concentration or changing pH. Size is the basis of gel filtration, and specific ligand binding is affinity chromatography.

questions.q: A protein with pI 8.0 is in buffer at pH 6.0. Which column will bind it?
o: An anion exchanger, such as DEAE resin
A net-positive protein is repelled by a positive anion exchanger.
Either exchanger equally well
Binding depends on matching opposite charges.
A cation exchanger, such as carboxymethyl (CM) resin
Correct: below its pI the protein is net positive and binds a negatively charged resin.
Neither, since the protein is neutral at pH 6.0
It is neutral only at pH 8.0, its pI.
questions.x: A protein carries a net positive charge when the pH is below its pI and a net negative charge above it. At pH 6.0, a protein with pI 8.0 is positive, so it binds a cation exchanger, a negatively charged resin such as carboxymethyl (CM). A positively charged anion exchanger such as DEAE would repel it.

questions.q: How are bound proteins typically eluted from an ion-exchange column?
o: By increasing the salt concentration of the buffer
Correct: salt ions compete for charged sites on the resin and displace proteins.
By adding SDS
SDS denatures proteins and is not used for ion-exchange elution.
By lowering the column temperature
Temperature is not the standard elution variable.
By adding imidazole
Imidazole elutes His-tagged proteins from nickel affinity resin.
questions.x: Proteins bind ion-exchange resins through electrostatic attraction. Raising the salt concentration adds ions such as Na⁺ or Cl⁻ that compete for the resin's charged sites and shield charges, releasing the bound proteins. Weakly bound proteins elute at lower salt and tightly bound ones at higher salt. Imidazole is for His-tag affinity columns.

questions.q: Proteins with pI 4.5, 6.5 and 9.0 are loaded onto a DEAE (anion-exchange) column at pH 7.5. Which protein flows through without binding?
o: The protein with pI 9.0
Correct: at pH 7.5 it is net positive and is repelled by the positive DEAE groups.
The protein with pI 4.5
It is strongly negative at pH 7.5 and binds tightly.
The protein with pI 6.5
It is mildly negative at pH 7.5 and binds.
None of them binds the column
Proteins with pI below 7.5 are negative and bind DEAE.
questions.x: DEAE is an anion exchanger with positive groups, so it binds proteins that are net negative, which means the buffer pH is above their pI. At pH 7.5, the proteins with pI 4.5 and 6.5 are negative and bind. For the pI 9.0 protein, pH 7.5 is below its pI, so it is net positive, is repelled, and flows through.

questions.q: Proteins with pI 4.5 and 6.5 are bound to DEAE at pH 7.5 and eluted with an increasing NaCl gradient. Which elutes last?
o: The protein with pI 6.5
Being less negative, it is displaced at lower salt.
Both elute together
Different net charges give different binding strengths.
The protein with pI 4.5
Correct: it carries more negative charge at pH 7.5, so it binds more tightly and needs more salt.
Neither elutes with salt
Salt competes for charged sites and elutes bound proteins.
questions.x: On an anion exchanger, the more negative a protein's net charge, the more tightly it binds and the more salt it takes to elute it. At pH 7.5, the protein with pI 4.5 is three units above its pI and carries more negative charge than the pI 6.5 protein. It therefore elutes last, at the highest salt.

questions.q: DEAE-cellulose is commonly used as an ion-exchange resin. What charge does it carry, and what does it bind?
o: Negative; it binds positively charged proteins
That describes cation exchangers like CM.
Positive; it binds negatively charged proteins
Correct: protonated diethylaminoethyl groups make DEAE an anion exchanger.
Positive; it binds positively charged proteins
Like charges repel, so no binding would occur.
No charge; it binds by size
DEAE carries charged amine groups.
questions.x: DEAE (diethylaminoethyl) cellulose carries tertiary amine groups that are protonated and positively charged at typical working pH. A positive resin attracts negatively charged proteins, so DEAE is an anion exchanger. Carboxymethyl (CM) cellulose carries negative carboxylate groups and is a cation exchanger.

questions.q: Affinity chromatography separates a protein from a mixture based on:
o: Net charge at the buffer pH
That is ion exchange.
Molecular size
That is gel filtration.
Boiling point
Proteins are not separated by volatility.
Specific binding to an immobilized ligand
Correct: only proteins that recognize the attached ligand are retained.
questions.x: Affinity chromatography attaches a ligand, such as a substrate analog, antibody or metal ion, to the resin. Only proteins that specifically recognize that ligand are retained, while everything else washes through. The bound protein is then released by adding a competing free ligand or changing conditions. It is usually the most selective purification step.

questions.q: A His₆-tagged protein is bound to a Ni²⁺–NTA column. Which reagent is typically used to elute it?
o: Glutathione
Glutathione elutes GST-tagged proteins from glutathione resin.
High concentration of NaCl alone
Salt reduces nonspecific ionic binding but does not break His–Ni coordination.
Imidazole
Correct: imidazole mimics the histidine side chain and competes for the nickel sites.
SDS
SDS denatures the protein and is not a standard affinity eluent.
questions.x: Ni²⁺–NTA resin holds proteins through coordination between nickel and the imidazole rings of the histidine tag. Free imidazole has the same ring and competes for the nickel sites, so a high imidazole concentration releases the tagged protein. Salt alone does not break metal coordination; glutathione is used only for GST tags.

questions.q: A His-tagged protein fails to bind a Ni²⁺–NTA column when the lysis buffer contains 50 mM EDTA. What is the most likely reason?
o: EDTA chelates and strips Ni²⁺ from the resin
Correct: without bound nickel, the column cannot coordinate histidines.
EDTA cleaves the His-tag
EDTA is a chelator, not a protease.
EDTA denatures the protein
EDTA does not unfold proteins.
EDTA protonates histidine side chains
EDTA is a metal chelator, not a strong acid.
questions.x: Ni²⁺–NTA columns depend on Ni²⁺ ions held by the NTA chelating groups. EDTA is a stronger chelator and pulls the nickel off the resin, leaving nothing to coordinate the histidines, so the tagged protein flows through. Lysis buffers for His-tag purification therefore avoid strong chelators such as EDTA.

questions.q: A lysate is passed over a column bearing an immobilized ATP analog. Which protein is most likely retained?
o: Hemoglobin
Hemoglobin binds O₂ via heme, not ATP.
Collagen
Collagen is a structural protein without an ATP site.
Albumin
Albumin binds fatty acids and drugs, not ATP specifically.
A protein kinase
Correct: kinases bind ATP and recognize the immobilized analog.
questions.x: Affinity chromatography retains proteins that specifically bind the immobilized ligand. An ATP analog column captures ATP-binding proteins, such as kinases, which use ATP as the phosphate donor. Hemoglobin, collagen and albumin have no specific ATP-binding site, so they wash through.

questions.q: During agarose gel electrophoresis, toward which electrode does DNA migrate?
o: The negative electrode (cathode)
DNA is negatively charged and moves away from the cathode.
The positive electrode (anode)
Correct: the negatively charged phosphate backbone is drawn toward the anode.
Neither, since DNA is neutral
Each phosphate carries a negative charge at running pH.
Toward whichever electrode is closer
Direction is set by charge, not distance.
questions.x: DNA's sugar-phosphate backbone carries one negative charge per phosphate at typical running pH. In an electric field, negatively charged molecules move toward the positive electrode, the anode. That is why samples are loaded at the cathode (black) end and run toward the red anode.

questions.q: Why does agarose gel electrophoresis separate linear DNA fragments primarily by length?
o: Longer fragments carry less total charge
Longer fragments carry more charge, in proportion to mass.
Charge-to-mass ratio is nearly constant, so the gel sieves by size
Correct: each nucleotide adds one negative charge, so mobility differences come from sieving.
Short fragments are more negatively charged per nucleotide
Charge per nucleotide is the same for all fragments.
The gel binds long fragments covalently
Agarose does not bind DNA covalently.
questions.x: Every nucleotide adds one phosphate charge and similar mass, so all linear DNA fragments have nearly the same charge-to-mass ratio. In free solution they would move at about the same speed. The agarose mesh acts as a sieve, slowing longer fragments more, so migration depends mainly on length.

questions.q: To better resolve DNA fragments of 100 to 300 bp, how should agarose concentration be changed?
o: Decrease it to make larger pores
Low-percentage gels suit large fragments; small ones would run together.
Leave it unchanged and raise the voltage
Voltage affects speed, not the sieving range.
Replace agarose with silica gel
Silica is not used for DNA electrophoresis.
Increase it to make smaller pores
Correct: a denser gel improves separation of small fragments.
questions.x: Agarose concentration sets pore size: a higher percentage gives a denser mesh with smaller pores. Small fragments of 100 to 300 bp pass easily through large pores and run together, but a denser gel separates them better. Low-percentage gels are used for large fragments. Voltage changes speed, not resolving range.

questions.q: Uncut plasmid DNA shows three bands: supercoiled, nicked circular and linear forms of the same length. Which form typically migrates fastest?
o: Supercoiled
Correct: its compact, twisted shape moves through agarose most easily.
Nicked (relaxed) circular
The open, floppy circle experiences the most drag and is usually slowest.
Linear
Linear DNA usually runs between supercoiled and nicked forms.
All migrate equally, since they have equal mass
Shape affects mobility, not just mass.
questions.x: Plasmid forms with the same length have the same mass and charge, so their mobility depends on shape. Supercoiled DNA is tightly twisted and compact, so it slips through the gel most easily and usually runs fastest. Nicked circles are open and floppy and run slowest, and linear DNA usually runs in between.

questions.q: On an agarose gel, a 1000 bp marker runs 4 cm and a 100 bp marker runs 8 cm. Migration distance is linear in log(size). About how large is a fragment that runs 6 cm?
o: 550 bp
Assumes size is linear with distance, not log(size).
300 bp
Correct: 6 cm is halfway in log scale, 10^2.5 ≈ 316 bp.
200 bp
Underestimates; the log midpoint of 100 and 1000 is about 316.
750 bp
Places the fragment too close to the 1000 bp marker.
questions.note: Use log(size) vs distance for gel standards.
questions.x: Over a gel's useful range, migration distance is roughly linear in the logarithm of fragment size. Here 4 cm corresponds to log 1000 = 3 and 8 cm to log 100 = 2, so 6 cm corresponds to log size = 2.5, which is 10^2.5 ≈ 316 bp, or about 300 bp. Assuming size itself is linear with distance gives the wrong answer of 550 bp.

questions.q: What is the main role of SDS in SDS-PAGE?
o: To reduce disulfide bonds
Reducing agents like β-mercaptoethanol break disulfides.
To give each protein a charge equal to its pI
SDS masks intrinsic charge rather than reflecting pI.
To denature proteins and coat them with uniform negative charge per mass
Correct: equal charge density lets the gel separate polypeptides by size.
To stain proteins for visualization
Staining is done afterward with dyes like Coomassie.
questions.x: SDS is an anionic detergent that unfolds proteins and binds along the chain at a roughly constant ratio per amino acid. The coating gives all polypeptides a similar negative charge-to-mass ratio and swamps their native charges, so migration through the gel depends mainly on size. Disulfide bonds must be broken separately by a reducing agent.

questions.q: An antibody runs at about 150 kDa on nonreducing SDS-PAGE but gives bands at about 50 and 25 kDa when β-mercaptoethanol is added. What explains this?
o: SDS breaks peptide bonds under reducing conditions
Neither SDS nor β-mercaptoethanol hydrolyzes peptide bonds.
The chains are held by noncovalent forces only
SDS alone would then separate them, even without reducing agent.
β-Mercaptoethanol removes carbohydrate from the antibody
It reduces disulfides; it does not deglycosylate.
Heavy and light chains are held together by disulfide bonds
Correct: reducing agent breaks interchain disulfides, releasing 50 kDa heavy and 25 kDa light chains.
questions.x: SDS breaks noncovalent interactions, but disulfide bonds survive unless a reducing agent like β-mercaptoethanol is added. An IgG antibody has two heavy and two light chains joined by interchain disulfides, so it runs intact at about 150 kDa without reduction. Reduction releases separate heavy (about 50 kDa) and light (about 25 kDa) chains.

questions.q: A protein is a noncovalent homodimer of 40 kDa subunits with no disulfide bonds. Where does it run on SDS-PAGE without reducing agent?
o: At 80 kDa
Only covalently (disulfide) linked subunits would stay together.
At 40 kDa
Correct: SDS disrupts noncovalent subunit contacts, so only monomers are seen.
At both 40 and 80 kDa equally
SDS fully dissociates noncovalent dimers.
At 20 kDa
SDS does not cleave the polypeptide chain.
questions.x: SDS unfolds proteins and breaks all noncovalent contacts between subunits. A dimer held together only by noncovalent forces therefore falls apart, and each 40 kDa subunit runs on its own, even without a reducing agent. Only disulfide-linked subunits stay joined under nonreducing SDS-PAGE.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the stacking gel in discontinuous SDS-PAGE?
o: To separate proteins by pI
Separation by pI is isoelectric focusing.
To denature proteins before they enter the gel
Denaturation is done by SDS and heat before loading.
To concentrate proteins into a sharp band before the resolving gel
Correct: the low-percentage, low-pH stacking gel compresses samples into a thin zone.
To remove salt from the samples
Desalting is done by dialysis or gel filtration.
questions.x: In discontinuous SDS-PAGE, the stacking gel has large pores and a lower pH (about 6.8) than the resolving gel. Ion mobility differences there squeeze all proteins into a very thin zone before they reach the resolving gel. Starting from that sharp band, proteins separate by size with crisp bands. Denaturation happens earlier, by heating with SDS.

questions.q: In SDS-PAGE, toward which electrode do the proteins migrate?
o: The positive electrode (anode)
Correct: SDS-coated proteins are negatively charged.
The negative electrode (cathode)
SDS makes proteins negative, so they move away from the cathode.
Basic proteins toward the cathode and acidic ones toward the anode
SDS overwhelms intrinsic charge, so all move toward the anode.
They do not migrate without a pH gradient
A pH gradient is needed for IEF, not SDS-PAGE.
questions.x: SDS binds proteins densely and gives them all a strong negative charge that overwhelms their intrinsic charge. Negative molecules move toward the positive electrode, the anode. So in SDS-PAGE every protein runs the same direction regardless of its pI, unlike native PAGE where charge depends on buffer pH.

questions.q: Which property of a protein cannot be determined from SDS-PAGE alone?
o: Its native oligomeric state
Correct: SDS dissociates noncovalent subunits, so native assembly is lost.
Its approximate subunit molecular weight
Subunit mass is exactly what SDS-PAGE estimates.
The number of different polypeptide sizes in a sample
Distinct bands reveal differently sized polypeptides.
Its relative purity in a sample
A single band versus many bands indicates purity.
questions.x: SDS-PAGE denatures proteins and breaks apart noncovalent subunits, so it reports subunit masses, how many sizes of polypeptide are present, and rough purity. Because the native structure is destroyed, it cannot reveal how subunits assemble in the living protein. Native methods such as gel filtration or native PAGE are needed for that.

questions.q: A researcher wants to detect an enzyme's activity directly in the gel after electrophoresis. Which method should be used?
o: SDS-PAGE with β-mercaptoethanol
SDS and reduction denature the enzyme.
SDS-PAGE without reducing agent
SDS alone still unfolds the enzyme.
Native PAGE
Correct: without SDS or reducing agent, proteins keep their folded, active structure.
Agarose gel with ethidium bromide
That system is for nucleic acids.
questions.x: Detecting enzyme activity in a gel requires the enzyme to stay folded and active. Native PAGE uses no SDS or reducing agent, so proteins keep their native structure and can be detected by an activity stain. SDS unfolds proteins even without a reducing agent, so any SDS-PAGE gel would destroy activity.

questions.q: Two globular proteins of 60 kDa have pI values of 5.0 and 6.5. They are run on native PAGE at pH 8.8 toward the anode. Which migrates farther?
o: The protein with pI 6.5
It is less negatively charged at pH 8.8.
The protein with pI 5.0
Correct: farther below its pI, it carries more negative charge at pH 8.8 and moves faster.
Both migrate equally, since they have equal mass
Native PAGE depends on charge and shape, not just mass.
Neither enters the gel
Both are negative at pH 8.8 and move toward the anode.
questions.x: In native PAGE, mobility depends on net charge and size and shape. At pH 8.8 both proteins are above their pI and are negative, but the protein with pI 5.0 is farther below the buffer pH and carries more negative charge. With equal mass and similar shape, the more highly charged protein moves farther toward the anode.

questions.q: Isoelectric focusing separates proteins on the basis of:
o: Molecular weight
Mass is the basis of SDS-PAGE.
Hydrophobicity
That is the basis of reverse-phase chromatography.
Ligand binding specificity
That is affinity chromatography.
Isoelectric point
Correct: each protein stops where the gradient pH equals its pI and its net charge is zero.
questions.x: In isoelectric focusing, proteins move through a stable pH gradient in an electric field. A protein's net charge changes as it moves, and it stops where the gradient's pH equals its pI because its net charge is zero there. IEF therefore separates by pI, not mass. In 2D gels it is followed by SDS-PAGE to separate by size.

questions.q: In an IEF gel, a protein with pI 6.0 is applied at the pH 8 region. Which way does it move?
o: Toward the cathode into higher pH, stopping at pH 6.0
pH 6.0 lies toward the acidic, anode end, not the cathode end.
It stays at pH 8, since it is already neutral
It is neutral only at pH 6.0.
Toward the anode into lower pH, stopping at pH 6.0
Correct: at pH 8 it is negative, moves toward the acidic anode end, and stops where it becomes neutral.
Toward the cathode, migrating off the gel
A negative protein moves toward the anode.
questions.note: In IEF the anode is the acidic end and the cathode the basic end.
questions.x: In IEF the anode end is acidic and the cathode end is basic. A protein with pI 6.0 sitting at pH 8 is above its pI, so it is net negative and moves toward the anode, into lower pH. As it moves, it gains protons until it reaches pH 6.0, where its net charge is zero and it stops.

questions.q: Two forms of a protein differ only by a single phosphate group. In 2D gel electrophoresis (IEF then SDS-PAGE), how are they best distinguished?
o: By a shift in the IEF dimension toward lower pI
Correct: the added negative phosphate lowers the pI, while the mass change is too small to resolve by SDS-PAGE.
By a large shift in the SDS-PAGE dimension
About 80 Da is negligible relative to protein mass.
By a shift toward higher pI
Adding a negatively charged group lowers pI.
They cannot be separated in 2D gels
IEF readily resolves charge isoforms.
questions.x: A phosphate group adds negative charge, which lowers a protein's pI, so the phosphorylated form focuses at a slightly more acidic position in the IEF dimension. Its mass rises by only about 80 Da, which is too small to resolve by SDS-PAGE for a typical protein. 2D gels therefore show phosphoforms as a horizontal row of spots at nearly the same size.

questions.q: Glycine (pI ≈ 6.0) is placed in an electric field in a buffer at pH 3. Which way does it migrate?
o: Toward the anode
That occurs at pH above the pI, where glycine is net negative.
It does not move
It is stationary only at pH = pI.
It splits evenly toward both electrodes
Rapid proton exchange gives every molecule the same average positive charge, so all move the same way.
Toward the cathode
Correct: below its pI, glycine carries a net positive charge on average, so it moves to the negative electrode.
questions.x: Below its pI, an amino acid has more protons than at neutrality and carries a net positive charge. At pH 3, every glycine has NH₃⁺, and a sizable share still has an un-ionized COOH, so the average net charge is positive and it migrates toward the cathode. It would move toward the anode only above its pI and would stay put at pH 6.0.

questions.q: A mixture of aspartate (pI 2.8), glycine (pI 6.0) and lysine (pI 9.7) undergoes electrophoresis at pH 6.0. What happens?
o: All three move to the anode
Lysine is positive at pH 6.0 and glycine is neutral.
Aspartate moves to the anode, glycine stays, lysine moves to the cathode
Correct: compare pH to each pI; above pI is negative, below pI is positive.
Lysine moves to the anode and aspartate to the cathode
Reverses the charges; lysine is positive and aspartate negative here.
None move, since all are zwitterions
Only glycine is net neutral at pH 6.0.
questions.x: Compare the buffer pH to each pI: if pH is above pI the molecule is negative, if below it is positive, and if equal it is neutral. At pH 6.0, aspartate (pI 2.8) is negative and moves to the anode, glycine (pI 6.0) is neutral and stays put, and lysine (pI 9.7) is positive and moves to the cathode.

questions.q: In differential centrifugation of a cell homogenate, which component pellets first, at the lowest speed?
o: Ribosomes
Ribosomes are small and require very high g forces.
Nuclei
Correct: nuclei are the largest and densest organelles and sediment first.
Mitochondria
Mitochondria pellet at intermediate speeds, after nuclei.
Soluble cytosolic enzymes
Soluble proteins remain in the final supernatant.
questions.x: Differential centrifugation separates components by sedimentation rate, which depends mainly on size and density. Large, dense nuclei (and unbroken cells) pellet at the lowest speeds. Mitochondria pellet at intermediate speeds, microsomes and ribosomes need ultracentrifugation, and soluble proteins stay in the final supernatant.

questions.q: Of these components, which requires the highest g force to pellet during differential centrifugation?
o: Nuclei
Nuclei pellet at low speed.
Mitochondria
Mitochondria pellet at moderate speed.
Unbroken cells
Intact cells pellet at very low speed.
Ribosomes
Correct: small ribonucleoprotein particles pellet only in ultracentrifugation.
questions.x: In differential centrifugation, smaller particles sediment more slowly and need higher g force to pellet. Intact cells and nuclei pellet at low g, mitochondria at moderate g. Ribosomes are small ribonucleoprotein particles that pellet only at around 100,000 g in an ultracentrifuge, the highest force among these.

questions.q: In equilibrium (isopycnic) CsCl density-gradient centrifugation, where does a DNA molecule come to rest?
o: Where its buoyant density equals the density of the medium
Correct: there is no net force where the densities match.
At the bottom of the tube
DNA bands within the gradient, not at the bottom.
At a position set mainly by its length
Isopycnic separation depends on density, not size.
At the top of the tube
DNA is denser than the top of the gradient and sinks to its matching density.
questions.x: In isopycnic centrifugation, a dense CsCl solution forms a density gradient as it spins. A DNA molecule sinks where the medium is less dense than it and rises where the medium is denser, so it settles where its buoyant density equals the medium's. The final position depends on density, such as GC content or ¹⁵N labeling, not on length.

questions.q: A bacterial ribosome is 70S even though its subunits are 50S and 30S. Why are the values not additive?
o: Some RNA is lost when subunits combine
Assembly does not remove RNA.
S values measure density only
S reflects sedimentation rate, which depends on mass, shape and density.
Sedimentation coefficients depend on shape and friction as well as mass
Correct: the assembled particle is more compact than the sum of its separate parts.
The 30S value is measured at a different speed
S values are intrinsic and independent of rotor speed.
questions.x: A sedimentation coefficient (S) measures how fast a particle sediments, which depends on mass, density and shape (friction), not on mass alone. When the 50S and 30S subunits join, the combined particle is more compact than two separate pieces, so it experiences relatively less friction per mass. So the assembled ribosome is 70S, not the 80S that simple addition would give.

questions.q: In rate-zonal centrifugation through a sucrose gradient, particles separate according to sedimentation rate. Why is the run stopped before completion?
o: Sucrose crystallizes if the run continues
Sucrose stays dissolved during centrifugation.
Particles would reverse direction at equilibrium
Particles denser than the gradient keep sinking; they do not reverse.
Longer runs denature all proteins
Time is limited to preserve separation, not to prevent denaturation.
Given enough time, all particles would reach the bottom and the separation would be lost
Correct: rate-zonal separation captures particles mid-migration, separated by size and shape.
questions.x: Rate-zonal centrifugation separates particles by how fast they sediment through a shallow gradient, which depends on size and shape. Particles denser than the gradient keep moving, and given enough time all of them would reach the bottom and pile together. The run is stopped while the particles are still separated into bands at different depths.

questions.q: How does adding a high concentration of ammonium sulfate precipitate proteins?
o: Sulfate covalently cross-links proteins
Salting out is a reversible solubility effect, not covalent.
Salt ions sequester water, reducing protein solvation
Correct: salting out lowers solubility, and proteins precipitate at different salt concentrations.
It denatures proteins by reducing disulfides
Ammonium sulfate is not a reducing agent and usually preserves folding.
