It shifts every protein's pI to the buffer pH
Salt does not change a protein's pI.
questions.x: At high concentration, ammonium sulfate ions bind many water molecules, leaving less water to solvate proteins. Protein–protein hydrophobic interactions then dominate and the proteins aggregate and precipitate, which is called salting out. Different proteins precipitate at different salt levels. The effect is reversible and usually preserves the native fold.

questions.q: A protein sample is dialyzed in tubing with a 10 kDa molecular weight cutoff against a large volume of buffer. What happens?
o: The 45 kDa protein diffuses out while salts are retained
Reverses the size selectivity of the membrane.
Both salt and protein are retained
Small ions pass freely through a 10 kDa cutoff membrane.
Salts diffuse out while a 45 kDa protein is retained
Correct: small solutes cross the membrane down their gradient, and large proteins cannot.
Proteins separate by charge across the membrane
Dialysis separates by size, not charge.
questions.x: A dialysis membrane has pores that let molecules smaller than the cutoff pass while retaining larger ones. Salt ions are far below 10 kDa, so they diffuse out into the large volume of buffer until their concentration evens out. A 45 kDa protein is too large to cross the membrane and stays inside the tubing.

questions.q: A crude extract has 200 mg protein and 1000 units of enzyme activity. After a column step, 10 mg protein with 600 units remains. What is the fold purification?
o: Divides 600 units by 100 instead of comparing specific activities (60 vs 5 units/mg).
Correct: specific activity rises from 5 to 60 units/mg, a 12-fold purification.
Uses the protein ratio (200/10) and ignores activity loss.
That is the fractional yield, not the fold purification.
questions.note: Fold purification = new specific activity / original specific activity.
questions.x: Specific activity is activity per mass of protein. It begins at 1000/200 = 5 units/mg and becomes 600/10 = 60 units/mg after the column. Fold purification is the ratio of specific activities, 60/5 = 12. The 20-fold choice uses only the drop in total protein and ignores that 40% of the activity was also lost.

questions.q: As a protein purification proceeds through successive steps, what typically happens to total activity and specific activity?
o: Total activity falls while specific activity rises
Correct: some enzyme is lost at each step, but contaminating protein is lost faster.
Both rise
Total activity cannot increase without added enzyme.
Total activity rises while specific activity falls
Reverses both trends.
Both stay constant
Purification removes contaminants, raising specific activity.
questions.x: Each purification step loses some of the target enzyme, so total activity falls (yield goes down). However, contaminating proteins are removed faster than the enzyme, so the activity per milligram of protein, the specific activity, rises. Total activity cannot increase unless more enzyme is added.

questions.q: Why is size-exclusion chromatography usually placed late in a protein purification scheme?
o: It accepts only small sample volumes, so it follows steps that concentrate the protein
Correct: gel filtration has low load capacity and dilutes samples, suiting final polishing.
It denatures proteins, so it must come last
Gel filtration is gentle and nondenaturing.
It removes salt, which must be present for earlier steps
Desalting is not the main reason for its late placement.
It has the highest capacity of any method
Its capacity is relatively low.
questions.x: Gel filtration has a low loading capacity: the sample must be a small fraction of the column volume, and it dilutes the protein. It is therefore placed late, after higher-capacity steps such as ion exchange or affinity that remove most contaminants and concentrate the sample. It is gentle, so denaturation is not a reason for its place in the order.

questions.q: Protein concentration is often estimated by absorbance at 280 nm. Which residues are mainly responsible?
o: Glycine and alanine
Small aliphatic side chains do not absorb at 280 nm.
Lysine and arginine
Basic side chains lack aromatic chromophores.
Tryptophan and tyrosine
Correct: their aromatic side chains absorb strongly near 280 nm.
Serine and threonine
Hydroxyl side chains do not absorb at 280 nm.
questions.x: Absorbance at 280 nm comes mainly from the aromatic rings of tryptophan and, to a lesser degree, tyrosine, with a small contribution from phenylalanine and disulfides. Because most proteins contain these residues, A₂₈₀ gives a quick estimate of protein concentration. Aliphatic, basic and hydroxyl side chains lack the needed chromophore.

questions.q: His-tagged protein eluted from Ni²⁺–NTA shows a target band plus a few contaminants of different size. Which next step best removes them while keeping the protein native?
o: SDS-PAGE followed by gel extraction
SDS denatures the protein.
Size-exclusion chromatography
Correct: contaminants of different size separate by gel filtration under native conditions.
A second identical Ni²⁺–NTA column under the same conditions
Contaminants that co-purified once will likely co-purify again.
Boiling the sample to precipitate contaminants
Boiling would likely denature the target protein too.
questions.x: Gel filtration separates proteins by size under native conditions, so it is ideal for removing contaminants of different size left after an affinity step. Repeating the same Ni²⁺–NTA column would likely retain the same contaminants, because they co-purified for a reason. SDS-PAGE and boiling would denature the target protein.

questions.q: A racemic carboxylic acid is resolved by reacting it with an enantiomerically pure amine. Why does this allow separation?
o: It converts one enantiomer into the other
Salt formation does not invert stereocenters.
It forms enantiomeric salts with different boiling points
Enantiomers have identical physical properties in an achiral environment.
It destroys one enantiomer selectively
Both enantiomers form salts; neither is destroyed.
It forms diastereomeric salts with different physical properties
Correct: diastereomers differ in solubility, so they can be separated by crystallization.
questions.x: Enantiomers have identical physical properties in an achiral environment, so they cannot be separated directly by crystallization. Reacting a racemic acid with a single enantiomer of a chiral amine produces two diastereomeric salts, (R,R) and (S,R). Diastereomers have different solubilities, so they can be separated by crystallization, then each acid is recovered by acidifying.

questions.q: Which method can directly separate the two enantiomers of a racemic mixture?
o: Fractional distillation
Enantiomers have identical boiling points.
Silica gel column chromatography
Achiral silica cannot distinguish enantiomers.
HPLC on a chiral stationary phase
Correct: a chiral phase interacts differently with each enantiomer, giving different retention.
Acid–base extraction
Enantiomers have identical pKa values.
questions.x: Separating enantiomers needs a chiral environment, because in an achiral one they behave identically. A chiral stationary phase forms short-lived diastereomeric complexes with each enantiomer that differ in stability, giving different retention times. Distillation, silica columns and acid–base extraction are all achiral, so they cannot separate enantiomers.

questions.q: Why can't a racemic mixture be separated by recrystallization from an ordinary achiral solvent in the usual way?
o: Enantiomers have identical solubilities in an achiral solvent
Correct: in an achiral environment, enantiomers share all physical properties.
Racemic mixtures are always liquids
Many racemates are crystalline solids.
Enantiomers react with achiral solvents
Enantiomers react identically with achiral reagents and are not consumed by solvents.
Enantiomers have different melting points
Pure enantiomers have identical melting points.
questions.x: Enantiomers are mirror images with identical physical properties, including solubility, in any achiral solvent. Ordinary recrystallization depends on solubility differences, so it cannot separate them. To resolve a racemate, a chiral environment must be introduced, for example by forming diastereomeric salts with a chiral resolving agent.

questions.q: A neutral organic product is contaminated with a carboxylic acid and an amine. Which wash sequence removes both impurities from the ether solution?
o: Two washes with dilute HCl
HCl removes the amine but leaves the carboxylic acid neutral in ether.
Two washes with brine
Brine dries the organic layer but does not ionize either impurity.
Aqueous NaHCO₃ only
Bicarbonate removes the acid but leaves the amine neutral in ether.
Dilute HCl, then aqueous NaHCO₃
Correct: acid protonates the amine into water, then bicarbonate deprotonates the carboxylic acid into water.
questions.x: A neutral product stays in the ether no matter the wash pH, so impurities are removed by ionizing them. Dilute HCl protonates the amine to a water-soluble ammonium salt, and NaHCO₃ deprotonates the carboxylic acid to a water-soluble carboxylate. Each wash removes only one kind of impurity, so both are needed.

questions.q: In ion-exchange chromatography, a protein at a buffer pH equal to its pI will:
o: Bind tightly to a cation exchanger
Binding requires net positive charge, which occurs below pI.
Not bind to either cation or anion exchanger
Correct: with zero net charge, the protein has no electrostatic attraction to the resin.
Bind tightly to an anion exchanger
Binding requires net negative charge, which occurs above pI.
Bind to both exchangers equally
A net-neutral protein binds neither strongly.
questions.x: Ion-exchange binding requires net charge. At a pH equal to its pI, a protein's positive and negative charges balance, so its net charge is zero and it has no overall attraction to either a cation or an anion exchanger. Below the pI it is positive and binds a cation exchanger; above it, it is negative and binds an anion exchanger.

questions.q: A protein of interest precipitates between 40% and 60% ammonium sulfate saturation. Which procedure enriches it?
o: Bring to 60%, keep the supernatant
The target would be in the 60% pellet, not the supernatant.
Bring to 40%, discard the pellet, then bring the supernatant to 60% and keep the pellet
Correct: the first cut removes proteins that precipitate earlier; the second collects the target.
Bring to 40%, keep the pellet
The target is still soluble at 40%.
Bring to 100% and keep the pellet
This precipitates nearly all proteins with little enrichment.
questions.x: Fractional precipitation uses two cuts. Bringing the extract to 40% saturation precipitates proteins that come out earlier while the target stays dissolved, so that pellet is discarded. Raising the supernatant to 60% then precipitates the target, which is collected as the pellet. Going straight to 100% precipitates nearly everything and gives little enrichment.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO?
o: Butanal
Correct: four carbons including the carbonyl carbon, aldehyde suffix -al.
Propanal
Forgets that the aldehyde carbon is counted in the parent chain.
Butan-2-one
A ketone; here the C=O is at the chain end and bears an H, so it is an aldehyde.
Butan-1-ol
An alcohol suffix; CHO is a carbonyl, not a hydroxyl.
questions.x: IUPAC names count every carbon in the longest chain that contains the principal group, and for an aldehyde that includes the CHO carbon itself, which is always C1. CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO has four carbons, so it is butanal. Propanal is the trap: it drops the carbonyl carbon from the count, as if CHO were a substituent.

questions.q: A molecule contains a ketone, a hydroxyl group and a carboxylic acid. Which group supplies the suffix of its IUPAC name?
o: The ketone (-one)
Ketones rank below carboxylic acids and their derivatives.
The carboxylic acid (-oic acid)
Correct: carboxylic acids outrank ketones and alcohols, which become oxo- and hydroxy- prefixes.
Whichever group has the lowest locant
Priority sets the suffix first; locants are assigned afterward.
The hydroxyl (-ol)
Alcohols rank below both carbonyl groups here.
questions.note: Priority: acid > anhydride > ester > acid halide > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine.
questions.x: The highest-priority functional group sets the suffix, and all lower groups become prefixes. Carboxylic acids outrank every other common group, so this compound is named as an -oic acid, with the ketone written as oxo- and the alcohol as hydroxy-. Locants are assigned only after the principal group is chosen, so the lowest locant never decides the suffix.

questions.q: What is the correct name of CH₃COCH₂CH₃?
o: Butan-3-one
Numbering must give the carbonyl the lowest possible locant.
Propanone
Propanone has three carbons; this molecule has four.
Butanal
Butanal has a terminal CHO; this carbonyl is internal, so it is a ketone.
Butan-2-one
Correct: four-carbon chain, ketone at C2 (numbered from the end nearer the C=O).
questions.x: CH₃COCH₂CH₃ has four carbons with an internal C=O, so it is a ketone named butanone. The chain is numbered from the end that gives the carbonyl the lowest locant, so the ketone is at C2 rather than C3, giving butan-2-one. Butan-3-one describes the same molecule numbered from the wrong end, which IUPAC rules do not allow.

questions.q: An ester is made from ethanol and propanoic acid. What is its name?
o: Propyl ethanoate
Reverses the roles; this ester would come from propanol and acetic acid.
Propanoyl ethyl ether
Esters are not named as ethers; the C=O makes it an ester.
Ethyl propanoate
Correct: the alcohol-derived group is named first (ethyl), then the acid as -oate (propanoate).
Ethyl propanol
Mixes ester and alcohol naming; esters end in -oate.
questions.x: Esters are named in two words: first the alkyl group from the alcohol, then the acid part with -ic acid changed to -oate. Ethanol supplies the ethyl group and propanoic acid becomes propanoate, so the ester is ethyl propanoate. Propyl ethanoate is the tempting reversal; it is an isomer that would come from propanol and ethanoic (acetic) acid.

questions.q: Which structure is 2-methylpropan-2-ol?
o: (CH₃)₂CHOH
That is propan-2-ol; it lacks the C2 methyl substituent.
(CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH
That is 2-methylpropan-1-ol; the OH is on C1, not C2.
(CH₃)₃COH
Correct: three-carbon chain with OH and a methyl on C2, a tertiary alcohol.
CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃
That is butan-2-ol, which has no methyl branch.
questions.x: Propan-2-ol is a three-carbon chain with OH on the middle carbon; the 2-methyl prefix adds a methyl to that same carbon. That carbon then bears three methyls and an OH, giving (CH₃)₃COH, tert-butyl alcohol, a tertiary alcohol. (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH has the same branched skeleton, but the OH is on C1, so it is 2-methylpropan-1-ol.

questions.q: A compound has two hydroxyl groups on the same carbon atom. This arrangement is called a:
o: Enol
An enol has an OH on a C=C carbon.
Hemiacetal
A hemiacetal has one OH and one OR on the same carbon.
Vicinal diol
Vicinal diols have OH groups on adjacent carbons.
Geminal diol
Correct: geminal means both groups on one carbon, as in a carbonyl hydrate.
questions.x: Geminal (from Latin for twins) means two groups on the same carbon, and vicinal means groups on adjacent carbons. A geminal diol is the hydrate a carbonyl forms when water adds across C=O. A hemiacetal also has two oxygens on one carbon, but one is OR rather than OH, so it is not a diol.

questions.q: In an alkene, the higher-priority substituents on each carbon lie on opposite sides of the double bond. How is it designated?
o: R
R/S describes tetrahedral stereocenters, not double bonds.
E
Correct: E (entgegen) means the CIP higher-priority groups are on opposite sides.
Z
Z (zusammen) means higher-priority groups are on the same side.
Always trans
Cis/trans compares identical groups; an E alkene is not always trans by that definition.
questions.x: E/Z naming ranks the two groups on each alkene carbon by CIP rules: E means the higher-priority groups are on opposite sides, and Z means they are on the same side. Cis/trans compares like groups instead, so E and trans do not always match: a heavy atom such as Br can reverse the ranking. R/S applies to tetrahedral stereocenters, not double bonds.

questions.q: Which property differs between two enantiomers measured in an achiral environment?
o: Direction of rotation of plane-polarized light
Correct: enantiomers rotate light by equal magnitudes in opposite directions.
Boiling point
Enantiomers have identical boiling points in achiral settings.
Solubility in water
Water is achiral, so both enantiomers dissolve equally.
Density
Physical properties other than optical rotation are identical.
questions.x: Enantiomers are mirror images with identical energies, so in an achiral setting they share every scalar property: boiling point, density, and solubility in achiral solvents such as water. They differ only when they interact with something chiral, and plane-polarized light is chiral. Each enantiomer rotates it by the same amount but in opposite directions.

questions.q: A compound has three stereocenters and no internal symmetry. What is the maximum number of stereoisomers?
o: That is the maximum for two stereocenters.
Correct: 2ⁿ with n = 3 gives 8 when no meso forms are possible.
Uses 2n instead of 2ⁿ.
Uses 3² instead of 2³.
questions.x: Each stereocenter can be R or S, so n independent stereocenters give at most 2ⁿ stereoisomers. With three centers that is 2³ = 8. The count drops below the maximum only when internal symmetry produces meso forms, which this stem rules out. The wrong answers come from using 2n or n² instead of the exponential.

questions.q: How many stereoisomers exist for 2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic acid (tartaric acid)?
o: Tartaric acid has only two stereocenters.
Ignores the meso form, which is a distinct diastereomer.
Correct: the (R,R) and (S,S) enantiomers plus one achiral meso form.
2² overcounts; (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) are the same meso compound.
questions.note: Identical substituent sets on two stereocenters signal a possible meso form.
questions.x: Tartaric acid has two stereocenters, so 2² = 4 configurations are possible. Because both centers carry the same set of substituents, (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) are the same achiral meso compound with an internal mirror plane. That leaves the chiral (R,R)/(S,S) pair plus one meso form, for 3 stereoisomers. Answering 4 misses the meso overlap.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a meso compound?
o: It is a 50:50 mixture of enantiomers
That is a racemic mixture, not a single meso compound.
It rotates plane-polarized light strongly
Being achiral, a meso compound is optically inactive.
It has no stereocenters
Meso compounds by definition contain stereocenters.
It has stereocenters but is achiral because of an internal mirror plane
Correct: the internal symmetry makes it superimposable on its mirror image.
questions.x: A meso compound has two or more stereocenters but also an internal mirror plane, so it is superimposable on its mirror image and is achiral. It therefore shows no optical rotation, even though it is one pure compound. A racemic mixture is also optically inactive, but for a different reason: it is a 50:50 mix of two chiral enantiomers whose rotations cancel.

questions.q: What is the relationship between (2R,3R)- and (2S,3R)-2-bromo-3-chlorobutane?
o: Diastereomers
Correct: only one of the two stereocenters differs, so they are non-mirror-image stereoisomers.
Constitutional isomers
Connectivity is the same; only spatial arrangement differs.
Identical
The two ends carry different halogens, so no meso form is possible.
Enantiomers
Enantiomers require inversion at every stereocenter.
questions.x: Compare the configuration at each stereocenter: if every center is inverted, the two molecules are enantiomers; if only some are inverted, they are diastereomers. (2R,3R) and (2S,3R) differ only at C2, so they are diastereomers. They cannot be identical or meso, because the different halogens on C2 and C3 rule out any internal mirror plane.

questions.q: What is the relationship between (2R,3S)- and (2S,3R)-2-bromo-3-chlorobutane?
o: Identical meso compound
Meso requires identical substituents on both centers; Br and Cl differ.
Diastereomers
Diastereomers differ at some but not all stereocenters.
Conformers
Conformers interconvert by bond rotation; these differ in configuration.
Enantiomers
Correct: every stereocenter is inverted, giving nonsuperimposable mirror images.
questions.x: Going from (2R,3S) to (2S,3R) inverts every stereocenter, which is the test for enantiomers. A meso relationship would need the two halves of the molecule to be identical, but C2 bears Br and C3 bears Cl, so no internal mirror plane exists. The two compounds are therefore nonsuperimposable mirror images, not one meso compound.

questions.q: How are (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane and (2S,3R)-2,3-dibromobutane related?
o: They are the same meso compound
Correct: with identical ends, R,S and S,R are superimposable through an internal mirror plane.
They are enantiomers
Inverting both centers of a meso compound gives back the same molecule.
They are a racemic pair
A racemic pair requires chiral molecules; this one is achiral.
They are diastereomers
Both centers changed, and the molecule is symmetric, so they are identical.
questions.note: Trap: R,S vs S,R are enantiomers only when the two ends differ.
questions.x: Inverting every center normally gives the enantiomer, unless the molecule has an internal mirror plane. In 2,3-dibromobutane both stereocenters carry identical substituent sets (H, Br, CH₃ and the other CHBr), so the R,S form is meso, and its mirror image is itself. (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) are therefore one compound, numbered from opposite ends.

questions.q: The pure R enantiomer of compound X has [α] = +40°. A synthetic sample of X shows [α] = +10°. What percentage of the sample is the R enantiomer?
o: That is the enantiomeric excess, not the percent R.
Adds the ee to half of 100% instead of half of the racemic remainder.
That is the percent of the S enantiomer.
questions.x: Enantiomeric excess equals observed rotation divided by the rotation of the pure enantiomer: 10/40 = 25%. That 25% is extra R; the other 75% is racemic and splits evenly into 37.5% R and 37.5% S. Total R = 25% + 37.5% = 62.5%. Answering 25% mistakes the ee for the percent of R.

questions.q: Why does a racemic mixture show no net optical rotation?
o: Its molecules are achiral
Each molecule is chiral; the cancellation is from the mixture.
Its molecules lack stereocenters
Racemates are made of chiral molecules that have stereocenters.
Equal amounts of enantiomers rotate light equally in opposite directions
Correct: the rotations cancel exactly.
It contains a meso compound
A racemate contains two enantiomers, not a meso form.
questions.x: Each molecule in a racemic mixture is chiral and optically active by itself. The mixture holds equal amounts of the two enantiomers, which rotate plane-polarized light by the same amount in opposite directions, so the rotations cancel exactly. A meso compound is also inactive, but for an internal reason: the molecule itself is achiral.

questions.q: At a single stereocenter, any two of the four substituents are swapped. What happens to the configuration?
o: It is unchanged
Two swaps restore the configuration; one swap inverts it.
It inverts (R becomes S)
Correct: one swap reverses the handedness of the center.
The center becomes achiral
The four groups are still different, so it remains a stereocenter.
It depends on which groups are swapped
Any single exchange of two groups inverts the center.
questions.note: Shortcut: if the lowest-priority group is toward you, swap it to the back and flip the answer.
questions.x: Swapping any two of the four groups on a stereocenter gives its mirror image, so R becomes S. A second swap restores the original, so an even number of swaps keeps the configuration and an odd number inverts it. The center stays a stereocenter because it still bears four different groups; only their arrangement in space has changed.

questions.q: When assigning configuration, the lowest-priority group points toward the viewer and priorities 1→2→3 trace clockwise. What is the configuration?
o: S
Correct: with the lowest group toward you, the observed direction must be reversed.
E
E/Z applies to alkenes, not tetrahedral centers.
R
Clockwise means R only when the lowest-priority group points away.
Cannot be assigned from this view
The assignment is possible; just reverse the result.
questions.x: The R/S rule assumes the lowest-priority group points away from the viewer. If it points toward you, the 1→2→3 direction you see is reversed from the true one, so the result must be flipped: an apparent clockwise (R) becomes S. The view is still usable, so the configuration can be assigned without redrawing.

questions.q: Which substituent has the highest Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priority?
o: –CH₂OH
Its carbon bears (O, H, H).
–CHO
Its carbon bears (O, O, H), which loses to (O, O, O).
–COOH
Correct: its first carbon bears (O, O, O) counting the duplicated C=O oxygen.
–CH(CH₃)₂
Its carbon bears (C, C, H); carbon ranks below oxygen.
questions.x: CIP priority is decided at the first atom: list the atoms attached to it, with a double bond counted as two bonds to that atom. The COOH carbon bears (O, O, O): the OH oxygen plus the C=O oxygen counted twice. CHO gives (O, O, H) and CH₂OH gives (O, H, H), and an isopropyl carbon bears only carbons and H, so COOH ranks highest.

questions.q: A newly synthesized compound has the R configuration. What can be concluded about its sign of optical rotation?
o: It is dextrorotatory (+)
R does not correspond to (+); there is no general correlation.
It is optically inactive
A single enantiomer of a chiral compound is optically active.
It is levorotatory (−)
R/S and the sign of rotation are independent.
Nothing; the sign must be measured experimentally
Correct: R/S is a naming convention and does not predict (+) or (−).
questions.x: R and S come from a geometric naming rule (CIP priorities), while the sign of rotation, (+) or (−), is a physical property found only by measurement with a polarimeter. The two are not linked, and an R compound may be either dextrorotatory or levorotatory. A single enantiomer of a chiral compound is optically active, so it is not inactive.

questions.q: The anti and gauche forms of butane are best described as:
o: Enantiomers
Butane has no stereocenters and these forms interconvert freely.
Constitutional isomers
The connectivity is identical in both forms.
Configurational diastereomers
Configurational isomers require bond breaking to interconvert.
Conformational isomers
Correct: they interconvert rapidly by rotation about the C2–C3 single bond.
questions.x: Anti and gauche butane differ only by rotation about the C2–C3 single bond, which is fast at room temperature, so they are conformers, not isomers you could isolate. Configurational isomers, such as enantiomers and cis/trans diastereomers, can interconvert only by breaking bonds. Butane has no stereocenter, so enantiomers are not possible.

questions.q: In the chair conformation of methylcyclohexane, the methyl group prefers the equatorial position mainly because:
o: Equatorial bonds are shorter
Axial and equatorial C–C bonds have essentially the same length.
Axial positions are electron-poor
The preference is steric, not electronic.
It avoids 1,3-diaxial steric interactions
Correct: an axial methyl clashes with axial hydrogens on C3 and C5.
It gains hydrogen bonding
A methyl group cannot hydrogen bond.
questions.x: An axial substituent on a chair points parallel to the ring axis and sits close to the axial hydrogens on C3 and C5 on the same side, which causes steric strain. In the equatorial position the methyl points outward, away from those hydrogens. This 1,3-diaxial strain is steric, not electronic, and bond lengths are essentially unchanged.

questions.q: Which dimethylcyclohexane can adopt a chair conformation with both methyl groups equatorial?
o: trans-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane
Correct: adjacent trans substituents can be one-up/one-down and both equatorial.
cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane
Adjacent cis groups always place one axial and one equatorial.
trans-1,3-Dimethylcyclohexane
For 1,3-substitution, trans forces one axial group.
cis-1,4-Dimethylcyclohexane
For 1,4-substitution, cis forces one axial group.
questions.note: Di-equatorial: cis-1,3; trans-1,2 and trans-1,4.
questions.x: On a chair, adjacent carbons alternate up/down for equatorial positions, so trans-1,2 groups (one up, one down) can both be equatorial. For 1,3-substitution the pattern flips, so cis-1,3 is the diequatorial isomer, and for 1,4 it flips back to trans. Cis-1,2, trans-1,3 and cis-1,4 always place one group axial in either chair.

questions.q: Which of these alcohols is chiral?
o: Propan-2-ol
C2 carries two identical methyl groups.
Butan-2-ol
Correct: C2 bears H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃, four different groups.
Ethanol
No carbon in ethanol has four different substituents.
Pentan-3-ol
C3 carries two identical ethyl groups.
questions.x: A carbon is a stereocenter when it bears four different groups. In butan-2-ol, C2 carries H, OH, methyl and ethyl, so the molecule is chiral. In propan-2-ol and pentan-3-ol the carbinol carbon has two identical alkyl groups (two methyls or two ethyls), so a mirror plane runs through it and neither molecule is chiral.

questions.q: A racemic carboxylic acid is treated with an enantiopure (R)-amine to form salts. Why can these salts be separated by crystallization?
o: They are enantiomers with different solubilities
Enantiomers have identical solubilities in achiral solvents.
The amine racemizes the acid
The amine does not change the acid's configuration.
They are diastereomers with different physical properties
Correct: (R,R) and (S,R) salts are not mirror images, so solubilities differ.
Only one enantiomer of the acid reacts
Both enantiomers form salts; the salts simply differ.
questions.note: Resolution works by turning enantiomers into diastereomers.
questions.x: Enantiomers have identical physical properties, so they cannot be separated by crystallization directly. Reacting the racemic acid with one enantiomer of a chiral amine gives (R,R) and (S,R) salts, which are diastereomers, not mirror images. Diastereomers differ in solubility, so they can be crystallized apart, and the pure acids are then recovered with acid.

questions.q: (R)-2-Bromobutane reacts with NaOH in acetone by an SN2 mechanism. What is the product?
o: (S)-Butan-2-ol
Correct: backside attack inverts the center, and OH takes Br's top priority, so R becomes S.
(R)-Butan-2-ol
SN2 inverts geometry; with matching priority order the label flips.
Racemic butan-2-ol
Racemization is typical of SN1, not a concerted SN2.
But-2-ene only
The stem specifies an SN2 pathway, which gives substitution, not elimination.
questions.x: SN2 is concerted backside attack, so the stereocenter inverts its geometry (Walden inversion). Here OH replaces Br as the highest-priority group, and ethyl, methyl and H keep their order, so the geometric inversion also flips the label: R becomes S. Do not assume inversion always flips the label; check the priorities after the substitution.

questions.q: Enantiopure (S)-3-bromo-3-methylhexane is heated in water. What best describes the alcohol formed?
o: An achiral meso alcohol
The product has one stereocenter, so it cannot be meso.
A nearly racemic mixture
Correct: SN1 goes through a planar carbocation attacked from both faces.
Pure (R)-alcohol by inversion
Inversion requires SN2, which a tertiary center cannot undergo.
Pure (S)-alcohol by retention
The planar carbocation erases the original configuration.
questions.x: A tertiary halide in water, a polar protic solvent, reacts by SN1. The leaving group departs first to give a planar sp² carbocation, which water can attack from either face. The original configuration is therefore lost and the alcohol forms nearly racemic. Pure inversion would need SN2, which is blocked at a crowded tertiary carbon.

questions.q: In methanol, a polar protic solvent, which halide ion is the strongest nucleophile?
o: F⁻
F⁻ is strongly hydrogen-bonded by protic solvent, which blunts its nucleophilicity.
Cl⁻
Cl⁻ is more solvated and less polarizable than I⁻.
Br⁻
Br⁻ is good but still less nucleophilic than I⁻ in protic solvent.
I⁻
Correct: large, polarizable I⁻ is least tightly solvated by hydrogen bonds.
questions.x: In protic solvents such as methanol, small, charge-dense anions are held tightly by hydrogen bonds and must lose some of that solvent shell before they can attack. I⁻ is large and polarizable, so it is the least solvated and the best nucleophile, and the order is I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻. F⁻ is the most basic halide but the most strongly caged by solvent.

questions.q: In DMSO, a polar aprotic solvent, which halide ion is the strongest nucleophile?
o: I⁻
I⁻ wins in protic solvents, where small anions are caged by hydrogen bonds.
F⁻
Correct: unsolvated anions follow basicity, and F⁻ is the strongest base of the halides.
Cl⁻
Cl⁻ is a weaker base than F⁻, so it is less nucleophilic in aprotic solvent.
Br⁻
Without hydrogen bonding, nucleophilicity tracks basicity, and Br⁻ is a weak base.
questions.note: Trap: the halide nucleophilicity order reverses between protic and aprotic solvents.
questions.x: Polar aprotic solvents such as DMSO solvate cations well but leave anions free, because they have no O–H or N–H to donate hydrogen bonds. Freed from solvent effects, halide nucleophilicity follows basicity, F⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻, so F⁻ is the strongest. The protic-solvent order (I⁻ best) is the trap, since it comes from hydrogen-bond caging.

questions.q: Why is an alcohol converted to a tosylate before an SN2 reaction?
o: Tosylate forms a carbocation more easily
Tosylation improves leaving ability; it does not force an SN1 path.
Tosylation makes the carbon more nucleophilic
The substrate carbon must be electrophilic, not nucleophilic.
Tosylate is a weak, resonance-stabilized base and thus a good leaving group
Correct: hydroxide is a strong base and a poor leaving group.
Tosylation removes the stereocenter
The C–O bond is untouched, so configuration is kept.
questions.x: Hydroxide is a strong base, so it is a poor leaving group and alcohols do not undergo SN2 directly. Converting the OH to a tosylate (OTs) turns it into a group that leaves as a weak, resonance-stabilized sulfonate anion, conjugate base of a strong acid. Tosylation forms an O–S bond and does not break the C–O bond, so the carbon keeps its configuration.

questions.q: Which is the best leaving group?
o: I⁻
Correct: as the conjugate base of the strongest acid (HI), it is the weakest base.
OH⁻
Hydroxide is a strong base and leaves poorly.
F⁻
F⁻ is the most basic halide and a poor leaving group.
NH₂⁻
Amide ion is an extremely strong base and essentially never leaves.
questions.note: Good leaving groups are weak bases.
questions.x: Leaving-group ability tracks weak basicity: the more stable the departing anion, the more easily it leaves. I⁻ is the conjugate base of HI, a very strong acid, so it is a very weak base and leaves readily. F⁻, OH⁻ and NH₂⁻ are conjugate bases of weak acids (HF, H₂O, NH₃), so they are strong bases and poor leaving groups.

questions.q: Which atom of a carbonyl group is attacked by nucleophiles?
o: Neither; carbonyls are unreactive
Carbonyls are among the most reactive electrophiles in biochemistry.
The α-carbon
The α-carbon becomes nucleophilic when deprotonated; it is not the electrophile.
The oxygen, which carries a partial negative charge
The electron-rich oxygen is attacked by electrophiles such as H⁺.
The carbon, which carries a partial positive charge
Correct: oxygen's electronegativity polarizes C=O, leaving the carbon electrophilic.
questions.x: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon and pulls the C=O π electrons toward itself, leaving the carbonyl carbon with a partial positive charge. Nucleophiles therefore attack that carbon, and the π electrons shift onto oxygen. The oxygen reacts with electrophiles such as H⁺, and the α-carbon becomes nucleophilic only after it is deprotonated to an enolate.

questions.q: Which species is the strongest nucleophile?
o: CH₃O⁻
Correct: a localized negative charge on oxygen makes methoxide strongly nucleophilic.
CH₃OH
The neutral alcohol is much weaker than its conjugate base.
H₂O
Water is a neutral, weak nucleophile.
CH₃COO⁻
Acetate's charge is delocalized by resonance, lowering nucleophilicity.
questions.x: Within one attacking atom, negatively charged species are stronger nucleophiles than neutral ones, and a localized charge is stronger than one spread out by resonance. Methoxide carries its full negative charge on one oxygen. Acetate is also an anion, but resonance spreads its charge over two oxygens, which makes it a much weaker nucleophile.

questions.q: 2-Bromopropane is heated with potassium tert-butoxide. Which reaction predominates?
o: SN1 substitution
A strong base and a secondary substrate favor E2, not ionization.
SN2 substitution to an ether
Steric bulk prevents tert-butoxide from performing backside attack.
No reaction
A strong base readily removes a β-hydrogen.
E2 elimination to propene
Correct: tert-butoxide is a strong but bulky base that cannot easily reach carbon for substitution.
questions.x: Potassium tert-butoxide is a strong base, but its bulk keeps it from reaching a carbon for backside attack. It removes an exposed β-hydrogen instead, so a secondary halide such as 2-bromopropane gives propene by E2. A small strong base such as ethoxide would give more substitution, but steric hindrance blocks SN2 for tert-butoxide.

questions.q: Which species acts as a Lewis acid (electrophile)?
o: NH₃
Ammonia donates its lone pair; it is a Lewis base.
CN⁻
Cyanide is an electron-pair donor and nucleophile.
BF₃
Correct: boron has an empty p orbital and accepts an electron pair.
H₂O
Water usually acts as a Lewis base through its oxygen lone pairs.
questions.x: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair. Boron in BF₃ has only six valence electrons and an empty p orbital, so it readily accepts a lone pair, for example from NH₃, to form an adduct. NH₃, CN⁻ and H₂O all have lone pairs to donate, so they act as Lewis bases (nucleophiles), not acids.

questions.q: The concentration of nucleophile in an SN1 reaction is doubled. How does the rate change?
o: It halves
Adding nucleophile cannot slow the ionization step.
It does not change
Correct: rate = k[substrate]; the nucleophile enters after the rate-limiting step.
It quadruples
That would require second-order dependence on nucleophile.
It doubles
That would be true for SN2, which is first order in nucleophile.
questions.x: SN1 is two steps: slow ionization of the substrate to a carbocation, then fast capture by the nucleophile. Only species involved in or before the rate-limiting step appear in the rate law, so rate = k[substrate] and the rate is zero order in nucleophile. Doubling the nucleophile does not change the rate; it would double the rate only for SN2.

questions.q: In an SN2 reaction, both the substrate and nucleophile concentrations are doubled. By what factor does the rate change?
o: Accounts for only one reactant.
SN2 rate depends on both concentrations.
Treats the reaction as third order.
Correct: rate = k[substrate][Nu], so 2 × 2 = 4.
questions.x: SN2 is one step in which the nucleophile and substrate collide in the transition state, so rate = k[substrate][Nu], first order in each. Doubling both concentrations multiplies the rate by 2 × 2 = 4. Answering 2 treats the reaction as first order overall, as SN1 would be.

questions.q: Which compound reacts fastest with NaCN in acetone?
o: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane
Tertiary centers are too hindered for SN2.
2-Bromobutane
Secondary centers react more slowly by SN2.
1-Bromobutane
Correct: primary, unhindered carbon allows fast backside attack.
Bromobenzene
sp² aryl carbons do not undergo SN2 backside attack.
questions.x: Cyanide in acetone, a strong nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent, reacts by SN2, and SN2 rates fall sharply with steric crowding: methyl > primary > secondary, with tertiary not reacting at all. 1-Bromobutane is primary and unhindered, so it reacts fastest. Bromobenzene cannot react, because backside attack on an sp² ring carbon is impossible.

questions.q: Which alkyl bromide undergoes solvolysis in ethanol fastest?
o: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane
Correct: ionization gives a stable tertiary carbocation.
1-Bromopropane
Primary carbocations are very unstable.
2-Bromopropane
A secondary cation forms, but more slowly than a tertiary one.
Bromomethane
A methyl cation is far too unstable for SN1.
questions.x: Solvolysis in ethanol, a weak nucleophile in a protic solvent, follows SN1, whose rate is set by carbocation stability: tertiary > secondary >> primary > methyl. 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane ionizes to the tertiary tert-butyl cation, stabilized by hyperconjugation and induction, so it reacts fastest. Primary and methyl cations are too unstable to form.

questions.q: 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane is warmed in water. What is the major alcohol product?
o: 3-Methylbutan-2-ol
Ignores the hydride shift that forms the more stable tertiary carbocation.
2-Methylbutan-2-ol
Correct: the secondary cation undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to a tertiary cation before water attacks.
3-Methylbutan-1-ol
No step places OH on a terminal carbon.
2,2-Dimethylpropan-1-ol
A methyl shift here would give a less stable cation, and the skeleton would change.
questions.note: Carbocations rearrange toward greater substitution.
questions.x: Ionizing 2-bromo-3-methylbutane gives a secondary cation at C2. A hydride on the adjacent C3 shifts over, moving the positive charge to C3, which bears two methyls and an ethyl, so it is tertiary and more stable. Water then attacks C3, giving 2-methylbutan-2-ol. 3-Methylbutan-2-ol is the trap: it assumes the cation is captured before it rearranges.

questions.q: Why does switching the solvent from methanol to DMSO accelerate an SN2 reaction of cyanide with bromoethane?
o: DMSO is a better nucleophile than cyanide
The solvent is not the nucleophile in this reaction.
DMSO does not hydrogen-bond the anion, leaving it more reactive
Correct: polar aprotic solvents solvate cations but leave anions free.
DMSO stabilizes the carbocation intermediate
SN2 has no carbocation intermediate.
DMSO increases the leaving ability of bromide by protonating it
DMSO is aprotic and cannot protonate anything.
questions.x: Methanol hydrogen-bonds to cyanide, wrapping it in a solvent shell that must be stripped off before it can attack. DMSO is polar aprotic: it solvates the Na⁺ or K⁺ counterion but leaves the anion poorly solvated and much more reactive, which speeds SN2. Stabilizing a carbocation is irrelevant, since SN2 has no intermediate.

questions.q: A chemist triples [N₃⁻] in a reaction with 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, and the rate stays the same. What does this indicate?
o: That azide is too weak to react
Product still forms; the nucleophile just is not in the rate law.
An E2 mechanism
E2 rate depends on base concentration.
An SN1 mechanism with rate-limiting ionization
Correct: zero-order dependence on nucleophile points to a unimolecular rate-limiting step.
An SN2 mechanism with backside attack
SN2 rate would triple with tripled nucleophile.
questions.x: A rate law includes only the species that take part in or before the rate-limiting step. If tripling azide leaves the rate unchanged, the nucleophile is not involved until after that step, which fits SN1, where the slow step is ionization of the tertiary chloride. SN2 and E2 are both bimolecular, so tripling [N₃⁻] would triple their rates.

questions.q: Why do benzylic halides react readily by SN1 even when the carbon is primary?
o: The aromatic ring is a good leaving group
The halide leaves, not the ring.
Benzylic carbons are sterically unhindered
Low hindrance helps SN2, not ionization.
Benzylic C–X bonds are stronger
Stronger bonds would slow ionization.
The carbocation is stabilized by resonance with the ring
Correct: positive charge delocalizes into the aromatic π system.
questions.x: SN1 rates depend on how stable the carbocation is. A benzylic cation is next to an aromatic ring, so its empty p orbital overlaps the π system and the positive charge spreads by resonance onto the ortho and para carbons. This makes even a primary benzylic cation easy to form. Low steric hindrance speeds SN2, not ionization.

questions.q: 1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentyl bromide) reacts extremely slowly by SN2 even though it is primary. Why?
o: Bulky groups on the adjacent carbon block backside attack
Correct: the β tert-butyl group hinders the nucleophile's approach.
It has no hydrogens on the α-carbon
The α-carbon is CH₂; it does have hydrogens.
Its carbocation is too stable
Stability of a cation is irrelevant to SN2, and this cation is primary.
Bromide is a poor leaving group
Bromide is a good leaving group in other primary systems.
questions.x: SN2 needs the nucleophile to reach the back of the C–Br bond. In neopentyl bromide the reacting carbon is primary, but the carbon next to it carries three methyl groups, and they crowd the backside approach, so SN2 is extremely slow. SN1 is also poor here, because ionization would give a highly unstable primary carbocation.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the SN2 mechanism?
o: The nucleophile attacks from the same side as the leaving group
SN2 attack is from the back side, opposite the leaving group.
The rate depends only on substrate concentration
SN2 is second order overall.
Bond formation and bond breaking occur in a single concerted step
Correct: there is one transition state and no intermediate.
A carbocation intermediate forms first
That describes SN1.
questions.x: In SN2 the nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group, and the new bond forms as the old one breaks. There is a single transition state with five partial bonds to carbon and no intermediate, so the rate is first order in both substrate and nucleophile, and the center inverts. A carbocation intermediate belongs to SN1.

questions.q: S-Adenosylmethionine (SAM) transfers its methyl group to an amine nucleophile. Why is this methyl carbon a good SN2 electrophile?
o: Sulfur is more electronegative than oxygen
Sulfur is less electronegative than oxygen.
The methyl group is a strong nucleophile
The methyl carbon is the electrophile being attacked.
It forms a stable methyl carbocation
Methyl cations are extremely unstable; this transfer is SN2.
It is unhindered and bonded to a positively charged sulfonium leaving group
Correct: a neutral thioether departs easily from the cationic sulfur.
questions.x: In SAM the methyl group is attached to a positively charged sulfonium sulfur. When the nucleophile attacks the methyl carbon, the leaving group departs as a neutral thioether (S-adenosylhomocysteine), a very weak base and so an excellent leaving group. A methyl carbon is also completely unhindered, making it an ideal SN2 electrophile.

questions.q: A primary alcohol is treated with PCC in dichloromethane. What is the product?
o: An aldehyde
Correct: PCC is a mild, anhydrous oxidant that stops at the aldehyde.
An alkene
PCC oxidizes; it does not dehydrate.
A carboxylic acid
Overoxidation needs water and a strong oxidant such as chromic acid.
A ketone
Ketones come from secondary alcohols.
questions.x: Oxidizing a primary alcohol gives an aldehyde first, and the aldehyde goes on to a carboxylic acid only when water is present to form a gem-diol hydrate that can be oxidized again. PCC is used in dry dichloromethane, so no hydrate forms and the reaction stops at the aldehyde. Strong aqueous oxidants such as chromic acid carry it on to the acid.

questions.q: Butan-1-ol is treated with excess Na₂Cr₂O₇ in aqueous H₂SO₄. What is the main product?
o: Butane
Dichromate oxidizes; it does not reduce.
Butanoic acid
Correct: strong aqueous oxidants take primary alcohols past the aldehyde to the acid.
Butanal
The aldehyde is an intermediate that is further oxidized via its hydrate.
Butan-2-one
Oxidation does not move the functional group to C2.
questions.x: Excess dichromate in aqueous acid is a strong oxidant in water. It first turns a primary alcohol into the aldehyde, which then adds water to form a hydrate that is oxidized again to the carboxylic acid, so butan-1-ol becomes butanoic acid. Stopping at butanal requires an anhydrous mild oxidant such as PCC.

questions.q: 2-Methylpropan-2-ol is mixed with acidified dichromate. What is observed?
o: A carboxylic acid forms
Only primary alcohols give carboxylic acids.
No oxidation occurs
Correct: the carbinol carbon of a tertiary alcohol has no H to remove.
A ketone forms
Forming a ketone would require breaking a C–C bond.
An aldehyde forms
Aldehydes come from primary alcohols.
questions.x: Alcohol oxidation removes the H on the carbinol carbon (the carbon bearing OH) along with the O–H hydrogen to form C=O. Primary and secondary alcohols have that C–H, but a tertiary alcohol's carbinol carbon is bonded to three carbons and has none. Forming a carbonyl would require breaking a C–C bond, so dichromate leaves 2-methylpropan-2-ol unchanged.

questions.q: Ethyl benzoate is treated with LiAlH₄, followed by aqueous workup. What products form?
o: Benzaldehyde and ethanol
The aldehyde intermediate is reduced further by LiAlH₄.
No reaction
LiAlH₄ is strong enough to reduce esters, unlike NaBH₄.
Benzoic acid and ethanol
That is hydrolysis, not reduction.
Benzyl alcohol and ethanol
Correct: LiAlH₄ reduces esters to two alcohols, one from each half.
questions.x: LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the ester carbonyl, and the tetrahedral intermediate expels ethoxide to give benzaldehyde, which is more reactive than the ester and is reduced again at once. After workup the acyl half becomes benzyl alcohol and the alkoxy half becomes ethanol. The aldehyde cannot be isolated with LiAlH₄; NaBH₄ is too weak to reduce esters at all.

questions.q: What is the oxidation state of carbon in formaldehyde (H₂C=O)?
o: Correct: two C–H bonds give −2 and the C=O double bond gives +2.
Ignores the two C–H bonds, which each lower the oxidation state by 1.
That is carbon in CO₂.
That is carbon in methanol.
questions.x: To find carbon's oxidation state, count −1 for each bond to a less electronegative atom (H), +1 for each bond to a more electronegative atom (O, counted per bond), and 0 for bonds to carbon. In H₂C=O, the two C–H bonds give −2 and the C=O double bond gives +2, so the total is 0. Carbon runs from −4 in CH₄ to +4 in CO₂.

questions.q: When alcohol dehydrogenase converts ethanol to acetaldehyde, what happens to NAD⁺?
o: It accepts a phosphate group
NAD⁺ carries electrons, not phosphate.
It donates a hydride and is oxidized
NAD⁺ is already the oxidized form; NADH is the hydride donor.
It accepts a hydride and is reduced to NADH
Correct: the alcohol is oxidized as NAD⁺ takes H⁻.
It is unchanged and acts only as a spectator
NAD⁺ is a stoichiometric cosubstrate here.
questions.x: Oxidizing ethanol to acetaldehyde removes two hydrogens: a proton from O–H and a hydride from the carbinol carbon. NAD⁺, the oxidized carrier, accepts the hydride on its nicotinamide ring and becomes NADH, which is a reduction. The common error is to swap roles: NADH is the hydride donor, used in the reverse direction to reduce carbonyls.

questions.q: N,N-Dimethylbenzamide is treated with LiAlH₄, then water. What is the product?
o: Benzaldehyde
LiAlH₄ does not stop at the aldehyde stage with amides.
Benzyl alcohol and dimethylamine
Amide oxygen is lost; the C–N bond survives the reduction.
Benzoic acid
That is hydrolysis, which requires acid or base and water.
N,N-Dimethylbenzylamine
Correct: LiAlH₄ reduces the amide C=O fully to CH₂, giving an amine.
questions.x: Esters are reduced to alcohols because their alkoxide oxygen can leave, but in an amide, nitrogen is a much poorer leaving group. With LiAlH₄ the carbonyl oxygen, bound to aluminum, is expelled instead, giving an iminium ion that a second hydride reduces. The C=O becomes CH₂ and the C–N bond survives, so a tertiary amide gives a tertiary amine.

questions.q: Which transformation is an oxidation of the organic substrate?
o: Aldehyde → carboxylic acid
Correct: carbon gains a bond to oxygen.
Carboxylic acid → primary alcohol
Losing C–O bonds and gaining C–H bonds is a reduction.
Alkene → alkane
Adding H₂ is a reduction.
Ketone → secondary alcohol
Gaining a C–H bond is a reduction.
questions.x: In organic chemistry, oxidation means more bonds from carbon to oxygen (or other electronegative atoms) or fewer bonds to hydrogen. An aldehyde becomes a carboxylic acid by gaining a C–O bond, so carbon goes from +1 to +3. Adding H₂ to an alkene, or hydride to a ketone or acid, adds C–H bonds, which are reductions.

questions.q: Ethanol boils at 78 °C, while dimethyl ether (same formula, C₂H₆O) boils at −24 °C. What explains the difference?
o: Dimethyl ether has stronger London forces
Dispersion forces are similar for these isomers.
Dimethyl ether is more polar
The ether is less able to form intermolecular attractions.
Ethanol molecules hydrogen-bond to one another
Correct: the O–H group lets ethanol donate and accept hydrogen bonds.
Ethanol has a higher molar mass
They are isomers with identical molar mass.
questions.x: Ethanol and dimethyl ether have the same formula and mass, so their London forces are similar. Only ethanol has an O–H bond, so its molecules can donate and accept hydrogen bonds to one another, which takes extra energy to break during boiling. The ether oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond but has no O–H to donate, so the pure ether has no hydrogen bonding.

questions.q: Which alcohol is the most acidic?
o: Ethanol
Lacks electron-withdrawing groups to stabilize the conjugate base.
2,2,2-Trifluoroethanol
Correct: three electronegative F atoms inductively stabilize the alkoxide.
2-Methylpropan-2-ol
Its bulky alkoxide is poorly solvated, making it the least acidic here.
Methanol
More acidic than ethanol but far less than the fluorinated alcohol.
questions.x: An alcohol's acidity depends on how stable its alkoxide conjugate base is. Three fluorines pull electron density through the σ bonds (induction) and spread out the negative charge on oxygen, so CF₃CH₂OH (pKa ≈ 12.4) is far more acidic than ethanol (≈ 16). Alkyl groups do the opposite, and the bulky tert-butoxide is poorly solvated, so t-butanol is the weakest.

questions.q: Which alcohol is least soluble in water?
o: Butan-1-ol
A shorter chain than hexanol makes it more water-soluble.
Methanol
Methanol is fully miscible with water.
Hexan-1-ol
Correct: the long hydrocarbon chain outweighs the single polar OH group.
Ethanol
Ethanol is fully miscible with water.
questions.x: Water solubility reflects a balance between the polar OH, which hydrogen-bonds with water, and the nonpolar hydrocarbon chain, which does not. Methanol, ethanol and propanol are fully miscible, butanol is only moderately soluble, and solubility keeps falling as the chain grows. With six carbons and one OH, hexan-1-ol is the least soluble choice.

questions.q: 2-Methylpropan-2-ol reacts with concentrated HBr to give 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. Which sequence describes the mechanism?
o: Protonation of OH, loss of water to a carbocation, then bromide attack
Correct: SN1 at a tertiary center via a good water leaving group.
Direct backside attack of Br⁻ on the C–OH carbon
Tertiary centers cannot undergo SN2, and OH⁻ is a poor leaving group.
Bromide removes the O–H proton, then the oxygen leaves
Bromide is not basic enough, and O²⁻ cannot leave.
Radical abstraction of hydrogen by bromine
Ionic conditions with HBr do not follow a radical path.
questions.x: OH⁻ is a poor leaving group, so strong acid first protonates the alcohol to an oxonium ion, which can leave as neutral water. A tertiary substrate then ionizes to a stable tert-butyl carbocation, and bromide captures it, which is an SN1 path. Backside SN2 is blocked by the three methyl groups, so direct displacement is not the mechanism.

questions.q: (R)-Butan-2-ol is converted to its tosylate with TsCl and pyridine, then treated with NaBr in DMSO. What is the final product?
o: (S)-Butan-2-ol
The tosylate is displaced by bromide, not hydroxide.
(S)-2-Bromobutane
Correct: tosylation retains configuration (C–O untouched); SN2 then inverts.
Racemic 2-bromobutane
Neither step passes through a carbocation in a polar aprotic solvent.
(R)-2-Bromobutane
Assumes retention in both steps; the SN2 step inverts.
questions.note: Tosylation keeps configuration; the displacement is where inversion happens.
questions.x: TsCl reacts at the alcohol oxygen, forming an O–S bond without breaking the C–O bond, so the tosylate keeps the R configuration. Bromide in polar aprotic DMSO then performs SN2 with backside attack, inverting the carbon. Br has top priority and OTs did too, so the inversion also flips the label to S. Racemization would need a carbocation, which neither step forms.

questions.q: 2-Methylbutan-2-ol is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄. What is the major organic product?
o: 2-Methylbutane
No reducing agent is present to give an alkane.
3-Methylbutan-2-ol
Acid and heat eliminate water; they do not move the OH.
2-Methylbut-1-ene
This less substituted alkene is the minor product.
2-Methylbut-2-ene
Correct: E1 dehydration favors the more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene.
questions.x: Hot concentrated H₂SO₄ protonates the tertiary OH, which leaves as water to give a tertiary carbocation (E1). A β-hydrogen is then lost from whichever neighbor gives the more stable alkene, so the trisubstituted 2-methylbut-2-ene is the major (Zaitsev) product. 2-Methylbut-1-ene, a less stable disubstituted alkene, is the minor one.

questions.q: Why are aldehydes generally more reactive than ketones toward nucleophilic addition?
o: Aldehydes have a more electronegative oxygen
The oxygen is the same element in both.
Ketones lack a carbonyl π bond
Ketones have the same C=O double bond.
Aldehydes form more stable tetrahedral intermediates only because of hydrogen bonding
Steric and electronic effects at carbon are the main reasons.
Less steric hindrance and less electron donation to the carbonyl carbon
Correct: one alkyl group instead of two leaves the carbon more open and more positive.
questions.x: Two factors favor aldehydes. Sterically, an aldehyde has one alkyl group and one small H, so the nucleophile can approach more easily and the crowded tetrahedral product is less strained. Electronically, each alkyl group donates electron density and reduces the carbonyl carbon's partial positive charge, so a ketone, with two, is the weaker electrophile.

questions.q: Which carbonyl compound has the largest equilibrium constant for hydrate formation in water?
o: Formaldehyde
Correct: no alkyl groups to donate electrons or crowd the tetrahedral hydrate.
Acetaldehyde
Its methyl group donates electrons and adds some steric strain.
Acetone
Two alkyl groups stabilize the carbonyl and disfavor the hydrate.
Pentan-3-one
Two ethyl groups make hydration even less favorable.
questions.x: Hydrate formation turns a planar sp² carbonyl into a tetrahedral gem-diol, which is favored when the carbonyl carbon is strongly electrophilic and has room for four groups. Formaldehyde has no alkyl groups to donate electrons or add steric strain, so it is almost entirely hydrated in water. Each added alkyl group shifts the equilibrium back toward the carbonyl.

questions.q: Which conditions convert an aldehyde into an acetal most efficiently?
o: NaBH₄ in ethanol
That reduces the aldehyde to an alcohol.
Excess alcohol, catalytic acid, and removal of water
Correct: acid activates the carbonyl and removing water drives the equilibrium.
One equivalent of alcohol in aqueous base
Base cannot make the hemiacetal OH leave as water.
Excess water and catalytic acid
Water drives the reverse reaction, hydrolyzing acetals.
questions.x: Acetal formation is a reversible, acid-catalyzed equilibrium: the aldehyde adds one alcohol to form a hemiacetal, then loses water and adds a second alcohol. Acid activates the carbonyl and turns the hemiacetal OH into water, a good leaving group. Using excess alcohol and removing water drives the equilibrium forward by Le Chatelier's principle, while excess water and acid reverse it.

questions.q: Imine formation from a ketone and a primary amine is slow at pH 1. Why?
o: Water cannot leave at low pH
Low pH actually helps the OH leave as water.
Acid hydrolyzes the amine
Amines are not hydrolyzed by acid; they are protonated.
The amine is almost fully protonated and no longer nucleophilic
Correct: R–NH₃⁺ has no lone pair to attack the carbonyl.
The ketone is converted to an enol and cannot react
Enol formation does not block imine formation.
questions.note: Imine formation peaks near pH 4–5: enough acid to protonate OH, not so much that the amine is tied up.
questions.x: Imine formation needs a free amine lone pair to attack the carbonyl, and also acid to protonate the carbinolamine OH so it leaves as water. At pH 1 nearly all of the amine is protonated to R–NH₃⁺, so it has no lone pair and the first step stalls. The rate is highest near pH 4–5, where both needs are met; strong acid does not block the water-loss step.

questions.q: Cyclohexanone reacts with a secondary amine such as pyrrolidine under mild acid. What forms?
o: An imine
Imines need a primary amine so nitrogen can lose its second H.
An amide
Amides form from carboxylic acid derivatives, not ketones.
An enamine
Correct: with no N–H left after addition, a proton is lost from the α-carbon instead.
A hemiacetal
Hemiacetals form from alcohols, not amines.
questions.x: A secondary amine adds to the ketone to form a carbinolamine, which loses water to give an iminium ion. A primary amine would then lose an N–H proton to form a neutral imine, but a secondary amine's nitrogen has no H left. A proton is lost from the α-carbon instead, forming a C=C–N unit called an enamine.

questions.q: In the visual pigment rhodopsin, retinal is covalently attached to a lysine side chain. What type of linkage is this?
o: A protonated Schiff base (imine)
Correct: the lysine ε-amine condenses with retinal's aldehyde.
A disulfide bond
Disulfides link two cysteine thiols.
An amide bond
Amides come from carboxylic acids; retinal has an aldehyde.
A glycosidic bond
Glycosidic bonds involve sugar anomeric carbons.
questions.x: In rhodopsin, the aldehyde of 11-cis-retinal condenses with the ε-amino group of a lysine, losing water to form a C=N bond, an imine (Schiff base) that is protonated in the protein. An amide would require a carboxylic acid derivative, not an aldehyde. The same imine chemistry links pyridoxal phosphate to enzymes and appears in aldolase intermediates.

questions.q: Why are the α-hydrogens of a ketone much more acidic (pKa ≈ 20) than ordinary alkane hydrogens?
o: α-C–H bonds are unusually long
Acidity comes from conjugate base stability, not bond length.
The carbonyl oxygen donates electrons to the α-carbon
Oxygen withdraws electron density; it does not donate here.
The α-carbon is sp hybridized
The α-carbon is sp³ before deprotonation.
The resulting enolate is resonance-stabilized with charge on oxygen
Correct: delocalization onto the electronegative oxygen stabilizes the base.
questions.x: An acid's strength reflects the stability of its conjugate base. Removing an α-hydrogen gives an enolate in which the negative charge is shared by resonance between the α-carbon and the electronegative carbonyl oxygen. An ordinary alkane carbanion has no such delocalization, so alkane C–H bonds have pKa values near 50, while ketone α-H values are near 20.

questions.q: The keto and enol forms of acetone are best described as:
o: Resonance structures
Resonance structures differ only in electron placement, not atom positions.
Tautomers, which are constitutional isomers
Correct: they differ in the position of a proton and a double bond.
Enantiomers
Neither form is chiral.
Conformers
Interconversion requires moving a proton, not just rotating a bond.
questions.note: Trap: if an atom moves, it is not resonance.
questions.x: Tautomers are constitutional isomers that interconvert rapidly by moving a hydrogen and shifting a double bond, as in the keto (C=O with α-C–H) and enol (C=C–OH) forms. Because an atom actually moves, they are distinct compounds in equilibrium, not resonance structures. Resonance structures differ only in where electrons are drawn, and all nuclei stay in place.

questions.q: Which hydrogens in pentane-2,4-dione (CH₃COCH₂COCH₃) are the most acidic?
o: All hydrogens are equally acidic
Position relative to the carbonyls makes a large difference.
None; diketones are not acidic
β-Diketones are unusually acidic carbon acids.
The terminal CH₃ hydrogens
These are next to only one carbonyl (pKa ≈ 20).
The CH₂ hydrogens between the two carbonyls
Correct: the carbanion is delocalized over both carbonyls (pKa ≈ 9).
questions.x: The CH₂ between the two carbonyls of a β-diketone is unusually acidic: losing its proton gives a carbanion whose negative charge spreads by resonance onto both oxygens. This extra delocalization lowers the pKa to about 9, compared with about 20 for the terminal CH₃ groups, which are next to only one carbonyl. Acidity depends on position.

questions.q: Two molecules of acetaldehyde react in cold dilute NaOH. What is the aldol addition product?
o: 3-Hydroxybutanal
Correct: the enolate of one adds to the carbonyl of the other, giving a β-hydroxy aldehyde.
Ethyl acetate
Ester formation is not an aldol process.
But-2-enal
That is the dehydrated condensation product formed on heating.
Butane-1,3-diol
No reducing agent is present to reduce the aldehyde.
questions.x: In base, one acetaldehyde loses an α-hydrogen to form an enolate, which adds as a nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon of a second acetaldehyde. Protonating the alkoxide gives a β-hydroxy aldehyde, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO, which is 3-hydroxybutanal. In cold dilute base the reaction stops at this addition product; heating dehydrates it to but-2-enal.

questions.q: The aldol product 3-hydroxybutanal is heated with base. What forms?
o: Butan-1-ol
No reduction occurs.
But-2-enal, an α,β-unsaturated aldehyde
Correct: dehydration gives a C=C conjugated with the C=O.
Butanoic acid
Heating with base does not oxidize the aldehyde.
Two molecules of acetaldehyde only
Retro-aldol can occur, but dehydration to the conjugated product dominates on heating.
questions.x: On heating in base, the β-hydroxy aldehyde loses water. The α-hydrogen is removed to form an enolate, which then expels hydroxide from the β-carbon (an E1cB elimination). The new C=C is conjugated with the C=O, and that conjugation stabilizes the product enough to drive the reaction, giving the α,β-unsaturated aldehyde CH₃CH=CHCHO, but-2-enal.

questions.q: In a crossed aldol reaction between benzaldehyde and acetone in base, why are few side products formed?
o: Base prevents acetone from self-condensing entirely
Self-condensation is suppressed by the more reactive aldehyde acceptor, not by the base.
Acetone has no α-hydrogens
Acetone has six α-hydrogens and serves as the enolate donor.
Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogens, so it acts only as the electrophile
Correct: only acetone forms an enolate, and benzaldehyde is the better acceptor.
Benzaldehyde is not electrophilic
Aldehydes are good electrophiles; it is the acceptor.
questions.x: A crossed aldol is clean when only one partner can form an enolate. Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogens, so it cannot act as the nucleophile and serves only as an acceptor, and as an aldehyde it is a better electrophile than acetone. Acetone forms the enolate and adds mostly to benzaldehyde rather than to itself, which keeps mixed and self-condensation products low.

questions.q: In glycolysis, aldolase splits fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. Chemically, this step is a:
o: Nucleophilic acyl substitution
No acyl derivative or leaving group is involved.
Hydrolysis of an ester
No ester bond is broken.
Oxidation by NAD⁺
No electrons are transferred in this step.
Retro-aldol reaction
Correct: a β-hydroxy carbonyl is cleaved into two carbonyl compounds.
questions.x: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate has a ketone at C2 and an OH at C4, which makes it a β-hydroxy carbonyl, the same pattern as an aldol product. Aldolase breaks the C3–C4 bond, the reverse of aldol addition, releasing two three-carbon carbonyl compounds, DHAP and G3P. No electrons go to NAD⁺ and no ester is hydrolyzed, so it is neither an oxidation nor a hydrolysis.

questions.q: Acetone is treated with CH₃MgBr, followed by aqueous acid workup. What is the product?
o: Propan-2-ol
That requires hydride addition, not a methyl group.
2-Methylpropan-2-ol
Correct: methyl adds to the ketone carbon, giving a tertiary alcohol.
2-Methylpropan-1-ol
The new OH stays on the former carbonyl carbon, which is tertiary.
Butan-2-one
Grignard addition gives an alcohol, not a new ketone.
questions.x: A Grignard reagent acts as a carbanion nucleophile: the methyl group of CH₃MgBr adds to the carbonyl carbon of acetone and forms a new C–C bond. Protonating the resulting alkoxide in workup gives (CH₃)₃COH, 2-methylpropan-2-ol. In general, a ketone plus a Grignard gives a tertiary alcohol, and propan-2-ol would need a hydride, not a carbon nucleophile.

questions.q: Why must Grignard reactions be performed in dry ether rather than in water or ethanol?
o: The Grignard reagent is a strong base and is protonated by protic solvents
Correct: R–MgX + H₂O gives R–H, destroying the reagent.
Water oxidizes the magnesium to Mg²⁺
Magnesium is already Mg²⁺-like in the reagent; protonation is the problem.
Grignard reagents are insoluble in all polar solvents
Ethers are polar and dissolve them well.
Ether is a better nucleophile than water
Ether stabilizes the reagent; it is not the nucleophile.
questions.x: The C–Mg bond is strongly polarized, so the carbon in a Grignard reagent behaves like a carbanion, which is an extremely strong base (an alkane conjugate acid, pKa ≈ 50). Any O–H or N–H proton, as in water or ethanol, protonates it at once to give R–H, destroying the reagent. Dry ethers are aprotic and stabilize magnesium by coordinating it.

questions.q: An aldehyde reacts with HCN in the presence of a little cyanide. What is the product?
o: An acetal
Acetals require alcohols.
An imine
Imines require amines.
A cyanohydrin
Correct: CN⁻ adds to the carbonyl carbon and the alkoxide is protonated.
A nitrile with loss of oxygen
The oxygen remains as an OH group.
questions.x: Cyanide is a good carbon nucleophile. It adds to the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide that HCN then protonates, giving a cyanohydrin, R–CH(OH)–CN, and regenerating CN⁻. A trace of cyanide is needed because HCN itself is a weak acid and a poor nucleophile. The carbonyl oxygen becomes an OH and is not lost.

questions.q: Which compound gives a positive Tollens' (silver mirror) test?
o: Propanal
Correct: aldehydes are oxidized to carboxylates as Ag⁺ is reduced to Ag.
Propanone
Ketones resist mild oxidation.
Propanoic acid
Carboxylic acids are already fully oxidized for this test.
Propan-2-ol
Tollens' reagent is too mild to oxidize this alcohol.
questions.x: Tollens' reagent, Ag(NH₃)₂⁺, is a mild oxidant that oxidizes aldehydes to carboxylates while Ag⁺ is reduced to metallic silver, which coats the glass as a mirror. Aldehydes react because they have an H on the carbonyl carbon, but ketones lack it and resist such mild oxidation. Acids are already highly oxidized, and Tollens' cannot oxidize secondary alcohols.

questions.q: Butan-2-one is reduced with NaBH₄ in methanol. What is the stereochemical outcome?
o: Pure (R)-butan-2-ol
No chiral influence favors one face.
Pure (S)-butan-2-ol
Both faces are attacked equally without a chiral catalyst.
Meso butan-2-ol
A molecule with one stereocenter cannot be meso.
A racemic mixture of butan-2-ol
Correct: hydride attacks either face of the planar carbonyl equally.
questions.x: The carbonyl carbon of butan-2-one is trigonal planar, and its two faces are mirror images. An achiral reagent such as NaBH₄ in an achiral solvent attacks both faces at the same rate, so equal amounts of (R)- and (S)-butan-2-ol form, a racemic mixture. Getting one enantiomer requires a chiral reagent or catalyst, as enzymes provide.

questions.q: What is the hybridization and approximate bond angle of a carbonyl carbon?
o: sp², about 90°
Trigonal planar angles are near 120°, not 90°.
sp², about 120°
Correct: trigonal planar geometry around the carbonyl carbon.
sp³, about 109.5°
That describes a tetrahedral carbon, such as in the addition product.
That describes nitriles or alkynes.
questions.x: The carbonyl carbon forms three σ bonds, using three sp² hybrid orbitals, and one π bond, using its unhybridized p orbital. Three electron domains arranged in a plane give trigonal planar geometry with angles near 120°. Nucleophilic addition converts this carbon to sp³ and tetrahedral, about 109.5°, which is why crowding matters in addition reactions.

questions.q: In an α,β-unsaturated ketone, which carbon other than the carbonyl carbon is electrophilic?
o: The α-carbon
Resonance puts positive character on alternating carbons, skipping α.
The carbonyl oxygen
Oxygen is the electron-rich end of the system.
The β-carbon
Correct: resonance places a partial positive charge on the β-carbon (conjugate addition site).
The γ-carbon only
The γ-carbon is outside the conjugated system.
questions.note: Michael acceptors react at the β-carbon.
questions.x: In an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl, the C=C is conjugated with the C=O, so resonance can push π electrons toward oxygen and leave a positive charge on the β-carbon. Nucleophiles can attack there, called conjugate or 1,4 addition (as in the Michael reaction), as well as at the carbonyl carbon. The α-carbon does not carry positive character in these resonance forms.

questions.q: Carboxylic acids boil at higher temperatures than alcohols of similar molar mass mainly because they:
o: Are ionic in the liquid phase
Neat carboxylic acids are mostly un-ionized.
Have no dipole moment
Carboxylic acids are polar.
Have weaker London forces
Weaker attractions would lower the boiling point.
Form hydrogen-bonded dimers
Correct: two hydrogen bonds link pairs of acid molecules.
questions.x: A carboxylic acid group has both an O–H donor and a C=O acceptor, so two molecules can join through two hydrogen bonds into a cyclic dimer. The dimer behaves as a much larger, tightly held unit, so more energy is needed to boil it. An alcohol forms only single hydrogen bonds, so it boils lower at similar molar mass.

questions.q: Which is the strongest acid?
o: Chloroacetic acid
One chlorine helps, but less than two.
Dichloroacetic acid
Correct: two α-chlorines inductively stabilize the carboxylate most.
Propanoic acid
The ethyl group is slightly electron-donating, making it the weakest.
Acetic acid
No electron-withdrawing substituent.
questions.x: Electronegative substituents near the carboxyl group pull electron density away by induction, stabilizing the carboxylate and strengthening the acid. The effect adds up with each substituent: acetic acid has pKa ≈ 4.8, chloroacetic ≈ 2.9 and dichloroacetic ≈ 1.3. Alkyl groups donate weakly, so propanoic acid is slightly weaker than acetic acid.

questions.q: How does the acidity of 2-chlorobutanoic acid compare with that of 4-chlorobutanoic acid?
o: 2-Chlorobutanoic acid is more acidic
Correct: inductive withdrawal weakens rapidly with distance from the carboxyl.
Neither is more acidic than butanoic acid
Chlorine at either position increases acidity.
4-Chlorobutanoic acid is more acidic
Farther substituents have a weaker inductive effect.
They are equally acidic
Same atoms, but the distance to the COOH differs.
questions.x: Inductive effects travel through σ bonds and weaken quickly with each intervening carbon. In 2-chlorobutanoic acid, chlorine sits on the α-carbon next to the carboxyl group and stabilizes the carboxylate strongly. In 4-chlorobutanoic acid it is three carbons away, so it raises acidity only slightly above butanoic acid. Same atoms, different distance, different pKa.

questions.q: Acetic acid has pKa 4.8. In a solution at pH 6.8, what is the ratio of acetate to acetic acid?
o: Inverts the ratio; above the pKa, the base form dominates.
That holds only when pH equals pKa.
Correct: pH − pKa = 2, so [A⁻]/[HA] = 10² = 100.
Uses the pH difference directly instead of as an exponent.
questions.x: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), rearranges to [A⁻]/[HA] = 10^(pH − pKa). Here pH − pKa = 6.8 − 4.8 = 2, so the ratio is 10² = 100 : 1 acetate to acid. When pH is above pKa the deprotonated form dominates, and each pH unit changes the ratio tenfold, not by a factor of the pH difference.

questions.q: Why are carboxylic acids (pKa ≈ 5) far more acidic than alcohols (pKa ≈ 16)?
o: The O–H bond in acids is much longer
Acidity comes mainly from conjugate base stability.
The carboxylate charge is delocalized over two oxygens by resonance
Correct: the stabilized conjugate base makes ionization favorable.
Alkoxides are stabilized by resonance
Alkoxide charge is localized on one oxygen.
Carboxylic acids contain more hydrogens
Number of hydrogens does not set acidity.
questions.x: Acidity is set mainly by the stability of the conjugate base. In a carboxylate, the negative charge is delocalized by resonance equally over two oxygens, which greatly stabilizes it. An alkoxide's charge sits on a single oxygen with no resonance. That difference of about 11 pKa units means carboxylic acids are roughly 10¹¹ times more acidic.

questions.q: Which compound is most reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?
o: Acetyl chloride
Correct: Cl⁻ is an excellent leaving group and gives little resonance donation.
Acetamide
Amides are the least reactive of these derivatives.
Ethyl acetate
Alkoxide is a poor leaving group and the ester is resonance-stabilized.
Acetic anhydride
Reactive, but carboxylate is a poorer leaving group than chloride.
questions.note: Reactivity: acyl halide > anhydride > thioester > ester > amide > carboxylate.
questions.x: Reactivity toward nucleophilic acyl substitution depends on how electrophilic the carbonyl is and how easily the leaving group departs. Chlorine donates little electron density by resonance, because its 3p orbital overlaps poorly with carbon's 2p, and Cl⁻ is a very weak base and an excellent leaving group. Anhydrides come next, since carboxylate is a weaker leaving group than chloride.

questions.q: Why are amides the least reactive carboxylic acid derivatives?
o: Amides have no carbonyl group
Amides contain a C=O group.
Amides are too sterically hindered
Even simple formamide is unreactive; the reason is electronic.
Nitrogen donates its lone pair into the carbonyl, and the amide ion is a poor leaving group
Correct: strong resonance lowers carbonyl electrophilicity.
Nitrogen is more electronegative than oxygen
Nitrogen is less electronegative, which is why it donates well.
questions.x: In an amide, nitrogen's lone pair is strongly delocalized into the C=O. This resonance gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character and makes the carbonyl carbon much less electrophilic.
