Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so it donates better than the OR of an ester, and the amide ion (NH₂⁻) is a strong base and so a very poor leaving group.

questions.q: Acetyl-CoA is a thioester. Why are thioesters more reactive acyl donors than oxygen esters?
o: Sulfur is more electronegative than oxygen
Sulfur is less electronegative than oxygen.
Thioesters have two carbonyl groups
A thioester has one carbonyl.
The C–S bond is stronger than the C–O bond
A stronger bond would make the thioester less reactive.
Poor C–S orbital overlap reduces resonance donation, and thiolate is a better leaving group
Correct: both effects raise acyl transfer reactivity.
questions.x: Thioesters are activated acyl donors for two reasons. Sulfur's large 3p orbitals overlap poorly with carbon's 2p orbital, so the thioester gets little resonance donation and its carbonyl stays electrophilic. Thiolate is also a weaker base than alkoxide and leaves more easily. Both effects make acetyl-CoA a high-energy acyl donor, about as reactive as an anhydride.

questions.q: What intermediate forms during nucleophilic acyl substitution of an ester?
o: A free carbon radical
This is a polar, two-electron mechanism.
A pentacoordinate SN2 transition state at the carbonyl
Acyl substitution is addition–elimination, not SN2.
A tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate
Correct: addition to C=O gives a tetrahedral species before the leaving group is expelled.
A planar acylium ion formed first
Esters react by addition then elimination, not ionization.
questions.x: Nucleophilic acyl substitution goes by addition then elimination. The nucleophile adds to the sp² carbonyl carbon, giving a tetrahedral intermediate with a negative charge on oxygen. The C=O then re-forms and expels the leaving group, here the alkoxide. There is no single-step SN2 displacement at the carbonyl and no carbocation or radical intermediate.

questions.q: Acetic acid is esterified with ¹⁸O-labeled ethanol under acid catalysis. Where does the ¹⁸O label end up?
o: In the ester's carbonyl oxygen
The carbonyl oxygen comes from the acid.
Distributed equally among all oxygens
The alcohol oxygen's C–O bond is never broken.
In the water by-product
Water comes from the acid's OH, not the alcohol's oxygen.
In the ester's alkoxy (C–O–CH₂CH₃) oxygen
Correct: the alcohol oxygen attacks the carbonyl and is retained; the acid's OH leaves as water.
questions.note: Fischer esterification: the acid loses OH, the alcohol loses only H.
questions.x: In Fischer esterification the alcohol is the nucleophile: its oxygen attacks the protonated carbonyl carbon and stays bonded to its ethyl group throughout. The acid's own OH is protonated and leaves as water. The labeled ¹⁸O therefore ends up as the ester's alkoxy oxygen, and the water by-product is unlabeled. This labeling result showed that the acid loses OH and the alcohol loses only H.

questions.q: Why is base-promoted hydrolysis of an ester (saponification) effectively irreversible?
o: Esters cannot be re-formed from acids under any conditions
Fischer esterification re-forms esters under acid.
The carboxylic acid product is deprotonated to an unreactive carboxylate
Correct: carboxylate is resonance-stabilized and resists alkoxide attack.
The alcohol product evaporates
Volatility is not the reason.
Hydroxide is a catalyst that is regenerated
Hydroxide is consumed stoichiometrically.
questions.x: Hydroxide adds to the ester and expels alkoxide, which first gives a carboxylic acid. In base that acid is deprotonated at once to a carboxylate, a resonance-stabilized anion with no electrophilic carbonyl left, so alkoxide cannot attack it to reverse the reaction. This final acid–base step pulls the equilibrium forward and consumes a full equivalent of hydroxide.

questions.q: Aspirin is made by treating salicylic acid with acetic anhydride. Which group of salicylic acid is acylated?
o: The phenolic OH, forming an ester
Correct: the phenol oxygen attacks the anhydride and becomes an acetate ester.
The carboxylic acid OH, forming an anhydride
The carboxyl group remains free in aspirin.
The carboxyl carbon, forming an amide
No nitrogen is present.
The aromatic ring carbon, forming a ketone
No Friedel–Crafts catalyst is present.
questions.x: Acetic anhydride is an acylating agent: a nucleophilic oxygen attacks one of its carbonyls, and acetate leaves. In salicylic acid, the phenolic OH is acetylated to form the ester group of aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid), and the carboxylic acid stays free. Ring acylation would need Friedel–Crafts conditions with a Lewis acid, and forming an amide would need a nitrogen nucleophile.

questions.q: Two equivalents of methylamine are needed to convert one equivalent of acetyl chloride fully into N-methylacetamide. Why?
o: The amide must be protonated to form
Amide formation releases, not consumes, a proton.
The first equivalent reduces the acid chloride
Amines do not act as reducing agents here.
Two amines add to each carbonyl
Only one amine becomes part of the amide.
The second equivalent neutralizes the HCl by-product
Correct: otherwise HCl protonates the amine, removing it as a nucleophile.
questions.x: Methylamine attacks acetyl chloride and expels chloride, forming N-methylacetamide and releasing one equivalent of HCl. That HCl reacts at once with any remaining amine to form CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻, and the protonated amine has no lone pair, so it cannot react. A second equivalent of amine, or another base such as pyridine, is therefore needed to take up the acid.

questions.q: Peptide bond hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable, yet peptides persist for years in neutral water. Why?
o: Amide resonance gives a high activation energy
Correct: the reaction is favorable but kinetically very slow without catalysts.
Water cannot act as a nucleophile
Water can add to carbonyls; it is just slow with amides.
Peptide bonds are ionic
Peptide bonds are covalent amide linkages.
Hydrolysis is endergonic at pH 7
Hydrolysis has a negative ΔG; the barrier is the issue.
questions.note: Thermodynamics says if; kinetics says how fast.
questions.x: Thermodynamics and kinetics answer different questions. Peptide hydrolysis has a negative ΔG, but amide resonance stabilizes the C–N bond and makes the carbonyl weakly electrophilic, so the activation energy is very high and uncatalyzed hydrolysis takes years. Proteases speed it by lowering that barrier, but they do not change ΔG.

questions.q: Which acid loses CO₂ most readily on gentle heating?
o: Butanoic acid
Simple acids lack the β-carbonyl needed for easy decarboxylation.
3-Oxobutanoic acid
Correct: β-keto acids decarboxylate through a cyclic six-membered transition state.
Benzoic acid
Aromatic acids are resistant to thermal decarboxylation.
4-Oxopentanoic acid
A γ-keto acid cannot form the cyclic transition state.
questions.x: β-Keto acids decarboxylate easily because the ketone oxygen can accept the carboxyl hydrogen through a cyclic six-membered transition state as CO₂ leaves. This gives an enol that tautomerizes to a ketone, so 3-oxobutanoic acid gives acetone. A simple acid or a γ-keto acid has no carbonyl in the right position to form that ring, so it needs much harsher conditions.

questions.q: Which reagent reduces a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol?
o: H₂O and H⁺
These conditions do not supply hydride.
PCC
PCC is an oxidant.
LiAlH₄
Correct: a strong hydride donor reduces acids fully to primary alcohols.
NaBH₄
NaBH₄ is too mild to reduce carboxylic acids.
questions.x: Reducing a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol requires a strong hydride donor, because the acid is first deprotonated to a carboxylate, which is a poor electrophile. LiAlH₄ is reactive enough to overcome this and gives RCH₂OH after workup. NaBH₄ is a milder hydride that reduces aldehydes and ketones but not acids or esters, so it is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: The β-lactam ring of penicillin is a:
o: Cyclic amide
Correct: lactams are cyclic amides.
Cyclic ester
Cyclic esters are lactones.
Cyclic anhydride
Anhydrides have two acyl groups on one oxygen.
Cyclic ether
Ethers lack a carbonyl group.
questions.x: Ring forms of carboxylic acid derivatives have their own names: a cyclic amide is a lactam and a cyclic ester is a lactone. The Greek letter gives the ring size by naming which carbon the nitrogen is bonded to, so in a β-lactam the N is on the β-carbon, which closes a four-membered ring. Penicillin's β-lactam therefore contains an N–C=O group in the ring, not an ester oxygen.

questions.q: Why does the β-lactam of penicillin acylate the active-site serine of bacterial transpeptidase much faster than a normal amide would?
o: The lactam nitrogen is positively charged
The nitrogen is neutral.
Serine is a stronger nucleophile than water only in bacteria
The key factor is the strained acyl donor.
Ring strain and reduced amide resonance make its carbonyl unusually electrophilic
Correct: the four-membered ring prevents planar N–C=O overlap.
β-Lactams are esters, not amides
β-Lactams are cyclic amides.
questions.x: A normal amide is stable because the nitrogen lone pair overlaps the C=O in a planar arrangement. In the four-membered β-lactam ring, fused to a second ring in penicillin, nitrogen is pyramidalized, which weakens that resonance, and ring strain is released when the ring opens. The carbonyl therefore behaves more like a reactive ketone, and the active-site serine attacks it quickly.

questions.q: Methyl acetate is treated with excess ethanol and catalytic sodium ethoxide. What is the main product?
o: Diethyl ether
Ethoxide does not convert esters into ethers.
Ethyl acetate and methanol
Correct: transesterification swaps the alkoxy group, driven by excess ethanol.
Acetic acid and methanol
Without water, hydrolysis does not occur.
Acetaldehyde
No reducing agent is present.
questions.x: Under alkoxide catalysis, an ester exchanges its OR group with the solvent alcohol, which is called transesterification. Ethoxide adds to the carbonyl and methoxide leaves from the tetrahedral intermediate, giving ethyl acetate and methanol. The reaction is an equilibrium, and the large excess of ethanol drives it forward. With no water present, hydrolysis to acetic acid cannot occur.

questions.q: Which compound is the weakest base?
o: Ammonia
More basic than aniline because its lone pair is localized.
Dimethylamine
Two donating alkyl groups make it one of the stronger bases here.
Methylamine
An alkyl group donates electron density, making it more basic than ammonia.
Aniline
Correct: the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic ring.
questions.x: An amine's basicity depends on how available its nitrogen lone pair is. Alkyl groups donate electron density, so alkylamines are slightly more basic than ammonia. In aniline, the lone pair is delocalized into the benzene ring by resonance, which makes it much less available for protonation: anilinium has a pKa near 4.6, while methylammonium is near 10.6.

questions.q: Which nitrogen atom is the least basic?
o: The nitrogen of triethylamine
A localized lone pair on an alkylamine is strongly basic.
The nitrogen of ethylamine
A typical alkylamine with pKa of its conjugate acid near 10.7.
The nitrogen of acetamide
Correct: its lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl, so amides are essentially neutral.
The nitrogen of pyridine
Pyridine's sp² lone pair is available, giving modest basicity.
questions.x: A nitrogen is basic only if its lone pair is free to bind a proton. In acetamide the lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl by resonance, so amides are essentially nonbasic (protonated amides have a pKa near 0, and they protonate on oxygen). Pyridine's sp² lone pair is localized but held closer to the nucleus, so it is weakly basic (pKa ≈ 5), still more basic than an amide.

questions.q: How is (CH₃)₃C–NH₂ (tert-butylamine) classified?
o: Tertiary amine
The tertiary label describes the carbon, not the nitrogen.
Secondary amine
A secondary amine has two carbons on nitrogen.
Quaternary ammonium ion
Quaternary nitrogen bears four carbons and a positive charge.
Primary amine
Correct: amines are classified by the number of carbons bonded to nitrogen, which is one.
questions.note: Trap: amine and alcohol degree are counted at different atoms.
questions.x: Amines are classified by how many carbons are bonded to the nitrogen: one is primary, two is secondary, three is tertiary. In tert-butylamine the nitrogen bears one carbon and two hydrogens, so it is a primary amine, even though that carbon is tertiary. Alcohols are classified the other way, by the carbinol carbon, which is why tert-butyl alcohol is a tertiary alcohol.

questions.q: Choline contains a quaternary ammonium group, (CH₃)₃N⁺–R. How does this group behave across physiological pH?
o: It loses a proton at high pH to become neutral
There is no N–H proton to lose.
It stays positively charged and cannot act as a base
Correct: with no lone pair or N–H, it cannot gain or lose a proton.
It is protonated only below pH 4
It carries a permanent charge independent of pH.
It acts as a strong nucleophile
Without a lone pair, nitrogen cannot donate electrons.
questions.x: A quaternary ammonium nitrogen forms four bonds to carbon and carries a permanent positive charge. It has no N–H to lose and no lone pair to accept a proton, so its charge does not change with pH, unlike the R–NH₃⁺ groups of amino acids, which lose a proton around pH 9–11. For the same reason it is not a nucleophile.

questions.q: Why is pyridine basic while pyrrole is essentially nonbasic?
o: Pyrrole's nitrogen lone pair is part of its aromatic sextet; pyridine's is not
Correct: protonating pyrrole's N would destroy aromaticity.
Pyrrole has no lone pair on nitrogen
Pyrrole's N has a lone pair, but it is used in the π system.
Pyridine is not aromatic
Pyridine is aromatic, with 6 π electrons from its carbons and nitrogen.
Pyridine's nitrogen is sp³ hybridized
Pyridine's nitrogen is sp²; its lone pair lies in the ring plane.
questions.x: In pyrrole, the nitrogen's lone pair occupies a p orbital and supplies two of the six π electrons the ring needs to be aromatic. Protonating it would take those electrons out of the π system and destroy aromaticity, so pyrrole is essentially nonbasic. Pyridine's lone pair is in an sp² orbital in the ring plane, outside the aromatic sextet, so it can accept a proton.

questions.q: An ether solution contains an amine and a neutral hydrocarbon. It is shaken with 1 M HCl. Where does the amine end up?
o: In the ether layer, unchanged
Acid protonates the basic amine.
Split equally between layers
Protonation strongly favors the aqueous phase.
As a precipitate of the free amine
The salt dissolves in water rather than precipitating.
In the aqueous layer as an ammonium salt
Correct: protonation makes the amine ionic and water-soluble.
questions.x: Acid–base extraction relies on the fact that charged species dissolve in water, while neutral organic molecules stay in the organic layer. HCl protonates the basic amine to an ammonium salt, R–NH₃⁺Cl⁻, which moves into the aqueous layer, and the neutral hydrocarbon stays in the ether. Making the aqueous layer basic later regenerates the free amine.

questions.q: Ammonia is treated with one equivalent of bromoethane. A mixture of ethyl-, diethyl- and triethylamine results. Why?
o: Each alkylated amine is at least as nucleophilic as the starting amine
Correct: products compete for the alkyl halide, causing overalkylation.
The C–N bonds rearrange after formation
Product mixtures arise from successive alkylations.
Bromoethane reacts by SN1
Primary halides do not ionize; this is SN2 overalkylation.
Ammonia is not nucleophilic
Ammonia attacks; the products simply compete with it.
questions.x: Alkylating ammonia gives ethylamine, and the added ethyl group makes its nitrogen at least as nucleophilic as ammonia's. The product therefore competes with ammonia for the remaining bromoethane, and further SN2 reactions give diethylamine, triethylamine and even quaternary salts. This overalkylation is why chemists use reductive amination or the Gabriel synthesis to make primary amines cleanly.

questions.q: Methylamine (bp −6 °C) boils far below methanol (bp 65 °C). Why?
o: Methylamine has a much lower molar mass
Their molar masses are close (31 vs 32 g/mol).
Methanol is ionic
Methanol is a neutral molecular liquid.
N–H bonds are less polar than O–H bonds, giving weaker hydrogen bonds
Correct: nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen.
Methylamine cannot hydrogen bond
Primary amines can donate and accept hydrogen bonds.
questions.x: Both molecules can donate and accept hydrogen bonds, and their molar masses are almost the same (31 vs 32 g/mol). Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so the N–H bond is less polar than O–H, and the hydrogen bonds between amine molecules are weaker. Less energy is needed to separate methylamine molecules, so it boils much lower than methanol.

questions.q: Which reagents convert cyclohexanone into N-methylcyclohexylamine in one pot?
o: Methylamine alone
Without a reductant, the product stops at the imine.
Methylamine and NaBH₃CN
Correct: reductive amination reduces the iminium formed from the ketone and amine.
Methanol and acid
Those conditions form an acetal.
NaBH₄ followed by methyl bromide
This gives an alcohol and possible ether, not the amine.
questions.x: Reductive amination combines a ketone and an amine to form an iminium ion, which a mild hydride donor reduces to the amine. NaBH₃CN is chosen because, under weakly acidic conditions, it reduces the protonated iminium faster than it reduces the ketone. Methylamine alone stops at the imine, and alkylating an alcohol with methyl bromide cannot give an amine.

questions.q: Phenol (pKa ≈ 10) is much more acidic than cyclohexanol (pKa ≈ 16). Why?
o: Cyclohexanol forms stronger hydrogen bonds
This does not explain the large pKa difference.
Phenol has more hydrogens
Acidity is not set by the number of hydrogens.
The phenoxide negative charge is delocalized into the aromatic ring
Correct: resonance stabilizes the conjugate base.
The phenol O–H bond is ionic
The O–H bond is covalent in both.
questions.x: When phenol loses H⁺, the negative charge on oxygen delocalizes by resonance onto the ortho and para carbons of the ring, stabilizing the phenoxide. In cyclohexoxide the charge stays on one oxygen, because the ring is saturated and has no π system. That resonance stabilization makes phenol about a million times more acidic (pKa 10 vs 16).

questions.q: Which phenol is the most acidic?
o: p-Cresol (p-methylphenol)
Methyl donates electrons, destabilizing the phenoxide.
p-Nitrophenol
Correct: the nitro group withdraws electrons and delocalizes the phenoxide charge.
Phenol
No substituent to stabilize the anion further.
p-Methoxyphenol
Methoxy donates by resonance, lowering acidity.
questions.x: A substituent changes a phenol's acidity by stabilizing or destabilizing the phenoxide. A para-nitro group withdraws electrons by induction and also by resonance, taking the negative charge onto its own oxygens, so p-nitrophenol has a pKa near 7.2. Methyl and methoxy groups donate electron density, which destabilizes the anion and makes those phenols less acidic than phenol.

questions.q: A mixture of benzoic acid (pKa 4.2) and phenol (pKa 10) in ether is washed with aqueous NaHCO₃ (H₂CO₃ pKa ≈ 6.4). What happens?
o: Neither is deprotonated
Benzoic acid's pKa is below that of carbonic acid.
Both move to the aqueous layer
That requires a stronger base such as NaOH.
Only phenol moves to the aqueous layer
Phenol is too weak an acid to be deprotonated by bicarbonate.
Only benzoic acid is deprotonated and moves to the aqueous layer
Correct: bicarbonate is basic enough for the carboxylic acid but not the phenol.
questions.note: NaHCO₃ separates carboxylic acids; NaOH also pulls out phenols.
questions.x: An acid–base reaction favors the side with the weaker acid. Benzoic acid (pKa 4.2) is stronger than carbonic acid (6.4), so bicarbonate deprotonates it and the benzoate moves into the water. Phenol (pKa 10) is weaker than carbonic acid, so bicarbonate cannot deprotonate it and it stays in the ether. A stronger base such as NaOH would extract both.

questions.q: Hydroquinone (p-dihydroxybenzene) is oxidized by loss of two electrons and two protons. What is the product?
o: p-Benzoquinone
Correct: the two OH groups become C=O groups in a cyclohexadienedione.
Phenol
Losing an OH group is not an oxidation of this kind.
Benzoic acid
No carboxyl group forms.
Catechol
Catechol is the ortho-diol isomer, not an oxidation product.
questions.x: Hydroquinone and p-benzoquinone form a redox pair. Removing two electrons and two protons, one H from each OH, turns both C–OH groups into C=O groups and gives the nonaromatic, cross-conjugated p-benzoquinone. Catechol is a structural isomer of hydroquinone with the OH groups ortho, not an oxidation product, and no carbon is removed to form phenol.

questions.q: In the electron transport chain, ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) is reduced to ubiquinol. What does this reduction involve?
o: Gain of two electrons and two protons
Correct: the quinone C=O groups become phenolic OH groups.
Gain of two electrons only, giving a dianion that stays charged
In the membrane, the reduced form picks up protons to become neutral ubiquinol.
Addition of a phosphate group
Phosphorylation is not involved in Q reduction.
Loss of two electrons and two protons
That is oxidation of ubiquinol back to ubiquinone.
questions.x: Ubiquinone is a quinone with two ring C=O groups. Its full reduction adds two electrons and two protons, turning both carbonyls into phenolic OH groups to give ubiquinol, QH₂, a hydroquinone. This coupling of electrons with protons lets coenzyme Q carry protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane in the Q cycle. Losing electrons and protons would be oxidation.

questions.q: One-electron reduction of ubiquinone produces which species?
o: A carbocation
Adding an electron cannot create a cation.
A semiquinone radical
Correct: a single electron gives a resonance-stabilized radical intermediate.
Ubiquinol
Ubiquinol requires two electrons and two protons.
A hydroquinone dianion
A dianion needs two added electrons.
questions.x: Quinones can be reduced in two one-electron steps. Adding a single electron to ubiquinone gives the semiquinone, a radical anion (or neutral radical after protonation) whose unpaired electron is spread over the ring and both oxygens. This one-electron intermediate lets Q move between two-electron carriers such as NADH and one-electron carriers such as iron–sulfur clusters and cytochromes.

questions.q: Vitamin E (α-tocopherol) is a phenol that protects membranes from lipid peroxidation. How does it act?
o: It accepts electrons to become a carbanion
Antioxidant phenols donate, not accept, a hydrogen atom.
It forms disulfide bonds with lipids
It contains no thiol group.
It hydrolyzes oxidized fatty acids
It is a radical scavenger, not a hydrolase.
It donates its phenolic H atom, forming a resonance-stabilized phenoxyl radical
Correct: the stable radical stops the chain reaction.
questions.x: Lipid peroxidation is a radical chain reaction in which lipid peroxyl radicals take hydrogen atoms from neighboring fatty acids. α-Tocopherol transfers its phenolic O–H hydrogen atom to a peroxyl radical faster than lipids do. The resulting phenoxyl radical is stabilized by resonance and by its bulky substituents, so it is too unreactive to continue the chain, which ends the cycle.

questions.q: Phenol reacts with Br₂ much faster than benzene does, and substitution occurs at which positions?
o: Randomly at all positions
Resonance donation creates a strong positional preference.
At the carbon bearing OH (ipso)
The OH is not displaced in this reaction.
Ortho and para
Correct: the OH donates electrons by resonance, activating ortho and para positions.
Meta only
Meta direction is typical of electron-withdrawing groups.
questions.x: The OH group donates electron density into the ring through an oxygen lone pair, which makes the ring much more nucleophilic than benzene, so it is strongly activated. In the arenium intermediate formed by ortho or para attack, the positive charge can sit on the carbon bonded to OH, where oxygen's lone pair stabilizes it, so substitution occurs ortho and para. Meta direction is typical of electron-withdrawing groups.

questions.q: Which species is aromatic?
o: Cyclooctatetraene
It has 8 π electrons and adopts a nonplanar tub shape.
Cyclobutadiene
Its 4 π electrons make it antiaromatic.
Cyclopentadienyl cation
It has 4 π electrons, making it antiaromatic.
Cyclopentadienyl anion
Correct: planar, cyclic, fully conjugated with 6 π electrons (4n+2, n = 1).
questions.x: A species is aromatic if it is cyclic, planar, fully conjugated, and has 4n + 2 π electrons (Hückel's rule). Deprotonating cyclopentadiene leaves a lone pair in a p orbital, giving the anion 6 π electrons in a continuous ring, so it is aromatic. The cation has only 4 π electrons and is antiaromatic. Cyclooctatetraene avoids antiaromaticity by puckering into a nonplanar tub.

questions.q: Benzene reacts with Br₂/FeBr₃ by substitution rather than addition. Why?
o: Substitution preserves the aromatic stabilization of the ring
Correct: addition would destroy the aromatic sextet.
Benzene has no π electrons
Benzene has six π electrons.
Addition products are always unstable
Additions are common for simple alkenes.
FeBr₃ blocks addition sterically
FeBr₃ activates Br₂ as an electrophile.
questions.x: Benzene's six delocalized π electrons give about 150 kJ/mol of aromatic stabilization. Adding Br₂ across one double bond would destroy that sextet, so the reaction would be uphill. In electrophilic aromatic substitution, the arenium intermediate loses H⁺ and restores the aromatic ring. FeBr₃ is a Lewis acid that polarizes Br₂ into a stronger electrophile; it does not block addition.

questions.q: Fructose is best classified as a:
o: Aldohexose
Glucose and galactose are aldohexoses; fructose has a ketone.
Ketohexose
Correct: six carbons with a ketone at C2.
Ketopentose
Fructose has six carbons, not five.
Aldopentose
Ribose is an aldopentose.
questions.x: Monosaccharides are named by their carbonyl type (aldose for an aldehyde at C1, ketose for a ketone) and their number of carbons. Fructose has six carbons with its carbonyl at C2 as a ketone, so it is a ketohexose. Glucose and galactose are its common aldohexose isomers, and ribose is an aldopentose.

questions.q: How many stereoisomers are possible for the open-chain form of an aldohexose?
o: Corresponds to only two stereocenters.
That is 2³, the number for aldopentoses.
Correct: four stereocenters (C2–C5) give 2⁴ = 16.
Counts five stereocenters; C1 and C6 are not stereocenters in the open chain.
questions.x: In an open-chain aldohexose, C1 is the aldehyde carbon (sp², not a stereocenter) and C6 is CH₂OH (two H atoms), so only C2, C3, C4 and C5 are stereocenters. With no meso possibilities, that gives 2⁴ = 16 stereoisomers: 8 D-sugars and their 8 L enantiomers. Cyclization adds C1 as a new anomeric stereocenter, but that applies only to the ring form.

questions.q: In the Haworth projection of α-D-glucopyranose, where is the anomeric OH?
o: In the ring as the ring oxygen
The ring oxygen comes from C5's hydroxyl.
On C6
The anomeric carbon is C1 in glucose.
Above the ring, cis to the C6 CH₂OH group
That describes the β anomer.
Below the ring, trans to the C6 CH₂OH group
Correct: the α anomer has the C1 OH on the face opposite CH₂OH.
questions.x: In a Haworth projection of a D-sugar, the C6 CH₂OH group points up. The α anomer has its anomeric OH on C1 on the opposite face, pointing down, trans to CH₂OH, and the β anomer has it pointing up, cis to CH₂OH. The ring oxygen comes from the C5 hydroxyl, which attacked the C1 aldehyde to form the hemiacetal.

questions.q: A freshly prepared solution of pure α-D-glucose changes its specific rotation over time until it levels off. What explains this?
o: The ring opens and recloses, interconverting α and β anomers
Correct: mutarotation reaches an equilibrium mixture of anomers.
Glucose is converted to its enantiomer
L-glucose cannot form without breaking bonds at every stereocenter.
Glucose is oxidized by dissolved oxygen
Oxidation is not responsible for mutarotation.
The glycosidic bond hydrolyzes
Free glucose has no glycosidic bond.
questions.x: The cyclic hemiacetal of glucose is in equilibrium with a small amount of the open-chain aldehyde. Each time the ring opens and recloses, C1 can form either anomer, so pure α-glucose (+112°) gradually converts to an equilibrium mixture of about 36% α and 64% β (+52.7°). This change in rotation is called mutarotation. No bonds at other stereocenters change, so no enantiomer forms.

questions.q: At equilibrium in water, β-D-glucopyranose is more abundant than the α anomer. Why?
o: The β anomer is an open-chain form
Both anomers are cyclic pyranoses.
In the β anomer, all bulky ring substituents can be equatorial
Correct: the anomeric OH is equatorial in β, minimizing steric strain.
The β anomer has an axial anomeric OH
An axial anomeric OH is the α form.
The α anomer cannot form hydrogen bonds
Both anomers hydrogen-bond with water.
questions.x: In the chair form of β-D-glucopyranose, every bulky substituent, including the C1 OH and the C5 CH₂OH, can sit equatorial. In the α anomer the anomeric OH is axial, which adds 1,3-diaxial strain, so β is favored at equilibrium (about 64%). The anomeric effect slightly favors an axial C1 oxygen, but in water steric effects win.

questions.q: Fructofuranose forms when which groups in open-chain fructose react?
o: The C1 hydroxyl and the C2 ketone
Adjacent groups cannot cyclize into a stable ring.
The C6 hydroxyl and the C1 aldehyde
Fructose has no aldehyde; C1 is a CH₂OH.
The C5 hydroxyl and the C2 ketone
Correct: this forms a five-membered ring hemiketal.
The C4 hydroxyl and the C2 ketone
This would give a four-atom ring, too strained to form.
questions.x: A sugar ring forms when one of its own hydroxyl groups attacks the carbonyl carbon. Fructose's carbonyl is the C2 ketone, and attack by the C5 OH makes a ring of C2, C3, C4, C5 and the oxygen, a five-membered furanose that is a hemiketal. Attack by the C6 OH gives the six-membered fructopyranose instead. Hydroxyl groups closer to C2 would form strained three- or four-membered rings.

questions.q: Which sugar is nonreducing?
o: Lactose
The glucose unit has a free anomeric carbon.
Sucrose
Correct: both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond.
Glucose
Free glucose has a hemiacetal in equilibrium with the aldehyde.
Maltose
One glucose keeps a free hemiacetal that can open.
questions.x: A reducing sugar has a free anomeric carbon, a hemiacetal or hemiketal, that can open to a carbonyl and be oxidized. In sucrose, C1 of glucose is joined to C2 of fructose, so both anomeric carbons are locked as acetals and the ring cannot open. Maltose and lactose each keep one free anomeric OH on their reducing-end glucose, so they are reducing sugars.

questions.q: Humans digest starch but not cellulose, although both are glucose polymers. Why?
o: Cellulose is too hydrophilic to be reached by enzymes
The barrier is linkage stereochemistry, not polarity.
Cellulose contains fructose
Cellulose is made only of glucose.
Humans lack enzymes that hydrolyze β(1→4) glycosidic bonds
Correct: cellulose is β(1→4); starch is α(1→4) with α(1→6) branches.
Starch uses peptide bonds
Starch uses glycosidic bonds.
questions.x: Starch is joined by α(1→4) links (with α(1→6) branches) that coil into helices, which human amylases bind and hydrolyze. Cellulose uses β(1→4) links, which form straight chains that pack into hydrogen-bonded fibers. Enzymes are stereospecific, and humans make no β-glucosidase (cellulase) for this linkage, so the difference is anomeric configuration, not sugar identity or polarity.

questions.q: What type of glycosidic bond forms the branch points of glycogen?
o: Correct: branches join the C1 of one chain to C6 of another.
β(1→4) bonds are found in cellulose.
Glycogen branches are α, not β.
α(1→4) bonds form the linear chain segments.
questions.x: Glycogen consists of glucose chains joined by α(1→4) glycosidic bonds, with a branch about every 8–12 residues. At each branch point, C1 of one chain links to the C6 hydroxyl of a glucose in another chain, forming an α(1→6) bond. The many branches give glycogen many chain ends, so enzymes can release glucose quickly. β linkages are found in cellulose.

questions.q: Methyl β-D-glucopyranoside gives a negative Benedict's test. Why?
o: The methyl group oxidizes Cu²⁺ instead
Methyl groups do not react with Benedict's reagent.
β-Sugars never reduce Cu²⁺
Free β-glucose is a reducing sugar.
It has no stereocenters
It has five stereocenters.
Its anomeric carbon is an acetal and cannot open to an aldehyde
Correct: glycosides are locked and do not mutarotate.
questions.note: Reducing sugar = free hemiacetal/hemiketal.
questions.x: Benedict's test detects an aldehyde, so a sugar reduces Cu²⁺ only if its ring can open, which requires a free hemiacetal. In a methyl glycoside the anomeric OH has been replaced by OCH₃, turning the hemiacetal into an acetal that is stable in base and does not open or mutarotate. Free β-glucose is still a reducing sugar, so β configuration is not the reason.

questions.q: D-Glucose and D-galactose differ only in configuration at C4. What are they?
o: Epimers
Correct: diastereomers differing at exactly one stereocenter.
Constitutional isomers
Their connectivity is the same.
Anomers
Anomers differ only at the anomeric carbon (C1).
Enantiomers
Enantiomers differ at every stereocenter.
questions.x: Epimers are diastereomers that differ in configuration at exactly one stereocenter. D-Glucose and D-galactose differ only at C4, so they are C4 epimers, and D-mannose is the C2 epimer of glucose. Anomers are a special case of epimers that differ only at the anomeric carbon formed on cyclization, C1 in glucose.

questions.q: What is the relationship between D-glucose and L-glucose?
o: Epimers
Epimers differ at a single stereocenter.
Enantiomers
Correct: all four stereocenters are inverted, giving mirror images.
Anomers
Anomers differ at C1 in the cyclic form.
Identical
D and L forms are not superimposable.
questions.x: D and L name the configuration at the highest-numbered stereocenter (C5 in glucose), but L-glucose is the full mirror image of D-glucose, with all four stereocenters C2–C5 inverted. Inverting every stereocenter gives the enantiomer. Changing only one center gives an epimer, which is a diastereomer, not a mirror image.

questions.q: Fructose, a ketose, gives a positive Benedict's test. How can a ketose reduce Cu²⁺?
o: Fructose contains a hidden aldehyde at C6
C6 is a CH₂OH group.
Cu²⁺ oxidizes the ring oxygen
The ring oxygen is not the site of oxidation.
The ketone is directly oxidized to a carboxylic acid
Ketones resist mild oxidation without tautomerization.
Under basic conditions it tautomerizes through an enediol to aldoses
Correct: the aldose forms can be oxidized.
questions.x: Benedict's reagent is basic, and in base fructose's α-hydrogens let it tautomerize: the C2 ketone forms an enediol spanning C1 and C2, which can re-form a carbonyl at C1 as glucose or mannose. Those aldoses are then oxidized by Cu²⁺. Ketones themselves resist mild oxidation, so it is this conversion to an aldose that lets fructose test as a reducing sugar.

questions.q: D-Glucose is treated with NaBH₄. What is the product?
o: D-Fructose
Isomerization does not occur with hydride reduction.
2-Deoxyglucose
Removal of the C2 OH is not a NaBH₄ reaction.
D-Glucitol (sorbitol), an alditol
Correct: the aldehyde is reduced to a primary alcohol.
D-Gluconic acid
That is the oxidation product.
questions.x: NaBH₄ reduces the aldehyde of open-chain glucose, which is in equilibrium with the ring forms, to a primary alcohol at C1. The product, D-glucitol (sorbitol), is an alditol with OH groups on all six carbons and cannot cyclize. Oxidation of C1 would instead give gluconic acid, and NaBH₄ does not rearrange glucose to fructose.

questions.q: A triacylglycerol consists of:
o: Glycerol esterified to three fatty acids
Correct: three ester bonds link fatty acids to glycerol's three OH groups.
Sphingosine linked to one fatty acid
That describes a ceramide.
Glycerol linked to two fatty acids and a phosphate
That describes a phosphatidic acid.
Three fatty acids linked by amide bonds
Triglycerides use ester bonds to glycerol.
questions.x: A triacylglycerol (triglyceride) forms when each of glycerol's three hydroxyl groups is esterified to a fatty acid, giving three ester bonds. This neutral, nonpolar molecule is the body's main stored fuel. Phospholipids replace one fatty acid with a phosphate-containing head group, and sphingolipids use sphingosine instead of glycerol and attach the fatty acid by an amide bond.

questions.q: A triglyceride is boiled with aqueous NaOH. What products form?
o: Diacylglycerol and methanol
No methanol is present; that resembles transesterification.
Glycerol and free fatty alcohols
Hydrolysis yields carboxylates, not alcohols from the acyl chains.
Glycerol and sodium salts of fatty acids (soap)
Correct: saponification hydrolyzes the three esters.
Fatty acid methyl esters
That is biodiesel formation with methanol.
questions.x: Saponification is base hydrolysis of esters. Hydroxide attacks each of the triglyceride's three ester carbonyls, releasing glycerol and three fatty acid carboxylates, which in NaOH are the sodium salts that make up soap. The carboxylate step makes the reaction irreversible. The acyl chains become carboxylates, not alcohols; making fatty alcohols would require reduction.

questions.q: Bacteria shifted from 37 °C to 10 °C change their membrane lipid composition. Which change best maintains membrane fluidity?
o: Increasing the fraction of saturated fatty acids
That would make the membrane more rigid.
Converting cis double bonds to trans
Trans chains pack like saturated chains and reduce fluidity.
Lengthening fatty acid chains
Longer chains increase van der Waals contact and rigidity.
Increasing the fraction of cis-unsaturated fatty acids
Correct: cis kinks disrupt packing and keep the membrane fluid in the cold.
questions.x: Membrane fluidity depends on how tightly the fatty acid chains pack. Cis double bonds put a fixed bend in a chain, which keeps neighboring chains apart and lowers the melting temperature, so cells in the cold make more cis-unsaturated fatty acids (homeoviscous adaptation). Saturated chains, longer chains and trans double bonds all pack more tightly, making the membrane more rigid.

questions.q: Elaidic acid (trans-C18:1) and oleic acid (cis-C18:1) differ only in double-bond geometry. Which has the higher melting point?
o: They melt at the same temperature
Geometry changes packing and melting point.
Elaidic acid
Correct: the straighter trans chain packs more tightly.
It cannot be predicted without molar masses
They are isomers with the same molar mass.
Oleic acid
The cis kink disrupts packing and lowers the melting point.
questions.x: Melting point depends on how well molecules pack against one another. A trans double bond leaves the chain nearly straight, so elaidic acid packs like a saturated fatty acid and melts at about 45 °C. The cis double bond in oleic acid puts a kink near the middle of the chain, which keeps the molecules apart, so it is liquid at room temperature (melting point about 13 °C).

questions.q: How does phosphatidylcholine differ structurally from a triacylglycerol?
o: It lacks a glycerol backbone
Phosphatidylcholine is a glycerophospholipid.
It has four fatty acids
Phospholipids have two fatty acids.
Its fatty acids are attached by amide bonds
Fatty acids are ester-linked to glycerol.
One fatty acid is replaced by a phosphate linked to choline, making it amphipathic
Correct: the polar head lets it form bilayers.
questions.x: Both lipids are built on glycerol with ester-linked fatty acids. A triacylglycerol carries three fatty acids and is entirely nonpolar. In phosphatidylcholine, the third (sn-3) position holds a phosphate esterified to choline instead, giving a charged, polar head attached to two nonpolar tails. That amphipathic shape lets phospholipids form bilayers, while triglycerides cluster into fat droplets.

questions.q: Which membrane lipid is built on a sphingosine backbone rather than glycerol?
o: Cardiolipin
Built from glycerol units.
Phosphatidylserine
A glycerophospholipid.
Sphingomyelin
Correct: sphingolipids use the amino alcohol sphingosine.
Phosphatidylethanolamine
A glycerophospholipid.
questions.x: Most membrane phospholipids are glycerophospholipids built on glycerol, as are phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylethanolamine and cardiolipin (which joins two phosphatidyl units through a central glycerol). Sphingolipids instead use sphingosine, a long-chain amino alcohol, with the fatty acid amide-linked to its nitrogen to form a ceramide. Sphingomyelin adds a phosphocholine head group and is common in myelin.

questions.q: What is the effect of cholesterol on animal cell membranes?
o: It always decreases fluidity
At low temperature it disrupts tight packing.
It reduces fluidity at high temperature and prevents rigidity at low temperature
Correct: cholesterol buffers membrane fluidity.
It forms covalent bonds with phospholipids
It interacts noncovalently.
It always increases fluidity
At high temperature it restrains phospholipid motion.
questions.x: Cholesterol is a fluidity buffer. At high temperature its rigid fused rings slot between phospholipid tails and restrict their motion, which reduces fluidity. At low temperature it keeps the tails from packing tightly and crystallizing, which prevents the membrane from becoming rigid. It acts through noncovalent interactions, not covalent bonds to phospholipids.

questions.q: Which structural feature defines a steroid?
o: Four fused rings: three six-membered and one five-membered
Correct: the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene core.
A long unbranched hydrocarbon chain ending in COOH
That is a fatty acid.
A ring of five isoprene units with a phosphate
Steroids are fused-ring isoprenoids without phosphate.
A glycerol backbone with two fatty acids
That is a glycerophospholipid.
questions.x: All steroids share one core: four fused rings, three six-membered (A, B, C) and one five-membered (D), called the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene system. They are made from isoprene units by way of squalene, but the fused ring core is what defines them. A long unbranched chain ending in COOH is a fatty acid, and a glycerol with two fatty acids is a phospholipid.

questions.q: Squalene, the C₃₀ precursor of cholesterol, is built from how many isoprene (C₅) units?
o: Three units give a C₁₅ sesquiterpene.
Correct: 30 ÷ 5 = 6 isoprene units (a triterpene).
Four units give a C₂₀ diterpene.
Confuses carbon atoms with isoprene units.
questions.x: Terpenes are built from five-carbon isoprene units, so the number of units equals the carbon count divided by 5. Squalene has 30 carbons, so 30 ÷ 5 = 6 isoprene units, which makes it a triterpene (one terpene unit is two isoprenes, C₁₀). Squalene cyclizes to lanosterol, which is then converted to cholesterol (C₂₇), losing three carbons.

questions.q: Which vitamin is water-soluble rather than fat-soluble?
o: Vitamin D
Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid.
Vitamin A
Retinol is a fat-soluble isoprenoid.
Vitamin K
Vitamin K is a fat-soluble naphthoquinone.
Vitamin C
Correct: ascorbic acid is polar with many OH groups.
questions.note: Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K.
questions.x: Vitamins sort by polarity. Vitamins A, D, E and K are largely hydrocarbon (isoprenoid or sterol-derived), so they dissolve in fat, are stored in tissues and need dietary fat for absorption. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) and the B vitamins are polar molecules with many OH or charged groups, so they dissolve in water and excess amounts are excreted in urine.

questions.q: Prostaglandins and thromboxanes are synthesized from which precursor?
o: Arachidonic acid, a C₂₀ fatty acid
Correct: eicosanoids derive from this 20-carbon ω-6 fatty acid.
Palmitic acid
Palmitate is saturated C₁₆ and not an eicosanoid precursor.
Cholesterol
Cholesterol gives steroid hormones and bile acids.
Sphingosine
Sphingosine gives sphingolipids.
questions.x: Eicosanoids, a name taken from the Greek word for twenty, are signaling lipids made from 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acids, mainly arachidonic acid (20:4, ω-6). Phospholipase A₂ releases it from membrane phospholipids, and cyclooxygenase converts it to prostaglandins and thromboxanes; aspirin works by inhibiting that enzyme. Cholesterol is the precursor of steroid hormones, not eicosanoids.

questions.q: A fatty acid is described as 18:3 cis-Δ9,12,15. What omega class is it?
o: That would require the last double bond at C12.
Uses the first Δ position, counted from the carboxyl end.
Correct: the last double bond starts at C15, which is 18 − 15 = 3 carbons from the methyl end.
Δ numbering counts from the carboxyl carbon; ω counts from the methyl end.
questions.x: Δ numbers count from the carboxyl carbon (C1), while the ω number counts from the methyl end to the nearest double bond. For an 18-carbon chain whose last double bond begins at C15, ω = 18 − 15 = 3, so this is an ω-3 fatty acid (α-linolenic acid). The tempting error is reading the first Δ position (9) as ω, or using Δ15 directly as the ω number.

questions.q: Waxes such as beeswax are chemically best described as:
o: Esters of long-chain fatty acids with long-chain alcohols
Correct: very hydrophobic esters used for waterproofing.
Triglycerides with short chains
Waxes are not glycerol esters.
Steroids with a hydroxyl group
That describes sterols such as cholesterol.
Polymers of glucose
That describes polysaccharides.
questions.x: A wax is a single ester formed between a long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol, often 30 to 50 or more carbons in total. With only one small polar ester group buried among long hydrocarbon chains, waxes are extremely hydrophobic and solid at room temperature, which suits them for waterproofing leaves, feathers and honeycomb. Triglycerides instead are glycerol triesters.

questions.q: Why do fats yield more energy per gram than carbohydrates?
o: They are water-soluble and absorbed faster
Fats are insoluble in water.
They contain more oxygen atoms
Carbohydrates contain more oxygen, which makes them more oxidized.
Their ester bonds release most of the energy
Most energy comes from oxidizing the hydrocarbon chains.
Their carbons are more reduced, with mostly C–H and C–C bonds
Correct: more electrons are available for oxidation.
questions.x: Energy from fuel oxidation comes from electrons passed to O₂, and more reduced carbons have more electrons to give. Fatty acid chains are almost all C–H and C–C bonds, while carbohydrates already carry an O on nearly every carbon, so they are partly oxidized. Fats therefore yield about 9 kcal/g compared with 4 kcal/g for carbohydrates. Ester hydrolysis itself releases little energy.

questions.q: Phospholipase A₂ hydrolyzes a membrane phospholipid. What are the products?
o: Glycerol and three fatty acids
Phospholipids have two fatty acids, and PLA₂ removes only one.
Phosphatidic acid and free choline
That is the action of phospholipase D.
A free fatty acid from the sn-2 position and a lysophospholipid
Correct: PLA₂ cleaves the ester at glycerol C2.
Diacylglycerol and a phosphorylated head group
That is the action of phospholipase C.
questions.x: Phospholipases are named by the bond they cut. PLA₂ hydrolyzes the ester at the sn-2 carbon of glycerol, releasing that fatty acid, often arachidonic acid, the eicosanoid precursor, and leaving a lysophospholipid with one tail. PLC cuts before the phosphate, giving diacylglycerol plus a phosphorylated head group such as IP₃, and PLD cuts after it, giving phosphatidic acid and free choline.

questions.q: Soap molecules (one hydrocarbon tail) form micelles in water, but diacyl phospholipids form bilayers. What best explains the difference?
o: Micelles form only from uncharged molecules
Soaps are charged and readily form micelles.
Single-tailed amphiphiles are cone-shaped; two-tailed ones are roughly cylindrical
Correct: cylinders pack into flat sheets, cones into spheres.
Soaps lack a polar head group
The carboxylate is the polar head of a soap.
Phospholipids are not amphipathic
Phospholipids have polar heads and nonpolar tails.
questions.x: An amphiphile's shape decides how it packs. A soap has a large head and one thin tail, a wedge or cone shape whose tails fit together only in the center of a sphere, so it forms micelles. A diacyl phospholipid's two tails are about as wide as its head, so it is roughly cylindrical and packs side by side into flat bilayers. Both kinds of molecules are amphipathic.

questions.q: Which standard amino acid is achiral?
o: Alanine
Alanine's α-carbon has four different groups.
Glycine
Correct: its α-carbon carries two hydrogens.
Proline
Proline's α-carbon is a stereocenter within its ring.
Serine
Serine's α-carbon has four different groups.
questions.x: An amino acid is chiral when its α-carbon carries four different groups: H, NH₂, COOH and the side chain R. In glycine the side chain is just H, so the α-carbon carries two hydrogens and is not a stereocenter, which makes glycine the only achiral standard amino acid. Proline's α-carbon is part of a ring but still bonded to four different groups, so it is chiral.

questions.q: Most L-amino acids have the S configuration, but L-cysteine is R. Why?
o: L-Cysteine has the opposite spatial arrangement from other L-amino acids
Its geometry matches other L-amino acids; only the priority order changes.
Disulfide formation inverts the α-carbon
Oxidation of the thiol does not touch the α-carbon.
The sulfur in –CH₂SH gives the side chain higher CIP priority than –COOH
Correct: S (Z = 16) outranks the O atoms on the carboxyl carbon at the first point of difference.
Cysteine's α-carbon is not a stereocenter
It has four different substituents.
questions.note: D/L is about geometry; R/S is about priorities.
questions.x: D/L describes actual geometry compared with glyceraldehyde, while R/S depends on CIP priorities. In most amino acids the priority order is NH₂ > COOH > R > H, which makes L amino acids S. In cysteine the side-chain carbon bears a sulfur, and S (atomic number 16) beats the carboxyl carbon's (O, O, O), so CH₂SH outranks COOH. The geometry is the same, but the label becomes R.

questions.q: Alanine has pKa values of 2.3 (α-COOH) and 9.7 (α-NH₃⁺). What is its isoelectric point?
o: Correct: pI = (2.3 + 9.7)/2 for an amino acid with no ionizable side chain.
pI is set by the amino acid's own pKa values, not neutral pH.
Adds the pKa values without dividing by two.
Takes a difference instead of an average.
questions.x: The pI is the pH at which the neutral zwitterion dominates, which falls midway between the pKa values on either side of it. For an amino acid with no ionizable side chain, those are the α-COOH and α-NH₃⁺ values, so pI = (2.3 + 9.7)/2 = 6.0. At pH 7 alanine is therefore not quite neutral overall; pI depends on the molecule's own pKa values, not on neutral pH.

questions.q: Lysine has pKa values of 2.2 (α-COOH), 9.0 (α-NH₃⁺) and 10.5 (side-chain NH₃⁺). What is its pI?
o: Averages all three pKa values.
Averages the carboxyl and side-chain pKa values.
Averages the α-carboxyl and α-amino pKa values, ignoring the basic side chain.
Correct: average the two pKa values flanking the neutral species, (9.0 + 10.5)/2.
questions.x: Find the pI by tracking charge: lysine is +2 below pH 2.2, +1 once the carboxyl loses its proton, and 0 once the α-amino group (9.0) loses its proton. The neutral form exists between pKa 9.0 and 10.5, so pI = (9.0 + 10.5)/2 = 9.75. Averaging the α-groups alone (5.6) ignores the basic side chain, which keeps lysine positive across most of the pH range.

questions.q: In an electrophoresis gel at pH 7, toward which electrode does free lysine migrate?
o: The anode (positive electrode)
Net negative species, such as aspartate, move toward the anode.
It does not move
It would be stationary only at pH equal to its pI.
It moves in both directions equally
A molecule has a single net charge at a given pH.
The cathode (negative electrode)
Correct: with pI ≈ 9.7, lysine carries a net positive charge at pH 7.
questions.x: At a pH below its pI, a molecule carries net positive charge, and above its pI, net negative charge. Lysine's pI is about 9.7, so at pH 7 both amino groups are protonated while the carboxyl is ionized, giving a net charge near +1. Positive species migrate toward the negative electrode, the cathode, and lysine would stay put only at a pH equal to its pI.

questions.q: Which side chain is most likely to be buried in the interior of a water-soluble globular protein?
o: Serine
The polar hydroxyl hydrogen-bonds with water at the surface.
Leucine
Correct: its nonpolar isobutyl side chain avoids water.
Aspartate
Charged aspartate prefers the surface.
Lysine
Charged lysine prefers the aqueous surface.
questions.x: Water-soluble proteins fold so that nonpolar side chains are tucked away from water. Burying them releases ordered water molecules and raises entropy, which is the hydrophobic effect. Leucine's isobutyl side chain is entirely hydrocarbon, so it belongs in the core. Charged residues such as lysine and aspartate, and polar ones such as serine, are usually found on the surface, where they interact with water.

questions.q: Why is rotation about the C–N bond of a peptide bond restricted?
o: Bulky side chains always block rotation
Restriction occurs even in glycine peptides.
The nitrogen is sp³ hybridized
Amide nitrogen is effectively sp² and planar.
Resonance gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character
Correct: the nitrogen lone pair delocalizes into the carbonyl, making the unit planar.
The C–N bond is a full triple bond
It is intermediate between single and double.
questions.x: The amide nitrogen's lone pair delocalizes into the carbonyl, so the C–N bond has about 40% double-bond character. Rotating about it would break that π overlap, so the six atoms of the peptide unit (Cα, C, O, N, H, Cα) lie in one plane, usually trans. Backbone flexibility comes only from the φ and ψ rotations at the α-carbon, which is why even glycine peptides have planar amide units.

questions.q: Proline is often found at turns and tends to break α-helices. Why?
o: Its ring constrains backbone rotation and its amide N lacks an H for helix H-bonding
Correct: both features disrupt the regular helical pattern.
It has no α-carbon
Proline has an α-carbon that is part of its ring.
It is the only charged amino acid
Proline's side chain is nonpolar and uncharged.
It forms disulfide bonds
Only cysteine forms disulfides.
questions.x: Proline's side chain loops back and bonds to its own backbone nitrogen, forming a five-membered ring. That ring locks the φ angle near −60° and leaves the amide nitrogen with no H to donate to the i − 4 carbonyl, a hydrogen bond the α-helix depends on. These constraints break helices but suit the tight bends of β-turns, where proline is common.

questions.q: Formation of a disulfide bridge between two cysteine residues is what type of reaction?
o: Hydrolysis
No water is added across a bond.
Reduction
Reducing agents such as DTT break disulfides.
Oxidation
Correct: each sulfur loses a hydrogen (and an electron) as the S–S bond forms.
Decarboxylation
No CO₂ is lost.
questions.x: Forming a disulfide joins two thiols, 2 R–SH → R–S–S–R, with loss of two hydrogens, so two electrons and two protons are removed. That is an oxidation: each sulfur goes from −2 to −1. Disulfides form in oxidizing environments such as the ER lumen and outside the cell, and reducing agents such as DTT or β-mercaptoethanol break them back to thiols.

questions.q: How many peptide bonds are in a linear pentapeptide?
o: Counts one bond per residue rather than one between each pair.
Correct: n amino acids in a chain are joined by n − 1 peptide bonds.
Counts possible pairs, not adjacent links.
Overcounts by two.
questions.x: Each peptide bond joins two adjacent residues, so a linear chain of n amino acids has n − 1 bonds, just as five beads on a string need four links between them. A linear pentapeptide therefore has 4 peptide bonds, and forming them releases 4 water molecules. Counting one bond per residue (5) is the common fencepost error.

questions.q: In the tripeptide Gly-Ala-Ser, which residue has the free α-carboxylate?
o: Ala
The middle residue has both α-groups in peptide bonds.
Gly
Gly is written first and is the N-terminal residue, with the free amino group.
All three
Only the C-terminal residue keeps a free carboxylate.
Ser
Correct: peptides are written N- to C-terminus, so the last residue is C-terminal.
questions.x: Peptide sequences are written from the N-terminus to the C-terminus by convention. In Gly-Ala-Ser, glycine is first and keeps the free α-amino group, while serine is last and keeps the free α-carboxylate. Alanine in the middle has both its α-groups used in peptide bonds. Only the two ends of the chain carry free α-amino and α-carboxyl groups.

questions.q: A histidine side chain has pKa 6.0. At pH 7.0, approximately what fraction of histidine side chains are protonated?
o: About 9%
Correct: [protonated]/[neutral] = 10⁻¹, so the fraction is 0.1/1.1 ≈ 9%.
About 1%
That would correspond to a pH two units above the pKa.
About 91%
Inverts the ratio; above the pKa most groups are deprotonated.
About 50%
That is true only when pH equals pKa.
questions.x: From Henderson–Hasselbalch, pH − pKa = 7.0 − 6.0 = 1, so [neutral]/[protonated] = 10¹ = 10. For every 10 neutral side chains there is 1 protonated one, so the protonated fraction is 1/(10 + 1) ≈ 9%. Above the pKa the deprotonated form dominates, which is why 91% is the reversed answer. Having both forms near pH 7 makes histidine useful as a catalytic acid or base.

questions.q: In a Strecker synthesis, an aldehyde reacts with NH₃ and HCN, and the aminonitrile is hydrolyzed. What is the stereochemistry of the amino acid product?
o: Racemic
Correct: cyanide adds to the planar imine from either face equally.
Pure L
Without a chiral catalyst or enzyme, there is no facial preference.
Meso
An α-amino acid with one stereocenter cannot be meso.
Pure D
No chiral influence favors D.
questions.x: In the Strecker synthesis, the aldehyde and NH₃ condense to a planar imine (iminium), and cyanide adds to the C=N carbon to create the new α-stereocenter. The two faces of the imine are mirror images, so an achiral reagent attacks both equally, giving a racemic aminonitrile and, after hydrolysis, a racemic amino acid. Getting only L requires an enzyme or a chiral catalyst.

questions.q: Glycine is titrated from pH 1 with NaOH. At what point does the pH equal glycine's pI?
o: At the second half-equivalence point
There pH = pKa₂ (about 9.6).
At the second equivalence point
There glycine is fully deprotonated with net charge −1.
At the first half-equivalence point
There pH = pKa₁ (about 2.3), not the pI.
At the first equivalence point
Correct: after one equivalent of OH⁻, the zwitterion predominates.
questions.x: Starting at pH 1, glycine is fully protonated (+1). Adding one equivalent of OH⁻ removes the carboxyl proton completely, leaving the zwitterion (net charge 0), so the first equivalence point falls at the pI, (2.3 + 9.6)/2 ≈ 6.0. The half-equivalence points are where pH equals pKa₁ or pKa₂, with equal amounts of the two forms on either side of that proton.

questions.q: Amino acids melt or decompose above 200 °C, far higher than similar-sized organic molecules. Why?
o: They are covalently polymerized in the solid
Free amino acids are not linked in the crystal.
In the solid they exist as zwitterions held by ionic attractions
Correct: the crystal resembles an ionic salt lattice.
They have very high molar masses
Their molar masses are modest.
They lack polar groups
They have both amino and carboxyl groups.
questions.x: In the solid state, amino acids exist as zwitterions, +H₃N–CHR–COO⁻, so the crystal is held together by strong ionic attractions between charged groups, much like a salt. Breaking that lattice takes a great deal of energy, so amino acids decompose before they melt, typically above 200 °C. Neutral organic molecules of similar size are held only by weaker dipole forces and hydrogen bonds.

questions.q: Which two standard amino acids contain sulfur?
o: Serine and threonine
These contain hydroxyl groups, not sulfur.
Cysteine and serine
Serine has an OH where cysteine has SH.
Cysteine and methionine
Correct: cysteine has a thiol, methionine a thioether.
Methionine and tyrosine
Tyrosine has a phenol, not sulfur.
questions.x: Two of the standard amino acids contain sulfur: cysteine, whose side chain is a thiol (–CH₂SH) that can form disulfides, and methionine, whose side chain is a thioether (–CH₂CH₂SCH₃). Serine is the oxygen analog of cysteine, with OH in place of SH, which makes it a common distractor. Methionine is also the source of SAM's methyl group.

questions.q: Protein kinases transfer phosphate to which functional group on serine, threonine or tyrosine?
o: The α-carboxyl group, forming an anhydride
The backbone carboxyl is in a peptide bond.
The aromatic ring carbon
Phosphorylation occurs on oxygen, not ring carbon.
The α-amino group, forming a phosphoramide
Kinases target side-chain hydroxyls of these residues.
The side-chain hydroxyl, forming a phosphate ester
Correct: the OH oxygen attacks the γ-phosphate of ATP.
questions.x: Kinases transfer the terminal (γ) phosphate of ATP to a nucleophile. On serine, threonine and tyrosine that nucleophile is the side-chain hydroxyl oxygen, which attacks the γ-phosphorus and forms a phosphate monoester (phospho-Ser, phospho-Thr or phospho-Tyr). Adding the negatively charged phosphate changes the protein's shape or binding, and phosphatases hydrolyze it to reverse the signal.

questions.q: How does adenosine differ from adenosine monophosphate (AMP)?
o: Adenosine contains deoxyribose
Adenosine contains ribose; deoxyadenosine has deoxyribose.
Adenosine has a different base
Both contain adenine.
Adenosine lacks the phosphate group
Correct: a nucleoside is base plus sugar; a nucleotide adds phosphate.
Adenosine lacks the ribose
Adenosine contains ribose bonded to adenine.
questions.x: A nucleoside is a nitrogenous base joined to a sugar. A nucleotide is a nucleoside with one or more phosphates esterified to the sugar, usually at the 5′-OH. Adenosine is adenine bonded to ribose, and AMP is adenosine 5′-monophosphate, so the only difference is the phosphate. Deoxyadenosine is the version made with deoxyribose.

questions.q: Which atoms are joined by the phosphodiester linkages of a nucleic acid backbone?
o: The 3′-OH of one sugar and the 5′-phosphate of the next
Correct: chains grow 5′ → 3′ through 3′-O–P–O-5′ links.
The 2′-OH of one sugar and the 5′-phosphate of the next
Normal backbones use the 3′ oxygen, not the 2′.
C1′ of one sugar and the base of the next
C1′ bonds to its own base via an N-glycosidic bond.
The bases of adjacent nucleotides
Bases on one strand stack but are not covalently linked.
questions.x: In a nucleic acid backbone, each phosphate forms ester bonds to two sugars: one to the 3′ oxygen of one nucleotide and one to the 5′ oxygen of the next, written 3′-O–P–O-5′. Polymerases add each nucleotide to a free 3′-OH, so chains grow 5′ → 3′. The bases hang off C1′ by glycosidic bonds and are not covalently linked to one another.

questions.q: Why is the DNA backbone negatively charged at physiological pH?
o: DNA binds chloride ions
DNA binds cations, such as Mg²⁺, to offset its charge.
Each phosphodiester has an acidic OH (pKa ≈ 1) that is deprotonated
Correct: one negative charge per phosphate.
Deoxyribose hydroxyls are deprotonated
Sugar OH groups have pKa values far above 7.
The bases carry negative charges
The bases are mostly neutral at pH 7.4.
questions.x: Each phosphodiester link keeps one ionizable P–OH, which is a strong acid with a pKa around 1. At pH 7.4, far above that pKa, it is fully deprotonated, giving one negative charge per nucleotide. Sugar hydroxyls have pKa values above 12 and stay protonated. This polyanion is neutralized by cations such as Mg²⁺ and by positively charged histone lysines and arginines.

questions.q: RNA is rapidly cleaved in dilute base, whereas DNA is stable. What is the chemical reason?
o: RNA contains uracil, which is base-labile
Uracil is not the site of backbone cleavage.
DNA has a positive backbone that repels hydroxide
Both backbones are negatively charged.
RNA's 2′-OH attacks the adjacent phosphate, forming a 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate
Correct: deoxyribose lacks this internal nucleophile.
RNA lacks phosphodiester bonds
RNA has the same phosphodiester backbone.
questions.x: Ribose has a 2′-OH right next to the 3′-phosphodiester. In base it is deprotonated, and the alkoxide attacks the neighboring phosphorus intramolecularly, cleaving the chain and forming a 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate. Deoxyribose lacks the 2′-OH, so DNA has no internal nucleophile and is much more stable. This stability is one reason DNA serves as long-term genetic storage.

questions.q: Sample A of double-stranded DNA is 30% G + C, and sample B is 60% G + C. Which melts at the higher temperature, and why?
o: Sample B, because G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds and stronger stacking
Correct: higher GC content raises Tm.
They melt at the same temperature
Base composition strongly affects Tm.
Sample A, because A–T pairs have three hydrogen bonds
A–T pairs have two hydrogen bonds.
Sample A, because it has more purines
Purine content is 50% in any duplex.
questions.x: Melting temperature measures how much energy it takes to separate the two strands. G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds compared with two for A–T, and GC-rich stretches also stack more favorably, so DNA with more G + C melts at a higher temperature. Every duplex is 50% purines by Chargaff's rule, so purine content cannot explain the difference.

questions.q: Which pair of bases are both pyrimidines?
o: Adenine and thymine
Adenine is a purine.
Cytosine and uracil
Correct: single-ring nitrogenous bases.
Adenine and guanine
Both are two-ring purines.
Guanine and cytosine
Guanine is a purine.
questions.x: Nitrogenous bases fall into two structural classes. Pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine and uracil) have a single six-membered ring, and purines (adenine and guanine) have a fused six- and five-membered double ring. In each Watson–Crick pair one base is a purine and the other a pyrimidine, which keeps the helix width constant. The memory aid is CUT the PY.

questions.q: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 20% adenine. What percentage is guanine?
o: Equates G with A; Chargaff's rule pairs G with C.
That is G + C combined.
Subtracts only adenine from 100%.
Correct: A = T = 20%, leaving 60% for G + C, so G = 30%.
questions.x: Chargaff's rules for double-stranded DNA state that A = T and G = C, because each base pairs with its partner. If A = 20%, then T = 20%, so A + T = 40% and G + C = 60%. G and C are equal, so G = 30%. The common error is assuming G must equal A, when G pairs only with C.

questions.q: Hydrolysis of ATP's terminal phosphoanhydride bond is strongly exergonic. Which factor contributes?
o: Release of energy stored in the adenine ring
The base is not altered during hydrolysis.
Breaking bonds releases energy
Bond breaking costs energy; ΔG reflects the products' greater stability.
Formation of a new phosphoanhydride bond
Hydrolysis breaks, not forms, an anhydride.
Relief of electrostatic repulsion among adjacent negative phosphates
Correct: products are also better resonance-stabilized and hydrated.
questions.note: Trap: breaking a bond never releases energy by itself.
questions.x: Breaking any bond costs energy, so ATP hydrolysis is exergonic only because its products, ADP and Pᵢ, are much more stable than ATP plus water. In ATP, closely spaced negative phosphates repel one another, and splitting them apart relieves that strain. Pᵢ also gains more resonance forms and both products are better solvated, which together give ΔG°′ about −30.5 kJ/mol.

questions.q: Spontaneous deamination of cytosine produces uracil. How does using thymine in DNA help cells repair this damage?
o: Any uracil in DNA can be recognized as damage and removed
Correct: thymine (5-methyluracil) is distinguishable from deaminated cytosine.
Thymine prevents cytosine from deaminating
Thymine does not alter cytosine's reactivity.
Thymine cannot be deaminated
Thymine has no amino group, but this is not the repair logic.
Uracil pairs with guanine more strongly than cytosine
Uracil pairs with adenine, causing mutations if not repaired.
questions.x: Cytosine deaminates spontaneously to uracil fairly often. If DNA normally contained uracil, a repair enzyme could not tell the original U's from damaged C's. Because DNA uses thymine (5-methyluracil) instead, any uracil found in DNA must be damage, and uracil-DNA glycosylase removes it. Unrepaired, U pairs with A, turning a G–C pair into A–T after replication.

questions.q: Thymine differs structurally from uracil by:
o: An extra fused ring
Both are single-ring pyrimidines.
An amino group at C4
That describes cytosine.
A methyl group at C5
Correct: thymine is 5-methyluracil.
A 2′-hydroxyl group
The 2′-OH belongs to ribose, not the base.
questions.x: Thymine and uracil are both pyrimidines, and the only difference is a methyl group at C5, which makes thymine 5-methyluracil. DNA uses thymine, and RNA uses uracil. Both pair with adenine, because the methyl group does not take part in base pairing. Cytosine differs from uracil instead by an amino group at C4 in place of a carbonyl.

questions.q: In a nucleoside, the base is connected to C1′ of the sugar by which type of bond?
o: A peptide bond
Peptide bonds join amino acids.
A β-N-glycosidic bond
Correct: N9 of purines or N1 of pyrimidines bonds to C1′.
An α-O-glycosidic bond
The linkage is through nitrogen, with β geometry.
A phosphodiester bond
Phosphodiesters connect sugars in the backbone.
questions.x: In a nucleoside, the base attaches to the sugar's anomeric carbon, C1′, through a ring nitrogen: N9 of a purine or N1 of a pyrimidine. A bond from an anomeric carbon to nitrogen is an N-glycosidic bond, and in natural nucleosides the base sits on the same face as the C5′ group, the β configuration. Phosphodiester bonds instead join the sugars of adjacent nucleotides.

questions.q: A molecule contains both a ketone and an ester. To reduce only the ester with LiAlH₄, what should be done first?
o: Protect the ester as an acetal
Esters are not usually protected as acetals, and the ketone is the problem.
Convert the ketone into a cyclic acetal with ethylene glycol and acid
Correct: acetals are inert to hydride, then removed with aqueous acid.
Run the reaction in aqueous acid
LiAlH₄ is destroyed by water and acid.
Hydrolyze the ester to a carboxylic acid
The ketone would still be reduced by LiAlH₄.
questions.x: LiAlH₄ reduces ketones even faster than esters, so the ketone must be masked first. Ethylene glycol and an acid catalyst turn the ketone into a cyclic acetal, which is inert to hydride and to base. After LiAlH₄ reduces the ester to an alcohol, aqueous acid hydrolyzes the acetal and gives back the ketone. Hydrolyzing the ester instead would do nothing to protect the ketone.

questions.q: An alcohol is protected as a tert-butyldimethylsilyl (TBDMS) ether. Which reagent removes this group selectively?
o: NaBH₄
Hydride reagents do not cleave silyl ethers.
CH₃MgBr
Silyl ethers are stable to Grignard reagents; that is why they are used.
Tetrabutylammonium fluoride (TBAF)
Correct: the very strong Si–F bond drives cleavage.
PCC
PCC oxidizes free alcohols and leaves silyl ethers intact.
questions.x: Silyl ethers such as TBDMS protect alcohols because they survive bases, Grignard reagents, hydrides and many oxidants. They are removed with fluoride, usually from TBAF, because the Si–F bond is one of the strongest single bonds (about 565 kJ/mol), far stronger than Si–O. Fluoride attacks silicon and releases the free alcohol, leaving other functional groups untouched.

questions.q: In solution-phase peptide synthesis, why is the amino group of the first amino acid protected (for example, with Boc)?
o: To prevent it from reacting with the activated carboxyl and forming unwanted peptides
Correct: protection ensures coupling occurs only in the desired direction.
To increase its water solubility
Boc groups make molecules more hydrophobic.
To make the amino acid chiral
Protection does not create stereocenters.
To activate the carboxyl group
Activation is done separately, such as with DCC.
questions.x: A free amino acid has both a nucleophilic amine and a carboxyl group. If the carboxyl is activated without protecting the amine, molecules couple with copies of themselves, giving a mixture of oligomers and wrong sequences. Protecting the N-terminus with Boc or Fmoc leaves only one amine able to react, so each coupling forms the intended bond, and the protecting group is then removed for the next step.

questions.q: A chemist must add CH₃MgBr to an ester in a molecule that also has a free OH group. Why must the OH be protected first?
o: The OH would be reduced to an alkane
Grignard reagents do not reduce alcohols to alkanes.
The OH group makes the ester unreactive
The ester remains reactive; the OH consumes the reagent.
The OH would add to the ester first
Intramolecular transesterification is not the main concern.
The acidic OH would protonate and destroy the Grignard reagent
Correct: a silyl ether removes the acidic proton.
questions.x: A Grignard reagent behaves like a carbanion, a very strong base. Any O–H proton in the molecule, here the alcohol at pKa about 16, protonates it immediately to give methane and an alkoxide, which uses up the reagent before it reaches the ester. Converting the OH to a silyl ether removes the acidic proton, so the Grignard adds to the ester, and fluoride later removes the protecting group.

questions.q: An IR spectrum shows a broad, strong absorption at 3200–3550 cm⁻¹ and no peak near 1700 cm⁻¹. Which functional group is present?
o: Ketone C=O
A ketone would show a strong band near 1715 cm⁻¹.
Carboxylic acid
Acids also show a C=O band near 1710 cm⁻¹.
Alcohol O–H
Correct: hydrogen bonding broadens the O–H stretch.
Nitrile C≡N
Nitriles absorb near 2250 cm⁻¹.
questions.x: A broad, strong band from about 3200 to 3550 cm⁻¹ is the O–H stretch of an alcohol, broadened by hydrogen bonding. With no carbonyl band near 1700 cm⁻¹, any C=O compound is ruled out, including a carboxylic acid, whose O–H is even broader (2500–3300 cm⁻¹) and always comes with a C=O band. Nitriles absorb sharply near 2250 cm⁻¹.

questions.q: An IR spectrum shows a very broad band from 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹ and a strong band at 1710 cm⁻¹. What class of compound is this?
o: Carboxylic acid
Correct: very broad dimer O–H stretch plus a C=O stretch.
Alcohol
Alcohols lack the C=O band.
Ester
Esters show C=O near 1735 cm⁻¹ but no O–H.
Ketone
Ketones lack the very broad O–H band.
questions.x: Carboxylic acids give two signature IR bands. Their O–H stretch is extremely broad, from about 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹, because the acid exists as hydrogen-bonded dimers, and it often overlaps the C–H peaks. Their C=O stretch is strong, near 1710 cm⁻¹. Alcohols have the O–H band but no C=O, and esters and ketones have C=O but no O–H, so only an acid shows both.

questions.q: A secondary alcohol is oxidized to a ketone. How would IR spectroscopy confirm completion?
o: The C–H stretches near 2900 cm⁻¹ disappear
The alkyl C–H bonds remain in the ketone.
The broad ~3300 cm⁻¹ band disappears and a sharp ~1715 cm⁻¹ band appears
Correct: loss of O–H and gain of C=O.
A peak appears at 2250 cm⁻¹
That indicates a nitrile.
A new broad band appears at 3300 cm⁻¹
That signals an O–H, which is being removed.
questions.x: Oxidation turns the C–OH of the alcohol into a C=O, so the reaction can be followed by the loss of one band and the gain of another. The broad O–H stretch near 3300 cm⁻¹ should disappear, and a sharp, strong C=O stretch near 1715 cm⁻¹ should appear. The alkyl C–H stretches near 2900 cm⁻¹ stay, because those bonds are not involved in the oxidation.

questions.q: A ¹H NMR spectrum shows a singlet at 9.8 ppm integrating to 1H. Which group does this suggest?
o: A carboxylic acid OH
Acid protons are typically broad near 10–12 ppm.
An aromatic C–H
Aromatic protons appear near 6.5–8 ppm.
An alcohol OH
Alcohol OH signals usually appear between 1 and 5 ppm.
An aldehyde CHO proton
Correct: aldehyde protons appear near 9–10 ppm.
questions.x: Aldehyde protons sit on a carbonyl carbon and are strongly deshielded by the electronegative oxygen and the magnetic anisotropy of the C=O, so they appear near 9–10 ppm. Here the signal integrates to 1H, consistent with a CHO group. Carboxylic acid OH protons are usually farther downfield (10–12 ppm) and broad, while aromatic protons appear near 6.5–8 ppm.

questions.q: What pattern does the ethyl group of ethyl acetate show in ¹H NMR?
o: A 2H triplet and a 3H quartet
Reverses the splitting; a CH₂ next to CH₃ is a quartet.
Two singlets
Adjacent CH₂ and CH₃ protons couple to each other.
A 2H doublet and a 3H septet
That pattern does not match an ethyl group.
A 2H quartet and a 3H triplet
Correct: by the n + 1 rule, CH₂ is split by 3 H and CH₃ by 2 H.
questions.x: By the n + 1 rule, a set of protons is split into n + 1 peaks by n equivalent neighbors. In the OCH₂CH₃ group, the CH₂ has three neighbors on the CH₃ and appears as a quartet (2H), while the CH₃ has two neighbors on the CH₂ and appears as a triplet (3H). The acetyl CH₃ has no neighbors with H and is a singlet. Reversing the multiplicities is the usual error.

questions.q: Which compound gives only one signal in its ¹H NMR spectrum?
o: Methyl acetate
Its two methyl groups are in different environments, giving two signals.
Ethanol
Ethanol has three distinct proton environments.
Acetone
Correct: all six hydrogens are equivalent.
Propanal
Propanal has three distinct proton environments.
questions.x: The number of ¹H NMR signals equals the number of distinct proton environments. In acetone, (CH₃)₂C=O, the two methyl groups are related by symmetry, so all six H atoms are equivalent and give a single singlet. Methyl acetate also has two methyl groups, but one is on the carbonyl carbon and the other on oxygen, so they are in different environments and give two signals.

questions.q: Which methyl halide's protons appear farthest downfield in ¹H NMR?
o: CH₃Br
Bromine deshields less than F or Cl.
CH₃F
Correct: fluorine is most electronegative and deshields most strongly.
CH₃Cl
Chlorine is less electronegative than fluorine.
CH₃I
Iodine is least electronegative here, giving the most upfield signal.
questions.x: A proton's chemical shift moves downfield as nearby electronegative atoms pull electron density away from it, which reduces its shielding. Fluorine is the most electronegative halogen, so CH₃F protons are farthest downfield (about 4.3 ppm), followed by CH₃Cl (about 3.1), CH₃Br (about 2.7) and CH₃I (about 2.2). The heavier halogens are larger, but electronegativity is what controls the shift.

questions.q: A compound C₃H₇Br shows a 6H doublet and a 1H septet in its ¹H NMR spectrum. What is it?
o: 2-Bromopropane
Correct: two equivalent CH₃ groups split by one CH, and the CH split by six H.
