Bromocyclopropane
Its formula is C₃H₅Br.
1-Bromopropane
It would show three signals: triplet, sextet and triplet.
1-Bromo-2-methylpropane
Its formula is C₄H₉Br.
questions.x: A 6H doublet next to a 1H septet is the signature of an isopropyl group. The two equivalent methyls are split into a doublet by the single CH, and that CH is split into a septet by its six neighboring H (6 + 1 = 7). For C₃H₇Br, this fits (CH₃)₂CHBr, 2-bromopropane. 1-Bromopropane has three different environments and would show three signals.

questions.q: After a few drops of D₂O are shaken with an NMR sample, one broad signal disappears. What kind of proton produced it?
o: An aldehyde C–H
The aldehyde proton is bonded to carbon and does not exchange.
An aromatic C–H
C–H protons do not exchange with D₂O under these conditions.
An exchangeable O–H or N–H proton
Correct: these protons exchange with deuterium, which is silent in ¹H NMR.
A methyl C–H
Alkyl C–H protons do not exchange.
questions.x: Protons bonded to oxygen or nitrogen are acidic enough to exchange quickly with D₂O, so O–H and N–H become O–D and N–D. Deuterium does not appear in a ¹H NMR spectrum, so after shaking with D₂O those signals vanish, and they were often broad to begin with. Protons bonded to carbon, including aldehyde and aromatic C–H, do not exchange under these conditions.

questions.q: How many signals appear in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of pentan-3-one?
o: Correct: symmetry gives one carbonyl carbon, one CH₂ type and one CH₃ type.
Overlooks the carbonyl carbon.
That would be butan-2-one or another unsymmetrical ketone.
Ignores the mirror symmetry of the molecule.
questions.x: Each set of symmetry-equivalent carbons gives one ¹³C signal. Pentan-3-one, CH₃CH₂C(=O)CH₂CH₃, has a mirror plane through the carbonyl carbon, so its two CH₃ carbons are equivalent, as are its two CH₂ carbons. That leaves three environments (CH₃, CH₂ and C=O) and three signals. Counting all five carbons separately ignores this symmetry.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a state function?
o: Enthalpy
Enthalpy depends only on the current state of the system.
Work done by a gas during expansion
Correct: work depends on the path taken, not only on the initial and final states.
Internal energy
ΔU is fixed by the initial and final states alone.
Entropy
Entropy is a state function; ΔS is path independent.
questions.note: Heat and work are path functions, but their sum ΔU is a state function.
questions.x: A state function depends only on the current state of a system, so its change is fixed by the initial and final states. Enthalpy, internal energy and entropy all qualify. Work and heat are path functions: the same start and end points can be connected by paths doing very different amounts of work, even though their sum, ΔU, is path independent.

questions.q: A gas absorbs 300 J of heat and does 120 J of work on its surroundings. What is ΔU of the gas?
o: Adds the work done by the gas instead of subtracting it.
Reverses the signs of both heat and work.
Confuses the work term with the change in internal energy.
questions.note: Sign convention: heat in is +q; work done BY the system is −w.
questions.x: The first law is ΔU = q + w, where w is work done on the system. Heat absorbed is positive (+300 J), and work done by the gas on the surroundings is negative (−120 J), so ΔU = +180 J. The common error is adding 120 J, which treats work done by the gas as energy gained rather than energy spent.

questions.q: Surroundings do 250 J of work compressing a gas while the gas releases 400 J of heat. What is ΔU of the gas?
o: Treats the released heat as positive.
Treats work done on the gas as negative.
Reverses the sign of the overall result.
questions.x: With ΔU = q + w, heat released by the gas is negative (−400 J) and work done on the gas by compression is positive (+250 J). The gas loses more energy as heat than it gains as work, so ΔU = −150 J. Getting the magnitude right but the sign wrong usually comes from flipping the convention for one of the two terms.

questions.q: Which type of system can exchange energy, but not matter, with its surroundings?
o: Closed system
Correct: a closed system allows heat and work to cross the boundary but no mass.
Open system
An open system exchanges both matter and energy.
Isolated system
An isolated system exchanges neither matter nor energy.
Isothermal system
Isothermal describes constant temperature, not what crosses the boundary.
questions.x: Systems are classified by what crosses their boundary. Open systems exchange matter and energy, closed systems exchange only energy (as heat or work), and isolated systems exchange neither. A sealed flask that can be heated is closed. Isothermal is a tempting choice but describes a process condition (constant T), not a type of boundary.

questions.q: According to the third law of thermodynamics, which of the following has an entropy of exactly zero?
o: Any element in its standard state at 25 °C
That condition defines ΔH°f = 0, not S = 0; elements have positive S° at 25 °C.
A perfect crystal of a pure substance at 0 K
Correct: a perfect crystal at absolute zero has only one possible microstate.
An ideal gas at 0 °C
0 °C is 273 K, and gases have large positive entropies.
A pure liquid at its freezing point
A liquid at its freezing point still has substantial molecular disorder.
questions.note: Trap: zero ΔH°f for elements is a convention; zero S applies only to perfect crystals at 0 K.
questions.x: The third law sets an absolute zero of entropy: a perfect crystal of a pure substance at 0 K has a single microstate, so S = k ln 1 = 0. Every real substance above 0 K has positive absolute entropy. The trap is mixing this up with the formation-enthalpy convention, where elements in their standard states are assigned ΔH°f = 0, which says nothing about entropy.

questions.q: For an ideal gas undergoing a reversible isothermal expansion, which statement is true?
o: q = 0, so ΔU equals the work done
No heat flow describes an adiabatic process, not an isothermal one.
w = 0, so ΔU equals the heat absorbed
Zero work describes a constant-volume process.
ΔU is positive because the gas expands
Isothermal means T is constant, so an ideal gas has ΔU = 0.
ΔU = 0, so the heat absorbed equals the work done by the gas
Correct: ideal-gas internal energy depends only on T, so q = −w.
questions.x: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, so any isothermal ideal-gas process has ΔU = 0. Then q = −w: all the heat absorbed leaves as work done by the expanding gas. Thinking ΔU must rise because the gas expands is the trap; expansion changes volume, not the molecules' kinetic energy, when T is held constant.

questions.q: An ideal gas expands adiabatically against a constant external pressure. What happens to its temperature?
o: It decreases, because the gas does work with no heat input
Correct: q = 0, so ΔU = w < 0, and an ideal gas's T falls with U.
It stays constant because no heat is exchanged
No heat flow does not mean constant T; the work lowers internal energy.
It increases because the gas occupies more volume
Expansion work removes energy from the gas, so T cannot rise.
It cannot be predicted without the heat capacity
The heat capacity sets the size of ΔT, but the sign is fixed by ΔU = w < 0.
questions.x: Adiabatic means q = 0, so ΔU = w. An expanding gas pushes on its surroundings and does work, making w negative, so ΔU falls; for an ideal gas, lower U means lower T. No heat exchange does not mean constant temperature, because work alone can change internal energy. Heat capacity only sets how big the drop is, not its direction.

questions.q: According to the second law of thermodynamics, every spontaneous process:
o: Increases the entropy of the system
System entropy can fall if the surroundings gain more entropy.
Decreases the enthalpy of the system
Endothermic processes such as ice melting can be spontaneous.
Increases the entropy of the universe
Correct: ΔS_universe > 0 for any spontaneous process.
Increases the total energy of the universe
The first law says the energy of the universe is constant.
questions.x: The second law states that the entropy of the universe (system plus surroundings) increases in every spontaneous process. A system's own entropy can fall, as when water freezes below 0 °C, as long as the heat released raises the surroundings' entropy by more. Spontaneous processes can also be endothermic, so neither system entropy nor enthalpy alone decides spontaneity.

questions.q: A gas expands from 2.0 L to 5.0 L against a constant external pressure of 1.0 atm. Taking w as work done on the gas, what is w?
o: +3.0 L·atm
A gas doing work on its surroundings loses energy, so w is negative.
−5.0 L·atm
Uses the final volume instead of the change in volume.
−7.0 L·atm
Adds the two volumes instead of subtracting them.
−3.0 L·atm
Correct: w = −PΔV = −(1.0 atm)(3.0 L) = −3.0 L·atm (about −300 J).
questions.note: 1 L·atm ≈ 100 J.
questions.x: Expansion work against a constant external pressure is w = −P_ext ΔV, with w defined as work done on the gas. Here ΔV = +3.0 L, so w = −3.0 L·atm, about −300 J. The sign is negative because the gas spends energy pushing back the surroundings; using the final volume instead of ΔV is the other common slip.

questions.q: For a process at constant pressure in which only pressure–volume work occurs, the heat exchanged equals:
o: ΔU
ΔU equals the heat exchanged at constant volume, not constant pressure.
ΔH
Correct: enthalpy change is defined as the heat flow at constant pressure.
ΔG
ΔG is the maximum non-expansion work, not the heat.
TΔS
TΔS equals heat only for a reversible process.
questions.x: Enthalpy is defined as H = U + PV, so at constant pressure ΔH = ΔU + PΔV = q_p when only PV work occurs. That is why coffee-cup calorimetry measures ΔH. At constant volume no PV work is done and the heat equals ΔU instead, which is the tempting distractor here.

questions.q: Which statement about ΔS of the universe for an idealized reversible process is true?
o: It equals zero
Correct: reversible processes generate no net entropy; system and surroundings changes cancel.
It is always positive
Positive ΔS_universe describes irreversible, spontaneous processes.
It is always negative
A negative ΔS_universe would violate the second law.
It equals ΔH/T of the system
ΔH/T gives the system's ΔS for a reversible change at constant T and P, not the universe's.
questions.x: A reversible process is an idealized limit carried out through equilibrium states, so it generates no new entropy: the system's entropy change is exactly balanced by the surroundings', and ΔS_universe = 0. Real, irreversible spontaneous processes have ΔS_universe > 0. A negative value would mean a process running backward against the second law.

questions.q: Hess's law works because enthalpy is:
o: Always negative for real reactions
Many reactions are endothermic; sign is irrelevant to Hess's law.
Equal to the heat at constant volume
Heat at constant volume is ΔU, and this is not the basis of Hess's law.
A state function
Correct: ΔH depends only on initial and final states, so any path gives the same total.
Independent of the amounts of reactants
ΔH is extensive and scales with the amount reacting.
questions.x: Hess's law says the enthalpy change for an overall reaction equals the sum of the enthalpy changes for any set of steps that add up to it. This works only because H is a state function: ΔH depends on start and end states, not the route. The sign of ΔH is irrelevant, and ΔH does scale with amount, so neither explains the law.

questions.q: Given C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −394 kJ and CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −283 kJ, what is ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g)?
o: Correct: keep the first, reverse the second (+283 kJ), and add: −394 + 283 = −111 kJ.
Adds both equations without reversing the CO equation.
Reverses the wrong equation.
Uses only the second equation.
questions.x: Arrange the given equations so they sum to the target. Keep C + O₂ → CO₂ (−394 kJ) and reverse CO + ½O₂ → CO₂ to CO₂ → CO + ½O₂ (+283 kJ). CO₂ and ½O₂ cancel, leaving C + ½O₂ → CO with ΔH = −111 kJ. Forgetting to flip the sign of a reversed equation is the most common Hess's-law error.

questions.q: If ΔH for A → 2B is +80 kJ, what is ΔH for 4B → 2A?
o: Doubles the value but forgets to flip the sign for the reverse direction.
Correct: reversing flips the sign and doubling doubles it: −2(80) = −160 kJ.
−80 kJ
Flips the sign but forgets to double for twice the amount.
−40 kJ
Halves the value instead of doubling it.
questions.x: Enthalpy changes follow the reaction as written. Reversing a reaction flips the sign of ΔH, and multiplying the coefficients by a factor multiplies ΔH by the same factor because enthalpy is extensive. 4B → 2A is the reverse of A → 2B doubled, so ΔH = −2 × 80 = −160 kJ.

questions.q: Using ΔH°f (kJ/mol): CH₄(g) −75, CO₂(g) −394, H₂O(l) −286, what is ΔH° for CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)?
o: Counts only one mole of water.
Subtracts products from reactants instead of reactants from products.
Adds the ΔH°f of CH₄ instead of subtracting it.
questions.note: ΔH°rxn = ΣΔH°f(products) − ΣΔH°f(reactants); O₂ contributes zero.
questions.x: ΔH°rxn = ΣnΔH°f(products) − ΣnΔH°f(reactants), and elements in their standard states such as O₂ contribute zero. Products: −394 + 2(−286) = −966 kJ; reactants: −75 kJ. So ΔH° = −966 − (−75) = −891 kJ. Remember to weight each value by its coefficient and subtract the reactant sum, which here makes the answer less negative.

questions.q: What is ΔH°f of O₂(g) at 25 °C?
o: +498 kJ/mol
That is roughly the O=O bond energy, not a formation enthalpy.
−286 kJ/mol
That is ΔH°f of liquid water.
+142 kJ/mol
That is ΔH°f of ozone, O₃, which is not oxygen's standard state.
0 kJ/mol
Correct: an element in its standard state has a formation enthalpy of zero by definition.
questions.x: Standard enthalpies of formation are measured relative to elements in their most stable form at 1 bar and the stated temperature, which are assigned ΔH°f = 0. For oxygen that form is O₂(g). Ozone is a different allotrope and has a positive ΔH°f, and the O=O bond energy describes breaking O₂ into atoms, not forming it.

questions.q: Which reaction has a ΔH° equal to ΔH°f of NaCl(s)?
o: Na(s) + ½Cl₂(g) → NaCl(s)
Correct: one mole of product formed from elements in their standard states.
Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s)
That is the reverse of lattice dissociation, not formation from elements.
2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s)
This forms 2 mol, so its ΔH° is twice ΔH°f.
Na(s) + Cl(g) → NaCl(s)
Chlorine's standard state is Cl₂(g), not free atoms.
questions.x: A formation reaction makes exactly one mole of a compound from its elements in their standard states. For NaCl that means solid sodium and diatomic chlorine gas: Na(s) + ½Cl₂(g) → NaCl(s). Using gaseous ions gives the lattice-energy process instead, and writing the reaction for 2 mol doubles ΔH, so neither equals ΔH°f.

questions.q: A reaction vessel becomes cold to the touch as the reaction proceeds at constant pressure. Which is true?
o: ΔH < 0; the system releases heat
Releasing heat would warm the vessel.
ΔH > 0; heat flows from the surroundings into the system
Correct: the reaction absorbs heat, cooling the vessel and your hand.
ΔH > 0; the system releases heat
A positive ΔH means heat is absorbed, not released.
ΔH = 0; the cooling reflects only entropy
At constant pressure, heat flow into the system is ΔH, so ΔH is not zero.
questions.x: Heat flow is judged from the system's point of view. If the vessel and your hand get cold, heat is leaving them and entering the reacting system, so the reaction is endothermic and ΔH > 0. A warm vessel would signal an exothermic reaction. At constant pressure the heat absorbed is ΔH, so it cannot be zero here.

questions.q: Burning 2.0 mol of a fuel releases 1600 kJ. How much heat is released when 0.25 mol of the fuel burns?
o: 400 kJ
Uses 1600 kJ per mole instead of per 2 mol.
800 kJ
That is the heat per mole; it ignores the 0.25 mol.
200 kJ
Correct: 1600/2 = 800 kJ per mol; 0.25 × 800 = 200 kJ.
Divides by 0.25 instead of multiplying.
questions.x: Reaction enthalpy is extensive, so heat scales directly with the amount reacting. First find heat per mole: 1600 kJ ÷ 2.0 mol = 800 kJ/mol. Then 0.25 mol × 800 kJ/mol = 200 kJ. Forgetting that the 1600 kJ belongs to 2 mol, not 1 mol, doubles the answer to 400 kJ.

questions.q: Why is the molar enthalpy of vaporization of water much larger than its enthalpy of fusion?
o: Vaporization breaks covalent O–H bonds
Phase changes do not break covalent bonds within molecules.
Vaporization occurs at a higher temperature, and ΔH scales directly with T
Transition enthalpies reflect attractions overcome, not the temperature itself.
Liquid water has stronger hydrogen bonds than ice
Ice has the more complete, ordered hydrogen-bond network.
Vaporization overcomes nearly all hydrogen bonding, while melting disrupts only part of it
Correct: gas-phase molecules are essentially free of intermolecular attractions.
questions.x: Phase changes overcome intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds. Melting only loosens the hydrogen-bond network so molecules can slide past one another, while vaporization must separate molecules almost completely. That is why water's ΔHvap (about 41 kJ/mol) is roughly seven times its ΔHfus (about 6 kJ/mol). Ice actually has the more complete hydrogen-bond network, not weaker bonds.

questions.q: Given A → B, ΔH = +30 kJ; B → C, ΔH = −50 kJ; and D → C, ΔH = −10 kJ, what is ΔH for A → D?
o: −10 kJ
Correct: A → C is +30 − 50 = −20 kJ; then reverse D → C (+10 kJ): −20 + 10 = −10 kJ.
−30 kJ
Adds D → C without reversing it.
−20 kJ
Stops at C and omits the C → D step.
+10 kJ
Reports the value for the reverse reaction, D → A.
questions.x: Chain the steps so intermediates cancel. A → B (+30) plus B → C (−50) gives A → C at −20 kJ. To get from C to D, reverse D → C, which flips its sign to +10 kJ. Total A → D = −20 + 10 = −10 kJ. Adding −10 kJ without reversing is the tempting slip.

questions.q: Using bond energies (kJ/mol) H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 431, estimate ΔH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g).
o: Uses bonds formed minus bonds broken, reversing the sign.
Counts only one H–Cl bond formed: 679 − 431.
Counts only one H–Cl bond formed and ignores bonds broken.
questions.note: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
questions.x: Bond-energy estimates use ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed), because breaking bonds costs energy and forming bonds releases it. Broken: H–H + Cl–Cl = 436 + 243 = 679 kJ. Formed: two H–Cl = 862 kJ. ΔH ≈ −183 kJ, exothermic. Reversing the order of subtraction gives the right magnitude with the wrong sign.

questions.q: Breaking a chemical bond is always:
o: Exothermic
Energy is released when bonds form, not when they break.
Exothermic for weak bonds only
Even weak bonds require energy to break.
Endothermic only in the gas phase
Bond breaking requires energy regardless of phase.
Endothermic
Correct: separating bonded atoms requires an input of energy.
questions.note: Trap: 'ATP has high-energy bonds' does not mean breaking them releases energy; the overall reaction does.
questions.x: Atoms in a bond sit in a potential-energy well, so pulling them apart always requires energy input; bond breaking is endothermic and bond formation is exothermic. The energy released in reactions such as ATP hydrolysis comes from forming new, stronger bonds and better solvation of the products, not from the breaking itself.

questions.q: Using bond energies (kJ/mol) C–H 413, Cl–Cl 243, C–Cl 328, H–Cl 431, estimate ΔH for CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.
o: Uses bonds formed minus bonds broken.
Counts only the bonds broken.
Counts only the bonds formed.
questions.note: Only bonds that change need to be counted; the three spectator C–H bonds cancel.
questions.x: Count only the bonds that actually change. One C–H (413) and one Cl–Cl (243) break, costing 656 kJ; one C–Cl (328) and one H–Cl (431) form, releasing 759 kJ. ΔH ≈ 656 − 759 = −103 kJ. The three untouched C–H bonds appear on both sides and cancel, so including them is unnecessary.

questions.q: Why are reaction enthalpies estimated from bond energies less accurate than those from ΔH°f values?
o: Bond energies ignore whether bonds are broken or formed
The method explicitly tracks bonds broken and formed.
Bond energies apply only to liquids and solids
Bond energies are defined for gas-phase molecules.
Bond energies include entropy contributions
Bond enthalpies are purely enthalpic quantities.
Tabulated bond energies are averages over many different molecules
Correct: a given bond's strength varies with its molecular environment.
questions.x: Tabulated bond energies are averages: a C–H bond in methane is not exactly as strong as one in ethanol, because neighboring atoms and resonance change bond strength. Formation enthalpies are measured for the specific compounds, so they give exact reaction enthalpies through Hess's law. Bond energies are gas-phase values, which is a further limitation, but averaging is the main source of error.

questions.q: Which nitrogen–nitrogen bond has the largest bond dissociation energy?
o: N=N
A double bond is weaker than a triple bond between the same atoms.
N≡N
Correct: a triple bond (one σ, two π) is the strongest and shortest.
N–N
A single N–N bond is the weakest of the three.
All are equal because the atoms are identical
Bond order, not just atom identity, determines bond strength.
questions.x: Bond strength rises with bond order: more shared electron pairs hold the nuclei together more tightly and pull them closer. N≡N has one σ and two π bonds and a dissociation energy near 945 kJ/mol, far above N=N and N–N. That strength is why N₂ is so unreactive. Identical atoms do not mean identical bonds, because bond order differs.

questions.q: For A₂ + B₂ → 2AB, ΔH = −100 kJ. If the A–A bond energy is 200 kJ/mol and B–B is 300 kJ/mol, what is the A–B bond energy?
o: 600 kJ/mol
Forgets that two A–B bonds form.
200 kJ/mol
300 kJ/mol
Correct: 500 − 2x = −100, so 2x = 600 and x = 300 kJ/mol.
250 kJ/mol
Averages the A–A and B–B bond energies.
questions.x: Use ΔH = Σ(broken) − Σ(formed) and solve for the unknown. Breaking A–A and B–B costs 200 + 300 = 500 kJ; forming two A–B bonds releases 2x. So 500 − 2x = −100, giving x = 300 kJ/mol. Forgetting that the equation forms two A–B bonds gives 600, double the right value.

questions.q: A reaction forms bonds that are stronger overall than the bonds it breaks. What is most likely true?
o: ΔH < 0
Correct: more energy is released forming bonds than is absorbed breaking them.
ΔH > 0
That would require breaking stronger bonds than are formed.
ΔS > 0
Bond strengths relate to enthalpy, not entropy.
The activation energy is small
Product bond strengths do not set the height of the barrier.
questions.x: Reaction enthalpy reflects the balance between energy absorbed to break bonds and energy released when bonds form. If the bonds formed are stronger overall, more energy is released than absorbed, so ΔH < 0. Bond strengths in reactants and products say nothing direct about the activation energy, which depends on the transition state.

questions.q: Which process has a negative ΔS for the system?
o: Ice melting
Melting increases disorder.
Water vapor condensing to liquid
Correct: a gas becoming a liquid loses freedom of motion and microstates.
Dry ice subliming
Solid to gas is a large entropy increase.
N₂O₄(g) → 2NO₂(g)
The moles of gas increase, so entropy increases.
questions.x: Entropy reflects how many microstates are available, and it rises sharply from solid to liquid to gas. Condensation turns freely moving gas molecules into a much more constrained liquid, so ΔS < 0. Melting, sublimation, and reactions that increase moles of gas, such as N₂O₄ → 2NO₂, all increase entropy.

questions.q: Which reaction has the most positive ΔS°?
o: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g)
Moles of gas fall from 4 to 2, so ΔS° is negative.
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g)
Moles of gas fall from 3 to 2, so ΔS° is negative.
2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g)
Correct: a gas is produced from liquids only.
H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)
Moles of gas are unchanged, so ΔS° is small.
questions.note: Quick check: count moles of gas on each side.
questions.x: The quickest way to predict the sign of ΔS° is to compare moles of gas, since gases have far higher entropy than liquids or solids. Decomposing liquid H₂O₂ to produce O₂ gas creates gas from no gas, giving the largest increase. Reactions that combine gas molecules into fewer molecules, like ammonia synthesis, have negative ΔS°.

questions.q: Which substance has the highest standard molar entropy at 25 °C?
o: CH₄(g)
Also a gas, but fewer atoms means fewer accessible microstates.
H₂O(l)
Liquids have much lower molar entropies than gases.
C(s, diamond)
A rigid covalent crystal has one of the lowest molar entropies.
C₃H₈(g)
Correct: a gas with many atoms has the most rotational and vibrational microstates.
questions.x: Standard molar entropy depends first on phase (gas ≫ liquid > solid) and then, within a phase, on molecular complexity. More atoms give more ways to rotate and vibrate, so propane (about 270 J/(mol·K)) beats methane (about 186). Diamond's rigid lattice gives it one of the lowest molar entropies known.

questions.q: Why does a substance's entropy increase as its temperature rises within one phase?
o: More energy levels become accessible, so the number of microstates grows
Correct: higher T spreads energy over more molecular states.
Its molar mass increases
Heating does not change molar mass.
Its intermolecular forces become stronger
Intermolecular forces do not strengthen on heating.
Its volume always decreases
Most substances expand on heating, and volume loss would lower entropy.
questions.x: Raising the temperature gives molecules more energy to distribute among translational, rotational and vibrational levels, so more energy levels are populated and the number of accessible microstates grows. That is why S increases with T even without a phase change. Molar mass and intermolecular forces do not change on heating, so they cannot explain it.

questions.q: One mole of ice melts reversibly at 0 °C. If ΔH°fus = 6.0 kJ/mol, what is ΔS for the melting?
o: −22 J/(mol·K)
Melting absorbs heat and increases disorder, so ΔS is positive.
+22 J/(mol·K)
Correct: ΔS = q_rev/T = 6000 J ÷ 273 K ≈ +22 J/(mol·K).
Leaves ΔH in kJ while reporting the answer in J.
Undefined, because the temperature does not change
ΔS = q_rev/T uses the constant T, not ΔT.
questions.note: Always use kelvins in ΔS = ΔH/T.
questions.x: At a phase-transition temperature the change is reversible, so ΔS = q_rev/T = ΔHfus/T. Convert kJ to J and °C to K: 6000 J/mol ÷ 273 K ≈ +22 J/(mol·K). The sign is positive because melting absorbs heat and the liquid is more disordered. Leaving ΔH in kJ produces a value a thousand times too small.

questions.q: Two different ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure mix spontaneously when a partition is removed. The main driving force is:
o: A strongly negative ΔH of mixing
Ideal gases have no intermolecular interactions, so ΔH of mixing is zero.
Formation of attractions between the two gases
Ideal gas particles do not attract one another.
An increase in entropy as each gas spreads into a larger volume
Correct: each gas gains positional microstates; ΔH ≈ 0 for ideal gases.
A decrease in the total pressure
The total pressure stays the same in this setup.
questions.x: Ideal gas particles do not interact, so mixing them involves no enthalpy change at all. The driving force is entropy: once the partition is removed, each gas spreads over the whole volume, gaining positional microstates. This entropy-driven mixing is why gases always mix spontaneously, and why answers based on attractions or heat release fail here.

questions.q: A hot metal block cools in a cooler room, and the block's entropy decreases. Why is this process still spontaneous?
o: The room gains more entropy than the block loses, because it receives the heat at a lower temperature
Correct: q/T_room > q/T_block, so ΔS_universe > 0.
The entropy of the universe is conserved
Entropy is not conserved; it increases in spontaneous processes.
The first law requires heat to flow from hot to cold
The first law conserves energy but says nothing about direction.
The block's entropy actually increases as it cools
Cooling lowers the block's thermal energy and entropy.
questions.x: Heat q leaves the hot block and enters the cooler room. The block's entropy falls by about q/T_hot, while the room's rises by q/T_cold. Because T_cold is smaller, the room's gain is larger, so ΔS_universe > 0. The first law only says energy is conserved; the second law is what makes heat flow from hot to cold.

questions.q: A reaction at 300 K has ΔH = −60 kJ. What is ΔS of the surroundings?
o: Heat released by the system enters the surroundings, raising their entropy.
Leaves ΔH in kJ while reporting J/K.
Multiplies by T instead of dividing.
Correct: ΔS_surr = −ΔH/T = +60,000 J ÷ 300 K = +200 J/K.
questions.x: Heat released by the system is absorbed by the surroundings, so at constant T and P, ΔS_surr = −ΔH_sys/T. Here −(−60,000 J)/300 K = +200 J/K. Exothermic reactions always raise the entropy of the surroundings. Forgetting to convert kJ to J gives 0.20 J/K, a thousandfold error.

questions.q: Which change increases the entropy of a gas sample held at constant temperature?
o: Compressing it to a higher pressure
Compression reduces the volume available, lowering entropy.
Expanding it into a larger volume
Correct: more volume gives each molecule more positional microstates.
Condensing part of it to liquid
Condensation lowers entropy.
Dissolving part of it in water
A gas dissolving in a liquid loses freedom of motion.
questions.x: At constant temperature, a gas's entropy depends on how much volume its molecules can occupy; for an ideal gas ΔS = nR ln(V₂/V₁). Expanding into a larger volume increases positional microstates and raises S. Compression, condensation and dissolving all confine the molecules more and lower the gas's entropy.

questions.q: Dissolving a certain salt in water is endothermic, yet it dissolves spontaneously. What must be true?
o: ΔS is negative
With ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0, ΔG would be positive at every temperature.
ΔG is positive because ΔH is positive
A spontaneous process has ΔG < 0.
ΔS is positive, and TΔS exceeds ΔH
Correct: with ΔH > 0, ΔG < 0 requires TΔS > ΔH.
The process lowers the entropy of the universe
Spontaneous processes always raise ΔS_universe.
questions.x: Spontaneity at constant T and P requires ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0. With ΔH positive, the only way to make ΔG negative is a positive ΔS large enough that TΔS exceeds ΔH. Dissolving salts such as NH₄NO₃ works this way: the ions dispersing in water raise entropy enough to overcome the heat absorbed.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔG < 0 under a given set of conditions. Which conclusion is valid?
o: The reaction is thermodynamically favorable under those conditions
Correct: negative ΔG means the forward reaction proceeds spontaneously.
The reaction is fast
ΔG tells nothing about rate; that depends on the activation energy.
The reaction is endothermic
ΔG alone does not reveal the sign of ΔH.
K is less than 1
K relates to ΔG°, not ΔG; ΔG also depends on Q.
questions.note: Thermodynamics says whether; kinetics says how fast.
questions.x: ΔG < 0 means the forward process is thermodynamically favorable under the stated conditions: it can proceed without outside work. It says nothing about speed, which depends on the activation energy; diamond turning to graphite is favorable but immeasurably slow. Nor does ΔG alone reveal ΔH or K, since ΔG also depends on the current Q.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔH = +40 kJ/mol and ΔS = +100 J/(mol·K). Under what conditions is it spontaneous?
o: Only below 400 K
With ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, the −TΔS term wins at high T, not low T.
Only above 0.4 K
Fails to convert kJ to J before dividing.
At all temperatures
ΔH > 0 makes ΔG positive at low temperature.
Only above 400 K
Correct: ΔG < 0 when T > ΔH/ΔS = 40,000/100 = 400 K.
questions.x: With ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is positive at low T and becomes negative once TΔS outweighs ΔH. The crossover is T = ΔH/ΔS = 40,000 J ÷ 100 J/K = 400 K, so the reaction is spontaneous above 400 K. Entropy-driven reactions are favored by heat, not cold.

questions.q: Which combination of signs makes a reaction nonspontaneous at every temperature?
o: ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0
This is spontaneous at low temperatures.
ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0
Correct: both terms make ΔG = ΔH − TΔS positive at all T.
ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0
This is spontaneous at high temperatures.
ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0
This is spontaneous at all temperatures.
questions.x: In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, a positive ΔH adds a positive term, and a negative ΔS makes −TΔS positive too. With both terms positive, ΔG is positive at every temperature, so the reaction is never spontaneous as written. The opposite signs (ΔH < 0, ΔS > 0) make a reaction spontaneous at all temperatures.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔH = −80 kJ/mol and ΔS = −200 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG at 500 K?
o: −180 kJ/mol
Sign error: subtracts TΔS as if ΔS were positive.
−80 kJ/mol
Ignores the TΔS term.
+20 kJ/mol
+100 kJ/mol
Reports only −TΔS and ignores ΔH.
questions.x: Use ΔG = ΔH − TΔS with consistent units: ΔS = −200 J/(mol·K) = −0.200 kJ/(mol·K). Then −TΔS = −(500)(−0.200) = +100 kJ/mol, and ΔG = −80 + 100 = +20 kJ/mol. At this high temperature the unfavorable entropy term outweighs the favorable enthalpy, so the reaction is nonspontaneous.

questions.q: A protein folds with ΔH = −80 kJ/mol and ΔS = −200 J/(mol·K). Above about what temperature does unfolding become favored?
o: Correct: ΔG = 0 at T = ΔH/ΔS = 80,000/200 = 400 K; above this, −TΔS dominates.
Fails to convert kJ to J.
Inverts the ratio, dividing ΔS by ΔH.
It never unfolds because ΔH < 0
At high T, the positive −TΔS term makes folding unfavorable.
questions.x: Folding releases heat (ΔH < 0) but reduces the chain's conformational freedom (ΔS < 0), so it is favored only at low temperature. ΔG = 0 at T = ΔH/ΔS = 80,000 J ÷ 200 J/K = 400 K; above that, −TΔS dominates and unfolding is favored. A negative ΔH does not guarantee spontaneity at every temperature.

questions.q: For vaporization of a pure liquid at its normal boiling point and 1 atm, which is true?
o: ΔG < 0 and ΔH = 0
Vaporization always absorbs heat, and the phases are at equilibrium.
ΔG > 0 because ΔH > 0
At the boiling point, the TΔS term exactly offsets ΔH.
ΔS = 0 because the temperature is constant
Liquid to gas is a large entropy increase even at constant T.
ΔG = 0 and ΔS = ΔH/T
Correct: liquid and vapor are in equilibrium, so ΔH = TΔS.
questions.x: At the normal boiling point, liquid and vapor at 1 atm are in equilibrium, so ΔG = 0 for the transition. Since ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = 0, it follows that ΔS = ΔH/T. Vaporization is still strongly endothermic and has a large positive ΔS; the two contributions simply cancel exactly at this one temperature.

questions.q: A process has ΔG = −50 kJ. What is the maximum non-expansion (useful) work it can perform?
o: Unlimited work, given enough time
The work available is capped by the free energy released.
Equal to |ΔH|, regardless of ΔG
ΔH includes the TΔS energy that is unavailable for work.
50 kJ
Correct: −ΔG is the maximum non-PV work available at constant T and P.
Zero, because ΔG < 0 means all energy is lost as heat
Negative ΔG is exactly what makes useful work possible.
questions.x: At constant temperature and pressure, −ΔG is the maximum non-expansion work a process can deliver, reached only in the reversible limit. Part of ΔH is tied up in the TΔS term and cannot be converted to useful work, so |ΔH| is not the cap. A process with ΔG = −50 kJ can therefore do at most 50 kJ of useful work.

questions.q: ATP hydrolysis (ΔG°′ = −30 kJ/mol) is coupled to a reaction with ΔG°′ = +14 kJ/mol. What is ΔG°′ of the coupled process?
o: −16 kJ/mol
Correct: free energies of coupled reactions add: −30 + 14 = −16 kJ/mol.
−44 kJ/mol
Adds the magnitudes and ignores that one value is positive.
+16 kJ/mol
Reverses the sign of the sum.
−30 kJ/mol
Ignores the unfavorable reaction's contribution.
questions.x: Free energy is a state function, so the ΔG°′ of coupled reactions is the sum of the individual values. −30 + 14 = −16 kJ/mol, so the combined process is favorable even though the second reaction alone is not. This is how cells use ATP hydrolysis to drive uphill reactions through a shared intermediate.

questions.q: For a reaction with positive ΔH and positive ΔS, what happens to ΔG as temperature increases?
o: It becomes more positive
That happens when ΔS is negative.
It stays the same
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS depends on T whenever ΔS ≠ 0.
It becomes zero at all temperatures
ΔG = 0 only at the single temperature T = ΔH/ΔS.
It becomes more negative
Correct: the −TΔS term grows more negative as T rises.
questions.x: In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, a positive ΔS makes the −TΔS term more negative as T rises. So ΔG falls with temperature and eventually becomes negative above T = ΔH/ΔS. The tempting answer, that ΔG becomes more positive, is the behavior of reactions with negative ΔS.

questions.q: Plotting ΔG against T for a reaction (assuming ΔH and ΔS are constant) gives a straight line. What are the slope and y-intercept?
o: Slope = ΔS; y-intercept = ΔH
Misses the negative sign on the TΔS term.
Slope = −ΔS; y-intercept = ΔH
Correct: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS has the form y = b + mx with m = −ΔS.
Slope = −ΔH; y-intercept = ΔS
Swaps the roles of ΔH and ΔS.
Slope = ΔH/T; y-intercept = 0
ΔG at T = 0 equals ΔH, not zero.
questions.x: Written as ΔG = ΔH + (−ΔS)T, the Gibbs equation is a line y = b + mx with T on the x-axis. The slope is −ΔS and the intercept at T = 0 is ΔH. A reaction with positive ΔS therefore slopes downward. Dropping the minus sign is the usual error.

questions.q: Which process is spontaneous at 25 °C and 1 atm even though it is endothermic?
o: Liquid water freezing
Freezing is exothermic and not spontaneous at 25 °C.
Iron rusting
Rusting is exothermic.
Methane burning
Combustion is strongly exothermic.
Ice melting
Correct: above 0 °C, the entropy gain outweighs the heat absorbed.
questions.x: Melting ice absorbs heat (ΔH ≈ +6 kJ/mol) but increases entropy. Above 0 °C, TΔS exceeds ΔH, so ΔG < 0 and melting is spontaneous. Rusting and combustion are spontaneous too, but they are exothermic, and freezing is exothermic and not spontaneous at 25 °C.

questions.q: If ΔG° for a reaction is negative, what is true of K at that temperature?
o: Correct: ΔG° = −RT ln K, so a negative ΔG° requires ln K > 0.
K < 1 corresponds to a positive ΔG°.
K = 1 corresponds to ΔG° = 0.
K is never zero; it is a ratio of positive concentrations.
questions.x: The standard free energy and the equilibrium constant are linked by ΔG° = −RT ln K. A negative ΔG° requires ln K > 0, so K > 1 and products are favored at equilibrium. K = 1 corresponds to ΔG° = 0, and K < 1 to a positive ΔG°; K can never be zero.

questions.q: At 298 K, a reaction has K = 1.0. What is ΔG°?
o: −RT
That would require ln K = 1, i.e., K ≈ 2.7.
Correct: ΔG° = −RT ln 1 = 0.
+RT
That would require ln K = −1, i.e., K ≈ 0.37.
It cannot be determined without Q
ΔG° depends only on K; Q matters for ΔG, not ΔG°.
questions.x: From ΔG° = −RT ln K, K = 1 gives ln 1 = 0 and therefore ΔG° = 0. Neither products nor reactants are favored under standard conditions. ΔG° is a fixed property at a given temperature, so it does not depend on Q; only ΔG, the free energy for the actual mixture, does.

questions.q: At 298 K, ΔG° = −2.303RT log K, with 2.303RT ≈ 5.7 kJ/mol. If ΔG° = −11.4 kJ/mol, what is K?
o: Sign error: a negative ΔG° gives K > 1.
Reports log K instead of K.
Correct: log K = 11.4/5.7 = 2, so K = 10² = 100.
Treats the ΔG° value in kJ as if it were log K.
questions.x: Rearrange ΔG° = −2.303RT log K to log K = −ΔG°/(2.303RT) = 11.4/5.7 = 2. So K = 10² = 100. Each −5.7 kJ/mol of ΔG° at 298 K multiplies K by ten. Stopping at log K = 2 and reporting it as K is the tempting mistake.

questions.q: A reaction has K = 1.0 × 10⁻³ at 298 K. Using 2.303RT ≈ 5.7 kJ/mol, what is ΔG°?
o: −17 kJ/mol
Sign error: K < 1 means ΔG° is positive.
+5.7 kJ/mol
Forgets to multiply by log K = −3.
+3 kJ/mol
Reports −log K as if it were ΔG°.
+17 kJ/mol
questions.x: With K = 10⁻³, log K = −3, so ΔG° = −2.303RT log K = −5.7 × (−3) ≈ +17 kJ/mol. A K below 1 always means a positive ΔG°: reactants are favored under standard conditions. Each factor of ten in K is worth about 5.7 kJ/mol at room temperature.

questions.q: Which statement is true for a reaction mixture at equilibrium?
o: ΔG° = 0 and Q = K
ΔG° is zero only when K = 1.
ΔG = ΔG° and K = 1
ΔG = ΔG° only when Q = 1, which need not be equilibrium.
ΔG = 0 and Q = K
Correct: at equilibrium there is no net driving force, and Q has reached K.
The forward and reverse rate constants are equal
The forward and reverse rates are equal; the rate constants generally differ.
questions.x: At equilibrium the system has no further tendency to change, so ΔG = 0, and the reaction quotient has reached its equilibrium value, Q = K. ΔG° is generally not zero; it equals zero only for the special case K = 1. Equilibrium also means equal forward and reverse rates, not equal rate constants.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔG° = +10 kJ/mol. A mixture is prepared with Q much smaller than K. What happens?
o: ΔG stays positive because ΔG° is positive
ΔG depends on Q; small Q can make it negative.
ΔG is negative, so the reaction proceeds forward
Correct: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q becomes negative when Q ≪ K.
ΔG° becomes negative
ΔG° is fixed at a given temperature.
K increases until it equals Q
K is constant at a given temperature; Q changes, not K.
questions.x: The actual driving force is ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q. When Q is far below K, RT ln Q is large and negative, enough to outweigh a positive ΔG°, so ΔG < 0 and the reaction runs forward. A positive ΔG° only means K < 1; it does not forbid the forward reaction in mixtures with very little product.

questions.q: At 298 K (2.303RT ≈ 5.7 kJ/mol), a reaction has ΔG° = −5.7 kJ/mol. A mixture has Q = 10. Which is true?
o: ΔG = 0; the mixture is at equilibrium
Correct: ΔG = −5.7 + 5.7 log 10 = 0, so Q = K = 10.
ΔG = −11.4 kJ/mol; the forward reaction is favored
Sign error on the RT ln Q term.
ΔG = −5.7 kJ/mol; the forward reaction is favored
Ignores the RT ln Q term.
ΔG = +5.7 kJ/mol; the reverse reaction is favored
Drops ΔG° and keeps only the RT ln Q term.
questions.x: Use ΔG = ΔG° + 2.303RT log Q = −5.7 + 5.7 × log 10 = −5.7 + 5.7 = 0. A ΔG of zero means the mixture is already at equilibrium, which fits K = 10 implied by ΔG° = −5.7 kJ/mol. Ignoring the Q term, or getting its sign wrong, wrongly predicts a forward shift.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes ΔG from ΔG°?
o: ΔG° is defined only at 0 °C
Standard states fix concentration and pressure, not a temperature of 0 °C.
ΔG° changes as the reaction proceeds
ΔG changes as Q changes; ΔG° is constant at a given T.
ΔG is always zero at 25 °C
ΔG is zero only at equilibrium, at any temperature.
ΔG° refers to all species in standard states; ΔG reflects the actual concentrations present
Correct: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q.
questions.x: ΔG° is the free-energy change when every species is in its standard state (1 M, 1 bar), and it is fixed at a given temperature. ΔG describes the actual mixture and changes as the reaction proceeds: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q. As Q approaches K, ΔG approaches zero. ΔG° is not tied to 0 °C; standard states specify concentration and pressure.

questions.q: Which change makes ΔG for a reaction more negative at a fixed temperature without changing ΔG°?
o: Continuously removing product as it forms
Correct: lowering Q lowers RT ln Q, making ΔG more negative.
Adding a catalyst
Catalysts change neither ΔG nor ΔG°.
Adding more product
Raising Q makes ΔG more positive.
Raising the activation energy
Activation energy affects rate, not ΔG.
questions.x: ΔG° is fixed at a given temperature, but ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q changes with composition. Removing product keeps Q low, so RT ln Q stays very negative and ΔG stays negative; this is how coupled pathways keep reactions running in cells. Catalysts and activation energy change only how fast equilibrium is reached, not ΔG.

questions.q: A plot of ln K versus 1/T for a reaction is a straight line with a positive slope. The reaction is:
o: Endothermic
An endothermic reaction gives a negative slope.
Exothermic
Correct: slope = −ΔH°/R, so a positive slope means ΔH° < 0.
Thermoneutral, with ΔH° = 0
ΔH° = 0 would give a horizontal line.
Impossible to classify without ΔS°
The slope alone gives ΔH°; ΔS° sets the intercept.
questions.note: van 't Hoff: ln K = −ΔH°/(RT) + ΔS°/R.
questions.x: The van 't Hoff equation, ln K = −ΔH°/(RT) + ΔS°/R, makes ln K vs 1/T a line with slope −ΔH°/R. A positive slope means ΔH° is negative, so the reaction is exothermic and K falls as temperature rises (moving left on the 1/T axis). An endothermic reaction would give a negative slope.

questions.q: How much heat raises 100 g of water from 20 °C to 30 °C? (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C))
o: Omits the temperature change.
Omits the mass.
Uses the final temperature (30 °C) instead of ΔT.
questions.x: Heat for a temperature change within one phase is q = mcΔT. Here q = 100 g × 4.18 J/(g·°C) × 10 °C = 4180 J ≈ 4.18 kJ. The temperature term is the change, ΔT, not the final temperature. Using 30 °C instead of 10 °C triples the answer.

questions.q: Equal masses of aluminum (c ≈ 0.90 J/(g·°C)) and copper (c ≈ 0.39 J/(g·°C)) absorb the same amount of heat. Which warms more?
o: Aluminum
A higher specific heat means a smaller temperature change for the same heat.
Both warm equally because the heat and mass are equal
Different specific heats give different ΔT.
Copper
Correct: ΔT = q/(mc), so the lower specific heat gives the larger ΔT.
It depends on their starting temperatures
ΔT depends on q, m and c, not on the starting temperature.
questions.x: Rearranging q = mcΔT gives ΔT = q/(mc). With q and m equal, the material with the smaller specific heat must change temperature more. Copper's c is less than half of aluminum's, so it warms over twice as much. A high specific heat means a substance resists temperature change, not that it heats faster.

questions.q: A 100 g metal block at 85 °C is placed in 100 g of water at 20 °C. The final temperature is 25 °C. What is the metal's specific heat? (c_water = 4.2 J/(g·°C))
o: Correct: water gains 100 × 4.2 × 5 = 2100 J; metal: 2100 = 100 × c × 60, so c = 0.35.
Assumes the metal has the same specific heat as water.
Uses a metal ΔT of 65 °C (to the water's initial temperature) instead of 60 °C.
Swaps the two temperature changes, using 5 °C for the metal and 60 °C for the water.
questions.note: Heat lost by the hot object = heat gained by the cold one.
questions.x: In an insulated mixing, heat lost by the hot object equals heat gained by the cold one. Water gains 100 × 4.2 × (25 − 20) = 2100 J. The metal cools by 85 − 25 = 60 °C, so 2100 = 100 × c × 60 and c = 0.35 J/(g·°C). Each object's ΔT is measured from its own starting temperature to the shared final temperature.

questions.q: In a coffee-cup calorimeter, a dissolving solid makes the solution warmer. What is the sign of ΔH for the dissolution?
o: Positive, because the solution gained heat
The solution is the surroundings; the system lost that heat.
Zero, because the calorimeter is insulated
Insulation keeps the heat inside, but the process still releases it.
It cannot be determined from a temperature change
At constant pressure, a temperature rise signals an exothermic process.
Negative, because the process releases heat into the solution
Correct: the water absorbs heat released by the system, so ΔH < 0.
questions.x: In coffee-cup calorimetry the reaction is the system, and the water is the surroundings. A temperature rise means the water absorbed heat, which must have come from the process, so the dissolution is exothermic and ΔH < 0. The calorimeter's insulation just keeps that heat in the water so it can be measured.

questions.q: A bomb calorimeter operates at constant volume. The heat it measures corresponds most directly to:
o: ΔH
ΔH is heat at constant pressure, as in a coffee-cup calorimeter.
ΔU
Correct: with no volume change, w = 0 and q_v = ΔU.
ΔG
Calorimeters measure heat, not free energy.
ΔS
Entropy is not measured directly as heat.
questions.x: A bomb calorimeter is rigid, so ΔV = 0 and no pressure–volume work is done. Then ΔU = q + w reduces to ΔU = q_v. A coffee-cup calorimeter, open to the atmosphere, measures heat at constant pressure, which is ΔH. For most reactions the two differ only slightly, by Δn_gas·RT.

questions.q: A bomb calorimeter has a heat capacity of 10 kJ/°C. Burning a 0.50 g sample raises its temperature by 2.0 °C. How much heat is released per gram?
o: 20 kJ/g
Reports total heat without dividing by mass.
10 kJ/g
Multiplies by the sample mass instead of dividing.
40 kJ/g
Correct: q = 10 × 2.0 = 20 kJ; 20 kJ ÷ 0.50 g = 40 kJ/g.
5.0 kJ/g
Divides the heat capacity by ΔT.
questions.x: For a calorimeter with known heat capacity, q = C_cal × ΔT = 10 kJ/°C × 2.0 °C = 20 kJ. Dividing by the sample mass gives 20 kJ ÷ 0.50 g = 40 kJ/g. Reporting 20 kJ/g forgets that the sample was only half a gram, so a full gram would release twice as much.

questions.q: Coastal cities tend to have smaller daily temperature swings than inland deserts. The main reason is that water:
o: Has a low specific heat, so it changes temperature quickly
A low specific heat would amplify temperature swings.
Reflects all incoming sunlight
Water absorbs much sunlight; reflection is not the main effect.
Has a lower boiling point than sand
Boiling point is irrelevant to daily temperature buffering.
Has a high specific heat, so it absorbs or releases much heat with little temperature change
Correct: the ocean buffers air temperature.
questions.x: Water has an unusually high specific heat because so much energy goes into its hydrogen bonds. Oceans absorb heat during the day and release it at night with only small temperature changes, which buffers the air of nearby cities. Sand and rock have low specific heats, so deserts heat and cool quickly.

questions.q: Liquid water's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·K). What is its molar heat capacity?
o: About 75 J/(mol·K)
Correct: 4.18 J/(g·K) × 18 g/mol ≈ 75 J/(mol·K).
About 0.23 J/(mol·K)
Divides by molar mass instead of multiplying.
Treats specific heat as if it were molar heat capacity.
18 J/(mol·K)
Reports the molar mass, not the heat capacity.
questions.x: Specific heat is per gram; molar heat capacity is per mole. Multiply by the molar mass: 4.18 J/(g·K) × 18 g/mol ≈ 75 J/(mol·K). Dividing instead of multiplying gives a tiny, meaningless number. The unit analysis (g in the denominator cancels with g/mol) shows which way to convert.

questions.q: Which sample has the greatest heat capacity?
o: 1 kg of iron
Iron's specific heat is far lower than water's.
1 kg of liquid water
Correct: heat capacity = mc, and water has a large c and the largest mass here.
100 g of liquid water
Same c as the 1 kg sample but one-tenth the mass.
1 kg of ethanol
Ethanol's specific heat is lower than water's.
questions.note: Specific heat is intensive; heat capacity is extensive.
questions.x: Heat capacity C = mc is extensive: it depends on both the material's specific heat and the amount. Water's c (4.18 J/(g·°C)) is far higher than that of iron (0.45) or ethanol (about 2.4), and 1 kg is the largest mass offered. So 1 kg of water has the largest heat capacity; 100 g of water has the same c but one-tenth the capacity.

questions.q: 100 g of water at 80 °C is mixed with 300 g of water at 20 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?
o: Takes a simple average and ignores the different masses.
Weights the temperatures with the masses swapped.
20 °C, because the larger mass sets the temperature
The larger mass dominates but still warms.
questions.x: When the same substance mixes in an insulated container, heat lost equals heat gained, and the final temperature is a mass-weighted average: (100 × 80 + 300 × 20) ÷ 400 = 35 °C. The larger, cooler mass pulls the result toward 20 °C but still warms by 15 °C. A simple average of 50 °C ignores the different masses.

questions.q: In a coffee-cup calorimetry experiment on an exothermic reaction, some heat escapes to the room. How does this affect the calculated magnitude of ΔH?
o: It is too small
Correct: the measured ΔT is smaller than it should be, so less heat is attributed to the reaction.
It is too large
Lost heat lowers the observed temperature rise, not raises it.
It is unaffected
The calculation uses ΔT, which heat loss reduces.
Its sign is reversed
The solution still warms, so the sign is still negative.
questions.x: The calculation assumes all the reaction's heat warms the solution. If some escapes, the measured ΔT is smaller, so q = mcΔT underestimates the heat released, and the computed |ΔH| comes out too small. The sign stays negative because the solution still warms. Heat loss in calorimetry nearly always biases magnitudes low.

questions.q: When 0.020 mol of a solute dissolves in 100 g of solution (c ≈ 4.0 J/(g·°C)), the temperature rises 5.0 °C. What is ΔH of solution?
o: +100 kJ/mol
A temperature rise means heat was released, so ΔH is negative.
−2.0 kJ/mol
Reports total heat without dividing by moles.
−10 kJ/mol
Divides by 0.20 mol instead of 0.020 mol.
−100 kJ/mol
Correct: q = 100 × 4.0 × 5.0 = 2.0 kJ released; 2.0 ÷ 0.020 = 100 kJ/mol, exothermic.
questions.x: Heat absorbed by the solution is q = mcΔT = 100 × 4.0 × 5.0 = 2000 J = 2.0 kJ. Since the solution warmed, that heat came from the dissolving solute, so ΔH is negative. Per mole: −2.0 kJ ÷ 0.020 mol = −100 kJ/mol. Forgetting to divide by moles gives the total heat, not the molar enthalpy.

questions.q: While water boils at 1 atm, heat is added but the temperature stays at 100 °C. The added energy mainly:
o: Increases the average kinetic energy of the molecules
Constant temperature means average kinetic energy is unchanged.
Overcomes intermolecular attractions, raising potential energy
Correct: during a phase change, energy goes to separating molecules, not speeding them up.
Breaks covalent O–H bonds
Boiling does not break bonds within water molecules.
Raises the pressure above the liquid
The pressure remains 1 atm in an open container.
questions.x: Temperature measures average molecular kinetic energy. During boiling, temperature is constant, so the added heat goes not into speeding molecules up but into separating them against intermolecular attractions, raising their potential energy. Covalent O–H bonds stay intact; water vapor is still H₂O.

questions.q: How much heat converts 36 g of ice at 0 °C into liquid water at 10 °C? (ΔHfus = 6.0 kJ/mol; c = 4.2 J/(g·°C))
o: 12 kJ
Includes melting but omits warming the liquid.
About 13.5 kJ
Correct: melting 2.0 mol takes 12 kJ; warming takes 36 × 4.2 × 10 ≈ 1.5 kJ; total ≈ 13.5 kJ.
About 1.5 kJ
Includes warming but omits melting.
About 7.5 kJ
Uses 1 mol instead of 2 mol for the melting step.
questions.x: Heating through a phase change is done in segments. Melting: 36 g ÷ 18 g/mol = 2.0 mol × 6.0 kJ/mol = 12 kJ, with no temperature change. Warming the liquid: 36 × 4.2 × 10 ≈ 1.5 kJ. Total ≈ 13.5 kJ. Notice that melting needs far more energy than warming the water by 10 °C.

questions.q: On a phase diagram, the triple point is where:
o: Solid, liquid and gas coexist in equilibrium
Correct: all three phase boundaries meet at one T and P.
The liquid–gas boundary ends
That is the critical point.
The vapor pressure equals 1 atm
That defines the normal boiling point.
The solid melts at 1 atm
That is the normal melting point.
questions.x: A phase diagram's lines mark conditions where two phases coexist. The triple point is the single temperature and pressure where the solid–liquid, liquid–gas and solid–gas lines meet, so all three phases are in equilibrium. The liquid–gas line ends at a different point, the critical point.

questions.q: Above its critical temperature and pressure, a substance:
o: Must be a solid
High temperature does not force a solid.
Is a liquid that cannot vaporize
Above the critical point, liquid and gas cannot be distinguished.
Boils continuously at constant temperature
There is no boiling transition above the critical point.
Is a supercritical fluid with no distinct liquid and gas phases
Correct: the liquid–gas boundary ends at the critical point.
questions.x: The liquid–vapor line ends at the critical point. Beyond the critical temperature and pressure, the densities of liquid and gas become equal and there is no phase boundary, so the substance is a supercritical fluid with properties of both. No amount of compression above T_c will produce a separate liquid phase.

questions.q: The solid–liquid line on water's phase diagram slopes to the left (negative slope). What does this imply?
o: Ice is denser than liquid water
A negative slope means the solid is less dense.
Raising the pressure raises water's melting point
That is true for a positive slope, not water's negative slope.
Increasing the pressure on ice just below 0 °C can melt it
Correct: ice is less dense than liquid water, so pressure favors the liquid.
Water cannot sublime at any pressure
Water sublimes below its triple-point pressure.
questions.x: By the Clapeyron relationship, a solid–liquid line with negative slope means the liquid is denser than the solid. Ice is less dense than liquid water, so applying pressure favors the denser liquid, and ice just below 0 °C can melt under pressure. For most substances the solid is denser and the slope is positive.

questions.q: The triple point of CO₂ is at 5.1 atm. What happens when dry ice is warmed at 1 atm?
o: It melts and then boils
A liquid phase requires a pressure above 5.1 atm.
It melts and stays liquid
Liquid CO₂ is not stable at 1 atm.
It sublimes directly to gas
Correct: below the triple-point pressure, liquid CO₂ cannot exist.
It stays solid at any temperature
Warming eventually crosses the solid–gas boundary.
questions.x: Liquid CO₂ can exist only at pressures above its triple point, 5.1 atm. At 1 atm, warming solid CO₂ moves the sample across the solid–gas line, so it sublimes directly (at about −78 °C) with no liquid stage. That is why dry ice leaves no puddle.

questions.q: A gas sample is held at a temperature below its triple-point temperature, and the pressure is raised steadily. Which phase change occurs?
o: Deposition (gas to solid)
Correct: below the triple-point temperature, the gas region borders only the solid region.
Condensation (gas to liquid)
The liquid region exists only above the triple-point temperature.
Freezing (liquid to solid)
The sample starts as a gas, not a liquid.
Sublimation (solid to gas)
Raising pressure moves the sample toward the denser phase, not the gas.
questions.x: Below the triple-point temperature, the liquid region of a phase diagram is absent, so a vertical path upward (increasing pressure) goes straight from the gas region into the solid region. Crossing that line is deposition. Condensation to a liquid can only happen at temperatures between the triple point and the critical point.

questions.q: A liquid's normal boiling point is the temperature at which:
o: Its vapor pressure equals zero
Vapor pressure rises with temperature and is not zero at boiling.
Its vapor pressure equals 1 atm
Correct: boiling occurs when vapor pressure equals external pressure; 'normal' means 1 atm.
Its solid and liquid coexist at 1 atm
That is the normal melting point.
It reaches its critical temperature
The critical temperature is well above the normal boiling point.
questions.x: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the external pressure, because bubbles of vapor can then form within the liquid. The normal boiling point is the temperature at which this happens under exactly 1 atm. Water's is 100 °C; at lower pressures the same condition is met at lower temperatures.

questions.q: Why does water boil at a lower temperature at high altitude?
o: There is less oxygen in the air
Oxygen content does not affect boiling point.
Water's vapor pressure is higher at altitude at the same temperature
Vapor pressure depends on temperature, not altitude.
Water's enthalpy of vaporization is lower at altitude
ΔHvap barely changes; the lower external pressure is what matters.
The atmospheric pressure is lower, so the vapor pressure matches it at a lower temperature
Correct: boiling occurs when vapor pressure equals external pressure.
questions.x: Boiling occurs when vapor pressure equals the external pressure. At altitude the atmospheric pressure is lower, and water's vapor pressure, which depends only on temperature, reaches that lower value at a lower temperature, so water boils below 100 °C. ΔHvap and the vapor pressure curve themselves barely change; only the external pressure does.

questions.q: Why does a steam burn at 100 °C usually cause more damage than a burn from the same mass of liquid water at 100 °C?
o: Steam has a higher temperature than boiling water
Both are at 100 °C in this comparison.
Steam releases its enthalpy of vaporization as it condenses on the skin
Correct: condensation adds a large heat release before the water even begins to cool.
Steam has a higher specific heat than liquid water
Steam's specific heat is actually lower than liquid water's.
Condensation absorbs heat from the skin
Condensation is exothermic; it releases heat.
questions.x: When steam touches skin it first condenses, releasing ΔHvap (about 41 kJ/mol, roughly 2260 J/g), and only then cools as liquid water. Liquid water at 100 °C can only release heat by cooling, about 4.2 J/g per degree. That extra condensation heat makes steam burns far worse. Condensation releases heat; it does not absorb it.

questions.q: On a heating curve (temperature vs heat added), the slope of a single-phase segment is inversely proportional to:
o: The heat capacity of that phase
Correct: ΔT/q = 1/(mc), so a larger heat capacity gives a shallower slope.
The enthalpy of vaporization
ΔHvap sets the length of the boiling plateau, not a sloped segment.
The density of that phase
Density does not set how temperature responds to heat.
The boiling point
The boiling point sets the plateau's height, not the slope.
questions.x: In a single-phase region of a heating curve, ΔT = q/(mc), so the slope of temperature versus heat added is 1/(mc). A phase with larger heat capacity warms more slowly and shows a shallower line. Liquid water's high c gives a gentle slope compared with ice or steam. Enthalpies of phase change set plateau lengths, not slopes.

questions.q: A liquid in a sealed container is at equilibrium with its vapor. The temperature is raised. What happens to the vapor pressure?
o: It decreases
Vapor pressure rises with temperature.
It stays the same because the container is sealed
Sealing fixes the volume, not the equilibrium vapor pressure.
It increases
Correct: more molecules have enough energy to escape the liquid.
It drops to zero as the liquid evaporates
Vapor pressure does not drop on heating.
questions.x: Vapor pressure is the pressure of vapor in equilibrium with its liquid, and it depends only on temperature. Raising T gives a larger fraction of molecules enough kinetic energy to escape, so evaporation outpaces condensation until a new, higher vapor pressure is reached. Sealing the container fixes the volume but does not change this equilibrium property.

questions.q: How is the enthalpy of sublimation related to the enthalpies of fusion and vaporization (at the same temperature)?
o: ΔHsub = ΔHvap − ΔHfus
Melting must be added, not subtracted, to get from solid to gas.
ΔHsub = ΔHvap alone
Omits the energy needed to melt the solid.
ΔHsub = ΔHfus × ΔHvap
Enthalpies of sequential steps add; they do not multiply.
ΔHsub = ΔHfus + ΔHvap
Correct: by Hess's law, solid → liquid → gas equals solid → gas.
questions.x: Enthalpy is a state function, so the direct path solid → gas has the same ΔH as solid → liquid → gas. By Hess's law, ΔHsub = ΔHfus + ΔHvap at the same temperature. Subtracting fusion reverses the melting step, which would describe going from liquid back to solid.

questions.q: Evaporation of sweat cools the skin because:
o: Evaporation is exothermic
Evaporation is endothermic; it absorbs heat.
Sweat has a low specific heat
Water's specific heat is high; the cooling comes from vaporization.
Water vapor is colder than liquid water
The cooling comes from energy carried away, not cold vapor.
The highest-energy molecules escape, lowering the average kinetic energy of what remains
Correct: evaporation also absorbs ΔHvap from the skin.
questions.x: Evaporation is endothermic. The molecules that escape are the most energetic ones at the surface, so the remaining liquid has a lower average kinetic energy and absorbs heat from the skin, carrying away ΔHvap. Water vapor is not cold; the cooling comes from the energy taken away by the escaping molecules.

questions.q: A substance's solid–liquid line has a positive slope. A liquid sample just above its melting point is compressed at constant temperature. What can happen?
o: It vaporizes
Compression favors denser phases, not the gas.
It can freeze, because higher pressure raises the melting point
Correct: a positive slope means the solid is denser, so pressure favors the solid.
It stays liquid because pressure always lowers the melting point
Pressure lowers the melting point only for a negative slope, as in water.
It sublimes
Sublimation goes from solid to gas and needs low pressure.
questions.x: A positive solid–liquid slope means the solid is denser than the liquid, as for most substances. Increasing pressure at constant temperature favors the denser phase, raising the melting point above the current temperature, so the liquid can freeze. Water is the familiar exception, with a negative slope, which is why the 'pressure always lowers melting point' choice fails.

questions.q: At constant temperature, lowering the pressure moves a sample from the liquid region across the liquid–gas line of its phase diagram. Which process occurs?
o: Vaporization
Correct: crossing from liquid to gas is vaporization.
Condensation
Condensation is gas to liquid, the reverse direction.
Sublimation
Sublimation goes from solid directly to gas.
Melting
Melting crosses the solid–liquid line.
questions.x: On a phase diagram, each line separates two phases, and crossing a line means a phase change. Starting in the liquid region and lowering the pressure at constant temperature moves the sample downward across the liquid–gas line into the gas region, which is vaporization. Condensation is the same line crossed the other way, from gas to liquid.

questions.q: For 2A → 3B, A is consumed at 0.20 M/s. At what rate is B formed?
o: Ignores the stoichiometric ratio.
Inverts the ratio, using 2/3 instead of 3/2.
Correct: rate of B = (3/2)(0.20) = 0.30 M/s.
Multiplies by 3 without dividing by 2.
questions.x: Rates of consumption and formation are related by the stoichiometric coefficients: rate = −(1/2)Δ[A]/Δt = (1/3)Δ[B]/Δt. For every 2 mol of A used, 3 mol of B form, so B appears 3/2 as fast as A disappears: 1.5 × 0.20 = 0.30 M/s. Using 2/3 instead of 3/2 inverts the ratio.

questions.q: A reaction has rate = k[A][B]². What is its overall order?
o: Correct: overall order is the sum of exponents, 1 + 2 = 3.
Counts only the exponent on B.
Counts only the exponent on A.
It cannot be determined without the balanced equation
The rate law itself gives the order directly.
questions.x: The overall reaction order is the sum of the exponents in the experimentally determined rate law. For rate = k[A][B]², that is 1 + 2 = 3, so the reaction is third order overall, first order in A and second order in B. The rate law itself gives the order; the balanced equation is not needed.

questions.q: For rate = k[A]²[B], [A] is tripled and [B] is halved. By what factor does the rate change?
o: It increases 1.5-fold
Treats A as first order: 3 × ½.
It increases 9-fold
Ignores the halving of [B].
It increases 3-fold
Ignores both the square and the change in [B].
It increases 4.5-fold
questions.x: Each concentration's effect is raised to its order, and the effects multiply. Tripling [A] in a second-order term multiplies the rate by 3² = 9; halving [B] in a first-order term multiplies it by ½. Overall the rate changes by 9 × ½ = 4.5. Forgetting to square the tripling gives 1.5.

questions.q: Initial rates: [A] 0.10 M, [B] 0.10 M → 2.0 × 10⁻³ M/s; [A] 0.20 M, [B] 0.10 M → 4.0 × 10⁻³ M/s; [A] 0.10 M, [B] 0.20 M → 8.0 × 10⁻³ M/s. What is the rate law?
o: rate = k[A]²[B]
Swaps the orders of A and B.
rate = k[A][B]²
Correct: doubling A doubles the rate (first order); doubling B quadruples it (second order).
rate = k[A][B]
Misses that doubling B quadruples the rate.
rate = k[B]²
Misses that the rate depends on A.
questions.note: Compare two runs in which only one concentration changes.
questions.x: Use the method of initial rates: compare two runs where only one concentration changes. Doubling [A] (runs 1 and 2) doubles the rate, so the order in A is 1. Doubling [B] (runs 1 and 3) quadruples it, so the order in B is 2. The rate law is rate = k[A][B]².

questions.q: For rate = k[A][B]², a run with [A] = 0.10 M and [B] = 0.10 M gives a rate of 2.0 × 10⁻³ M/s. What is k?
o: Uses [B] to the first power instead of squaring it.
Multiplies the rate by the concentrations instead of dividing.
2.0 M⁻²·s⁻¹
2.0 M²·s⁻¹
Gets the number right but inverts the units; k must cancel M³.
questions.x: Rearrange the rate law: k = rate/([A][B]²) = (2.0 × 10⁻³ M/s) ÷ (0.10 M × 0.010 M²) = 2.0 M⁻²·s⁻¹. For a third-order reaction the units must be M⁻²·s⁻¹ so the rate comes out in M/s. Forgetting to square [B] gives 0.20.

questions.q: Doubling [B] has no effect on the initial rate of a reaction. What is the order with respect to B?
o: First
First order would double the rate.
Second
Second order would quadruple the rate.
Zero
Correct: rate ∝ [B]⁰, so changing [B] does not change the rate.
Negative first
A negative order would decrease the rate.
questions.x: If changing a reactant's concentration leaves the rate unchanged, the rate does not depend on it: its order is zero, since [B]⁰ = 1. This often happens when B is involved only after the rate-determining step. First order would double the rate, and second order would quadruple it.

questions.q: Initial rates: [A] 0.10, [B] 0.10 → rate r; [A] 0.20, [B] 0.20 → 8r; [A] 0.10, [B] 0.20 → 2r. What is the rate law?
o: rate = k[A][B]²
Swaps the orders of A and B.
rate = k[A]³
Attributes the entire 8-fold change to A.
rate = k[A][B]
First order in each would give only 4× when both double.
rate = k[A]²[B]
Correct: B alone doubles the rate (first order); doubling both gives 8×, so A contributes 4× (second order).
questions.x: First isolate B: from run 1 to run 3 only [B] doubles and the rate doubles, so B is first order. From run 1 to run 2 both double and the rate rises 8-fold; B accounts for 2×, so A must account for 4×, making A second order. Rate = k[A]²[B]. Assigning the whole 8× to A ignores B's contribution.

questions.q: For a multistep reaction, the rate law generally cannot be determined from:
o: The coefficients of the balanced overall equation
Correct: orders must be found experimentally or from the mechanism.
Initial-rate experiments
This is the standard experimental method for finding orders.
The rate-determining step of a known mechanism
The slow step's molecularity sets the rate law.
Graphs of integrated rate laws
Linear plots of [A], ln[A] or 1/[A] vs time reveal the order.
questions.x: The coefficients of an overall equation describe stoichiometry, not how the reaction actually happens. For a multistep reaction, orders depend on the mechanism and must be found experimentally, by initial rates or integrated-rate-law plots, or deduced from a known rate-determining step. Only for an elementary step do the coefficients give the orders.

questions.q: What is the rate law for the elementary step 2NO₂ → NO₃ + NO?
o: rate = k[NO₂]
Ignores that two NO₂ molecules collide.
rate = k[NO₂]²
Correct: for an elementary step, the coefficients give the orders.
rate = k[NO₃][NO]
Uses products instead of reactants.
rate = k[NO₂]²/[NO]
Products do not appear in the forward rate law of an elementary step.
questions.x: An elementary step describes a single molecular event, so its rate law follows directly from its molecularity: the reactant coefficients become the exponents. Two NO₂ molecules colliding gives rate = k[NO₂]². Products never appear in the forward rate law of an elementary step; this shortcut fails for overall equations.

questions.q: Which change generally increases the rate of a reaction involving a solid reactant?
o: Grinding the solid into a fine powder
Correct: more surface area allows more collisions per second.
Lowering the temperature
Lower T decreases the fraction of molecules with enough energy.
Diluting the other reactant
Lower concentration means fewer collisions.
Raising the activation energy
A higher barrier slows the reaction.
questions.x: A reaction involving a solid can only occur at its surface. Grinding the solid into powder vastly increases surface area, so more reactant particles collide with it per second and the rate rises. Lowering temperature, diluting reactants or raising the activation energy all reduce the number of successful collisions.

questions.q: For rate = k[A], [A] is reduced to one-quarter of its original value. What happens to the rate?
o: It falls to one-sixteenth
That would be second order.
It is unchanged
That would be zero order.
It falls to one-quarter
Correct: first order means rate is directly proportional to [A].
It falls to one-half
Halving would require a square-root dependence.
questions.x: In a first-order rate law the rate is directly proportional to [A]. Cutting [A] to one-quarter therefore cuts the rate to one-quarter. A second-order reaction would drop to one-sixteenth, and a zero-order reaction would not change at all. The exponent tells you how strongly the rate responds.

questions.q: According to collision theory, why do most molecular collisions not lead to a reaction?
o: Most collisions occur between identical molecules
Collisions between identical molecules can react, as in 2NO₂ → products.
Colliding molecules need both enough energy and the proper orientation
Correct: only collisions with energy ≥ Ea and correct geometry react.
Reactions occur only at the walls of the container
Most gas reactions occur through collisions between molecules.
Molecules must collide three at a time
Most elementary steps are bimolecular.
questions.x: Collision theory says a reaction occurs only when molecules collide with kinetic energy at least equal to Ea and with an orientation that lets the reacting atoms meet. Most collisions fail one or both tests, so only a small fraction are productive. Identical molecules can react, and most elementary steps involve two molecules, not three.

questions.q: Mechanism: Step 1 (slow) NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO; Step 2 (fast) NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂. What is the rate law?
o: rate = k[NO₂][CO]
Uses the overall equation instead of the slow step.
rate = k[NO₃][CO]
Uses the fast step and includes an intermediate.
rate = k[NO₂]²[CO]
CO enters only after the rate-determining step.
rate = k[NO₂]²
Correct: the slow first step sets the rate, and it involves two NO₂.
questions.x: The rate-determining (slow) step limits the overall rate, so the observed rate law matches that step's molecularity when it is the first step. Step 1 is a bimolecular collision of two NO₂ molecules, giving rate = k[NO₂]². CO reacts only in the fast second step, after the bottleneck, so it does not appear in the rate law.

questions.q: Mechanism: Step 1 (fast, reversible) 2NO ⇌ N₂O₂; Step 2 (slow) N₂O₂ + O₂ → 2NO₂. What is the observed rate law?
o: rate = k[N₂O₂][O₂]
Contains an intermediate; it must be replaced using step 1.
rate = k[NO]²
Uses only the fast step and ignores the slow step.
rate = k[NO][O₂]
Ignores that step 1 involves two NO molecules.
rate = k[NO]²[O₂]
Correct: rate = k₂[N₂O₂][O₂], and the pre-equilibrium gives [N₂O₂] = K[NO]².
questions.note: Rate laws must contain only reactants (and catalysts), never intermediates.
questions.x: When the slow step involves an intermediate, write its rate law and then replace the intermediate using the fast pre-equilibrium. Here rate = k₂[N₂O₂][O₂], and step 1 gives [N₂O₂] = K[NO]². So rate = k₂K[NO]²[O₂] = k[NO]²[O₂]. Observed rate laws contain only reactants and catalysts, never intermediates.

questions.q: In a two-step mechanism, species X is formed in step 1 and consumed in step 2. X is a(n):
o: Catalyst
A catalyst is consumed first and regenerated later.
Transition state
A transition state is an energy maximum, not a species formed and consumed between steps.
Intermediate
Correct: intermediates are made and then used up, so they are absent from the overall equation.
Final product
A product is not consumed in a later step.
questions.x: An intermediate is produced in one elementary step and consumed in a later one, so it does not appear in the overall equation. A catalyst does the opposite: it is consumed first and regenerated later. A transition state is not a species formed between steps at all; it is the fleeting high-energy arrangement at the top of each barrier.

questions.q: An elementary step A + B + C → products would be described as:
o: Bimolecular, because only two particles can collide at once
There are three reactant particles in this step.
Termolecular, and rare because three-body collisions are improbable
Correct: three particles must collide simultaneously.
Unimolecular, because it forms a single product set
Molecularity counts reacting particles, not products.
Termolecular, and the most common type of elementary step
Most elementary steps are uni- or bimolecular.
questions.x: Molecularity counts the reactant particles that collide in a single elementary step. Three particles make a termolecular step. Such steps are rare because three particles must meet at the same instant with the right energy and orientation, which is far less likely than a two-body collision. Most mechanisms are built from uni- and bimolecular steps.

questions.q: Why do kinetics experiments typically measure initial rates?
o: At the start, the reverse reaction and changes in concentration are negligible
Correct: concentrations are known exactly and product has not built up.
The rate constant changes later in the reaction
k is constant at a fixed temperature.
The activation energy is lowest at the start
Ea does not change during the reaction.
Initial rates are always zero
Initial rates are usually the fastest, not zero.
questions.x: At the very start of a reaction, the reactant concentrations are known exactly and essentially no product has formed, so the reverse reaction and other product effects can be ignored. That makes it simple to relate rate to the starting concentrations. The rate constant and activation energy do not change during a run at fixed temperature.

questions.q: The absorbance of a colored reactant (proportional to its concentration) decreases linearly with time. What is the order with respect to that reactant?
o: First order
First order gives a linear ln[A] vs t plot, with [A] decaying exponentially.
Second order
Second order gives a linear 1/[A] vs t plot.
Order cannot be inferred from this data
Which plot is linear reveals the order.
Zero order
