Correct: a linear [A] vs t plot means a constant rate, independent of [A].
questions.x: Each order gives a characteristic linear plot: [A] vs t for zero order, ln[A] vs t for first order, and 1/[A] vs t for second order. A straight line of [A] (here absorbance) against time means the rate is constant, independent of concentration, which is zero order. First-order decay would curve as an exponential.

questions.q: If rate is in M/s, what are the units of k for a second-order reaction?
o: s⁻¹
Those are first-order units.
M⁻¹·s⁻¹
Correct: k = rate/[A]² = (M/s)/M² = M⁻¹·s⁻¹.
M·s⁻¹
Those are zero-order units.
M⁻²·s⁻¹
Those are third-order units.
questions.x: The units of k must make the rate law come out in M/s. For rate = k[A]², k = rate/[A]² = (M/s)/M² = M⁻¹·s⁻¹. In general k has units M^(1−n)·s⁻¹ for an nth-order reaction: M·s⁻¹ for zero order, s⁻¹ for first and M⁻²·s⁻¹ for third.

questions.q: A rate constant has units of M·s⁻¹. What is the overall order of the reaction?
o: Zero
Correct: k has the same units as the rate when rate = k.
First
First-order k has units of s⁻¹.
Second
Second-order k has units of M⁻¹·s⁻¹.
Third
Third-order k has units of M⁻²·s⁻¹.
questions.note: General rule: units of k = M^(1−n)·s⁻¹.
questions.x: For a zero-order reaction the rate law is rate = k, so k has the same units as the rate itself, M·s⁻¹. Using the general rule M^(1−n)·s⁻¹, M¹ means 1 − n = 1, so n = 0. First-order k is s⁻¹, which is the usual confusion.

questions.q: Which statement about the half-life of a first-order reaction is true?
o: It doubles when the initial concentration doubles
That describes a zero-order reaction.
It halves when the initial concentration doubles
That describes a second-order reaction.
It is independent of the initial concentration
Correct: t½ = 0.693/k, with no concentration term.
It shortens as the reaction proceeds
First-order half-lives stay constant throughout.
questions.x: For a first-order reaction, t½ = ln 2/k ≈ 0.693/k, which contains no concentration term. The same fraction reacts in each half-life, so every half-life is the same length no matter how much reactant is present. Zero-order half-lives get shorter as [A] falls, and second-order half-lives get longer.

questions.q: A first-order reaction has k = 0.0693 s⁻¹. What is its half-life?
o: Divides k by 0.693 instead of 0.693 by k.
Multiplies 0.693 by k.
Uses 1/k, omitting the factor ln 2.
questions.x: The first-order half-life is t½ = 0.693/k. With k = 0.0693 s⁻¹, t½ = 0.693/0.0693 = 10 s. The k units of s⁻¹ make the half-life come out in seconds. Using 1/k alone gives 14.4 s, which is the mean lifetime, not the half-life.

questions.q: For a second-order reaction (rate = k[A]²), which plot gives a straight line?
o: ln[A] vs time
That plot is linear for first-order reactions.
[A] vs time
That plot is linear for zero-order reactions.
1/[A] vs time
Correct: 1/[A] = 1/[A]₀ + kt.
[A]² vs time
No standard integrated rate law makes this linear.
questions.x: The integrated second-order rate law is 1/[A] = 1/[A]₀ + kt, so a plot of 1/[A] against time is a straight line with slope +k. First-order data are linear as ln[A] vs t, and zero-order data as [A] vs t. Testing which plot is linear is a standard way to find the order.

questions.q: How does the half-life of a zero-order reaction change as the reaction proceeds and [A] falls?
o: It stays constant
Constant half-life is the signature of first order.
Each successive half-life gets longer
That is the pattern for second order.
It always equals 0.693/k
That is the first-order half-life formula.
Each successive half-life gets shorter
Correct: t½ = [A]₀/(2k), so lower starting concentration means shorter half-life.
questions.x: For a zero-order reaction, [A] falls at a constant rate k, so t½ = [A]₀/(2k) is proportional to the starting concentration. Each successive half-life starts from a smaller amount and so is shorter (half as long as the previous one). Only first-order reactions have a constant half-life.

questions.q: A second-order reaction (rate = k[A]²) has a half-life of 20 s when [A]₀ = 0.10 M. What is the half-life when [A]₀ = 0.20 M?
o: Treats the half-life as concentration-independent, as in first order.
Correct: t½ = 1/(k[A]₀), so doubling [A]₀ halves t½.
Applies the zero-order relationship, where t½ ∝ [A]₀.
5 s
Applies an inverse-square dependence that does not exist.
questions.x: For a second-order reaction, t½ = 1/(k[A]₀), so the half-life is inversely proportional to the starting concentration. Doubling [A]₀ from 0.10 M to 0.20 M halves t½ from 20 s to 10 s. Higher concentration means more frequent collisions, so half the reactant is used up faster.

questions.q: A plot of ln[A] vs time is linear with a slope of −0.020 s⁻¹. What are the order and rate constant?
o: First order; k = −0.020 s⁻¹
Rate constants are positive; the slope equals −k.
First order; k = 0.020 s⁻¹
Correct: ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt, so slope = −k.
Second order; k = 0.020 M⁻¹·s⁻¹
Second order is linear in 1/[A], not ln[A].
Zero order; k = 0.020 M·s⁻¹
Zero order is linear in [A], not ln[A].
questions.x: The integrated first-order rate law is ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt, so a linear ln[A] vs t plot means first order, and its slope equals −k. A slope of −0.020 s⁻¹ gives k = +0.020 s⁻¹. Rate constants are always positive; the negative slope reflects the reactant decreasing.

questions.q: A drug is eliminated by first-order kinetics with a half-life of 4 h. Its plasma level is 80 mg/L. What is the level 12 h later?
o: 10 mg/L
Correct: three half-lives: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 mg/L.
20 mg/L
Counts only two half-lives.
40 mg/L
Counts only one half-life.
0 mg/L
Assumes a constant 40 mg/L lost per half-life (zero-order thinking).
questions.x: First-order elimination removes a constant fraction, not a constant amount, per unit time. With t½ = 4 h, 12 h is three half-lives, so the level halves three times: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 mg/L, or 80 × (½)³. Subtracting 40 mg/L each period is zero-order thinking and would predict the drug runs out.

questions.q: Which change alters the value of a reaction's rate constant k?
o: Doubling a reactant concentration
This changes the rate but not k.
Increasing the volume of the reaction vessel
Volume changes concentrations, not k.
Raising the temperature
Correct: k depends on T through the Arrhenius equation (and on catalysts), not on concentrations.
Letting the reaction run longer
k is constant throughout a run at fixed T.
questions.x: A rate constant is independent of concentration and of how long the reaction has run, but it depends on temperature through the Arrhenius equation, k = A·e^(−Ea/RT), and on whether a catalyst lowers Ea. Changing concentrations or volume changes the rate, not k.

questions.q: In the Arrhenius equation k = A·e^(−Ea/RT), why does raising the temperature increase k?
o: The activation energy decreases
Ea is essentially constant with temperature.
The pre-exponential factor A decreases
A decrease in A would lower k.
ΔH becomes more negative
Reaction enthalpy does not set the rate constant.
A larger fraction of collisions have energy at least equal to Ea
Correct: the exponential factor rises sharply with T.
questions.x: In k = A·e^(−Ea/RT), the exponential term is the fraction of collisions with energy at least Ea. Raising T makes −Ea/RT less negative, so this fraction grows sharply and k increases. The activation energy itself is essentially constant with temperature, and A does not decrease.

questions.q: A plot of ln k versus 1/T is linear. Its slope equals:
o: +Ea/R
Misses the negative sign in the exponent.
−Ea/R
Correct: ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T).
ln A
ln A is the y-intercept, not the slope.
−ΔH°/R
That is the slope of a van 't Hoff plot of ln K, not ln k.
questions.x: Taking the natural log of the Arrhenius equation gives ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T), a line in 1/T with slope −Ea/R and intercept ln A. A steeper negative slope means a larger activation energy. The similar-looking van 't Hoff plot uses ln K and gives −ΔH°/R instead.

questions.q: Reaction X has a larger activation energy than reaction Y. Both are warmed by 10 K. Which is true?
o: k for X increases by a smaller factor than k for Y
A high-Ea reaction is more, not less, temperature sensitive.
Both k values increase by the same factor
The factor depends on Ea in the exponent.
k for X decreases while k for Y increases
Raising T increases k for any reaction with positive Ea.
k for X increases by a larger factor than k for Y
Correct: a larger Ea makes the rate constant more sensitive to temperature.
questions.x: The temperature sensitivity of k comes from the exponent −Ea/RT: d(ln k)/dT = Ea/(RT²). A reaction with a larger Ea therefore has its rate constant multiplied by a larger factor for the same temperature rise. Every reaction with positive Ea speeds up on heating, but high-barrier reactions speed up most.

questions.q: Using the rule of thumb that a reaction's rate doubles for every 10 °C rise, by about what factor does the rate increase from 25 °C to 55 °C?
o: Correct: three 10 °C steps give 2³ = 8.
Counts the steps but does not compound the doublings.
Adds a doubling for each step (2 + 2 + 2) instead of multiplying.
Uses the temperature change itself as the factor.
questions.x: If the rate doubles for each 10 °C rise, the effect compounds multiplicatively, not additively. A 30 °C rise is three 10 °C steps, so the factor is 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8. Adding the doublings (to get 6) or counting the steps (to get 3) ignores that each step doubles the already-increased rate.

questions.q: In the Arrhenius equation, the pre-exponential factor A mainly reflects:
o: The fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea
That is e^(−Ea/RT), not A.
The equilibrium constant
A is a kinetic parameter, unrelated to K.
Collision frequency and the fraction with proper orientation
Correct: the energy requirement is handled by the exponential term.
The enthalpy change of the reaction
ΔH does not appear in the Arrhenius equation.
questions.x: The Arrhenius factor A, the frequency factor, reflects how often molecules collide and what fraction of collisions have a suitable orientation. The energy requirement is handled separately by the exponential term e^(−Ea/RT). A depends on the kinetics of collisions, not on thermodynamic quantities such as K or ΔH.

questions.q: Two reactions have the same pre-exponential factor. Reaction 1's Ea is lower than reaction 2's by 2.3RT. What is k₁/k₂ at that temperature?
o: About 10
Correct: k₁/k₂ = e^(2.3) ≈ 10.
About 2.3
Reports the exponent instead of evaluating e^2.3.
About 0.1
Inverts the ratio; the lower-Ea reaction is faster.
About 1
Equal A values do not mean equal k when Ea differs.
questions.x: With equal A values, k₁/k₂ = e^(−Ea₁/RT)/e^(−Ea₂/RT) = e^((Ea₂ − Ea₁)/RT). A difference of 2.3RT gives e^2.3 ≈ 10, since ln 10 ≈ 2.3. So lowering a barrier by about 2.3RT (roughly 5.7 kJ/mol at 298 K) speeds a reaction about tenfold.

questions.q: A catalyst is added to a reaction mixture that is already at equilibrium. What happens?
o: The equilibrium shifts toward products
A catalyst does not favor either direction.
The equilibrium shifts toward reactants
A catalyst does not favor either direction.
K increases
Only temperature changes K.
The equilibrium composition is unchanged
Correct: a catalyst speeds forward and reverse reactions equally, leaving K and Q unchanged.
questions.x: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount, speeding them equally. A system already at equilibrium therefore stays at the same composition, and K is unchanged. Catalysts help a reaction reach equilibrium faster; they never shift where equilibrium lies.

questions.q: A catalyst increases the forward rate constant of a reversible reaction 100-fold. By what factor does it change the reverse rate constant?
o: It leaves it unchanged
Then K would increase 100-fold, which a catalyst cannot do.
It increases it 100-fold
Correct: K = k_f/k_r is unchanged, so k_r must rise by the same factor.
It decreases it 100-fold
Then K would increase 10,000-fold.
It increases it 10,000-fold
Then K would decrease, which a catalyst cannot do.
questions.x: For a reversible reaction at equilibrium, K = k_f/k_r. A catalyst cannot change K because it does not change ΔG°, so any increase in k_f must be matched by the same increase in k_r. Raising k_f 100-fold therefore raises k_r 100-fold too, because the same lowered barrier is crossed in both directions.

questions.q: Platinum in a catalytic converter speeds reactions of exhaust gases on its surface. This is an example of:
o: Homogeneous catalysis
Homogeneous catalysts are in the same phase as the reactants.
Autocatalysis
Autocatalysis means a product catalyzes its own formation.
Heterogeneous catalysis
Correct: the catalyst is in a different phase (solid) from the reactants (gases).
Enzyme catalysis
Platinum is a metal, not a protein enzyme.
questions.x: Catalysts are classified by phase relative to the reactants. In a catalytic converter, gaseous exhaust molecules adsorb onto a solid metal surface, react there and then desorb, so the catalysis is heterogeneous. A homogeneous catalyst is dissolved in the same phase as the reactants, as an acid catalyst in solution is.

questions.q: Enzymes accelerate reactions primarily by:
o: Making ΔG of the reaction more negative
Catalysts do not change ΔG.
Stabilizing the transition state, which lowers the activation energy
Correct: binding the transition state tightly reduces Ea.
Shifting the equilibrium toward products
Catalysts do not change K.
Raising the temperature of the active site
Enzymes do not work by heating their substrates.
questions.x: Enzymes bind the transition state more tightly than the substrate, which lowers its energy and therefore lowers the activation energy. They may also orient substrates and provide acidic or basic groups. Like all catalysts, they speed both directions equally and leave ΔG and K unchanged; they do not heat the active site.

questions.q: Compared with the uncatalyzed pathway, a catalyzed pathway on a reaction coordinate diagram has:
o: A lower energy maximum but the same reactant and product energies
Correct: only the barrier changes; ΔH is unchanged.
Lower product energy, making ΔH more negative
Catalysts do not change the energies of reactants or products.
Higher reactant energy, so less energy is needed
Catalysts do not raise reactant energy.
The same peak height but fewer steps
Catalysts work by lowering the highest barrier.
questions.x: On a reaction coordinate diagram, a catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower highest barrier. The reactants and products are the same species with the same energies, so ΔH (and ΔG) are unchanged. Only the peak, the activation energy, is lowered, often by introducing new steps.

questions.q: Which statement is true of a catalyst?
o: It appears in the balanced overall equation
Because it is regenerated, it cancels from the overall equation.
It is consumed in stoichiometric amounts
Small amounts work because it is not used up.
It increases the equilibrium yield of product
Catalysts change rate, not yield at equilibrium.
It is regenerated by the end of the reaction mechanism
Correct: it is consumed in one step and re-formed in a later step.
questions.x: A catalyst takes part in the mechanism: it is consumed in an early step and regenerated in a later one. Because it is regenerated, it cancels out of the overall equation and works in small amounts. It speeds the approach to equilibrium but cannot change the equilibrium yield.

questions.q: A catalyzed reaction has rate = k[S][Cat]. What happens if the catalyst concentration is doubled?
o: The rate doubles and K doubles
Catalysts never change the equilibrium constant.
The rate is unchanged because catalysts never appear in rate laws
Catalysts can appear in rate laws, as here.
The rate doubles but K is unchanged
Correct: the catalyst is first order in the rate law yet cannot alter equilibrium.
The rate quadruples
First order in catalyst means doubling it doubles the rate.
questions.x: A catalyst can appear in the rate law because it participates in the rate-determining step. With rate = k[S][Cat], doubling the catalyst doubles the rate. But the catalyst speeds forward and reverse reactions equally, so K is unchanged. Faster rate and unchanged equilibrium are both true at once.

questions.q: On a reaction coordinate diagram, the forward activation energy is the energy difference between:
o: The reactants and the products
That difference is ΔH.
The products and the transition state
That is the reverse activation energy.
The reactants and the transition state
Correct: Ea is the climb from reactants to the highest point.
The intermediate and the products
This difference is not an activation energy for the forward reaction.
questions.x: Activation energy is measured from the starting species to the highest point on the path, the transition state. For the forward reaction that is the climb from reactants to the transition state. The gap between reactants and products is ΔH, and the climb from products back up to the transition state is the reverse activation energy.

questions.q: On a reaction coordinate diagram, reactants are at 50 kJ/mol, the transition state at 120 kJ/mol, and products at 20 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?
o: 70 kJ/mol
That is the forward activation energy, 120 − 50.
30 kJ/mol
That is the magnitude of ΔH.
120 kJ/mol
Uses the absolute transition-state energy instead of a difference.
100 kJ/mol
Correct: Ea(reverse) = 120 − 20 = 100 kJ/mol.
questions.x: The reverse reaction starts from the products, so its barrier is the climb from products to the transition state: 120 − 20 = 100 kJ/mol. The forward barrier is 120 − 50 = 70 kJ/mol, and ΔH = 20 − 50 = −30 kJ/mol. Note that Ea(reverse) − Ea(forward) = −ΔH, a useful check.

questions.q: Reactants are at 40 kJ/mol, the transition state at 100 kJ/mol, and products at 70 kJ/mol. Which is true?
o: ΔH = −30 kJ/mol and Ea(forward) = 60 kJ/mol
Products are higher than reactants, so ΔH is positive.
ΔH = +30 kJ/mol and Ea(forward) = 60 kJ/mol
Correct: ΔH = 70 − 40; Ea = 100 − 40.
ΔH = +30 kJ/mol and Ea(forward) = 100 kJ/mol
Uses the absolute transition-state energy as Ea.
ΔH = +30 kJ/mol and Ea(forward) = 30 kJ/mol
30 kJ/mol is the reverse barrier, 100 − 70.
questions.x: Read both quantities as differences from the reactant energy. ΔH = products − reactants = 70 − 40 = +30 kJ/mol, so the reaction is endothermic. Ea(forward) = transition state − reactants = 100 − 40 = 60 kJ/mol. Using the transition state's absolute energy (100) as Ea forgets that barriers are measured from the start.

questions.q: For an endothermic reaction, how do the forward and reverse activation energies compare?
o: Ea(forward) > Ea(reverse)
Correct: ΔH = Ea(forward) − Ea(reverse) > 0.
Ea(forward) < Ea(reverse)
That is true for an exothermic reaction.
Ea(forward) = Ea(reverse)
Equal barriers would mean ΔH = 0.
Ea(forward) < ΔH
The forward barrier must be at least as large as ΔH.
questions.x: On an energy diagram, ΔH = Ea(forward) − Ea(reverse). For an endothermic reaction products sit above reactants, so the reverse path starts higher and has a shorter climb to the same transition state. Thus Ea(forward) > Ea(reverse), and the forward barrier must be at least as large as ΔH.

questions.q: In a two-step reaction coordinate diagram, the first transition state is much higher than the second, with an intermediate in the valley between. Which is true?
o: Step 1 is rate-determining
Correct: the highest barrier controls the overall rate.
Step 2 is rate-determining
Step 2 has the lower barrier, so it is fast.
The intermediate is the transition state of step 1
An intermediate sits in a valley; transition states sit at peaks.
The overall reaction must be endothermic
Peak heights do not determine the overall ΔH.
questions.x: In a multistep reaction, the step with the highest transition state relative to the starting reactants controls the overall rate. Here the first peak is much higher, so step 1 is rate-determining and the intermediate, once formed, quickly crosses the lower second barrier. Intermediates sit in valleys, not at peaks, and peak heights alone do not set ΔH.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts a transition state with an intermediate?
o: A transition state lies at a minimum; an intermediate lies at a maximum
Reverses the two.
Both are stable species that can be isolated
Transition states exist only fleetingly at the peak.
An intermediate lies at a local energy minimum; a transition state lies at an energy maximum
Correct: intermediates can sometimes be detected; transition states cannot be isolated.
Transition states appear in the overall equation; intermediates do not
Neither appears in the overall equation.
questions.x: An intermediate is a real species sitting in a local energy minimum between steps; it has a finite lifetime and can sometimes be detected or even isolated. A transition state is the energy maximum of a single step, a fleeting arrangement with partial bonds that cannot be isolated. Neither appears in the overall balanced equation.

questions.q: A reaction proceeds through a three-step mechanism. Its reaction coordinate diagram shows:
o: Two peaks and three intermediate valleys
Swaps the number of transition states and intermediates.
Three peaks and two intermediate valleys
Correct: each step has a transition state, and an intermediate separates successive steps.
Three peaks and three intermediate valleys
Only the junctions between steps are intermediates.
One peak, since only the slow step appears
Every elementary step has its own transition state.
questions.x: Each elementary step crosses its own energy barrier, so a three-step mechanism shows three peaks (transition states). Between consecutive steps the system rests in a valley, an intermediate, giving two valleys for three steps. Reactants and products sit at the ends and are not counted as intermediates.

questions.q: According to the Hammond postulate, the transition state of a highly exothermic elementary step most closely resembles:
o: The products
Product-like transition states occur in endothermic steps.
An intermediate halfway along the coordinate
Highly exothermic steps have early, not midway, transition states.
Neither, because structure is unrelated to energy
Hammond's postulate links similar energy with similar structure.
The reactants
Correct: an early transition state is closer in energy, and structure, to the reactants.
questions.x: The Hammond postulate says a transition state resembles the species closest to it in energy. In a highly exothermic step the transition state is reached early, while it is still close in energy to the reactants, so it is reactant-like in structure. In a strongly endothermic step it comes late and resembles the products.

questions.q: For an exothermic reaction, where do products lie on the reaction coordinate diagram, and how do the activation energies compare?
o: Below the reactants; Ea(reverse) is greater than Ea(forward)
Correct: the reverse climb must cover |ΔH| plus the forward barrier.
Below the reactants; Ea(reverse) is less than Ea(forward)
The reverse path starts lower, so its barrier is larger.
Above the reactants; Ea(reverse) is greater than Ea(forward)
Products above reactants means endothermic.
Level with the reactants; the activation energies are equal
That describes ΔH = 0.
questions.x: Exothermic means the products have lower enthalpy, so they sit below the reactants on the diagram. Both directions share the same transition state, so the reverse reaction must climb |ΔH| plus the forward barrier: Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) + |ΔH|. That makes the reverse barrier larger, which is why exothermic reactions rarely reverse.

questions.q: What is the equilibrium expression for N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)?
o: Coefficients become exponents, not multipliers.
K = [NO]²/([N₂][O₂])
Correct: products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient.
K = [N₂][O₂]/[NO]²
This is the expression for the reverse reaction.
K = [NO]²/([N₂] + [O₂])
Reactant concentrations are multiplied, not added.
questions.x: The equilibrium expression is products over reactants, with each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation. For N₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2NO, K = [NO]²/([N₂][O₂]). Coefficients become exponents, not multipliers, and reactant concentrations are multiplied, never added.

questions.q: What is the equilibrium expression for CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g)?
o: K = [CaO][CO₂]/[CaCO₃]
Includes pure solids, which do not appear in K.
K = [CaO]/[CaCO₃]
Includes solids and omits the only gas.
K = 1/[CO₂]
This is the reverse reaction's expression.
K = [CO₂]
Correct: pure solids have activity 1 and are omitted.
questions.x: Pure solids and pure liquids have activity 1, so they are omitted from equilibrium expressions; their concentrations cannot change. Only the gas, CO₂, remains, so K = [CO₂] (or Kp = P_CO₂). This is why heating limestone in a closed container stops at a fixed CO₂ pressure regardless of how much solid is present.

questions.q: K = 4.0 for A ⇌ 2B. What is K for 4B ⇌ 2A?
o: Reverses the reaction but forgets to square for the doubled coefficients.
Squares K but forgets to invert it for the reverse direction.
Correct: reverse gives 1/4; doubling squares it: (1/4)² = 1/16 = 0.0625.
Multiplies 1/K by ½ instead of squaring it.
questions.note: Reverse → 1/K; multiply coefficients by n → Kⁿ.
questions.x: Two rules: reversing a reaction inverts K, and multiplying all coefficients by n raises K to the nth power. 4B ⇌ 2A is the reverse of A ⇌ 2B, doubled. So K = (1/4.0)² = 1/16 = 0.0625. Inverting without squaring gives 0.25, the most tempting partial answer.

questions.q: For A ⇌ B + C at equilibrium, [A] = 0.50 M, [B] = 0.20 M and [C] = 0.10 M. What is K?
o: Inverts the expression (reactants over products).
Adds the product concentrations instead of multiplying them.
Omits [C] from the expression.
questions.x: Write the expression and substitute equilibrium concentrations: K = [B][C]/[A] = (0.20)(0.10)/0.50 = 0.040. Product concentrations are multiplied in the numerator, not added. A K below 1 here means reactant A is somewhat favored at equilibrium.

questions.q: 2.0 mol H₂ and 2.0 mol I₂ are placed in a 1.0 L flask: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, K = 64. What is [HI] at equilibrium?
o: Reports x instead of 2x for [HI].
Assumes the reaction goes to completion.
That is the equilibrium [H₂] (2.0 − 1.6), not [HI].
questions.x: Set up an ICE table: H₂ and I₂ each fall from 2.0 to 2.0 − x, and HI rises to 2x. K = (2x)²/(2.0 − x)² = 64, and taking square roots gives 2x/(2.0 − x) = 8. So 2x = 16 − 8x, x = 1.6 M, and [HI] = 3.2 M. Because K is large but finite, the reaction does not go all the way to 4.0 M.

questions.q: A reaction has K = 1 × 10¹⁵ at 25 °C. What does this tell you?
o: The reaction reaches equilibrium very quickly
K says nothing about rate.
Reactants are strongly favored at equilibrium
That would correspond to a very small K.
The reaction is endothermic
The size of K alone does not reveal the sign of ΔH.
Products are strongly favored at equilibrium
Correct: a huge K means the equilibrium mixture is almost all product.
questions.x: K compares product and reactant concentrations at equilibrium. A value of 10¹⁵ means the equilibrium mixture is overwhelmingly product. K is a thermodynamic quantity, though, so it says nothing about how quickly equilibrium is reached, and its size alone does not reveal whether the reaction is exothermic.

questions.q: Which statement describes a system at dynamic chemical equilibrium?
o: Reactant and product concentrations are equal
Constant does not mean equal.
Both the forward and reverse reactions have stopped
Equilibrium is dynamic; both reactions continue.
The forward and reverse rates are equal, and concentrations stay constant
Correct: both reactions continue, with no net change.
The forward and reverse rate constants are equal
Rates are equal; rate constants generally differ (K = k_f/k_r).
questions.x: Chemical equilibrium is dynamic: forward and reverse reactions keep occurring, but at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant. Constant does not mean equal; reactant and product concentrations can be very different. Equal rates do not require equal rate constants either, since K = k_f/k_r is usually not 1.

questions.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), how is Kp related to Kc?
o: Kp = Kc
That holds only when moles of gas are unchanged (Δn = 0).
Kp = Kc(RT)
Uses Δn = +1; the reaction loses one mole of gas.
Kp = Kc(RT)²
Uses the product coefficient instead of Δn.
Kp = Kc(RT)⁻¹
Correct: Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn with Δn = 2 − 3 = −1.
questions.x: Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn is moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants. Here Δn = 2 − (2 + 1) = −1, so Kp = Kc(RT)⁻¹. Kp equals Kc only when the reaction has the same number of moles of gas on both sides.

questions.q: Which change alters the numerical value of K for a gas-phase reaction?
o: Changing the temperature
Correct: K depends only on temperature for a given reaction.
Changing the total pressure by compression
Compression shifts the position, but K is unchanged.
Adding more reactant
Adding reactant changes Q, not K.
Adding a catalyst
Catalysts do not affect K.
questions.x: For a given reaction, K depends only on temperature, because it is set by ΔG° = −RT ln K. Compressing the system, adding a reactant or adding a catalyst can shift concentrations or speed things up, but the system returns to the same K. Changing temperature shifts K according to the sign of ΔH°.

questions.q: For A ⇌ B, K₁ = 10. For B ⇌ C, K₂ = 5. What is K for A ⇌ C?
o: Adds the K values instead of multiplying.
Divides K₁ by K₂.
Correct: when reactions are added, their K values multiply: 10 × 5 = 50.
Divides K₂ by K₁.
questions.x: When reactions are added together, their equilibrium constants multiply, because free energies add and ΔG° = −RT ln K turns sums into products. A ⇌ B plus B ⇌ C gives A ⇌ C with K = 10 × 5 = 50. Adding the K values (15) is the tempting but wrong analogy with adding ΔH values.

questions.q: Which species appear in the equilibrium expression for CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)?
o: All four species, including H₂O
A pure liquid solvent has activity 1 and is left out.
CH₃COOH, CH₃COO⁻ and H₃O⁺ only
Correct: water is the pure-liquid solvent and is omitted.
CH₃COO⁻ and H₃O⁺ only
Aqueous reactants such as CH₃COOH must be included.
CH₃COOH and H₂O only
Products always appear in the numerator.
questions.x: Pure liquids and solids are left out of K because their activity is 1. Water here is the solvent, present in huge, essentially constant excess, so it is omitted. All aqueous species, including the reactant CH₃COOH, appear: Ka = [CH₃COO⁻][H₃O⁺]/[CH₃COOH].

questions.q: For A(aq) ⇌ B(aq) + C(aq), K = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶. Starting with [A] = 1.0 M only, what is [B] at equilibrium?
o: Forgets to take the square root.
Halves K instead of taking its square root.
Squares K instead of taking its square root.
Correct: x²/(1.0 − x) ≈ x² = 10⁻⁶, so x = 10⁻³ M.
questions.note: Small K: assume x ≪ initial concentration, then check.
questions.x: Let x = [B] = [C] at equilibrium, with [A] = 1.0 − x. Since K is tiny, x ≪ 1.0, so x²/1.0 ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ and x = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M. The check confirms x is only 0.1% of 1.0 M. Forgetting the square root leaves x equal to K.

questions.q: For the elementary reversible reaction A ⇌ B, k_forward = 0.40 s⁻¹ and k_reverse = 0.10 s⁻¹. What is K?
o: Correct: at equilibrium k_f[A] = k_r[B], so K = k_f/k_r = 4.0.
Inverts the ratio.
Multiplies the rate constants.
Adds the rate constants.
questions.x: At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates of an elementary reaction are equal: k_f[A] = k_r[B]. Rearranging gives [B]/[A] = k_f/k_r = K = 0.40/0.10 = 4.0. A faster forward than reverse reaction means products are favored at equilibrium. Inverting the ratio gives 0.25.

questions.q: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) at equilibrium, more N₂O₄ is added at constant volume. What happens?
o: The equilibrium shifts left
Adding reactant drives the reaction forward, not backward.
Nothing, because K is unchanged
K is unchanged, but Q drops below K, so a shift occurs.
The equilibrium shifts right, forming more NO₂
Correct: the system consumes some added reactant.
K increases
K changes only with temperature.
questions.x: Adding N₂O₄ at constant volume raises its concentration, so Q = [NO₂]²/[N₂O₄] drops below K. The system responds by converting some N₂O₄ into NO₂ until Q returns to K. K itself does not change, because only temperature can change it.

questions.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −198 kJ. Which change increases the equilibrium yield of SO₃?
o: Adding a catalyst
A catalyst speeds equilibrium but does not change yield.
Lowering the temperature
Correct: for an exothermic reaction, cooling favors the forward direction and raises K.
Removing some O₂
Removing a reactant shifts the equilibrium left.
Increasing the container volume
Lower pressure favors the side with more moles of gas (reactants).
questions.x: The forward reaction is exothermic, so heat acts like a product. Lowering the temperature removes 'product', shifting the equilibrium right and increasing K, which raises the SO₃ yield. A catalyst only speeds equilibration, removing O₂ shifts left, and expanding the volume favors the side with more gas moles, the reactants.

questions.q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) at equilibrium, the container volume is reduced at constant temperature. What happens?
o: No shift occurs, because both sides have 2 mol of gas
Correct: the pressure change affects both sides equally.
The equilibrium shifts right
There is no side with fewer moles of gas to favor.
The equilibrium shifts left
There is no side with fewer moles of gas to favor.
K increases
Only temperature changes K.
questions.x: Changing volume shifts an equilibrium only when the two sides have different numbers of moles of gas. H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI has 2 mol of gas on each side, so compressing raises all partial pressures by the same factor and Q stays equal to K. No shift occurs, and K is unchanged at constant temperature.

questions.q: Argon is added to a rigid, fixed-volume vessel containing PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) at equilibrium. What happens?
o: A shift toward PCl₅, because the total pressure increased
Total pressure rises, but each reacting gas's partial pressure is unchanged.
A shift toward PCl₃ and Cl₂
Nothing has lowered Q below K.
K decreases
K depends only on temperature.
No shift, because the partial pressures of the reacting gases are unchanged
Correct: at constant volume, an inert gas does not change Q.
questions.note: Inert gas at constant V: no shift. At constant P (volume grows): shift toward more moles.
questions.x: Adding an inert gas at constant volume raises the total pressure but leaves the moles and volume of each reacting gas, and so their partial pressures and concentrations, unchanged. Q still equals K, so there is no shift. If the argon were added at constant total pressure, the volume would grow and the equilibrium would shift toward the side with more gas moles.

questions.q: For Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq), FeSCN²⁺ is deep red. A reagent that removes Fe³⁺ from solution is added. What is observed?
o: The equilibrium shifts right and the red deepens
Removing reactant cannot drive the forward reaction.
The equilibrium shifts left and the red color fades
Correct: removing a reactant shifts the equilibrium toward reactants.
No change, because K is constant
K is constant, but Q now exceeds K, so a shift occurs.
SCN⁻ concentration decreases
The leftward shift releases SCN⁻, increasing its concentration.
questions.x: Removing Fe³⁺ lowers a reactant concentration, so Q = [FeSCN²⁺]/([Fe³⁺][SCN⁻]) rises above K. The system responds by breaking down some FeSCN²⁺ to replace Fe³⁺, shifting left. The red complex decreases, so the color fades, and the released SCN⁻ increases in concentration.

questions.q: In a sealed soda, CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq). When the bottle is opened, the pressure of CO₂ gas above the liquid drops. What happens?
o: More CO₂ dissolves
That would require raising the gas pressure.
Nothing, because the liquid volume is unchanged
The equilibrium depends on the CO₂ partial pressure.
Dissolved CO₂ comes out of solution, forming bubbles
Correct: lowering gas pressure shifts the equilibrium toward the gas.
The soda's temperature rises sharply
Opening the bottle mainly affects pressure, not temperature.
questions.x: For gas dissolved in a liquid, the equilibrium amount dissolved depends on the partial pressure of the gas above the liquid (Henry's law). Opening the bottle lowers P_CO₂, so the equilibrium CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq) shifts toward the gas and dissolved CO₂ escapes as bubbles. The liquid's volume is irrelevant.

questions.q: H₂ is added to N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at equilibrium. After the system re-equilibrates, how does [N₂] compare with its original equilibrium value?
o: It is higher
The shift is toward NH₃, which uses up N₂.
It is lower
Correct: the forward shift consumes some N₂ along with the added H₂.
It is the same
The forward shift must consume N₂.
It falls to zero
A shift only partly consumes N₂; equilibrium is re-established.
questions.x: Adding H₂ makes Q smaller than K, so the reaction shifts forward to form NH₃. That forward reaction consumes N₂ along with H₂, so [N₂] ends up below its original equilibrium value. Le Châtelier's principle only partly offsets a disturbance; N₂ is reduced, not used up.

questions.q: For A(g) ⇌ B(g) + C(g) with ΔH > 0, which change shifts the equilibrium to the left?
o: Increasing the volume
Lower pressure favors the side with more moles of gas (right).
Removing some C
Removing a product shifts the equilibrium right.
Raising the temperature
Adding heat to an endothermic reaction shifts it right.
Lowering the temperature
Correct: removing heat from an endothermic reaction favors the reverse direction.
questions.x: For an endothermic reaction, heat behaves like a reactant. Lowering the temperature removes heat, so the equilibrium shifts left, and K becomes smaller. Raising the temperature, removing product C, or expanding the volume (favoring the side with more gas moles) all shift this equilibrium right.

questions.q: For Hb + O₂ ⇌ HbO₂, people living at high altitude (low P_O₂) produce more hemoglobin. How does Le Châtelier's principle explain the benefit?
o: More Hb increases K for oxygen binding
Changing concentration does not change K.
More Hb raises the partial pressure of O₂ in the air
Hemoglobin cannot change atmospheric P_O₂.
More Hb shifts the equilibrium toward HbO₂, partly offsetting the low O₂
Correct: increasing a reactant pushes the reaction forward.
More Hb shifts the equilibrium toward free O₂
Adding a reactant shifts toward products, not reactants.
questions.x: In Hb + O₂ ⇌ HbO₂, low P_O₂ at altitude pulls the equilibrium left, reducing oxygen loading. Making more Hb raises a reactant concentration, which pushes the equilibrium toward HbO₂, so more total oxygen can be bound and carried. K is unchanged; only the position shifts.

questions.q: For A ⇌ B, K = 2.0. A mixture has [A] = 1.0 M and [B] = 4.0 M. Which is true?
o: Q > K, so the net reaction proceeds in reverse
Correct: Q = 4.0/1.0 = 4.0 > 2.0, so B converts to A.
Q < K, so the net reaction proceeds forward
Q = 4.0, which is greater than K.
Q = K, so the mixture is at equilibrium
Q > K, so the net reaction proceeds forward
When Q > K, there is too much product, so the reaction runs in reverse.
questions.x: Compare Q to K to predict direction. Q = [B]/[A] = 4.0/1.0 = 4.0, which exceeds K = 2.0, so there is too much product relative to equilibrium. The net reaction runs in reverse, converting B to A until Q falls to 2.0. Q > K always means a reverse shift.

questions.q: A reaction mixture has Q < K. What happens?
o: Net reverse reaction until Q = K
That occurs when Q > K.
K decreases until it equals Q
K is fixed at a given temperature.
Nothing; the mixture is at equilibrium
Equilibrium requires Q = K.
Net forward reaction until Q = K
Correct: too little product is present, so more forms.
questions.x: The reaction quotient Q has the same form as K but uses current concentrations. If Q < K, there is too little product compared with equilibrium, so the net reaction proceeds forward, raising Q until it equals K. K itself is fixed at a given temperature and does not move toward Q.

questions.q: For 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), Kc = 5.0. A mixture has [NO₂] = 0.50 M and [N₂O₄] = 0.50 M. What happens?
o: Q = 1.0, so there is net formation of N₂O₄
Forgets to square [NO₂].
Q = 2.0, so there is net formation of N₂O₄
Correct: Q = 0.50/(0.50)² = 2.0 < 5.0, so the reaction proceeds forward.
Q = 2.0, so there is net formation of NO₂
Q < K means the reaction proceeds forward, not in reverse.
Q = 0.50, so there is net formation of NO₂
Inverts Q and then misreads the direction.
questions.x: Q has the same form as K: Q = [N₂O₄]/[NO₂]² = 0.50/(0.50)² = 0.50/0.25 = 2.0. Since Q < K = 5.0, there is too little product, and the reaction proceeds forward, forming N₂O₄. Forgetting to square [NO₂] gives Q = 1.0, which gives the right direction but the wrong value.

questions.q: At the moment a reaction begins, with only reactants present, what is the value of Q?
o: Infinity
Infinite Q would mean only products are present.
Q = 1 requires specific nonzero concentrations.
Correct: product concentrations in the numerator are zero.
Equal to K
Q = K only at equilibrium.
questions.x: Q places products in the numerator. If only reactants are present, every product concentration is zero, so Q = 0. Because Q = 0 is less than any K, the reaction must proceed forward at first. Infinite Q would describe the opposite case, a mixture containing only products.

questions.q: If Q > K for a reaction, what is the sign of ΔG for the forward reaction?
o: Positive
Correct: ΔG = RT ln(Q/K) > 0, so the reverse reaction is spontaneous.
Negative
Negative ΔG corresponds to Q < K.
Zero
ΔG = 0 only when Q = K.
Equal to ΔG°
ΔG = ΔG° only when Q = 1.
questions.x: Since ΔG° = −RT ln K, the free energy of a mixture can be written ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q = RT ln(Q/K). If Q > K, then Q/K > 1 and ΔG > 0, so the forward reaction is nonspontaneous and the reverse reaction proceeds. ΔG is zero only at Q = K.

questions.q: Under kinetic control, the major product is the one that:
o: Is the most thermodynamically stable
That defines the thermodynamic product.
Has the largest entropy
Entropy alone does not determine kinetic outcome.
Forms through the pathway with the lowest activation energy
Correct: the fastest-forming product dominates when reactions are irreversible.
Releases the most heat on formation
Exothermicity does not set which product forms fastest.
questions.x: When products form irreversibly, the product made fastest dominates, and the fastest pathway is the one with the lowest activation energy. That is kinetic control, typical of low temperatures and short times. The thermodynamic product, the most stable one, dominates only when products can revert and equilibrate.

questions.q: Which conditions favor formation of the thermodynamic product?
o: Higher temperature and longer reaction times
Correct: these allow product formation to reverse, so the system reaches the more stable product.
Low temperature and short reaction times
These conditions favor the kinetic product.
Adding a catalyst for the faster pathway
This favors the kinetic product.
Removing products as soon as they form
This prevents equilibration, favoring the kinetic product.
questions.x: The thermodynamic product wins when products can interconvert. Higher temperature supplies enough energy to cross the reverse barriers, and longer times let the mixture reach equilibrium, which favors the lowest-free-energy product. Low temperature, short times or removing products as they form lock in whichever product forms fastest.

questions.q: From the same reactant, product P1 forms with Ea = 50 kJ/mol (ΔG° = −10 kJ/mol) and P2 with Ea = 80 kJ/mol (ΔG° = −40 kJ/mol). At low temperature and short times, which product dominates?
o: P2, because it is more stable
Stability decides the outcome only under equilibrating conditions.
Equal amounts, because both are spontaneous
Spontaneity does not set the product ratio.
P2, because it has the larger activation energy
A larger barrier slows formation.
P1, because its lower barrier makes it form faster
Correct: kinetic control favors the lower-Ea pathway.
questions.x: At low temperature and short times, products cannot revert, so the ratio reflects relative rates, which depend on the activation energies. P1 has the lower barrier (50 vs 80 kJ/mol), so it forms much faster and dominates as the kinetic product. P2's greater stability matters only once the system can equilibrate.

questions.q: Product P1 forms with Ea = 50 kJ/mol (ΔG° = −10 kJ/mol) and P2 with Ea = 80 kJ/mol (ΔG° = −40 kJ/mol); both form reversibly. After prolonged heating, which product dominates?
o: P1, because it forms faster
Faster formation matters only when products cannot revert.
P2, because it is lower in free energy
Correct: with reversibility and enough energy, the mixture equilibrates to the more stable product.
Equal amounts, because both pathways are open
Equilibrium ratios depend on relative stability.
Neither; both revert to reactant
Both products are favored over reactant (ΔG° < 0).
questions.x: With prolonged heating and reversible formation, both pathways can run backward, so the mixture equilibrates. At equilibrium, product ratios depend on relative free energies, not barriers. P2 has the more negative ΔG° (−40 vs −10 kJ/mol), so it is the thermodynamic product and dominates. Rate matters only when products are locked in.

questions.q: The conversion of diamond to graphite has ΔG° < 0 at room temperature and pressure, yet diamonds persist for millions of years. Why?
o: ΔG° for the conversion is actually positive
The stem states ΔG° < 0, which is correct for diamond → graphite.
K for the conversion is less than 1
ΔG° < 0 means K > 1.
The conversion has a very large activation energy
Correct: diamond is thermodynamically unstable but kinetically stable.
Diamond has higher entropy than graphite
Entropy does not explain the slow rate.
questions.x: ΔG° < 0 means diamond → graphite is thermodynamically favorable, but ΔG says nothing about rate. Converting diamond's three-dimensional sp³ network into graphite's layered sp² sheets requires breaking many strong C–C bonds, giving an enormous activation energy. Diamond is thus thermodynamically unstable but kinetically stable at room temperature.

questions.q: HBr adds to 1,3-butadiene. At −80 °C the 1,2-adduct is the major product; at 40 °C the 1,4-adduct is major. Which inference is correct?
o: The 1,2-adduct is more stable; the 1,4-adduct forms faster
Reverses the kinetic and thermodynamic roles.
The 1,2-adduct forms faster; the 1,4-adduct is more stable
Correct: low T gives the kinetic product; higher T allows equilibration to the stable one.
Both adducts have the same stability
Different equilibrium outcomes reflect different stabilities.
Temperature changes ΔG° so much that the faster product changes
The barrier order is unchanged; reversibility at high T is what changes.
questions.x: At −80 °C the additions are effectively irreversible, so the product that forms fastest, the 1,2-adduct, dominates: it is the kinetic product. At 40 °C the adducts can revert and interconvert, so the mixture reaches equilibrium and favors the more stable 1,4-adduct with its more substituted double bond. The barriers do not swap; reversibility does the work.
